What makes an Atlantic City home sale different?

Atlantic City is a barrier-island city of about 11 square miles of land, and three things shape what a buyer offers and how fast a deal closes: casino tourism, flood maps and a renter-heavy housing stock. Your three realistic paths are a traditional listing, a sale handled by yourself, or an as-is cash purchase.

Any of the three still needs the same local paperwork: a smoke and carbon monoxide compliance certificate, whatever occupancy or landlord filings the city attaches to the property, and a deed recorded with Atlantic County. Each piece is covered below, along with the office that handles it.

Casinos set the rhythm of the local economy, and that carries into housing demand. Expect buyers to ask detailed questions about condition, flood status and rent rolls, so having answers ready speeds things up.

Atlantic City housing numbers

Atlantic City had an estimated 38,787 residents in mid-2025, up slightly from the 38,497 people counted in April 2020. Just 30.3% of homes are occupied by their owners, which means renters fill most of the housing.

Atlantic City population and housing, survey years 2020 to 2024 except where dated

Population estimate, July 202538,787

These figures describe the whole city, from Ducktown to the Marina District, so a house near the Boardwalk and one in an inland block can sit far apart on price. Recent sales on your own street tell you more than a citywide median can.

Do flood maps change how an Atlantic City house sells?

Yes. The whole city sits on a barrier island, and buyers and lenders look at flood zone status early. Superstorm Sandy struck on October 29, 2012, caused flooding and power outages, and destroyed the northern boardwalk section fronting Absecon Inlet in the South Inlet neighborhood.

The city's website carries a Property Flood Information page, a Flood Insurance Rate Map, links to the FEMA flood map viewer and a floodplain development form. Before you list, look up your lot's flood zone and pull any elevation certificate you have, since a buyer's insurance quote can change their offer.

Inspections and certificates

Atlantic City's Licensing and Inspection division runs occupancy inspections, and its Fire Prevention forms include a Smoke Detector Application and a Smoke Certificate Affidavit. Call the division before you list so you know which certificate your sale needs.

The city publishes a checklist for the certificate of occupancy on a residential rental unit. Inspectors look at both outside and inside conditions, and the list works as a pre-sale walkthrough even for an owner-occupied house.

  • Outside: trip hazards in curbs and sidewalks, house number, siding, gutters, windows, railings, roof, fence, steps, foundation and high grass.
  • Inside: working deadbolt, smoke detectors on each level within 10 feet of sleeping areas, a 2A10BC fire extinguisher, carbon monoxide detection, GFCI outlets in bathrooms, two outlets per bedroom, working appliances and no leaks.
  • Seasonal items: window screens from May 1 to October 1 and heat at 68 degrees from October 1 to May 1.
  • Utilities must be on and the unit clean at the time of inspection.

Selling a rental or short-term rental

Atlantic City has a Landlord Registration form, a Short Term Rental Public Form and a short-term rental complaint hotline, so an owner with tenants or guests has paperwork to settle before a sale. If tenants live in the house, confirm your registration is current ahead of any contract.

The city also lists a Lead Certification form under Licensing and Inspection, with a list of certified lead evaluation contractors. Landlords should ask the department whether a lead certificate is on file for the unit. Give any buyer copies of the leases so they know what they are taking over, and clear any open violations first.

Deed recording and sale fees

Atlantic County Clerk's Office staff review and record every Atlantic City deed. The main office is at 5901 Main Street in Mays Landing, with a satellite office at 1333 Atlantic Avenue in Atlantic City. Checks for recording and realty transfer fees go to the Atlantic County Clerk's Office, while Gross Income Tax checks go to the State of NJ Division of Taxation.

A seller covers the New Jersey realty transfer fee. Sales at or under $350,000 follow the lower state schedule, counted per $500 of price: $2.00 through $150,000, $3.35 from $150,000 to $200,000, and $3.90 from $200,000 to $350,000. Because owner-occupied homes here are valued around $207,400, plenty of Atlantic City deals fall on this lower schedule.

Sellers who live outside New Jersey file a GIT/REP form, and the state sets a minimum prepayment of 2% of the consideration shown in the deed. Your closing agent usually handles those filings.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Atlantic City houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Which sale route fits an Atlantic City house best?

The best route turns on the house's condition, your timeline and how much prep you want to take on. A listing may bring more buyers, though it usually brings repairs, showings, and the appraisal and inspection schedule that comes with a lender.

A cash sale as-is avoids the repair list and the mortgage wait, though the city certificate, deed recording and fee steps above still apply. If foreclosure, back taxes or a tenant problem is driving the sale, compare the written terms of every option, including who pays the transfer fee and whether any certificate work falls on you. The city also lists a First Time Homebuyer Program, which can matter if your likely buyer is a local household.

A practical order of work: call Licensing and Inspection, fix any checklist items, look up the flood zone, gather leases if there are tenants, and then ask each buyer or agent for their terms in writing.

On closing day expect these items to come off the seller's side: any mortgage payoff, the realty transfer fee, and the cost of any city certificate. Out-of-state owners add the GIT/REP prepayment. Having each number confirmed ahead of time lets you compare a cash offer and a listing on what you would actually walk away with, not on the headline price alone.

Owners of rentals near the Boardwalk or in Ducktown face a slightly longer list than owners of a single house on an inland block. Tenants, leases, registration forms and the lead certification question all sit between you and a clean closing. Start those conversations first, since the answers shape what a buyer is willing to pay, and clear anything open before a contract goes out. Flood status is the other early item: a buyer's insurance quote can move an offer, so a lot with an elevation certificate on hand has an edge over one without.

Frequently asked questions

Does Atlantic City require an inspection before I sell?

Ask Licensing and Inspection before listing, since the city issues occupancy permits and runs the smoke certificate process through Fire Prevention. The checklist covers smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, outlets, heat and exterior condition, so fixing those items in advance avoids delays.

Who pays the realty transfer fee on an Atlantic City sale?

The seller pays it. The state sets the rate in steps per $500 of consideration, and the clerk collects it at the counter when the deed is filed.

Where do I record the deed for an Atlantic City house?

Deeds go to the Atlantic County Clerk, whose main recording office is on Main Street in Mays Landing. A satellite office operates on Atlantic Avenue in Atlantic City.

Can I sell an Atlantic City house that has tenants or short-term guests?

Yes. Keep landlord registration and any short-term rental paperwork current, and hand the buyer the lease terms. The city has registration forms and a complaint hotline, so open violations are worth clearing first.

Does flood risk change how an Atlantic City house sells?

It can, because the city sits on a barrier island and buyers check flood zones and insurance costs. The city website links to its flood map, FEMA tools and a property flood information page you can review before you list.

What should I know before selling a house in Bayonne?

Bayonne is a dense Hudson County city, with 74,744 residents on a peninsula that has 5.82 square miles of land. A sale there involves a resale certificate through the city, a deed recorded by the Hudson County Register, and for many sellers a look at short-term rental and rent control rules.

This page covers the local numbers, the city steps and the county and state filings, so you can decide whether to list, sell on your own or accept an as-is cash purchase.

Bayonne housing numbers

Bayonne sits on a peninsula bounded by Newark Bay, the Kill Van Kull and Upper New York Bay, and it borders Jersey City to the north. The 2020 census counted 71,686 people, up 13.7% from 63,024 in 2010, and the estimate for mid-2025 is 74,744. Density was 12,315.1 people per square mile in 2020.

For 2020 to 2024, owners occupied 36.2% of homes. The median owner-occupied home was valued at $460,100, owner costs with a mortgage ran $3,348 a month, and median gross rent was $1,682. The city has 28,951 households, and the average commute is 33.7 minutes.

With about 36% of homes owner-occupied, two- and three-family houses and condos are a large part of the market, and landlords are common sellers. The $460,100 median sets the price range most buyers will compare against. The Hudson-Bergen Light Rail has four stops in Bayonne, and the Newark Bay Extension of the New Jersey Turnpike (Interstate 78) serves drivers, so listings near transit tend to say so.

The Bayonne resale certificate

Bayonne requires a resale certificate whenever a building is sold, and a May 2026 city notice moved that process to the Fire Prevention Bureau at City Hall. Applicants pick up the application from the Fire Prevention office, complete the inspection, and the Fire Department issues the certificate for the sale.

This replaced an earlier arrangement. On October 1, 2025, the Building Department stopped issuing Continuing Certificates of Occupancy and began issuing Resale Certificates for one-family, two-family and multi-family dwellings and commercial buildings. The city described the change as a new name with a shorter application. Because the office handling it moved again in 2026, call the Fire Prevention Bureau before you schedule closing. The Building Department lines at 201-858-6334 and 201-858-6073 may help with permit history on the property.

Can I sell a Bayonne house that has been a short-term rental?

Yes, but the city's short-term rental ordinance sets rules that a buyer will want proof of. Under Chapter 33, a short-term rental is occupancy of 60 consecutive days or fewer, and only a property owner can hold the license.

  • Applications go through the city's Spatial Data Logic online portal.
  • Fire safety, building and zoning inspections come first, and a license follows within 30 calendar days of satisfactory inspections.
  • Applicants show no outstanding taxes or water and sewer charges, prior code violations abated and open construction permits closed.
  • A zoning determination letter costs $50 and is requested from the zoning officer at City Hall.
  • A tenant cannot hold the license.

If you hold a license, have the approval and inspection records ready for the buyer's attorney, and confirm that nothing is open before you sign a contract. A buyer who plans to keep the property as a short-term rental will need to apply for their own license, because a license is held by the owner, so tell prospective buyers early which approvals will and will not carry over. If the house was never rented short term, say so in the listing to head off questions.

Rent control and landlord sellers

The city has a Rent Control board and a Small Landlord Emergency Grant Program page. If your building has tenants, ask the Planning, Zoning and Development office whether rent control covers it before you list.

Buyers of tenant-occupied buildings will want copies of the leases and a clear picture of current rents. Gathering them early shortens attorney review and cuts down on last-minute price talks. Landlords who sell a building with tenants often find that a tidy rent record, signed leases and proof of any rent control filing do more for the sale price than a cosmetic repair would.

Deed recording and state filings

Bayonne is in Hudson County, so the deed is recorded by the Hudson County Register of Deeds and Mortgages, reachable at 201-395-4760. Sellers pay the state realty transfer fee. For sales over $350,000, the schedule starts at $2.90 per $500 on the first $150,000 and rises to $4.80 per $500 between $200,000 and $550,000.

If you own a Bayonne house but live outside New Jersey, the state requires a GIT/REP form with the deed. Nonresident sellers prepay the larger of 10.75% of their gain or 2% of the deed consideration, so a landlord with a rental in Bayonne should ask the closing agent to calculate the payment before settlement day.

Should I list, sell myself, or take a cash offer in Bayonne?

Compare the three on time, cost and risk, using written numbers from each buyer or agent. A cash purchase as-is can avoid repair work and showings, while a listing may reach more buyers on a $460,100 median market.

Whichever way you go, schedule the resale inspection early, since the certificate gates the closing. Mortgage payoff, tax bills and any water and sewer balance come off the proceeds at settlement, and the city has online payment pages for taxes and water and sewer so you can pull current balances. The city also has an Emergency Rescue Mortgage Assistance page, which is worth reading if missed payments are pushing you to sell.

A workable order for a Bayonne seller looks like this. Call the Fire Prevention Bureau and book the resale inspection. Fix whatever the inspector flags. Pull your tax and water balances from the city's payment pages. Ask the Planning, Zoning and Development office about rent control if tenants live in the building. Then collect written offers, whether from a listing agent or a cash buyer, and compare what each would leave in your hands after the transfer fee, the payoff and any certificate costs.

Owners who live outside New Jersey should add one more step early on: ask the closing agent to estimate the GIT/REP prepayment, so the number is known before the contract is signed and the proceeds are not reduced by a surprise at settlement.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Bayonne resale certificate?

It is the certificate the city requires whenever a building is sold. As of the city's May 2026 notice, the Fire Prevention Bureau at City Hall issues it after an inspection.

Did Bayonne get rid of the continuing certificate of occupancy?

Yes. The Building Department replaced the CCO with a Resale Certificate on October 1, 2025, and the city described the change as a rename with a shorter application.

Where is a Bayonne deed recorded?

The Hudson County Register of Deeds and Mortgages records it. That office can be reached at 201-395-4760.

Can I sell a Bayonne property that I rent short term?

Yes. The city's Chapter 33 ordinance limits short-term rentals to 60 days or fewer and requires an owner license with inspections, so confirm your license status before you sign a contract.

Do out-of-state owners owe tax when selling in Bayonne?

They owe a prepayment with the GIT/REP form. The minimum is 2% of the consideration shown on the deed, and the state formula can produce a higher amount based on the gain.

Selling in Bergenfield?

Ways to sell a Bergenfield house quickly

Three routes exist in Bergenfield: an agent, a do-it-yourself sale, or a buyer paying cash. All of them finish at the same borough checkpoints covering permits, alarms and taxes.

Your choice depends on the condition of the house and the date you need to close. A listing reaches the most buyers, but it brings open houses, repair requests after the inspection and a lender's timetable. A cash buyer pays less and skips most of that. It can suit you if relatives left you the house, tenants live in a two-family, repairs have piled up, or your moving date is fixed.

  • Agent: widest audience, a fee paid from proceeds, and a schedule set by the buyer's bank.
  • On your own: no agent fee, but pricing, showings and borough inspections are your job.
  • Cash buyer: the house is bought as it stands, and a fast closing is possible.

Bergenfield housing at a glance

Bergenfield is a dense inner suburb of 28,754 people, and owners live in 70.6 percent of the housing units. The median owner-occupied house is $491,500, median household income is $130,045 and median gross rent is $1,752. Population climbed from 8,816 in 1930 to 17,647 in 1950, so many houses you will sell are decades old. Buyers and inspectors often ask about finished basements, additions and garage conversions in that kind of stock, so have the paperwork for any of those ready.

What must be in order before closing

Start by asking your attorney to order a municipal tax search from the Tax Collector. Then ask the Construction Office to confirm that every permit has its final inspection. Both offices work out of the municipal building at 198 North Washington Avenue.

Open permits cause most of the trouble. If no certificate of occupancy is on file, or an added or omitted assessment is pending, the buyer's and seller's attorneys settle the fines or assessments in the closing documents. Closing old permits before you list costs less than haggling over them at the table.

New Jersey also wants proof that smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms and a portable extinguisher meet code. On a one- or two-unit house the town alone can issue that paper, and it expires in six months, so apply late in the process. Fire Prevention, in the same municipal building, enforces the State Uniform Fire Code.

Costs that come out of your proceeds

Only one cost here is set by statute: the state realty transfer fee. The seller owes it, the county recording officer collects it as the deed is lodged, and it follows the price stated in that deed.

Some deeds avoid it entirely. A parent deeding to a son or daughter qualifies, as does an executor passing the house to an heir named in the will, but a stepchild only counts after a legal adoption. Prices over $1,000,000 also trigger a 1 percent charge on the buyer, a rarity in a borough like this.

  • The transfer fee.
  • An agent's commission, negotiated case by case and not set by statute.
  • Payoff of the mortgage, an equity line or any lien.
  • Your share of the current quarter's tax, prorated to the closing day.
  • Money to clear open permits or settle related fines.
  • A New Jersey attorney to handle contract and closing.

Have your attorney itemize these in writing before you accept an offer, so the take-home number is real.

Assessment changes and added assessments

The Tax Department values every property under state guidelines and checks building permits to update those values. Additions, finished basements, garage conversions, in-ground pools, fireplaces, decks and kitchen or bathroom remodels can trigger an added assessment. Paint, fences, replacement windows, skylights, air conditioning and above-ground pools do not.

An added assessment bill goes out in October and is payable on November 1, then February 1 and May 1, before merging into the regular bill the next June. Appeals of a regular assessment are due by April 1, with applications available from the Bergen County Board of Taxation after February 1. Appeals of an added assessment are due by December 1. A late bill can follow the house to the buyer, so order the tax search early.

Commuting and schools buyers ask about

Washington Avenue, which is County Route 39, is the borough's spine. NJ Transit routes 166 and 167 go to Midtown's Port Authority Bus Terminal, and route 186 goes to the George Washington Bridge Bus Station. Passenger rail on the West Shore line ended in 1959, so commuters rely on those buses.

Bergenfield Public Schools run five elementary schools, Roy W. Brown Middle School and Bergenfield High School. Students may also apply to Bergen County Technical Schools programs. Mention the bus lines and schools in your listing or your pitch to a buyer.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Bergenfield houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Is a cash buyer right for you?

It is when speed or condition matters more than a slightly higher price. Picture a house with permits nobody wants to chase, an estate whose heirs live in other states, a two-family with tenants, or an owner leaving town on a deadline.

The borough steps still apply. Someone has to order the tax search, review permits and get the alarm certificate, so settle in writing who does it and whether the cost is deducted from what you receive. Put any cash figure next to what a listing would clear once commission, repairs and holding costs are paid, and have a New Jersey attorney read the agreement first.

A cash sale usually skips the buyer's mortgage approval, the appraisal gap and repair negotiations after an inspection. It does not skip the municipal paperwork, so start the tax search and permit review in the first week.

On closing day the attorneys total the payoffs, the prorated tax and any fines, then the deed goes to the county recording officer. Keep your keys, garage openers and any warranty papers for the handover, and bring photo ID to the table.

Frequently asked questions

Which alarm certificate does Bergenfield require?

You need a certificate of compliant smoke and carbon monoxide alarms before a one or two family house is sold. The municipality issues it for six months. Contact the Fire Prevention Bureau at the municipal building and time the application near closing.

Who owes the state transfer fee in Bergenfield?

The seller. The county recording officer collects it at recording. A buyer owes a further 1 percent only on prices above $1,000,000.

What is the Bergenfield assessment appeal deadline?

April 1 for a regular assessment. The Bergen County Board of Taxation supplies the form after February 1, following your assessment notice. Added assessments follow a separate December 1 deadline.

What does a Bergenfield municipal tax search cover?

It covers unpaid taxes, open building and plumbing permits and pending added or omitted assessments. The Tax Collector's Office charges $10 and needs 2 to 4 days, and your attorney normally orders it for the closing.

Can I sell in Bergenfield with permits still open?

Yes, but fix them first if you can. Ask the Construction Office to confirm permits and final inspections before closing. A missing certificate of occupancy is dealt with in the closing documents, and any fines or assessments can reduce your proceeds.

Selling a Bridgeton house fast

A cash purchase is the quickest exit in Bridgeton, since no lender appraisal or repair haggling slows it down. Listing opens the door to more buyers but adds showings, inspections and the city's resale form. A sale without an agent lands between the two and carries the same certificate and recording work.

Bridgeton has 28,307 residents on 6.23 square miles of land, and most blocks mix single-family houses, doubles and small rentals.

Bridgeton housing market

Bridgeton is a renter-heavy city with modest values. Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $145,500, rent is $1,340, and only 36.4% of the 7,481 households own. Median household income is $55,781. Many sellers here are landlords or heirs rather than long-term single-family owners.

The city sits on the tidal Cohansey River and is the Cumberland County seat, in three sections: Northside, Southside and Hillside. Philadelphia is about an hour away, Wilmington about 50 minutes, and Atlantic City and Cape May roughly an hour. A low entry price and a reachable job market draw investors, which is one reason cash offers are common.

  • Victorian and Federal-era houses near the downtown core often need roof, porch and plumbing work.
  • Many blocks of "doubles" were built as working-class housing and are now often rentals.
  • Occupied rentals can be sold with tenants in place, but the buyer will ask for the rental registration and inspection record.

Does the historic district affect a sale?

For a large share of the city it can. The Bridgeton Historic District covers about a quarter of the city and includes more than 2,000 properties ranging from early Federal buildings to 1920s construction.

If your house is inside the district, ask the city's Historic District Administrative Officer, who works alongside Code Enforcement, what review applies to exterior work before you replace windows, siding or porches ahead of a sale. Buyers who plan renovations will ask the same question.

Getting around Bridgeton

Routes 49 and 77 and County Route 552 are the main roads, and NJ Transit's 410 bus runs between Bridgeton and Philadelphia. Bridgeton Public Schools runs eight schools for pre-kindergarten through grade 12, and students can also apply to the Cumberland County Technical Education Center in Millville. Mention the bus line and school options in your listing.

Resale and rental requirements

The Code Enforcement Office enforces the 2015 International Property Maintenance Code and also handles home sales. On the sale of any property in the city, a resale Certificate of Property Compliance (CPC) form must be filled out and filed with the office. Ask about inspection timing early, because a failed inspection means a notice, repairs and a re-inspection before a certificate issues. The Housing and Code department is at 181 E. Commerce Street.

Landlords carry extra steps. Every rental unit must be registered each year by March 1, whether vacant or occupied, and must pass inspection before tenants move in or whenever occupancy changes. The city also has a rent leveling ordinance, Ordinance 25-28, which matters to anyone buying or selling an occupied building. Tree removal above set trunk sizes needs an application too.

Property taxes for a Bridgeton seller

Bridgeton's tax load is heavy relative to its home values, which is a common reason owners want out. Ask the tax collector for the current rate before you quote a monthly carrying cost to a buyer.

The tax collector bills property tax in four installments due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. The same office collects water, sewer and the solid waste charge, listed at $150 for residents and $90 for seniors. Unpaid balances can attach to the sale, so ask for a payoff or statement before closing.

  • Assessment appeals go to the Cumberland County Board of Taxation, 2475 S. Delsea Drive, Vineland, (856) 453-7425, by April 1 or 45 days after notices are mailed, whichever is later, or May 1 after a municipal-wide revaluation.
  • Assessments above $1,000,000 may be filed directly with the State Tax Court.
  • Senior, disabled and veteran deductions are $250 each and require an application to the assessor.

Inherited and family sales

Many Bridgeton sales involve an estate or a relative, and New Jersey's Realty Transfer Fee has exemptions that fit those cases. Deeds that skip the fee include a parent giving title to a child, one spouse to another, an estate representative passing the house to an heir under a will or intestacy, and a transfer recorded within 90 days after a divorce decree. A seller claiming an exemption files Form RTF-1 with the deed.

An ordinary sale is different: the seller owes the fee at recording, calculated per $500 of the price. On a sale of $150,000 or less, the schedule for deals not over $350,000 starts at $2.00 per $500, so the fee on a typical Bridgeton price is modest compared with the repair cost of an older house.

If you inherited the house, a deed from the executor to you is exempt, but your later sale to a buyer is a regular conveyance. Plan for the fee at recording and ask your attorney to confirm which form applies.

Steps from offer to closing

Once you accept an offer, file the resale CPC form with Code Enforcement and book the inspection. Fix anything on the notice, pay the $18 re-inspection if needed, and keep the certificate for the closing file. Ask the tax collector for a statement of taxes, water, sewer and the solid waste charge so no balance follows the sale. If tenants live in the house, gather the unit registration and rent records for the buyer. Your attorney then schedules the closing, the deed is recorded and the seller's fee is paid at recording.

Landlords selling a building with several units should also set aside time for the rent leveling rules. Pull each lease, list the current rents and confirm that every unit's yearly registration is on file, because a buyer's attorney will ask for all of it before the contract becomes final. An older house with open repair notices from the city will move faster if you clear those notices first.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need an inspection to sell my house in Bridgeton?

The city requires a resale Certificate of Property Compliance form to be filed with Code Enforcement on the sale of any property. Call the Housing and Code department at 856-455-3230 to schedule and ask what the inspector checks.

Can I sell a Bridgeton house with tenants in it?

Yes. Keep the unit registered (due each March 1) and have the current Certificate of Property Compliance and rent records ready, because the buyer takes the property subject to the city's rent leveling ordinance.

How much is the annual rental registration in Bridgeton?

It costs $45 per unit if filed by March 1 and $75 per unit after that date. The registration renewal also covers the rental certificate fees.

Where do I appeal my Bridgeton tax assessment?

Appeal to the Cumberland County Board of Taxation in Vineland at (856) 453-7425, by April 1 or 45 days from the mailing of notices, whichever is later. Properties assessed over $1,000,000 can go straight to the State Tax Court.

Is the realty transfer fee owed if I inherited the house and sell it?

The fee applies to the sale deed. A deed from an executor to an heir is exempt, but the later sale to a buyer is a regular conveyance, so plan for the seller's fee at recording.

Selling a Camden house fast

In Camden the quickest sale is a cash purchase from a buyer who accepts the house as it is and handles the city's sale certificate. A listing can work for houses in good shape in neighborhoods with active demand, but the city's resale rules add steps whichever way you go. Selling yourself without an agent is allowed, with the same paperwork.

Camden is the county seat on the Delaware River, directly across from Philadelphia, with 71,430 residents.

Camden home values and ownership

Camden values sit far below the rest of the Philadelphia area. The median owner-occupied value is $112,000, median gross rent is $1,226, and just 34.4% of the city's 24,443 households own. Median household income is $40,546, so many sellers are carrying a house they cannot afford to repair, or an heir inheriting one.

The most common housing type is the rowhouse. The city recognizes more than 20 neighborhoods, including Cooper Grant, Cramer Hill, East Camden, Parkside, Waterfront South, Rosedale, Pyne Point and Gateway.

  • Rowhouses share walls and roofs, so a buyer's inspection will look closely at party walls and roof drainage.
  • Vacant or fire-damaged houses can still sell, but the buyer may sign an agreement not to occupy until permits are closed.
  • Homes near the waterfront, the Rutgers campus and the hospital district sit close to the city's largest employers.

Transit and schools

Transit is a real selling point. The PATCO Speedline runs 24 hours to Philadelphia and to Collingswood, Haddonfield, Cherry Hill and Lindenwold, and NJ Transit's River Line light rail runs from Camden to Trenton with four stops in the city. The Walter Rand Transportation Center at Martin Luther King Boulevard and Broadway joins PATCO, River Line and NJ Transit buses. By road, Interstate 676 and U.S. 30 lead to the Benjamin Franklin Bridge. Mean travel time to work is 23.8 minutes.

Camden City School District runs 19 schools, and charter and renaissance schools operate alongside it, which buyers with children will ask about.

Certificate of Continued Occupancy

Camden requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy (the building bureau also calls it a Camden Resale Occupancy Certificate) to be applied for and issued before any property in the city is sold or conveyed. The seller is responsible for applying, though the buyer may apply with the seller's written permission. The certificate is issued to the buyer, not the seller. If a buyer closes without one, the buyer stays liable for penalties of up to $2,000 until it issues.

The process starts with a zoning permit at City Hall, then an application to the Construction and Building Bureau, followed by four inspections: building, plumbing, electric and fire. All open building permits must be closed first. If the house is not habitable, the buyer can sign an Agreement to Not Occupy and commit to pulling permits and doing the work. Plan submissions are digital only. A change of tenant in a rental is a different step and goes through the Housing Department.

Rules for Camden rental properties

The Bureau of Housing enforces the city's property maintenance code. Rental properties must be inspected at a change of ownership or occupancy and hold a Rental Approval Certificate before anyone moves in, and buildings with three or more units need a license. To schedule an inspection, all taxes must be current, utilities must be on, the fee is paid when scheduling, and the property must be registered with both the Rent Control office and the Municipal Clerk.

The city has had a rent control ordinance since March 12, 1981. At lease expiration a landlord may raise rent by no more than the lower of the 12-month average consumer price index for the Philadelphia area or 6% of the latest rent, and rent cannot rise during a lease. A buyer of a rental building takes on those limits, so a landlord selling should have the registration file ready.

Taxes and state fees when selling in Camden

The Office of Assessments maintains the tax map, processes senior and veteran deductions and exemptions, receives abatement requests, and handles assessment appeals filed with the Camden County Board of Taxation or the New Jersey Tax Court. The office is in City Hall, Room 329, at 520 Market Street. Check that taxes are current before listing, since a lien can hold up a closing.

New Jersey's Realty Transfer Fee falls on the seller. At Camden-level prices below $350,000, the schedule is $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $3.90 per $500 above that. Senior citizens, blind or disabled sellers and certain low and moderate income housing sales qualify for lower rates, starting at $0.50 per $500 on the first $150,000. Ask your attorney which rate applies to you before you compare offers.

How a cash sale fits Camden's rules

A cash buyer can take on the certificate process, which suits vacant, damaged or inherited houses. Settle in writing who applies, who pays the $200 application and the $64 fire fee, and who closes any open permits. If the house is not habitable, the Agreement to Not Occupy lets the buyer proceed while the work is done.

Compare a cash offer with what a listing would net after commission, repairs and the months you would carry taxes and utilities. Before you sign, have a New Jersey attorney read the contract and confirm how the certificate and any penalty are handled.

For a quick start, confirm that taxes are current, look up open permits with the Construction and Building Bureau and gather your deed. If tenants live in the house, bring the Rent Control registration and the Rental Approval Certificate so the buyer sees a clean file.

Expect the four inspections (building, plumbing, electric and fire) to be booked separately, so ask each inspector for a date as soon as the zoning permit is in hand. If an inspection fails, fix the listed items and request a repeat visit before the six-month application window runs out. On closing day your attorney confirms the certificate is in the buyer's name, pays off any lien and records the deed. Keep copies of every inspection report and receipt in one folder.

Frequently asked questions

Who applies for the Certificate of Continued Occupancy in Camden?

The seller. The buyer may file as the seller's agent with written permission, but the certificate is issued to the buyer. The application costs $200 plus a separate $64 fire safety fee.

How long is a Camden occupancy certificate application good for?

Six months. After that a new application must be filed and paid for, unless there are open permits on the property.

Can I sell a vacant or damaged house in Camden?

Yes. If the house is not habitable, the buyer can sign an Agreement to Not Occupy and then obtain permits, do the work and apply for the certificate. Open permits have to be closed before a certificate issues.

Is there rent control in Camden?

Yes. Camden has had a rent control ordinance since 1981, with a cap at the lower of the Philadelphia-area consumer price index or 6% at lease expiration, and landlords register each rental unit annually for $25.

Where do I appeal a Camden property assessment?

Appeals go to the Camden County Board of Taxation or the New Jersey Tax Court. The Office of Assessments, at 520 Market Street, Room 329, can explain the process and handles deductions.

Where to start a Carteret sale

Begin with the borough's occupancy inspection and a current tax bill. A Carteret sale can go through an agent, a for-sale-by-owner listing or an investor, and all three paths pass the same two checkpoints. After those, the deed gets filed in New Brunswick at the Middlesex County Clerk's Registry.

Roughly 55 percent of homes here are owner-occupied, so rentals fill much of the rest. That is why sellers range from landlords to heirs to people holding older houses with deferred repairs. For those owners the paperwork below weighs as much as the listing photos, so read it before you set a closing date.

Carteret housing and location

Carteret sits in northeastern Middlesex County, on the Arthur Kill across from Staten Island, and Woodbridge Township touches it on every land side. Local place names still in use include Chrome, Lamar, Canda, Silvan Beach and West Carteret, the part west of the Turnpike.

  • Residents: 25,781
  • Share of homes lived in by owners: 54.7%
  • Typical owner-occupied home value: $405,800
  • Typical gross rent: $2,032
  • Households: 8,224, averaging 3.10 people
  • Household income, midpoint: $96,862

The borough's occupancy form has separate lines for one-family and two-family houses, and a house with a clean certificate and working mechanicals gives a buyer fewer reasons to renegotiate.

Roads and the waterfront

Access is the strength here, though some buyers will want to talk about truck traffic. The New Jersey Turnpike is the only major highway through the borough, with Interchange 12 inside its limits. NJ Transit local buses run the 116 route toward Midtown Manhattan and Perth Amboy and the 48 route toward Elizabeth. The average commute is 31.4 minutes.

With an economy built around freight and warehousing, buyers may ask about noise, truck routes and flood exposure along the Arthur Kill and Rahway River edges. Walk the block at rush hour before you price the house so you can answer honestly.

  • Know how far the house sits from the Turnpike ramps and from CR 602.
  • Pull together any flood or sump-pump history, since tidal water borders the east side.

Certificate of continued occupancy

Carteret requires a residential certificate of continued occupancy, issued by the Department of Code Enforcement at 61 Cooke Avenue, before a house changes hands. The application asks for the owner, the purchaser, the realtor if there is one, the block and lot, one family or two, the listed price and the names and ages of everyone living there. Code enforcement answers at (732) 541-3925, and inspections are booked through (732) 541-3810.

An addendum to the application works as a plain checklist, and the inspector holds you to it. The seller certifies each item, and the form warns that false statements can be prosecuted with a fine of $2,000 per occurrence.

  • Smoke detectors on each level, plus a smoke detector and carbon monoxide alarm outside every sleeping area, within ten feet.
  • Battery-powered units that carry sealed 10-year batteries.
  • A 2A:10BC fire extinguisher mounted near the kitchen, also within ten feet.
  • Working heat, hot water, electric, water and sewer.
  • No unpermitted work and no open permits.

The base fee pays for the first visit and one follow-up. Since the application lapses after 90 days, file it close to your expected closing rather than months ahead. Pay by cash, certified check, or an attorney or broker check. The borough reserves the right to inspect again later.

Tax bills at closing

One bill arrives in July. Pay it in four pieces, on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, each with a ten day cushion before interest starts. Once grace ends, interest runs from the original due date at 8 percent a year on the first $1,500 owed and 18 percent on whatever exceeds it. Owing more than $10,000 adds a 6 percent penalty at year-end, and a balance that sits unpaid for a year or longer goes into the yearly tax sale.

Carry your newest bill to closing so the buyer's attorney can see the next installment due. The tax collector works from the finance department at 100 Cooke Avenue on weekdays between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. Call (732) 541-3820 extension 3818 for a payoff figure.

If you believe the assessment is off, take it up with the borough assessor first, at extension 3110. Next comes an appeal package from the Middlesex County Tax Board in New Brunswick. The state deadline is April 1, moved to May 1 in a revalued town, and the owner must show the assessed value is unreasonable next to market value. People who hold a senior or veteran deduction also send in an annual statement by March 1 to keep it.

Recording the deed and state tax forms

Recording happens at the Middlesex County Clerk's Registry, fourth floor, 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick. Hours are weekdays, so plan to arrive by 4 p.m. Most owners let their attorney or title company deliver the deed. Online records reach back to 1929 for deeds and 1950 for mortgages, which lets you pull your own chain of title before listing, though the staff will not run a title search for you.

Expect a $45 charge for deed page one, $10 per additional page, and $6 per name beyond the fifth. On top come state items. Sellers pay the realty transfer fee, and each seller files a gross income tax form. Residents of New Jersey sign a residency certification and settle income tax on their regular return. Someone who has moved out of state, even a longtime Carteret owner, prepays either two percent of the price or 8.97 percent of the net gain, unless the form lists an exemption that fits.

Two years of residence within the last five years shields the first $250,000 of profit from federal tax, or $500,000 for married couples, and the state takes the same view.

Which route sells a Carteret house fastest?

Speed comes from either a cash sale to an investor or a brief listing of a house that is ready, and the borough certificate stands in front of both. A cash purchase removes the lender's appraisal and underwriting, yet the inspection, the tax payoff and the deed filing still apply.

  • An agent suits a house in good shape when you can tolerate showings and wait on a buyer's lender.
  • An as-is investor purchase suits a house needing work, one with tenants, back taxes or an estate behind it.
  • Choose a sale by owner only with an attorney lined up for the contract, the certificate and the closing forms.

Whichever way you go, order the inspection early, replace alarms and the extinguisher yourself, and ask the buyer's attorney who will book the final walk-through. If a repair cannot be finished before the closing date, ask the borough code office whether a temporary certificate is available.

Frequently asked questions

Is an occupancy inspection mandatory for Carteret sellers?

Yes. The Department of Code Enforcement issues a residential certificate of continued occupancy after an inspection, and the application lapses 90 days after issuance, so time it close to closing.

How much does the Carteret inspection run?

It is $100 for a one-family house and $150 for a two-family house. A temporary certificate is $75, and every extra inspection after a failure or no-show is $50.

What are Carteret's quarterly tax dates?

Installments fall on the first of February, May, August and November, with ten days of grace. Late balances accrue 8 percent a year up to $1,500 and 18 percent on anything above that.

Which Middlesex County office files a Carteret deed?

The County Clerk's Registry at 75 Bayard Street in New Brunswick. A closing attorney or title agent usually delivers it with the state transfer and income tax forms.

Can a Carteret house with tenants or open repairs still sell?

Yes, but the occupancy inspection still applies and the application lists everyone living in the home. Ask the code office about open permits first, since none may be open.

Selling a house in Cliffside Park, NJ

Cliffside Park is one of the most densely packed boroughs in New Jersey, so a sale here is often a condominium, a co-op unit or a house on a very small lot. The borough requires a certificate of continued occupancy for a sale, issued through its building department, and the deed is filed in Hackensack through the Bergen County Clerk.

This page walks through the local paperwork, the tax calendar and the Bergen County steps that apply when you sell.

Housing market snapshot

The borough holds about 26,539 residents in under a square mile. The middle value of an owner-occupied home is $588,200, far above the national $332,700, and a little over half the homes (51.4%) are lived in by their owners. A seller with a condo, a rented unit or an inherited multifamily building is dealing with a different market than a suburban house seller.

Getting buyers: transit, views and listing details

Commuting is what many buyers ask about first. The average trip to work runs 35.5 minutes, well above the 26.4 minutes for the country as a whole. Anderson Avenue and Palisade Avenue carry most north-south traffic, and Palisade Avenue has views toward the Hudson River and the Manhattan skyline. NJ Transit bus lines 156, 159 and 181 go to Manhattan, the 22 serves Jersey City, and the 751 and 755 run locally.

About 65 percent of households speak a language other than English at home, so listing materials in more than one language can widen your buyer pool.

  • Name the bus line and the walking distance to it in your listing.
  • Photograph the view if you have one, and note which floor you are on.
  • For a condo or co-op, collect the association's budget and rules before the first showing.

Certificate of occupancy for a sale

The building department requires a Certificate of Occupancy for the sale of property. It is at the Municipal Complex, 525 Palisade Avenue, Room 220, phone 201-313-2042, with counter hours of 8:30 to 4:30. The applications page carries a form titled Certificate of Continued Occupancy for Sale, with a separate form for rentals.

After the inspections are done and the requirements are met, the Construction Code Official issues either a Certificate of Occupancy or a Certificate of Approval. The same office issues permits for alterations, demolitions and interior renovations, which means unpermitted work can come to light during a sale. Cash is no longer taken in any borough department, so plan to pay by check, debit or credit card.

The Planning Board sits on the first Monday of each month and the Board of Adjustment on the fourth, which matters if you need a variance before selling. Ask the department for the current fee for the sale certificate before you file.

Property tax due dates and where to pay

Real estate tax is collected in four installments, due the first of February, May, August and November. The tax collector sits on the second floor of 525 Palisade Avenue, phone 201-313-2050. You can pay through the borough's online lookup page, mail a check to the Tax Collector at that address, or use the drop box by the Borough Hall entrance.

Taxes here run modest for Bergen County. A borough release put the average residence at an assessed $373,110 with a yearly bill of $9,982, ninth lowest of the county's 70 municipalities. That figure is from an earlier year, so rely on your own current bill for closing math.

For state relief programs, start at the Division of Taxation's relief page. Selling while you collect a homestead benefit? Say so on the application, or take the benefit as a credit at closing. If you do neither, it goes toward the new owner's taxes.

How to appeal your assessment before selling

Tax appeals are filed with the Bergen County Board of Taxation in Hackensack, and the calendar is tight: April 1, or May 1 following a revaluation. The board encourages online filing and can be reached at 201-336-6300. Start with the borough assessor at 201-313-2009, whose office also defends appeals.

The board starts from the assumption that your assessment is right. To change that you need proof it exceeds market value, and proof means recent comparable sales rather than frustration over the bill. Any savings mostly go to whoever owns the unit after the ruling, so talk to your attorney before filing on a property you are about to sell.

  • Compare your assessment with recent sales of similar units in your building or block.
  • Check that the assessor shows the correct square footage and unit count.
  • Ask whether a pending appeal could affect the closing adjustments.

Deed filing, transfer fees and income tax forms

Deeds, mortgages and liens for the county are recorded by the Bergen County Clerk. Sellers pay the state realty transfer fee. On residential and cooperative-unit deeds over $1,000,000 an extra graduated fee kicks in, starting at 1 percent of the price between $1,000,000 and $2,000,000 and climbing to 3.5 percent above $3,500,000. With a middle value of $588,200, most Cliffside Park sales land under that line, but a penthouse or a multifamily building can cross it. The buyer pays a separate 1 percent fee on certain purchases above $1 million.

At closing the seller hands over a gross income tax form. Residents of New Jersey sign a residency certification, while an owner who has moved out of state prepays estimated income tax, figured at either two percent of the price or the 8.97 percent rate on the gain. On the federal side, the rule for a principal residence can shelter $250,000 of profit, or $500,000 for a married couple.

Which routes sell a Cliffside Park home fastest?

Two routes move fastest: an investor purchase, or a well-priced listing with the certificate already in hand. A unit with a clean inspection history and complete association paperwork leaves a buyer fewer open questions.

If you inherited a unit, have tenants or owe back taxes, get permit status and a tax payoff in writing before you accept an offer. An as-is buyer will still need the occupancy certificate and a clear deed, so put those items on your checklist whichever route you choose.

A short to-do order keeps a Cliffside Park sale moving: call the building department about the sale certificate, ask the tax collector for a payoff or current balance, gather association documents if the unit is a condo or co-op, and have your attorney or title agent order the deed work. Selling for cash removes the buyer's mortgage underwriting and appraisal, two common sources of delay. The occupancy certificate and the deed filing still happen.

Frequently asked questions

Is a certificate required to sell in Cliffside Park?

Yes. The borough building department requires a Certificate of Occupancy for the sale of property, and its applications page carries a separate sale form.

Where is the Cliffside Park sale certificate filed?

At the building department, Municipal Complex, 525 Palisade Avenue, Room 220, or by phone at 201-313-2042. The borough accepts check, debit or credit card, not cash.

What are the Cliffside Park tax installment dates?

The first of February, May, August and November. You can pay online, by mail, or in the drop box by the Borough Hall entrance.

When can I appeal my Cliffside Park assessment?

Appeals are due April 1, or May 1 after a revaluation, to the Bergen County Board of Taxation. Call the borough assessor first to review your numbers.

Which office records a Cliffside Park deed?

The Bergen County Clerk in Hackensack files deeds and mortgages for the borough, usually through your attorney or title agent along with the state fee and income tax forms.

Selling a house in Clifton, NJ

No closing can take place in Clifton without a valid dwelling certificate from the Fire Prevention Bureau. On top of that, the city has been revaluing property, which changes assessed values. Those two items shape the timeline more than the listing does.

Clifton is the second-largest city in Passaic County and a bedroom community for New York. A seller usually owns a one- or two-family house or a condo, and the same city paperwork follows the property whether you list it, sell it yourself or accept an investor's offer. The steps below run in the order you will meet them.

Clifton housing and neighborhoods

About 91,127 people live in Clifton, up from 90,296 in the 2020 count. The owner-occupied rate is 59.6 percent, the median owner-occupied home is valued at $461,900, and median gross rent is $1,711. With roughly four in ten homes not owner-occupied, many sellers here are landlords as well as owner-occupants.

Buyers ask for neighborhoods by name, so use the right one in your listing.

  • Main Mall is the downtown, and Allwood is the other business district, along Route 3.
  • Athenia and Delawanna each have a train station, and Dutch Hill sits near downtown.
  • Botany Village is the northernmost neighborhood, and Lakeview runs along the western edge.
  • Montclair Heights and Rosemawr are among the wealthier residential areas, with Albion Place beside Garret Mountain Reservation.

Highways, trains and commute

Route 3, Route 21, Route 19 and U.S. Route 46 cross the city, and the Garden State Parkway runs through it with interchanges 153 through 156. NJ Transit trains stop at Clifton station and Delawanna station on the Main Line toward Hoboken and Suffern. Buses on the 190, 191, 192 and 195 routes go to the Port Authority Bus Terminal, and routes 13, 27 and 72 go to Newark. The mean commute is 28.3 minutes.

A listing that names the elementary school number and the nearest train station answers two of the first questions buyers ask.

How to get the Clifton dwelling certificate

You file a dwelling application with the Fire Prevention Bureau, at 900 Clifton Avenue, after checking with the Building Department that the property has no open permits. The application must be signed by both the seller and the buyer.

  • Call the Building Department at 973-470-5809 to confirm there are no open permits and to learn where to get the application stamped.
  • Bring the stamped application and payment to Clifton Fire Headquarters. An after-hours drop box is available.
  • Inspections are scheduled on Wednesdays from 9 a.m. to noon, and an adult over 18 has to be present with every area of the structure accessible.
  • Call about seven business days after the inspection, since certificates must be picked up in person.

The certificate depends on passing the building, tax and zoning departments, and it expires six months after the fire department inspection. Schedule it once you have a signed contract and a target closing date.

Fees are charged per dwelling unit, so a two-family house costs double. Pay by personal check, money order, cashier's check, exact-change cash or credit card with a transaction fee, all made out to the City of Clifton. The city takes neither an application without payment nor payment without an application.

Smoke, carbon monoxide and alarm checks

The inspector looks at smoke detectors, carbon monoxide alarms and a label for homes with backup power. Fix these before the appointment, because failing and rescheduling eats into a closing calendar that already hangs on a Wednesday slot.

  • Smoke detectors on every level, except crawl spaces and unfinished attics reached by pull-down stairs.
  • A detector within 10 feet of the outside of each bedroom door on any floor that has bedrooms.
  • All detectors under 10 years old, with 10-year sealed batteries when battery operated, and hardwired systems kept in service.
  • Carbon monoxide alarms within 10 feet of sleeping areas, with more on each additional floor that has sleeping areas.
  • A central station fire alarm tested beforehand, with the test record from a certified company handed over. Inspectors do not test those systems, and a missing report fails the inspection.

One- and two-family homes also need a label within 18 inches of the main electrical panel and meter, warning about secondary power sources such as generators, solar panels or battery storage. The Fire Prevention Bureau supplies and installs that label on inspection day, so owners with solar should expect it.

The citywide revaluation

Clifton has been carrying out a city-wide revaluation, described on the assessor's page and in a city presentation from January 2026. The last revaluation was in 1991, and the average ratio is 31.87. A ratio that low means assessments sit well below market value, so new values are expected to be higher while the tax rate is meant to fall.

The city's explanation is that a revaluation does not raise the total amount collected. School, county and municipal budgets set the levy, and the revaluation only redistributes it by value. Whether your own bill rises or falls depends on whether your house moved more or less than the city average.

The assessed value on old paperwork may not match the new notice. The appeal deadline is April 1, or May 1 in a newly revalued municipality, and an appeal has to prove value with comparable sales. Call the assessing department at 973-470-5838 for your property record.

Tax due dates and relief programs

Taxes are due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, with a ten-day grace period. The tax collector is at 900 Clifton Avenue, first floor, phone 973-470-5830. Online payment is by e-check only, and a lockbox at City Hall takes mailed or dropped-off payments, but no cash. A $35 fee applies to a returned check caused by wrong account numbers.

The assessor's page lists a $250 deduction for qualifying former service members or surviving spouses and a $250 deduction for seniors or disabled persons. The senior deduction requires age 65 or older, ownership and residence in the house, and annual income of $10,000 or less after permitted exclusions. The state's ANCHOR program for homeowners and renters is linked from the tax collector's page. If you receive any of these, tell your closing attorney so the adjustments come out right.

Where a Clifton deed is recorded

Deeds go to the Passaic County Clerk's Registry Division, 401 Grand Street, Room 113, in Paterson, open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:15 p.m. The office does not do title searches or record surveys. Recording rules to plan around:

  • Deeds must carry the words Prepared by, the tax block, lot and consideration.
  • Every document needs a record and return address, and original signatures with names printed beneath.
  • Use the official county cover sheet, or pay an extra $20 per document.
  • Pay the realty transfer fee with an attorney trust check, title agency trust check, certified check or cash.

The county posts the seller forms you need: the Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller, the Seller Residency Certification, the Nonresident Seller Tax Declaration and the waiver form. An owner who has moved out of New Jersey is treated as a nonresident for the sale, which can mean an estimated payment at closing. A federal principal residence exclusion may shelter up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 for a qualifying couple.

Frequently asked questions

Can I close on a Clifton house without a dwelling certificate?

No. The city's instructions state that no closing shall take place without a valid Certificate of Inspection, and the certificate expires six months after the fire department inspection.

How much does a Clifton sale certificate cost?

The standard fee is $125 per unit for a sale. Expedited service costs $200 per unit for a 4 to 20 day turnaround or $300 per unit for four business days.

When does the Clifton fire department inspect?

Inspections run on Wednesdays between 9 a.m. and noon, and an adult over 18 must be home. Call about seven business days afterward, because certificates are picked up in person.

When are Clifton property taxes due?

February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, with a ten-day grace period. Online payment is by e-check only.

When must I appeal a Clifton assessment?

The deadline is April 1, or May 1 in a municipality that has just been revalued. An appeal has to prove value with comparable sales.

Ways to sell in East Orange

East Orange owners generally pick among a listing, a private sale, and a direct cash purchase. Listing brings the most buyers, but here the paperwork often decides the closing date. The city requires a Certificate of Conformity before a property is sold, and the fire department issues a smoke alarm and carbon monoxide certificate for one and two family homes. Both take scheduling.

  • Agent listing: fits a house that can clear the city's certificate inspections with little work.
  • Cash purchase: fits an inherited or tenant-occupied house, or one carrying open code violations.
  • Private sale: still needs the Certificate of Conformity, a deed, and the state's seller forms.

The East Orange housing market

East Orange is a dense city, with an estimated 72,159 residents on 3.93 square miles. Owners live in just 31.0 percent of homes, so rentals make up a big slice of the stock. The middle value of an owned home is $365,900, against $454,400 across New Jersey, and median gross rent is $1,441. The city sits in Essex County beside Newark, South Orange, Orange, Glen Ridge and Bloomfield.

Buyers often ask for a neighborhood by name: Ampere in the northeast, Greenwood (the Teen Streets), Presidential Estates in the north with its larger homes, and Elmwood in the southeast around Elmwood Park.

Transit and highways

East Orange has two commuter rail stops, East Orange and Brick Church, both on NJ Transit's Morris and Essex Lines with daily trains to New York Penn Station and weekday trains to Hoboken. The East Orange station sits beside Interstate 280, directly across a parking lot from City Hall. More than a dozen NJ Transit bus routes, including the 5, 21, 24, 34, 41, 44, 71, 73, 79, 90, 92, 94 and 97, cover the city.

By road, the Garden State Parkway is reached at Interchange 145 for I-280 and Interchange 147 for Springdale Avenue. The average commute is 35.4 minutes, so naming the nearest station in a listing helps.

What is a Certificate of Conformity?

It is the city's pre-sale compliance certificate. Under Section 159-50, it must be in hand before a property is sold. It shows the property conforms to the city code, and the code holds seller and buyer both accountable for getting it. Apply in person at the Department of Property Maintenance, East Orange City Hall, 44 City Hall Plaza, third floor, paying by certified check or money order, since no cash is taken. The phone is 973-266-5320.

After an inspection, the city mails a Notice of Code Violations listing everything found and a correction deadline. Items left uncorrected can bring a summons and fines between $100 and $2,000 per offense. Ask Code Enforcement whether any open notices sit on your house before you list it.

Smoke alarm and carbon monoxide certificate

For a one or two family home, the Fire Department issues a Certificate of Smoke Alarm and Carbon Monoxide Compliance. Ask the buyer's attorney whether it is expected at your closing. Call the Fire Prevention Bureau at 973-266-5520 to book, at least a day ahead. Appointments run Monday to Thursday between 9 and 3. One and two family homes can also get free smoke detector installation from the city.

Other items that come up at closing

  • Service line: the piece beyond the curb box belongs to the owner, so a leak there is the owner's repair.
  • Superintendent license: a building with four or more dwelling units needs a designated, registered superintendent, renewed yearly.
  • Lead paint: the state inspection law applies to rentals built before 1978 and not to home sales, but federal rules still require a seller to disclose known lead hazards in a pre-1978 home.

Transfer fee and deed filing

The state's realty transfer fee is the seller's cost, charged on a schedule by price. Senior, blind or disabled sellers and certain affordable housing sales use a lower schedule. Your attorney or title agent can work out the figure for your price.

The Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages files East Orange deeds. It occupies Room 130 of the Hall of Records, 465 Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard in Newark, takes its last transaction at 4:15 on weekdays, and answers at 973-621-4960. A certified deed copy costs $8 for page one and $2 for each page after, and the staff will not conduct title searches.

Putting the steps in order

For an East Orange sale, start with the city, not the buyer. Call Code Enforcement to learn whether any Notice of Code Violations is open, then apply for the Certificate of Conformity at City Hall. Book the fire department detector appointment next, aiming for ten or more business days before closing to get the lowest fee. Ask the Water Department for a balance so nothing lands on the tax lien list, and tell your attorney about any tenants, since a building with four or more units adds the superintendent registration question.

A cash buyer can take the house as it stands and adjust the offer for open violations. A buyer using a mortgage will usually want them cleared before closing.

On the day of the closing, expect the title agent or attorney to ask for the Certificate of Conformity, the detector certificate where it applies, a final water balance, and your payoff letter. Having each of these in a single folder, with the Property Maintenance and Fire Prevention phone numbers written on the front, saves a scramble if a buyer's attorney asks a question late. Call the Fire Prevention Bureau again if the date moves, since the lead-time fee depends on how many business days remain. Sellers who inherited the house should also bring the estate papers so the attorney can confirm who has authority to sign the deed and the seller's tax form.

Frequently asked questions

Is a Certificate of Conformity mandatory for an East Orange sale?

Yes. The city requires it before a property is sold, and the code makes both seller and buyer responsible for obtaining it. Apply in person at the Department of Property Maintenance, third floor of City Hall.

What does the East Orange fire department charge for the detector certificate?

It is $100 with ten or more business days of notice, $125 with four to nine, and $175 with one to three. A failed inspection or a missed appointment costs $50.

Can a house with open code violations be sold in East Orange?

Yes. The violations stay with the property, and the owner receives a Notice of Code Violations with a deadline. A cash buyer can accept the house as it stands and adjust the offer for the open items.

Does the state lead paint inspection law reach home sales?

No, it covers rentals built before 1978. Federal law still requires a seller to disclose known lead hazards in a house older than 1978.

Which office files an East Orange deed?

The Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages in Newark, reachable at 973-621-4960. The seller's tax form goes with the deed, and the transfer fee is the seller's.

Selling a house in Elizabeth, NJ

Elizabeth is a dense port city: 141,675 residents on 12.32 square miles of land, about 11,145 people per square mile by the 2020 count. Only 25.6 percent of homes are owner occupied, so many houses for sale are two, three and four family buildings that investors and live-in owners both compete for. Median value of owner-occupied homes is $449,300, median gross rent is $1,523, and median household income is $66,555.

Price realistically against that $449,300 median rather than against figures from richer Union County suburbs. A bilingual listing, flyer and contract summary can reach more of the buyers in this city.

Layout and neighborhoods

The city sits in Union County between Newark to the north and Linden to the southwest. Newark Bay and the Arthur Kill form its eastern edge. The street plan is unusual for New Jersey: instead of a grid, it is largely circular, with streets radiating from the central railroad station. A house a block from Elizabeth station and one near Warinanco Park are very different propositions, so a good listing names the neighborhood and the number of units in the first line.

Elizabeth neighborhoods buyers ask about
NeighborhoodWhat it is known for
Midtown / UptownMain commercial district with the 1931 Art Deco Hersch Tower and the Ritz Theatre
BaywaySouthern end beside Linden; older, well kept homes and many affordable two to four family buildings
ElizabethportOldest neighborhood, east of 7th Street; renovated homes and new townhouses along the waterfront
ElmoraMiddle and working class western section on Elmora Avenue, with high-rises near the train station

Resale certificate and detector rules

Elizabeth has an online Resale Certificates application, and the form asks you to attach the smoke detector certificate if the property is occupied. Call the Bureau of Zoning for the current fee and inspection timing when you submit it.

Use these detector rules as a checklist before you apply:

  • Smoke detectors on every level, including the basement and any finished attic, mounted at the center of the ceiling within ten feet of bedrooms.
  • A carbon monoxide detector on every floor near sleeping areas, with combination units allowed.
  • A UL listed 2-A:10-B:C fire extinguisher, fully charged and mounted within ten feet of the stove in every kitchen.
  • Hardwired systems must have power on and all units sounding together; battery units cannot replace a hardwired system.

Everything has to be mounted and working before the inspector arrives.

Transit and roads

NJ Transit stops at Elizabeth station and North Elizabeth on the Northeast Corridor and North Jersey Coast lines, with service to Newark Penn, Secaucus Junction and New York Penn. Buses run to the Port Authority terminal and to Newark. By road, the New Jersey Turnpike, Interstate 278, U.S. 1 and 9, and Routes 27, 28, 81 and 439 all cross the city, and The Mills at Jersey Gardens anchors retail. Mean travel to work is 26.7 minutes. The Goethals Bridge lands here on the way to Staten Island, and the Port Newark Elizabeth Marine Terminal and part of Newark Liberty airport sit within the city, so buyers who work in logistics or at the airport often search here first. Say how far the house is from the station or the Turnpike, because commuters compare those two first.

Elizabeth Public Schools is one of 31 former Abbott districts, with five new academies and a smaller Elizabeth High School. Mention the zoned school in your listing, and confirm it with the district first, since buyers with children will ask before they book a showing.

What to gather before listing

  • The current block and lot numbers, confirmed with the Tax Assessor, since the city renumbered parcels starting January 1, 2023.
  • Proof of working, mounted detectors and extinguishers for every unit, ready for the smoke certificate attached to the resale application.
  • Permit records for any finished basement, converted attic or added unit, plus any boiler, roof or electrical paperwork.
  • Tenant names, lease terms and security deposit records if the building is occupied.
  • The deed, mortgage payoff figure and any lien letters.

Having all of this in one folder shortens the time between accepting an offer and sending a contract package to the buyer's attorney.

Deeds, transfer fee and appeals

Deeds are recorded with the Union County Clerk, whose land records site is clerk.ucnj.org. A notice there says the city began assigning new lot and block numbers on January 1, 2023, and that the person preparing the deed must confirm the correct numbers with the Tax Assessor or the county tax board association before recording. The clerk is not responsible for numbers copied from an old document.

On the state side, the seller pays the realty transfer fee on the deed. Rates run per $500 of price and step up in bands, and sales over $1,000,000 add a graduated percent fee. A seller who is a New Jersey resident signs GIT/REP-3. Sellers who are nonresidents use GIT/REP-1 or GIT/REP-2 unless a listed assurance applies. Appeals of an assessment must reach the county board of taxation by April 1.

How an Elizabeth sale usually unfolds

Start with the property record: confirm the block and lot with the Tax Assessor, because a deed copied from older paperwork can carry the wrong numbers. Next, walk every unit with the detector checklist and fix what fails. Then submit the online Resale Certificates application with the smoke certificate attached and ask the Bureau of Zoning when an inspection can happen.

If the building has tenants, tell them when the inspector is coming. If you inherited it, gather the estate papers so your attorney can confirm who signs. A cash buyer can take a two or three family building as it stands, while a buyer using a mortgage will want a clean certificate and an appraisal that supports the price.

Because so many Elizabeth houses have more than one unit, expect the buyer's attorney to ask for each unit's lease, rent roll and deposit records, and to ask whether every kitchen has its own extinguisher and every floor its own carbon monoxide detector. Answering those questions before they are asked is the easiest way to keep the closing date. If a unit was added without a permit, raise it with your attorney early, since it can affect both the certificate and the buyer's financing.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need an inspection to sell my Elizabeth house?

What does Elizabeth require for detectors and extinguishers?

April 1, filed with the Union County Board of Taxation, or May 1 where the city has just completed a revaluation. Properties assessed above $1,000,000 may go to the State Tax Court instead.

Selling a house in Englewood, NJ

Englewood is a small Bergen County city of 4.93 square miles with 30,035 residents, and it enforces a Certificate of Continued Occupancy on every sale of a one, two or multi-family house. The inspection is short, but the permit check that comes first can take longer than the visit itself, so begin early.

The median owner-occupied home is valued at $544,100, median household income is $102,571, and 54.5 percent of homes are owner occupied. The city has 11,274 households.

How the Certificate of Continued Occupancy works

City Ordinance 85-40, in Chapter 9 of the Revised General Ordinances, says a seller must receive a CCO before ownership transfers. New construction and buildings the state inspects, such as hotels and rooming houses, are outside it. The point is to check safety and to hand the new owner information about fire and occupancy rules.

  1. Once you have a buyer, the seller or agent visits the Englewood Municipal Building at 2-10 North Van Brunt Street, second floor, and tells the Building Department about the sale.
  2. Any open permits for work on the property must be closed out before an inspection can be scheduled.
  3. The application asks for the property address, owner and buyer contact details, the buyer's present address (or a mailing address for an LLC or corporation), and the number of people living there before and after the sale.
  4. You pay the fee to the City of Englewood and the inspector visits.
  5. The certificate is passed to the buyer at closing.

Selling without a CCO risks fines and delays at the closing table. The application asks about occupancy before and after the sale, so have the buyer's details ready when you go in, and keep a copy of the receipt for the fee. If the buyer is an LLC or corporation, bring its mailing address instead of a home address.

Inspection checklist and fees

Englewood CCO fees and what the inspector checks

Fee, multi-family building$250
