What if the inspector finds an illegal unit or unpermitted work?

The owner has to remove the extra unit, which means cutting off utility service and removing the added kitchen and bathroom. The certificate issues only after a second inspection confirms the work is done and the code is met. Work that needed a permit and did not get one must go through the Building Department first.

If you suspect an old basement apartment or an attic conversion has no paperwork, talk to the Building Department before you accept a contract. Raising it early leaves time to renegotiate before the closing date is fixed. Buyers rarely walk away from a clearly explained problem, but they do from a surprise at the inspection.

Englewood housing costs and neighborhoods

Median selected monthly owner costs are $3,464 with a mortgage and $1,500 or more without one, and median gross rent is $1,977. Englewood borders Bergenfield, Englewood Cliffs, Fort Lee, Leonia, Teaneck and Tenafly, and Highwood is an unincorporated community inside its lines. Street names such as Brinckerhoff, Van Brunt, Lydecker, Demarest and Van Nostrand recall the early families, and houses on Grand Avenue include several of the city's National Register sites.

Flat Rock Brook is a 150 acre preserve on Van Nostrand Avenue with 3.6 miles of trails, and MacKay Park on North Van Brunt Street has a pool, rink and athletic fields. Mention whichever is closest in your listing, along with the walk or drive to the bus stop, since commuters and families both read for that.

Compare your carrying costs against these medians when deciding how long to wait for an offer. An inherited house with a mortgage-free balance costs far less to hold than one carrying a payment, which changes how patient you can afford to be.

Commuting and schools

Interstate 95 clips the city for 0.43 miles near the Leonia line. Routes 4 and 93 and county routes 501 and 505 carry local traffic. NJ Transit bus 166 runs to the Port Authority Bus Terminal, while routes 171, 175, 178 and 186 serve the George Washington Bridge Bus Station, and Rockland Coaches also runs to Port Authority. Mean travel time to work is 30.9 minutes, so a listing that states the nearest bus line helps buyers who work in Manhattan.

The Englewood Public School District runs five schools, from the D. A. Quarles Early Childhood Center to Dwight Morrow High School, which also takes students from Englewood Cliffs. Bergen County students can apply to the Bergen County Academies and other county technical programs.

State fees at the deed and where it is recorded

Bergen County's Clerk acts as the recording officer for deeds, mortgages and liens. The state charges the seller a realty transfer fee on the deed, and any price above $350,000 uses a higher schedule: for example, $4.80 per $500 on the slice between $200,000 and $550,000. Sales above $1,000,000 add a graduated percent fee that starts at 1 percent.

A resident seller signs the state's GIT/REP-3 form for recording, and nonresident sellers use GIT/REP-1 or GIT/REP-2 unless a stated assurance applies. For a tax assessment challenge, the county board of taxation must receive your petition by April 1, or May 1 where a revaluation or reassessment took place.

Getting ready: a short timeline

Once a buyer is lined up, call the Building Department the same week. Ask whether any permit from past work is still open, close it out, and only then request the inspection. While you wait, test every smoke and carbon monoxide detector, put an ABC extinguisher of 2 to 10 pounds within 10 feet of each kitchen, and walk the stairs and railings for anything loose.

A cash buyer does not avoid the CCO. The ordinance applies whenever ownership changes hands, so the buyer's attorney will ask for the certificate at closing, and a missing one can push the closing date back. A cash sale does save you the lender's appraisal and the repair negotiations that often follow a mortgage buyer's inspection. If the house has a basement apartment or attic room, tell the buyer up front and fix the paperwork or remove the unit before the inspector arrives.

Do I need a CCO to sell a house in Englewood?

Yes. City Ordinance 85-40 requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy for one, two and multi-family houses before ownership changes hands.

How much is the Englewood CCO inspection?

$150 for a one or two family home and $250 for a multi-family building, paid to the City of Englewood with the application.

What does the Englewood inspector look at for fire safety?

A working smoke detector on each level, a working carbon monoxide detector within 10 feet of bedrooms, and an ABC extinguisher of 2 to 10 pounds within 10 feet of the kitchen.

Where in Englewood do I start the CCO process?

At the Building Department, second floor of the Municipal Building, 2-10 North Van Brunt Street. Have the buyer's name, phone and address ready, and close out any open permits first.

What happens if the inspector finds an illegal unit?

The owner removes the unit, including its kitchen and bathroom and utility service, and a second inspection confirms it before the certificate issues.

The Certificate of Continued Occupancy comes first

Fair Lawn is a Bergen County borough roughly 12 miles northwest of New York City. It had 34,927 residents in 2020 and an estimated 37,128 in 2025, up 6.3 percent. Only 5.14 square miles of land hold all those people, about 6,800 per square mile, so lots are tight and houses sit close together. Radburn, a planned community from 1929 and one of the first in the country, is inside the borough, and eight local sites are on the National Register of Historic Places. What does the Certificate of Continued Occupancy involve?

The certificate is required for any transfer of title on a one or two family dwelling, and the borough's published fee is $175. The Building Department is in Room 112 of the municipal building, open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and the phone is (201) 794-5307. Fire Prevention handles the smoke certificate at 201-794-5408.

  • You file an application and pay the $175 fee, then the department inspects the property and may photograph conditions.

If the buyer plans to do the repairs, the borough offers a Conditional Certificate for transfer of title only, with no occupancy. The buyer's attorney sends a letter confirming the buyer understands that, and after closing the buyer reapplies for the full certificate and pays another $175. Fair Lawn's hyphenated addresses

Most Fair Lawn addresses carry a hyphenated number, like the library's 10-01 Fair Lawn Avenue, and buyers searching online sometimes get no match unless they drop the dash. Nearly 10,000 addresses here use the system, almost half of all hyphenated addresses in New Jersey.

The first number gives the block distance from Broadway on north-south streets, or from the numbered street on east-west ones. Addresses south of Broadway or Route 4 begin with a zero. The system goes back to at least the 1930s and was built so emergency crews could find a house fast. Exceptions exist on the Glen Rock, Hawthorne and Saddle Brook sides and inside Radburn.

In your ad, write the address both with and without the dash, and check it against the tax record so title and survey work match the deed.

Commuting from Fair Lawn

Route 4 reaches the George Washington Bridge in under 10 miles from the Broadway district, and Route 208 runs northwest to Interstate 287. The Radburn and Broadway stations on NJ Transit's Bergen County Line serve Hoboken, with connections at Secaucus Junction to New York Penn Station. NJ Transit buses 144, 145, 148, 160, 164 and 196 run to the Port Authority Bus Terminal.

Local streets form a rough three-by-three grid. Saddle River Road, Plaza Road and River Road run north to south, while Broadway, Morlot Avenue and Fair Lawn Avenue run east to west. Buyers also ask about the neighborhoods: Berdan Grove around Berdan Grove Park, the Broadway District shopping strip, and Radburn with its own station and pathways.

Above $1 million, a graduated percent fee also falls on the seller, and your attorney will calculate it.

New Jersey resident sellers, estates and trusts included, complete a GIT/REP-3 to record the deed. In an estate sale, the executors who sign the deed also sign the form, and an executor who is also a beneficiary signs two forms. County clerks decide whether to accept a deed, so if one is rejected, resolve it with the clerk's office first and then with the state GIT/REP Unit at 609-322-9275.

Assessment appeals in Bergen County go to the Board of Taxation at 201-336-6300, which can give you the current filing deadline. For rent control questions on a rented house, the borough's rent leveling office is at (201) 564-6152.

Timeline for a quick sale

Order matters in Fair Lawn because the certificate gates everything. Apply for it first, and ask Fire Prevention for the smoke certificate at the same time. Check the public sidewalk in front of the house, since a failed one holds up approval until it is fixed. Once the Building Department signs off, your closing attorney prepares the deed, the transfer fee and the GIT/REP form. Bring the deed, your latest tax bill and a payoff statement to that first meeting.

If a cash buyer wants to do the work, the Conditional Certificate lets title transfer without occupancy. That can shorten the wait for a seller, but the buyer must then apply for the full certificate after closing.

Does Fair Lawn require an inspection before I sell?

Yes. The borough requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy for any transfer of title on a one or two family dwelling. The fee is $175, and applications go to Room 112 of the municipal building. Fire Prevention supplies the smoke certificate at 201-794-5408.

Yes, with a Conditional Certificate for transfer of title only. The buyer's attorney sends a letter confirming there is no occupancy, and a failed sidewalk still has to be fixed. After closing, the buyer reapplies for the full certificate and pays another $175.

Who signs the GIT/REP form when an estate sells a Fair Lawn house?

The executors who sign the deed sign it, or the administrator if there is no will. An executor who is also a beneficiary signs two forms, one for the estate and one personally. Residents use the GIT/REP-3.

Why do Fair Lawn addresses have a dash?

The dash comes from the borough's grid numbering, in use since at least the 1930s. The first number counts blocks from Broadway or follows the numbered street, and addresses south of Broadway start with a zero. Many online forms accept only the number without the dash.

Which county office records a Fair Lawn deed?

The Bergen County Clerk records deeds, and the Board of Taxation handles assessment appeals. The state transfer fee and the GIT/REP form go in with the deed. Your closing attorney or title company can confirm the filing method for your closing date.

Selling a unit in a tower can add association steps before the deed passes. Make that request at the start, before a contract is signed, so the closing date reflects the association's timetable.

The state classifies co-ops as Class 4C property, and the Division of Taxation applies the graduated percent fee to them on deeds above $1 million. It starts at 1 percent of the total price for sales between $1,000,000 and $2,000,000 and rises in steps to 3.5 percent above $3.5 million. The seller is responsible for it.

How do Fort Lee's roads and transit affect buyers?

Position at the George Washington Bridge shapes how buyers judge a property. The bridge, signed as I-95, U.S. 1-9 and U.S. 46, carries traffic into Washington Heights in Upper Manhattan. Corporations, partnerships and multi-member LLCs file a GIT/REP-3 and check Box 5, and so do single-member LLCs. Start with the building. Ask the management office for the resale package and any board approval steps, and ask Fire Prevention for the Certificate of Compliance packet. Then have your closing attorney prepare the deed and the transfer fee and GIT/REP filings, which go to the Bergen County Clerk at recording.

A cash buyer can often skip a mortgage appraisal timeline, but the borough certificate and any association approval still set the pace.

Bring a short folder to your attorney: the deed, your latest tax bill, a mortgage payoff statement, the association's contact details and, for a rental, the lease and deposit figure. If the frontage has a cracked or failed sidewalk, file the sidewalk permit application early so the repair does not hold up the certificate. A seller who lives outside New Jersey should also ask the attorney about the estimated Gross Income Tax payment well before the closing date, since it is collected at the table.

An owner who is an LLC or other entity should confirm which GIT/REP box applies before the closing date, because a wrong form can get the deed rejected at recording. It is the graduated percent fee on deeds above $1 million, and the seller pays it. It starts at 1 percent for sales up to $2 million and reaches 3.5 percent above $3.5 million. It applies to Class 2 residential and Class 4C cooperative units.

An LLC files the GIT/REP-3 and checks Box 5, which covers sellers that are not individuals, estates or trusts. Single-member LLCs follow the same instruction.

The Bergen County Clerk. The state Realty Transfer Fee and the Gross Income Tax form are filed with the deed, and your closing attorney or title company handles the submission and confirms the fee.

Selling in a city of renters and owners

Garfield is a compact Bergen County city where renters outnumber owners, and its sale paperwork is priced by unit count. It has an estimated 33,353 residents in 2025 on 2.11 square miles of land, about 15,469 per square mile at the 2020 count.

Just 44.7% of households own their home (2020 to 2024). Median home value is $475,500 and median gross rent is $1,688. With that split, a seller tends to see two kinds of buyer: an occupant, and an investor who plans to rent the units out. Both face the same city paperwork before title passes, starting with the resale certificate.

Old neighborhood names such as Belmont, Bogart Heights, Dundee Dam and Plauderville still appear on deeds and listings. One piece of local history matters for due diligence: the EPA identified groundwater contamination from a 1983 chromic acid spill at a former electroplating company in Garfield and announced a $37 million cleanup in 2016. Buyers and lenders sometimes ask about nearby cleanup sites, so look up your street in the EPA's records early.

What Garfield requires before a resale

Garfield requires a certificate of occupancy for resale plus a separate smoke, carbon monoxide and fire extinguisher certification. Submit the request through the Building Department citizen portal or by email, then wait for the email that tells you when fees are due.

Processing takes 10 business days from the day the application is received, so do not schedule a closing until the certificate is in hand. Ignoring the ordinance can bring a fine of $2,000.

  • Send the property address and the full names, current home addresses, phone numbers and emails of buyer and seller. Do not list a business, attorney or real estate office address.
  • If an LLC or corporation is selling, give the contact person's details as well.
  • For an estate sale, attach the Surrogate letter to the application.
  • Pay the certificate fee to the City of Garfield and the smoke certification fee to the Bureau of Fire Prevention, each with its own check or money order.

Fees are charged by building type, and the city asks sellers to wait for its fee email before paying.

Tenants, repairs and open estates

Each of these situations adds one step without blocking the sale. An as-is house can still receive its paperwork once the smoke and fire items pass.

The detector rules are specific. Ten-year sealed-battery smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms must sit within ten feet of every bedroom, and a common stairwell needs smoke alarms at the top and bottom. Inspectors also ask for access to the attic and basement.

  • A tenant-occupied house may also need a dwelling certificate. Ordinance 2213 requires one on any change of occupancy, with a $60 fee per unit that includes the smoke certification, unless an inspection happened within the previous eleven months.
  • A second visit costs another $60 per unit if the unit fails or the paperwork is not on site.
  • For a house with a deceased owner, the application asks for the Surrogate letter, so have it ready before you apply.

If repairs are the problem, fix the detector items first. They are the cheapest part of the checklist, and the state rule behind them is N.J.A.C. 5:70-2.3.

State filings recorded with the deed

The Bergen County Clerk records a Garfield deed, and the state attaches two filings to it: the Realty Transfer Fee and a gross income tax residency form. The seller owes the fee, and it is computed from the consideration recited in the deed.

For prices of $350,000 or less, the schedule starts at $2.00 per $500 of the first $150,000 and tops out at $3.90 per $500 for the slice between $200,000 and $350,000. A higher schedule applies above $350,000, opening at $2.90 per $500 and reaching $4.80 per $500 for the slice from $200,000 to $550,000.

The state exempts deeds between husband and wife or parent and child, and an executor's deed distributing an estate to an heir. An arm's-length purchase fits none of these.

The residency paperwork is the GIT/REP. A New Jersey resident signs the GIT/REP-3. A nonresident seller prepays estimated gross income tax, never less than 2% of the deed consideration, unless a listed assurance on the form applies. No deed gets recorded without a signed GIT/REP-1, -2 or -3.

Trains, roads and schools buyers ask about

Garfield sells on access: two NJ Transit rail stops and Route 46 both sit inside the city. The Garfield and Plauderville stations on the Bergen County Line run to Hoboken Terminal, with a transfer at Secaucus Junction for Penn Station. NJ Transit buses 160 and 161 run to the Port Authority terminal in Midtown Manhattan.

By road, U.S. Route 46 and County Route 507 pass through, and Midland Avenue, Outwater Lane, River Drive and Passaic Street are the other main streets. Mean commute time is 28.0 minutes. The public schools are Garfield Public Schools, a pre-K to grade 12 district. A buyer with children will ask, so have the district name ready.

Which sale route fits a Garfield owner?

Your deadline and the condition of the building decide it. Listing reaches the most buyers but puts showings and repair requests on you. A private sale or cash buyer trims the repair list, yet the city certificate and fire certification apply to all three.

  • List with an agent if the building is in good order and you can wait on a buyer's mortgage approval.
  • Sell privately if a buyer is already lined up, such as a tenant, relative or neighbor.
  • Consider a cash offer for a building that needs work, carries tenants or belongs to an estate, and settle in the contract who orders the certificate and pays the $50 or $100 city fee.

Fix the closing date first, then count back 10 business days to learn the last day to file with the city.

Frequently asked questions

Is an inspection mandatory when I sell in Garfield?

Yes. Garfield requires a certificate of occupancy for resale and a smoke, carbon monoxide and fire extinguisher certification. Processing takes 10 business days, so do not schedule a closing before the certificate is issued.

How much is the Garfield resale certificate?

One-family houses pay $50 and two-family houses pay $100. Bigger buildings pay $100 for two units plus $25 for each one after that. The Bureau of Fire Prevention charges its smoke and CO certification on the same scale.

Who pays the New Jersey realty transfer fee in a Garfield sale?

The seller. The county recording officer collects the state fee at recording, and the amount scales with the price in the deed. Spouse-to-spouse and parent-to-child deeds carry an exemption.

Can I sell a Garfield house that I inherited and have not cleared up yet?

Yes, once you have the right papers. Garfield wants the Surrogate letter with the certificate application on an estate sale. Selling to an outside buyer is a taxable transfer, though an executor's deed to an heir is exempt.

Do I need a dwelling certificate if tenants live in the house?

Possibly. Ordinance 2213 calls for a dwelling certificate on a change of occupancy, at $60 per unit, unless the unit was inspected in the previous eleven months. Ask the Fire Prevention Bureau whether your tenant situation triggers it.

What is the quickest way to move a house in Hackensack?

Whether you use an agent, a private buyer or a cash buyer, the city inspection, tax payoff and recording are the same. Cash only takes the lender's appraisal and approval out of the schedule.

Hackensack covers 4.35 square miles roughly 12 miles northwest of Midtown Manhattan, and one block can look nothing like the next. The west side has single-family homes, a few on an acre or larger. Older central blocks have two-family houses, Prospect Avenue and the garden complexes offer apartment living at scale, and downtown has mixed-use buildings.

Figures that should shape your asking price

Hackensack pairs a renter-heavy population with a large tax bill: the average home was billed $10,307 in 2025.

Fire inspection before a Hackensack sale

Before closing, a seller needs the compliance certificate for smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms and a portable fire extinguisher, which the Fire Prevention Bureau issues. The city form lists a $70 fee and a six-month validity period, and the certificate is issued the same day as the inspection.

A failed inspection, or an empty house at appointment time, means a new application and a new fee. Fill the form carefully with the buyer's name, the seller's name and the real estate company, because wrong details void the report.

The state Uniform Fire Code is the source, requiring a smoke alarm certificate when a one-family or two-family dwelling is sold, leased or changes occupants. Only the municipality can issue it. Get the house ready first:

  • Smoke alarms on each floor and in the basement, in shared stairwells and hallways, and within 10 feet of every sleeping area.
  • Sealed ten-year battery alarms in place of old ones, since the state Division of Fire Safety advises swapping alarms every decade.
  • A carbon monoxide alarm and a portable fire extinguisher, both listed on the city form.

The Building, Housing and Land Use department can tell you if your property type needs other resale paperwork.

What the tax collector expects

Four installments are due each year, on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, with a 10-day grace period after each. Interest on late balances is 8 percent a year up to $1,500 and 18 percent on the rest. Pay everything by November 10 to stay clear of the accelerated tax sale that starts November 11.

County recording can take three to six months before the city hears of a new owner, so a buyer should mail the collector an address after closing. As the seller, ask for a written balance before you review the closing statement.

If you believe the assessment is above market value, appeal to the Bergen County Board of Taxation, Two Bergen County Plaza in Hackensack, by the yearly April 1 date. Property assessed above $750,000 may skip ahead to the Tax Court, also by April 1.

Costs at the closing table

When the deed is recorded, the seller owes the state Realty Transfer Fee, taken from a rate table keyed to the sale price. Above $1,000,000 a graduated percent fee also applies, with its own published schedule.

  • The state transfer fee, collected at recording.
  • The $70 fire certificate.
  • Mortgage payoff and any recorded liens.
  • Your share of the current quarter's property tax.

New Jersey residents sign the GIT/REP-3 so the clerk will accept the deed. Sellers from out of state prepay Gross Income Tax of no less than 2 percent of the price, unless a listed assurance covers them. Estates have a special case: an executor's deed to an heir named in the will is an exempt transfer, while a sale to an outside buyer is taxed and still needs the fire certificate.

How should a landlord handle a Hackensack rental sale?

Renters occupy roughly 63 percent of homes, at a typical rent of $1,911. The same Building, Housing and Land Use department staffs the Rent Stabilization Board, so find out whether your building is covered before you price from market rents.

The fire certificate is needed for leases as well as sales, so a new tenant and a sale may each trigger an inspection. Time yours so the six-month certificate is still good on closing day. An attorney should read every lease, since the buyer inherits the occupancy.

Roads and rail lines buyers use

Interstate 80, Route 17, Route 4 and County Route 503 pass through, and the Hackensack River is crossed at Court Street, Midtown and Anderson Street. Pascack Valley Line trains stop at Anderson Street and Essex Street, heading to Hoboken and on to Penn Station New York. The Hackensack Bus Terminal sends buses to the Port Authority and the George Washington Bridge Bus Station. A listing close to a station or the terminal puts that commute in front of buyers.

Order of steps for a quick sale

Schedule the fire inspection first, then request a written balance from the tax collector. Gather the deed, newest tax bill and any lease or payoff statement for your attorney. With the certificate in hand, a cash buyer can close on the date you both pick, and the attorney records the deed with the state filings. If tenants are staying, ask the buyer to confirm that in the contract, and if the house must be empty, set the move-out date in writing before you sign.

Frequently asked questions

Is a fire inspection certificate mandatory for a Hackensack sale?

Yes. The state requires a smoke alarm certificate when a one- or two-family home sells. The city fire bureau issues it for $70, on a form that also covers carbon monoxide alarms and a fire extinguisher, and it lasts six months.

Who pays the state transfer fee on a Hackensack sale?

You do, at recording. The amount follows the state's schedule for your sale price, and only listed transfers, such as a deed from parent to child, are exempt.

Does a Hackensack house with unpaid taxes still sell?

It can, as long as the balance is cleared by closing. Current-year taxes should be paid by November 10 to avoid the tax sale starting November 11, and interest runs 8 percent up to $1,500 and 18 percent beyond.

May I sell while tenants live in the house?

Yes. Check rent stabilization with the Building, Housing and Land Use department and let an attorney review each lease.

What changes when the house came through an estate?

The estate completes a GIT/REP form for its residency status. A deed from the executor to an heir named in the will is exempt from the transfer fee, but a sale to an outsider is taxed and the fire certificate still applies.

Quickest ways to sell in Hoboken

Hoboken owners can list on the open market, sell privately, or accept an as-is cash offer. Which fits depends on what you own. A condo unit, a rowhouse and a small building with tenants each send you to different city offices.

Housing here is dense and mostly rented, so many sales involve a lease, a registration or a rent ordinance. Clearing those items first gets you to a closing date faster than any price cut would.

  • Traditional listing: best for a renovated unit in good shape, with showings, inspections and a buyer's financing to schedule.
  • Private sale: saves the commission, but disclosures, contracts and the city's compliance certificate are yours to manage.
  • Cash purchase: suits a unit with deferred repairs, tenants in place or a deadline, since no mortgage approval holds up the closing.

The Hoboken housing market

Hoboken sits on the west bank of the Hudson River in Hudson County, across from Manhattan's West Village and Chelsea. It is called the Mile Square City, though the land area is about 1.25 square miles. The ZIP code is 07030. The July 2025 population estimate is 59,027, a 1.7 percent drop from 2020.

Only about one in three housing units is owner-occupied, so a seller often competes with landlords as well as other owners. The old factory blocks of Maxwell House, Lipton and Hostess are now condominiums and shops, and the once industrial Northwest section has been rezoned and rebuilt as housing.

Flood history and what buyers ask

Buyers will ask about flooding, and the history gives them reason. In October 2012 Hurricane Sandy flooded about 1,700 Hoboken homes and caused roughly $100 million in damage, and it shut down the PATH station at Hoboken Terminal.

The response was large. The federal housing department set aside $230 million through the Rebuild by Design competition for Hoboken, Weehawken and Jersey City. The city's plan has four parts: resist surge with barriers, delay runoff with green infrastructure, store rainwater in basins and parks, and discharge it through upgraded sewers and pump stations. ResilienCity Park, which the city calls New Jersey's largest resiliency park, can hold up to 2 million gallons of rain.

If your building took water in 2012, have repair records, flood insurance history and any elevation paperwork ready. Buyers' attorneys ask for them.

Commuting and transit

Hoboken has the highest share of public transit commuters of any American city, with 56 percent of working residents riding each day. Hoboken Terminal in the southeast corner is a national historic landmark, built in 1907.

  • Rail and subway: NJ Transit's Main, Bergen County, Pascack Valley, Montclair-Boonton, Morris and Essex and Meadowlands lines end at the terminal, and PATH runs to 33rd Street, the World Trade Center and Journal Square.
  • Light rail, bus and ferry: the Hudson-Bergen line has three Hoboken stops, nine NJ Transit bus routes terminate at Hudson Place, and NY Waterway ferries cross to Battery Park City, Pier 11 and West Midtown.
  • Roads: the 14th Street Viaduct leads up to Jersey City Heights, and the Lincoln and Holland tunnels are nearby.

City rules for selling or renting out

Three city offices matter most: Construction Code, the Fire Department, and Rent Leveling and Stabilization. City Hall is at 94 Washington Street.

Construction Code issues certificates of occupancy for new buildings, additions and altered space, and a certificate of approval for other work. For a resale, ask about the application titled Certificate of Smoke Detector, CO and Fire Extinguisher Compliance. The fire inspection office can tell you whether your unit needs it.

Rent Leveling and Stabilization administers Chapter 155, the municipal rent control ordinance. Its staff can say which apartments are covered, what the legal base rent is, and how annual adjustments, vacancy decontrol and surcharges apply. Owners of single-family homes, condominiums, multiple dwellings and mixed-use buildings must register each year through the SDL portal. If you are selling a building with tenants, get the office's file on your property and hand a copy to the buyer's attorney.

Property taxes and payoffs

Hoboken sends one tax bill with four quarterly stubs. It combines municipal, school, county and library taxes, plus a Special Improvement District assessment for properties inside that district. Postmarks do not count, so a payment is on time only when the tax office receives it or it is paid online by the end of the grace period.

Added and omitted assessment bills for improvements go out in October and fall due November 1, with a grace period to November 10. For a lien payoff, call the Tax Collector for a redemption statement, because balances shown on the website may be wrong. Expect to pay by certified check or money order.

Deliver payments to City Hall at 94 Washington Street or pay online.

How to appeal your assessment

Appeals go to the Hudson County Board of Taxation, normally by April 1. A successful judgment is credited first to fourth-quarter taxes, then to any third-quarter balance, and any leftover is refunded to the petitioner or their attorney.

State fees at Hoboken prices

With a median owned-home value of $895,100, many Hoboken sales approach the $1,000,000 line. Above it, the seller owes a graduated fee of 1 percent of the total price up to $2,000,000, and the buyer owes an extra 1 percent. Residents who keep their New Jersey residency sign GIT/REP-3 at closing instead of making an estimated payment.

Ask your closing attorney for the exact fee schedule before you accept an offer, so the net figure you compare is accurate.

Selling a Hoboken unit for cash, step by step

A cash buyer takes away the mortgage approval, but not the city's paperwork. Start with the fire inspection office to learn whether your unit needs the smoke detector, CO and fire extinguisher certificate. If you own a rental building, pull the Rent Leveling file and your yearly registration. Next, call the Tax Collector for a redemption statement if a lien exists, and gather any flood repair records.

At the closing table, bring your deed, a recent tax bill, a mortgage payoff letter, leases for any tenants, and the residency form. A condo seller should also ask the association for its documents early, since those can take longer than anything the city does.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Is there a rent control law I should know about before selling a Hoboken rental?

Yes. Hoboken enforces Chapter 155, a municipal rent control ordinance, through its Rent Leveling and Stabilization office. The office can tell you which apartments are covered, the legal base rent and the allowed increases. Owners register their properties every year through the SDL portal.

Does Hoboken require a certificate to sell a home?

The city publishes an application for a Certificate of Smoke Detector, CO and Fire Extinguisher Compliance, and Construction Code issues certificates of occupancy for new or altered space. Ask the fire inspection office and your closing attorney which one your sale needs, since it can differ for a condo, a rowhouse and a multi-unit building.

Does Hoboken flood, and what should a seller have ready?

Parts of the city flooded badly in Hurricane Sandy in 2012, and the city has since built sewer, park and barrier projects with $230 million in federal funds. Gather repair records and insurance history for your address and review them with your attorney before listing.

When are Hoboken property taxes due?

In four quarterly installments listed on the single annual bill. The Tax Collector charges interest back to the due date once the grace period ends, and does not honor postmarks. Call the office for a redemption figure if a lien exists.

How long do I have to appeal my Hoboken assessment?

Generally until April 1, filed with the Hudson County Board of Taxation on Form A-1. Owners of properties assessed above $1,000,000 may go straight to the Tax Court by the same date. If you disagree with the board's judgment, the Tax Court appeal must be filed within 45 days.

City rules that matter when you sell

No new certificate of occupancy is issued in Jersey City for a purchase or sale. The sale-related fire rule comes from the state: a one- or two-family house needs a municipal smoke alarm certificate, valid six months, before it changes hands. Ask the city's fire prevention office for the form.

With tenants in place, give the buyer the lead-safe certificates or exemption papers alongside the leases.

Flooding near the waterfront

Buyers near the water ask about storms. Irene, in August 2011, flooded parts of Downtown and the waterfront, and Sandy, in October 2012, pushed storm surge into Downtown, the Country Village neighborhood, the West Side and Liberty State Park. The flooding damaged city utilities and shut down PATH and the Holland Tunnel for days.

For a waterfront property, gather flood insurance papers, elevation certificates and repair invoices before listing. A paper trail of dry basements and replaced systems settles the question before it turns into a price cut.

Transit and jobs

Transit explains much of the pricing. Four PATH stations serve the city (Exchange Place, Newport, Grove Street and Journal Square), with trains to Hoboken, 33rd Street in Midtown, Lower Manhattan's World Trade Center and Newark Penn Station. Thirteen of the Hudson-Bergen Light Rail's 24 stations are inside Jersey City. NJ Transit buses reach Newark and, through the Lincoln Tunnel, Midtown, and Hoboken Terminal runs commuter rail. Mean commute is 36.8 minutes.

The waterfront known as Wall Street West holds more than 13 million square feet of Class A office space, which keeps demand strong around Exchange Place and Newport. If your house is a short walk from a PATH or light rail stop, say so in the first line of your description.

The city's tax assessor page sends you to taxrecords-nj.com, where Records Search lets you pick Hudson County and Jersey City and search by address, owner or block and lot. The deed is filed in Hudson County, and the transfer fee comes out of the seller's proceeds. On a price over $1 million, check the graduated percent fee before anyone agrees on a net number. Two city offices handle questions outside the sale itself: the Division of Housing Preservation for lead inspections and the Division of Zoning for driveway determinations.

Closing a cash sale in Jersey City

A cash buyer takes the house without a lender, so the work left is local. Book the smoke alarm inspection through the fire prevention office, collect lead certificates and leases if tenants live there, and ask the tax collector for the current balance. If the house has flood history or a driveway question, hand the buyer the papers up front.

Bring your deed, a recent tax bill, any mortgage payoff letter and photo ID to the closing. Unpaid balances come out of your proceeds at the table.

Sequence matters. Order the smoke alarm certificate first, because it is valid six months and the fire prevention office issues it, so a late start can leave the paper expired before closing. Next, sort out tenants: with renters in place, a buyer will want leases, lead-safe certificates or exemption papers, and a clear picture of who pays what. Last, ask the tax collector for the balance and the next installment so the title company can put exact figures on the settlement statement.

If the house has a front-yard parking space, a Zoning Determination Letter can show whether it counts as legal, which saves a buyer's attorney a round of questions. For a condo, ask the association for its documents early, since those often take longer than anything the city does. A cash buyer does not change any of this paperwork, but it does remove the appraisal and the loan commitment that usually run on their own timetable.

Must I get a certificate of occupancy to sell in Jersey City?

Not a new one. The state does want a smoke alarm compliance certificate on a one- or two-family house before it sells, so reach the fire prevention office early.

How is the state transfer fee calculated here?

The seller owes it, in price bands per $500 that run from $2.90 to $6.05 for a standard sale above $350,000. Going over $1 million also brings the graduated percent fee. Your closing agent does the arithmetic.

Is lead paint a factor when selling a Jersey City rental?

Yes, for pre-1978 rentals. They need inspections every three years or at tenant turnover unless exempt, so have the certificate or exemption papers ready for the buyer.

Where do I look up my assessment?

At taxrecords-nj.com, through Records Search with Hudson County and Jersey City chosen. Enter an address, an owner name or block and lot.

Will past flooding hurt a Jersey City sale?

It can come up near the water, where Sandy flooded Downtown, Country Village, the West Side and Liberty State Park. Insurance and repair records let you answer buyers directly.

Kearny, in Hudson County, has an estimated 40,862 residents, down 2.7% from 2020. Only 42.9% of housing units are owner-occupied, so a good share of Kearny sellers are landlords as well as homeowners, and a few own buildings with tenants.

Kearny's housing stock

Kearny sits on a peninsula between two rivers: the Passaic separates it from Newark and Belleville, and the Hackensack separates it from Secaucus and Jersey City. The town has 8.84 square miles of land and splits into three areas: the Kearny Uplands, the Kearny Meadows and South Kearny.

The housing grew out of the mills. Clark Thread opened its Kearny plants in 1875, Nairn Linoleum followed in 1887, and Western Electric's Kearny Works, opened in 1928, employed as many as 24,000 people. Population rose from 777 in 1880 to 40,716 in 1930, so much of the older housing dates from that surge. Expect a buyer's inspector to look closely at older wiring, plumbing and roofs.

Certificates and permits at the construction office

The Construction Code Enforcement Department posts a residential certificate of occupancy package: a checklist, an application, and the smoke detector and carbon monoxide detector compliance form for one- and two-family houses.   • A building subcode construction permit costs $20 per $1,000 of listed work, with a $50 minimum.

These numbers matter if the house has unfinished work. A garage conversion or an addition done without permits is the kind of gap a buyer's attorney will ask about.

If you find unpermitted work in your own house, you have two choices. A building with tenants adds paperwork: lead certificates, the landlord registration and any rental inspection records, to go along with the smoke alarm certificate. A cash buyer who takes the property as it stands can skip repair negotiations, though the certificate and any open permits still have to be settled.

Bring your deed, a recent tax bill, any mortgage payoff letter and leases to the closing. Unpaid balances are paid out of your proceeds.

Working backward from the closing date helps. The construction office books certificate inspections only on select days, so call (201) 955-7880 as soon as a contract exists and ask which days are open. Bring the smoke detector and carbon monoxide compliance form with you to the visit, and clear any permit that was never closed. If a building has tenants, gather the lead certificates, the landlord registration and recent leases before the buyer's attorney asks.

The tax collector at (201) 955-7888 can say what is owed and when the next installment falls. If there is a lien, a redemption statement costs $20 and a duplicate bill costs $5, so request both in one visit. With a cash buyer there is no mortgage commitment to wait for, which leaves the inspection date as the main thing that can slip, so treat it as the first task rather than the last.

How far ahead should I book a Kearny inspection?

There is no fixed wait, because the construction office schedules those inspections only on select days. Leave significant time before closing, since last-minute inspections cannot be fitted in. Call (201) 955-7880 as soon as you have a contract.

Do I need a detector certificate to sell in Kearny?

Yes, for a one- or two-family house. The state requires a compliance certificate before a sale, and the town's residential certificate package includes the application. Once issued, it lasts six months.

Can I rent my Kearny house on a short-term basis?

Section 15-4 restricts short-term rentals of single-family homes, and the town has looked at widening the ban to every dwelling. Ask the town clerk which version is in force.

The seller does, when the deed is filed in Hudson County. Rates step up with price, and sales above $1 million add a graduated percent fee. The closing agent computes the total.

What happens to Kearny taxes at closing?

Ask the tax collector for the current balance and, if any lien exists, a redemption statement, which costs $20. Confirm there are no older balances before you set a closing date.

Collect receipts for sump pumps, waterproofing, boiler service and roof work, and find the paperwork for past permits. A tidy folder on day one tells buyers the house was looked after.

The assessor's office compares building permits with its records, and unpermitted work can still be assessed. Closing out old permits before you list prevents a surprise during the buyer's attorney review and gives a cash buyer less reason to cut an offer.

From contract to closing in Lodi

After you sign, the buyer's attorney orders a title search and asks the borough about the resale certificate and any open permits. Schedule the inspection the moment you have a contract, because the Zoning and Fire Prevention offices work by appointment and a failed item means a second visit and a few more days of waiting. If the house is a rental, line up the tenant's lease and the latest fire inspection record at the same time.

On closing day you sign the deed and the seller's tax forms. The attorney deducts your mortgage payoff, the transfer fee and your share of the open tax quarter, then the Bergen County Clerk records the deed. A cash buyer drops the lender's appraisal and underwriting from this list, which is why cash closings in Lodi can move so much faster than financed ones.

If the owner has died, bring the estate papers to the first meeting with the attorney, since the buyer cannot close until the person signing the deed has clear authority to do so.

When a cash buyer is the right choice

Cash suits a property that needs more repair than a retail buyer will finance, an inherited house, or a building with tenants, liens or a damp basement that would stall a listing. A well-kept home with time on your side usually earns more through a listing, since cash offers price in the buyer's repair costs and risk.

Get at least one cash offer and compare it with an agent's estimate of list price minus commission and repairs. Ask each buyer who covers recording costs, whether the offer is as-is, and how tenants and open permits would be handled.

Lodi's Zoning Department issues a Resale/New Tenant Certificate and posts the application among its forms. Phone the department before listing to find out whether your property needs one.

What is the last day to appeal a Lodi assessment?

Appeals go to the Bergen County Board of Taxation before April 1 each year. A separate bill for an added assessment can be appealed until December 1.

Who covers the transfer fee on a Lodi sale?

The seller covers it. Your closing attorney can quote the exact amount, since the state's table depends on the price.

Can I sell a Lodi house with tenants inside?

Yes, either with the tenants in place or empty. For a one- or two-family rental owned by someone who lives elsewhere, make sure the Fire Prevention Bureau inspection is current before closing.

Will flooding history hurt a Lodi sale?

It can lower offers, so disclose what you know. Parts of the borough take on water in heavy rain, and cash buyers typically accept the condition without demanding repairs.

The shortest path to a sale in Long Branch

The quickest route skips the lender's appraisal and the repair list: a buyer who pays cash and accepts the property as it stands. An agent listing also works in this shore city, though the city's own inspection step, described below, adds days to any sale that transfers title.

Line up these pieces before you accept an offer, since they are what most often slows a Long Branch closing.

  • Property tax paid through the current quarter, with a printout from the tax office.
  • Sewer charges paid to the current quarter at the Long Branch Sewerage Authority.
  • A sign-off from the Building Department that no construction permits are open.
  • Smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms and a fire extinguisher that meet the city's rules.

Long Branch neighborhoods and access

Long Branch sits on the Monmouth County shoreline with 5.12 square miles of land and 1.16 of water. Neighborhood names buyers use include Pier Village and the oceanfront, Downtown, Uptown, the North End, West End, Elberon, Branchport, Hollywood, Kensington Park and Pleasure Bay.

Elberon has its own train stop, and the main Long Branch station sits three blocks from the beach on NJ Transit's North Jersey Coast Line. Route 36 and Route 71 are the main highways. Local NJ Transit buses 831 and 837 run in the city, and Academy Bus serves New York City on its Route 36 and Shore Points lines.

Shore weather and your inspection

A buyer's inspector will look hard at roofs, siding, windows and basements for the wear that salt air and storm water cause. Precipitation averages about 52.5 inches a year, and winters bring nor'easters.

Hurricane Sandy struck on October 29, 2012, and flooding occurred in Long Branch even though the city avoided the worst of the surge. If your house took water then, keep repair records and any elevation or flood insurance paperwork, because buyers ask for them.

Long Branch housing numbers

Renters are the majority in this growing city, which is why small investors and landlords are common sellers. The 2020 census counted 14,944 housing units with 17.1 percent vacant, so a fair number of houses and apartments sit empty at any given time.

Population was 33,321 in the 2025 estimate, 5.3 percent above April 2020. Owners occupy 42.5 percent of homes, a typical owner-occupied home is valued at $574,000, and typical rent is $1,876 a month. The city counts 13,140 households, and the average commute is 29.6 minutes.

Compliance certificates required before a sale closes

The Fire Marshal's office issues the Residential Certificate of Compliance under city ordinance 262-25. For a one- or two-family home, a Smoke Alarm, Carbon Monoxide Alarm and Portable Fire Extinguisher certificate is required on a change of occupancy or transfer of title, and the compliance certificate itself is required before a change of occupancy.

Selling a Long Branch house as-is

The Fire Marshal publishes a Letter of Intent for Purchase of a Building in As-Is Condition. The buyer circles 30, 60 or 90 days to make repairs, accepts responsibility for permits, and agrees that nobody occupies the building until the Fire Prevention Bureau inspects it and issues a Certificate of Compliance.

That form is useful if your house has deferred maintenance. It lets a cash buyer close first and complete the repairs afterward, while still satisfying the city.

Once you accept an offer, book the Fire Marshal inspection first, since the city does not inspect occupied units and the application is valid for a limited window. Then collect the tax printout, the sewer payoff from the Sewerage Authority and the Building Department's open-permit form. Hand the originals to the city in person, because copies and mailed forms are not accepted.

At the closing table the closing agent records the deed with the Monmouth County Clerk, deducts the state transfer fee from your side and collects the GIT/REP form. A cash buyer removes the loan appraisal from the schedule, but the city's certificates still gate occupancy, so many cash buyers in Long Branch sign the as-is letter and finish repairs afterward.

Selling with tenants in place

Tell the buyer early. The compliance application asks for the type of occupancy (rental, sale or owner re-occupy), requires every lease to be attached, and lists the prospective occupants. Occupant names can be changed only within two weeks of the inspection date, after which a new application must be filed.

Because the inspector will not enter an occupied unit, a seller with a tenant in place usually has to wait until the lease ends or negotiate a move-out date. A buyer who plans to keep the tenant may prefer to complete the as-is letter and handle the certificate after closing. Either way, agree on the sequence in the contract so no one is surprised by a $95 fee or a missed appointment.

Taxes, appeals and closing costs

Installments come due at the start of February, May, August and November. The collector allows ten days before interest runs, records the day a payment arrives instead of its postmark, and wants the block and lot written on every payment. Checks go in a secure box at 344 Broadway, or you can pay online.

Monmouth County follows an alternate assessment calendar, so the appeal deadline is January 15 rather than April 1. The Monmouth County Board of Taxation answers at 732-431-7404. Owners who live in the home may also qualify for the state's property tax reimbursement (senior freeze) and homestead rebate programs.

The seller also pays the state's transfer fee when the closing agent records the deed, and the agent collects a GIT/REP form. Out-of-state sellers prepay estimated income tax of no less than two percent of the price. The Monmouth County Clerk charges $40 for page one of a deed and $10 for every page after it.

The residential certificate is $60 and the smoke, carbon monoxide and extinguisher certificate is $35, for $95 together on a one- or two-family home. Fees are payable to the City of Long Branch.

Do I need open permits closed before selling in Long Branch?

Yes for the compliance application, which needs a Building Department form stating there are no open construction permits on the property.

Can I rent my Long Branch house for a weekend?

No. Ordinance 16-26, adopted July 22, 2026, requires rentals of one- to four-family dwellings to run at least 60 days.

By what date must a Long Branch tax appeal be filed?

By January 15, because Monmouth County runs an alternate assessment calendar. Call the county board of taxation to confirm before you file.

My Long Branch house needs major work. Can I still sell?

Yes. Use the city's as-is letter of intent so the buyer takes 30, 60 or 90 days to complete repairs, and the Certificate of Compliance is issued before anyone occupies the house.

Millville is a Cumberland County city where the main local rule for a seller concerns tenants. Roughly 36 percent of occupied homes are rented, so many sales involve a registered rental unit, and the city's registration and inspection code shapes what a buyer inherits.

The city has about 28,098 residents and 11,845 households. Owner occupancy is 64.1 percent, the median owner value is $219,000, and median gross rent is $1,261. With a median value that low, comparable Cumberland County sales matter more to your price than any statewide average.

Rental registration and inspection

Chapter 11, Article VII of the Millville code requires every residential rental unit, single family homes included, to be registered and inspected each year and again with each change in occupancy. No one may live in an unregistered unit. After a satisfactory inspection the city issues a certificate of continued occupancy, and none is issued while violations remain open.

Getting around Millville

Buyers coming from Philadelphia or the shore compare Millville on drive time and price. Workers in Millville average 25.2 minutes getting to their jobs. The city sits between the southern ends of the New Jersey Turnpike, the Garden State Parkway, Route 55 and the Atlantic City Expressway.

  • Roads: Routes 47, 49 and 55 cross the city.
  • Transit: NJ Transit bus routes 313 from Cape May to Philadelphia, 408 between Millville and Philadelphia, and 553 toward Atlantic City.
  • Local draws: the Glasstown Arts District, Wheaton Arts, the Levoy Theatre, New Jersey Motorsports Park and Laurel Lake.

How Millville property taxes work

The Millville Tax Collector bills on a calendar year, mails bills in mid to late July, and each bill has four stubs for August, November, February and May. The city allows a 10-day grace period, and the collector cannot honor postmarks, so a payment must arrive by the 10th. Interest is 8 percent on the first $1,500 of delinquency and 18 percent above that, with a 6 percent year-end penalty on balances over $10,000 left on June 30. Charges unpaid on the 11th day of the 11th month are delinquent and subject to the annual tax sale.

The bill schedule matters if you sell mid-year, since a stub may be due soon after the closing date and the buyer's attorney will ask who covers it. If taxes are owed when you sell, the balance is settled from your proceeds at closing, so ask the tax collector for a current figure before you accept an offer.

Appealing your assessment

Cumberland County's Board of Taxation takes regular appeals from the first business day of January through April 1 at 4:00 PM, with no exceptions for lateness. Transfer fee and deed recording

The seller owes the state's Realty Transfer Fee at recording, and exemptions exist for deeds between spouses or from parent to child. A Millville deed is recorded with the Cumberland County Clerk, which keeps an office in Bridgeton and another at the Cumberland Mall. Ask the clerk's office for the current recording fee and cover sheet requirements before closing day, and ask your closing agent who files the deed and settles the transfer fee.

Steps for a tenant-occupied sale

The pieces of a tenant sale are different from an ordinary listing, and most of the delay comes from paperwork rather than repairs. Check the registration first. Confirm with the Bureau of Permits and Inspections that the unit is registered and that the latest inspection produced a certificate of continued occupancy. Collect the signed lease, the rent roll if there are several tenants, the Truth in Renting guide handed over at the last change of occupancy, and the name of the agent if you live outside the county.

Gather the money items next. Ask the tax collector which stubs are paid and whether anything is past the 10-day grace period, because delinquent balances grow at the stated interest rates and can head toward the annual tax sale. Ask the buyer's attorney how they want the tax stubs prorated. Settle any open charges before closing so the title search comes back clean, and keep receipts for every payment you make to the city.

Plan the timeline around the inspection calendar. Registration terms start on four dates a year, so find out which one applies to your unit and avoid a lapse that leaves you paying the higher late fee. If an inspection is needed at the change of occupancy, book it as soon as a contract is signed, and give tenants the notice their lease requires so the cancellation charge for under 48 hours' notice does not apply.

Decide whether the tenants stay. Talk to them early, since occupied houses show less well and tenants who feel informed are more likely to allow inspections and showings. Nothing in the registration rules forces them out, and the new owner simply keeps the registration current. A cash buyer may take the house with tenants in place, which spares you a vacancy while you wait on a mortgage-financed buyer.

What does Millville charge to register a rental house?

$100 per unit each year, rising to $125 when paid late. A single family house that is rented counts as a unit, and added inspections or short-notice cancellations cost $50 each.

When is the Cumberland County appeal deadline for a Millville assessment?

The regular deadline is April 1 at 4:00 PM, with no exceptions for lateness. When April 1 falls on a weekend the deadline moves to the next business day, and a municipality revalued that year gets until May 1.

When do Millville property taxes become delinquent?

Bills are due on the August, November, February and May stubs with a 10-day grace period. Charges still owed on the 11th day of the 11th month are delinquent and can go to the city's annual tax sale.

Do tenants have to move out before a Millville sale?

No rental registration rule requires it. The unit must stay registered and inspected at each change in occupancy, so the new owner must keep that registration current for anyone who stays.

Who pays the state transfer fee on a Millville sale?

The seller pays it when the deed is recorded. Exemptions exist for deeds between spouses or from parent to child.

Ways to sell a New Brunswick house fast

A New Brunswick owner has three realistic paths. An agent listing reaches the most buyers, a private sale saves the commission, and a direct as-is purchase trades some price for speed. Whichever you pick, the deed is recorded at the Middlesex County Clerk's office on Bayard Street, inside the city.

This is a renter city. The owner-occupied rate is just 21.4% for 2020 to 2024, across 15,676 households of about 3.13 people each, and the population estimate for July 2025 is 57,133. A sale here often involves a house with tenants or a landlord seller, so the rental rules below matter as much as the repair list. The middle owner-occupied value is $353,800.

  • Agent listing: the widest exposure, though showings, repairs and a lender's timetable come with it.
  • Private sale: no commission, but you still need an attorney, a deed and the municipal paperwork.
  • As-is purchase: often no lender and a closing date you set, with the house taken in its current state. Repairs and showings drop away.

Who buys in New Brunswick

Hospital staff, students and commuters make up much of the demand. Johnson & Johnson keeps its global headquarters here beside several medical teaching and research institutions, Rutgers has three campuses inside city limits, and Robert Wood Johnson Medical School spans New Brunswick and Piscataway.

Commuting shapes the buyer pool too. Residents spend 23.3 minutes getting to work on average, and the city sits on the Northeast Corridor rail line between New York and Trenton. Route 18, U.S. 1 and Route 27 cross the city.

  • Hospital and university staff looking for a short commute.
  • Landlords weighing a rental house against the city's rent control rules.
  • Households who want rail access to Penn Station.

When you describe your house to a buyer, name the neighborhood it sits in: the Fifth Ward, Feaster Park, Lincoln Park, Raritan Gardens or Edgebrook-Westons Mills. It paints a clearer picture than the street address alone.

Local steps before closing

Start with the alarm check. New Brunswick's Division of Fire Safety inspects smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms in one and two family houses being sold or leased, and it offers an online form for booking the visit. Schedule it early so a dead battery does not push the closing back.

The Construction Department, at 25 Kirkpatrick Street, also issues a Certificate of Continuing Occupancy when the city calls for one. Phone 732-745-5075 and ask whether your sale needs it. The answer depends on the property and its permit history.

If tenants live in the house, read the Rent Control Ordinance before you list. Most rental units in the city are regulated, and each regulated unit must register by April 1 every year. Owners of unregistered units face summonses and fines, so confirm your registration status with the Rent Control office first.

Winters bring snow, so clear the gutters and check the roof before the first showing.

Rent control and your rental's price

Rent control caps what a landlord can collect. Rents may rise only by the yearly allowance unless the unit has an approved vacancy decontrol or is exempt, so the rent roll you show is the figure a buyer will work from.

State fees on the seller

Filing the deed triggers the state realty transfer fee, and the seller pays it. Sellers who live out of state have an extra task at the closing table. At least two percent of the deed price is paid ahead toward New Jersey income tax unless a GIT/REP-3 assurance fits. Recording the deed with the county

Filings go to the Middlesex County Clerk's registry on the fourth floor of the County Administration Building, 75 Bayard Street. The office is open weekdays from 8:30 until 4:10, though the last arrivals are taken at 4 pm. The main line is 732-745-3002, and walk-ins are welcome, with appointments served first.

  • Documents must be readable English with original signatures, printed names and a proper acknowledgment.
  • A deed carries the drafter's name after the words Prepared by, plus tax block, lot and the price.
  • A return address is required.
  • Paper filings need a cover sheet or the county adds a $20 indexing charge.

Attorneys and title companies may instead send documents any hour of the day through the county's e-recording portal. Owners worried about fraud on an empty house can sign up for the clerk's email alerts, which announce any document recorded against their block and lot.

How a quick sale usually runs here

Order matters, because several offices have to be dealt with before a closing date can be firm. Book the Division of Fire Safety alarm check first, since it is online and fast. Call the Construction Department about the Certificate of Continuing Occupancy next. If the house has tenants, pull together the leases, the rent history and your Rent Control registration so a buyer can see what the units bring in.

Then sort out the deed. Your attorney drafts it with the tax block, lot and price, you sign it with the proper acknowledgment, and the county records it after closing. If you live out of state, the GIT/REP form is signed at the same table. A buyer paying cash and taking the house as it stands skips the lender's appraisal and repair demands, which is where many conventional closings slip. The paperwork above still applies either way.

Frequently asked questions

Can a New Brunswick house be sold while tenants are still in it?

Yes. A sale does not end a tenancy. Keep your rent control registration current and have each lease and the rent history on hand, because regulated units register by April 1 every year and unregistered ones risk fines.

Is an inspection required before selling a small home in New Brunswick?

At minimum a smoke and carbon monoxide alarm check through the Division of Fire Safety for one and two family houses. Call the Construction Department at 732-745-5075 to learn whether a Certificate of Continuing Occupancy is also needed.

Which office files the deed after a New Brunswick sale?

The Middlesex County Clerk's registry, in the County Administration Building on Bayard Street. Your closing attorney or title company usually submits it, either on paper or electronically.

I own the house but live in another state. What changes?

You complete a GIT/REP form at the closing table. A nonresident seller prepays at least two percent of the deed price toward state income tax unless the GIT/REP-3 assurances apply, and can request a refund later if less is owed.

Which transfer fee schedule applies to a New Brunswick sale?

The lower schedule applies at $350,000 or less: $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 per $500 up to $200,000, then $3.90 per $500 on the rest. One dollar over that figure moves the whole sale to the higher schedule.

Choosing the quickest route in Newark

Pick the route that removes the most waiting. For one owner that means a buyer paying cash with no lender in the way, and for another it means a listing priced to move. A vacant house needing a new roof and a rented three-family with open violations call for different answers, so let condition, occupancy and your deadline decide.

Renters outnumber owners here. Only 24.4% of Newark's occupied homes are owner-occupied, and the city counts 113,384 households. Many of the buildings that sell are therefore two to four family properties with tenants inside, which is why the rental registration rules further down deserve an early look.

  • Collect the deed, the latest tax bill and any violation notices.
  • Decide whether tenants will stay, and read their leases.
  • Ask a closing attorney which seller forms apply to you.

Newark's five wards

Buyers think in wards first and neighborhood names second, and Newark has five wards.

  • Central: University Heights, beside NJIT, Rutgers-Newark, Essex County College and the medical school.
  • North: Branch Brook Park is the anchor, with Mount Pleasant, Upper Roseville and the Forest Hill Historic District, known for its older mansions.
  • West: Vailsburg, Ivy Hill, West Side and Fairmount.
  • South: Weequahic, Clinton Hill, Dayton and South Broad Valley.
  • East: Downtown plus the Ironbound, dense with apartment buildings, rowhouses and restaurants.

The airport, seaport and heavy industry cluster in the East and South wards. Most homes sit in the North, Central and West wards. When you advertise, say which ward the house is in and what surrounds it.

Newark grew fast during its industrial years and left a great many older blocks, so expect a buyer's inspector to study roofs, wiring and heating systems closely.

Why buyers keep coming

Work and rail. Over 100,000 workers travel into the city on a typical weekday, giving Newark the biggest job base in New Jersey across insurance, finance, healthcare, law and government. Prudential Financial keeps its home office downtown, and close to 50,000 students attend the local universities and medical and law schools.

Port Newark handles more cargo than any other terminal in the Port of New York and New Jersey, and part of Newark Liberty International Airport lies within city lines. At Newark Penn Station riders can change between PATH, three NJ Transit rail lines and Amtrak, and the Newark Light Rail runs from there to the northern neighborhoods, Belleville and Bloomfield.

Workers who live here average 32.6 minutes to their jobs, and about 40% of households own no car, so say how far the house is from a station in your listing.

Portions of the city fall in an Urban Enterprise Zone where eligible shops charge half the state sales tax rate. For property taxes, request the current bill and any balance due at closing from the tax office.

A median of $373,700 sits above the $350,000 line where the state's higher transfer fee schedule begins. Treat it as a rough anchor only, because prices swing widely from ward to ward.

Landlord requirements before selling

Every rented unit in the city has to be registered with the Department of Economic and Housing Development. Landlords list contacts for themselves, for the person who handles upkeep, and for fuel delivery and round-the-clock emergencies, and each unit may be inspected once every three years or when the occupants change.

A unit that passes earns a Certificate of Habitability, the document that allows it to be rented. One that fails must stay unleased until the problems are corrected, and the certificate can be suspended or revoked for overcrowding or danger. Purchasers of rental buildings will ask for these certificates, so pull them together before listing.

Registration and rent control are different matters. Ask Newark's Office of Rent Control which units are regulated and what each legal base rent is, then pass that answer to the buyer's attorney.

What a Newark seller pays and who files the deed

New Jersey's transfer fee is the seller's cost and rises in bands as price rises. Above $350,000 the banded schedule tops out at $6.05 per $500 once a price passes $1,000,000, and a separate graduated percent fee, starting at 1%, applies to those higher-priced homes.

Deeds for Newark properties are recorded by the Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages, an office that handles all 22 municipalities in the county. A title company or closing attorney usually takes the paperwork there with the seller's residency form.

Lead service lines have been a problem in Newark's water system, and the city hired a contractor to replace them at many properties. Ask the water department what material the service line is at your address, since a buyer's inspector may bring it up.

Getting a Newark sale ready to close

Work backward from the closing date. A few weeks out, order the open-violation list from the city's building office and ask the water department about your service line. Gather the registration and habitability paperwork for any rented unit, and have the tax office confirm the balance due.

Closer to the date, your attorney or title company prepares the deed and the seller's residency form. A cash buyer who takes the house as it stands can skip the lender's repair conditions, so open items are negotiated between the two of you instead of being fixed first. Either way, the seller covers the transfer fee and the deed is filed in Essex County.

If you rent out part of the building, tell the buyer early which units are occupied, what each tenant pays and whether any unit has failed an inspection. Buyers of two to four family houses price these details in, and a clean paper trail shortens the back and forth. If the house is empty and needs work, a short listing description that names the ward, the condition and the closing timeline you can offer saves everyone time. Ask your attorney to confirm which forms you sign, and keep copies of every certificate you hand over.

Frequently asked questions

Can a Newark house with open code violations still be sold?

Yes, though the buyer pool narrows. A purchaser paying cash can take the house as it is, while a lender-backed buyer may need the violations cleared first. Ask the city's building office for a list of open items before you set a price.

Do rentals have to be registered with Newark before a sale?

Yes. The city requires registration of every rented unit, and a Certificate of Habitability follows a passed inspection. Buyers of rental buildings tend to ask for both.

Which transfer fee schedule would apply near the Newark median value?

The state's over-$350,000 schedule, with rates that climb in bands from $2.90 per $500 on the first $150,000. Your attorney will show the total on the settlement statement.

Where is a Newark deed filed?

With the Essex County Register of Deeds and Mortgages, which covers all 22 county municipalities. The closing attorney or title company submits it along with the seller's residency form.

If I live out of state, do the closing steps change?

Yes. A seller who lives outside New Jersey prepays at least 2% of the deed price toward state income tax on form GIT/REP-1, unless an assurance on form GIT/REP-3 applies. A refund can follow later if less is owed.

Routes to a fast Paramus sale

Three routes lead to a closing here: an agent listing, a private sale, or an investor who takes a house left as is. All three finish at the same borough inspection and the same deed filings, so what changes is the amount of preparation you do first.

Paramus is a borough in central Bergen County, roughly 15 to 20 miles northwest of Midtown Manhattan. It is best known for its two retail corridors along Routes 4 and 17, yet it is also a suburban bedroom community of New York City. To compare the routes, start with this short list:

  • Check whether any permit for past work on the house is still open at the Building Department.
  • Decide whether you can wait for a conventional buyer's financing and inspection period.
  • Locate the deed, a payoff letter from your lender and, if you inherited, the estate papers.
  • Have a closing attorney confirm which deed forms the sale needs.

Skipping the marketing stage saves weeks. The borough's Certificate of Compliance stays in the path, and Paramus describes it as mandatory for closings.

Homes, owners and values

Paramus skews toward owners and high values: more than four in five homes are occupied by their owners. Treat these numbers as a borough-wide picture rather than a price for any single street.

More than one resident in four is 65 or older, so downsizing and the care of a parent's house come up often. If that sounds like you, the estate and tax pointers below deserve as much attention as the price.

Neighborhoods, roads and commuting

The borough names five residential areas: Arcola, Bergen Place, Dunkerhook, Fairway Oaks and Spring Valley. Van Saun County Park (146 acres, with the county zoo) lies on the east side, and Saddle River County Park runs along the west side with a six-mile bike path.

Most trips here are by car. The borough counts 121.92 miles of road, including Route 17, Route 4 and Garden State Parkway Interchange 165, and NJ Transit buses reach the Port Authority Bus Terminal and the George Washington Bridge Bus Station. Sellers who live near the highways should expect buyers to ask about traffic noise and commute time, since the mean trip to work is 30.8 minutes.

The Certificate of Compliance

Paramus requires a Certificate of Compliance for any resale or rental, and the borough states that this certificate is mandatory for closings. The Building Department asks sellers to confirm first that every earlier permit has been closed out, then file an application with a $100 fee for a sale.

After the application is accepted, an inspector visits. Resale inspections run weekday mornings from 9:00 to 12:00, and someone needs to be at the house to let the inspector in. The inspection covers:

  • Smoke alarms on every level and near bedrooms, plus carbon monoxide detectors near sleeping areas, following the borough's NFPA-based guidelines.
  • A permanent label within 18 inches of the electrical panel and meter if the house has solar panels, a generator or battery storage.
  • The street number visible from the street on the mailbox, front door or garage.
  • Borough-issued garbage and recycling containers on the property with their serial numbers.
  • A fence around any pool.

Open permits cause the most delays. Unpermitted renovations must be permitted and inspected before the certificate is released, and permitted jobs lacking a final inspection hold up the Certificate of Occupancy. Close open permits a full week ahead of the resale inspection. Call the Building Department at 201-265-2100, extension 2230, for the current process.

State transfer fee and tax forms

The seller carries the Realty Transfer Fee, which the county collects at recording. The state steps the charge from $2.90 to $6.05 for each $500 of price on sales above $350,000, and a Graduated Percent Fee is layered on once a sale passes $1,000,000. Your closing attorney or title agent can turn the schedule into a dollar figure for your deed.

Estate sales are one common exemption: an executor's deed to an heir following a will is excused, as is a deed between parent and child. Form RTF-1 goes on record with the deed for any seller claiming relief.

Recording also requires a GIT/REP form under N.J.S.A. 54A:8-9, so the state can tell whether a seller living outside New Jersey owes prepaid income tax. Whoever signs the deed completes it, and only sheriff's sales and bankruptcy trustee sales are left out.

Flood disclosure

A Paramus seller has to answer flood questions on the property condition disclosure statement before a buyer is committed to the contract: whether the lot falls inside a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area or Moderate Flood Hazard Area, and whatever flood history you personally know.

The Department of Environmental Protection runs a Flood Risk Notification Tool that helps sellers look up the answers. Check your own parcel on that tool instead of assuming the answer. Cash buyers and conventional buyers receive the same disclosure.
