Property taxes and appeals

Every New Jersey county assesses at 100 percent of market value as of October 1, and the local rate applied to that figure produces your bill. Because Paramus lies in Bergen County, contested assessments go to the Bergen County Board of Taxation.

  • Filing: Form A-1, in the board's hands by April 1.
  • After a revaluation: the cutoff moves to May 1.
  • Large assessments: above $1,000,000 can skip to the State Tax Court.
  • Next level: 45 days to take a board ruling to the Tax Court.

The burden is yours: prove the figure is out of line with market value or with the district's common level range. Ask the Paramus tax collector for your payoff and quarterly status before closing, so any open installment is cleared at the closing table and the buyer inherits no surprise.

A short plan for closing quickly

Order matters. Start by finding any permit that was never finalized, because the certificate waits on it and the borough wants permits closed a week before the inspection. Then file the Certificate of Compliance application with the $100 fee and arrange for someone to be home during the morning inspection window. Replace dead alarms, label solar or generator equipment, and put the house number where it can be seen.

While that runs, answer the flood questions, request your tax payoff and have your attorney prepare the deed and the GIT/REP form. A cash buyer can skip lender conditions, but the borough steps stay the same, so ask in writing who will handle them.

Frequently asked questions

Is a borough certificate really required to close a sale in Paramus?

Yes. The borough treats the resale Certificate of Compliance as mandatory at closing. The seller applies to the Building Department, pays $100 and passes the inspection.

What happens if I made changes to the house without permits?

The resale certificate is withheld until the missing permits are applied for and the work is inspected. Permitted work that never received a final inspection holds up the Certificate of Occupancy.

Is the New Jersey transfer fee my bill in Paramus?

Yes, the seller pays it. It is a state charge collected at recording, sized by the price brackets on the Division of Taxation schedule.

At what point must a buyer receive flood information?

Before the buyer is committed to the purchase contract. The statement covers FEMA flood zone status and any flood problems the seller knows about.

How late can I file a Paramus assessment appeal?

April 1, or May 1 following a revaluation or reassessment, and the petition must reach the county board by then. Ask the Bergen County Board of Taxation for the form and current filing steps.

What is the fastest way to sell a Passaic house?

Selling for cash as the house stands is usually the shortest path, since it drops repairs, showings and a buyer's loan approval. A listing or private sale takes longer. Every route, though, has to clear the city's occupancy certificate and fire certification before closing.

Many Passaic buildings hold more than one unit, and owners live in just 23.8 percent of homes. Sellers here are often landlords, heirs, or owners of condos and co-ops. Whichever you are, gather these items first:

  • The deed and the block and lot numbers, which every city application asks for.
  • Tenant leases and rent rolls, if any unit is occupied.

  • The name the buyer will take title in, because Passaic issues the occupancy certificate under the buyer's name.

Passaic housing at a glance

Passaic is a dense city of 71,337 residents in the 2025 estimate, packed into 3.13 square miles. Renters outnumber owners about three to one, and households run large at an average of 3.29 people across 21,151 households. The median owned home is valued at $429,900, typical rent is $1,465 and median household income is $55,371.

Condo and co-op owners in Passaic Park, in complexes such as the 21-floor Carlton Tower and the Barry Gardens garden apartments, should ask their association what documents a buyer needs. About 72.3 percent of residents speak another language at home, so bilingual listing and closing papers can help buyers follow what they sign.

Occupancy certificate and fire certification

A sale in Passaic needs two approvals: an occupancy certificate, and a smoke detector and carbon monoxide certification. The one-family application goes to the Division of Housing under Inspections and Code. It asks for the seller's details and the buyer's name, because the certificate is issued to the buyer. A company buying through an LLC or corporation must supply the registered agent and the certificate of formation.

The fire inspector looks for a smoke detector on each level, detectors and a carbon monoxide alarm outside every sleeping area, working units, and a fire extinguisher within ten feet of the kitchen. A 90-day temporary certification is available when items fail. The occupancy certificate confirms the property meets Passaic's zoning and property maintenance laws. It does not replace construction permits or health approvals. Condo, one, two and three family homes all use the fire form.

How the Passaic approval process runs

Start the paperwork once you have a signed contract and the buyer's exact legal name. File the occupancy application with the Division of Housing, then book the fire inspection with Fire Prevention. If you want the faster handling, ask for the $300 expedite option when you file.

When the inspector finds problems, you have two ways forward. Fix the items and request a reinspection at $25, or ask for the 90-day temporary fire certification and agree with the buyer on who finishes the work. Tell your closing attorney which route you chose so the closing date reflects it.

Bring the same set of papers to every office: the deed, block and lot numbers, payoff figures and, for an entity buyer, the registered agent and certificate of formation. A short call to the Division of Housing before you file saves a second trip.

State transfer fee and forms

Trenton charges a Realty Transfer Fee, and in Passaic the seller pays it when the deed is recorded. Above $350,000 the schedule opens at $2.90 per $500 of price. A GIT/REP form is recorded alongside the deed too. Its job is to tell the State whether an out-of-state seller owes prepaid income tax, and the person who signs the deed fills it out. Your attorney or closing agent normally prepares the deed, the fee paperwork and this form, and you sign at the closing table.

Flood disclosure has been mandatory since March 20, 2024. The river borders the city, so check the FEMA zone for your lot in the DEP Flood Risk Notification Tool and answer the statement honestly before the buyer is bound.

How to appeal your Passaic assessment

An owner who thinks the city's figure is too high files Form A-1 with the Passaic County Board of Taxation. The board must have it by April 1, or by May 1 where Passaic has carried out a revaluation or reassessment.

You carry the proof. Show that the assessment is out of line with market value or with the district's common level range. Anything assessed above $1,000,000 can go straight to the State Tax Court, and a county board decision can be carried to that court within 45 days. The city tax collector can give you your balance and open charges. The county board can tell you where to deliver the petition and how its hearings are scheduled.

Before you file, pull your latest assessment notice and compare it with what similar homes nearby have sold for. Have your block and lot numbers ready, since the petition and every city form key off them. If you are selling this year, tell your attorney about the appeal so any refund or balance is handled at closing.

A cash buyer taking the house as it stands removes the repair list, the showings and the wait for a lender. It does not remove the city's certificates. The occupancy certificate and fire certification are still needed, and the buyer's name still goes on both.

Before you accept an offer, ask who files the occupancy application, who pays the $65 certificate fee and any $300 expedite charge, and who pays for a fire reinspection. For a multi-unit building, add the lease and rent roll question: tell the buyer which units are occupied and on what terms. Compare offers by what you net after payoff, transfer fee and carrying costs.

Passaic's mix of two and three family buildings, condos and co-ops means the buyer's plan matters. An investor keeping tenants cares about the leases, while an owner-occupant needs a vacant unit at closing. Settle that in writing before the certificate application goes in, because the form asks who will take title and the city will not issue the certificate until it has that name.

The buyer's. The one-family application issues the certificate under the buyer's name, and an LLC buyer must supply its registered agent and certificate of formation.

Three months from approval, and only for the person named on it. When the inspection finds problems, a 90-day temporary certification can be issued.

Yes. The State bills the seller at recording, and the fee steps up with the sale price.

Paterson is Passaic County's seat and its largest municipality, with 161,793 residents in the 2025 estimate on 8.41 square miles of land. It has 49,865 households, and renters hold most of the housing. The median owned home is valued at $360,100, typical rent is $1,548 and median household income is $55,997.

The Passaic River runs through the city. In August 2011 Hurricane Irene pushed it to levels unseen in about a century, so a riverside seller should prepare an honest flood answer before a buyer asks. Neighborhood demand changes from ward to ward, so price against recent sales on your own street. Ask your agent or attorney which comparable sales are closest to your block, and be ready to explain any open code items.

Vacant, foreclosed and rental property rules

Building, electrical, plumbing and fire inspectors enforce the state construction code in Paterson. They issue permits and final approvals, including Certificates of Occupancy and Continued Certificates of Occupancy. Inspections, licenses, permits and certificates of occupancy all run through the Division of Community Improvements, which posts weekday hours on its construction code page. Call 973-321-1232 to find out what your sale requires.

A vacant building owner names a local agent aged 21 or older who can be reached at all hours. Once a vacant property is sold or transferred, the owner gives the city proof within 30 days. Rent leveling registration is filed under Chapter 381 of the municipal code.

When Paterson calls a property abandoned

A property can be deemed abandoned once it has gone six months without legal occupancy and meets another test: no rehabilitation, stalled construction, an unpaid and delinquent tax installment, or a nuisance finding by the public officer. Inspectors look for boarded windows, disconnected utilities, piled-up mail and overgrown yards when they decide a building is vacant.

Check with the Division of Community Improvements whether your house has been flagged before you sign a contract. A flag can affect the fees you owe and what the buyer will want settled at the table.

If you are inheriting or taking over a house that has sat empty, sort out the registration first. The 30-day clock starts when you take ownership, and a buyer's attorney will ask for proof that it was filed.

What to have ready for a Paterson sale

Most delays in Paterson come from paperwork that was never started. Before you accept an offer, pull together the deed, your mortgage payoff figure and every code violation notice you have received. Note the dates of any registration filings for a vacant or foreclosed building, since the buyer's attorney will ask for proof.

If the building is a rental, find the annual rent leveling registration form and confirm it was returned within 30 days of receipt. Tenants in place stay in place, so the buyer inherits the leveling rules along with the leases. Give the buyer's side copies of leases and security deposit records early.

When the house is vacant, expect questions about utilities, boarded windows and the local agent named on the registration. Fixing those before listing keeps the city from treating the property as abandoned and keeps the closing calendar clear.

Realty transfer fee and state forms

Trenton sets the Realty Transfer Fee, and the seller pays it. Rates climb in bands from $2.90 up to $6.05 per $500 for prices above $350,000, and from $2.00 up to $3.90 per $500 for prices at or below that line. Your closing attorney can give you the exact dollar amount for your price.

Sellers who are seniors, blind or disabled pay reduced bands, and the claim is made on a form recorded with the deed. An estate deed to an heir is exempt. A GIT/REP form is recorded too, signed by whoever signs the deed, so the State can tell whether a seller from another state must prepay income tax.

Flood answers are required as well. Since March 20, 2024, the disclosure statement has to state the FEMA flood zone and any known flooding before the buyer signs. The DEP Flood Risk Notification Tool can help you look up your lot.

How can I appeal Paterson property taxes?

Appeals go to the Passaic County Board of Taxation, and the petition must be in its hands by April 1. After a citywide revaluation or reassessment the date is May 1.

Show that the assessment misses market value or falls outside the district's common level range, which is 15 percent either side of the average ratio. Property assessed above $1,000,000 can skip to the State Tax Court, and a county board ruling can be taken to that court within 45 days. Your balance comes from the Paterson tax collector. File before you list if you think the assessment is high, because a pending appeal is something a buyer will ask about.

Steps for selling a Paterson house for cash

Cash suits a building with code problems, tenants you no longer want to manage, or a vacancy registration piling up at $2,000 a year. The buyer takes the property in its present state, which removes the repair list and the showing schedule.

The city's paperwork still applies. Work through it in this order:

  1. Call the Division of Community Improvements and ask what a change of occupancy needs for your address.
  2. Register the building if it counts as vacant, and confirm any rent leveling registration is current.
  3. Gather the deed, the payoff figure and any code violation notices for the buyer's attorney.
  4. Agree in writing on who orders inspections and who pays any reinspection.

Some sellers also use a cash sale to end a vacancy registration that renews every year. Compare offers by what you net after payoff, the seller's transfer fee and the months a listing could take. Where tenants are in place, ask how leases and deposits will be handled before you sign.

Frequently asked questions

Must I register a vacant Paterson house?

Yes, when it fits the city's definition of a vacant building. Registration is due within 30 days, with a $2,000 yearly fee.

How does Paterson treat foreclosed properties?

The creditor that files the foreclosure complaint registers the property within seven days, at $500 for the first year and each renewal.

Which office issues certificates of occupancy in Paterson?

The Division of Community Improvements, which enforces the Uniform Construction Code. Its construction code page posts weekday office hours.

Does the seller cover the state transfer fee in Paterson?

Yes. The State bills the seller at recording, in bands that rise with the price.

What is the Paterson tax appeal deadline?

April 1, or May 1 after a revaluation, at the Passaic County Board of Taxation.

What should I know before selling a house in Perth Amboy?

Perth Amboy has its own sale rule: a Certificate of Code Compliance must be in hand before a house is transferred, whether the buyer pays cash or finances. That single step shapes timing, repairs and who takes on what, so deal with it before a listing goes live.

About 56,739 people lived in the city by the mid-2025 estimate, on 4.66 square miles of land. The fee schedule in the city code covers everything from one-family homes to four-family buildings. The median owned home is valued at $370,600, and Victorian houses on the hills above the waterfront sit alongside many multi-unit buildings.

What the Certificate of Code Compliance requires

Chapter 181 of the city code bars any transfer, conveyance or sale of a residential, commercial or industrial building until the Department of Code Enforcement issues the certificate. The inspection checks zoning, the fire safety code and substantial conformity with the property maintenance code.

The code gives sellers several ways to keep a closing on schedule:

  • A conditional certificate can run 45 days, and the Director may grant a second 45 days on request.
  • A buyer who says in writing that the purchase is as-is can receive a temporary, nonrenewable certificate good for up to six months from transfer, unless a life-safety hazard exists.
  • A certificate may issue even when the building falls short of full code compliance, provided it is in substantial compliance and safe, sound and sturdy.
  • A denial can be appealed in writing within 10 days to a three-member Certificate of Code Compliance Appeals Board.

Some transfers are exempt, including those between immediate family members, transfers through probate, sales of a building inspected or certified within the previous six months, and purchases made to demolish the building. Violations carry a fine up to $1,000, jail up to 90 days, or both, with each day counted separately. The code also lists a $25 per unit residential reinspection fee and exempts holders of a senior citizen property tax exemption from the fees. Call Code Enforcement for the current inspection charges.

Selling a Perth Amboy rental

Most Perth Amboy homes are rentals. Only 35.4 percent are occupied by their owners, median gross rent is $1,688 and median household income is $61,977.

A buyer of a tenant-occupied building steps into the city's rent control ordinance, Chapter 353, which a Rent Leveling Board enforces. Since November 1, 2022, increases are capped at 3 percent where water is included in rent and 2.5 percent where it is not. Periodic tenants on terms shorter than a year cannot be charged an increase until the tenancy passes twelve months. Anyone pricing a sale on rent growth should work from those caps.

With 83.6 percent of residents Hispanic or Latino and 79.5 percent of those aged five and up speaking another language at home, many sellers and tenants read Spanish first. The city posts its rent control information in English and Spanish, and a seller who does the same with notices will answer questions sooner.

Historic district rules

They can affect a sale if the building stands in or beside a historic district. The Historic Preservation Commission, formed in 1993, reviews proposed changes to designated sites and structures and new construction within or next to districts, under Chapter 258 of the city code.

The historic waterfront neighborhood holds much of the old building stock, including the Proprietary House built in 1764 as a royal governor's residence, and Market Square across from City Hall. Deeds for Perth Amboy parcels go to the Middlesex County Clerk's registry in New Brunswick, where walk-in filers must arrive by 4 p.m. on weekdays. A paper deed without its cover sheet draws a $20 indexing charge, and title agents can skip the counter by filing electronically.

If the house sits in an estate, the executor signs the seller's Gross Income Tax form on the estate's behalf, and the city's code exempts probate transfers from the compliance certificate. Heirs who sell after taking title sign for themselves, using the form that matches their own residency. The seller also pays the state realty transfer fee at recording, set by bracket on the sale price.

Order of steps for a Perth Amboy sale

Start with Code Enforcement. Ask whether your transfer is exempt, for example a family or probate transfer, or a building inspected or certified in the previous six months. If it is not exempt, request the inspection early enough that a conditional certificate of 45 days, with one more 45-day extension, covers any repairs.

Next, line up the paperwork a buyer will ask for: leases, security deposit records and the rent level for each unit if tenants are in place. Then order the tax search and payoff, and have your attorney or title agent prepare the deed and the state tax forms. If the inspection is denied, remember you have 10 days to appeal in writing.

When does a cash offer help a Perth Amboy seller?

A cash offer helps when the building would fail the code inspection, carries tenants a seller no longer wants to manage, or must close before a conditional certificate runs out. In each case the as-is certificate route can let the buyer take the repairs after closing.

Ask any buyer whether the offer assumes the temporary certificate, who pays for inspections, and how existing leases and security deposits will be handled. Compare offers by net proceeds, not by the top-line price. A buyer who will keep tenants needs the rent cap history, while a buyer who will demolish may qualify for the demolition exemption, so ask what the plan is.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a certificate to sell a house in Perth Amboy?

Yes. Chapter 181 of the city code requires a Certificate of Code Compliance before a residential or commercial building is transferred, for cash and financed sales alike.

Yes, with limits. If the buyer states in writing that the purchase is as-is, the city can issue a temporary, nonrenewable certificate for up to six months, unless a life-safety condition exists.

Are probate and family transfers exempt in Perth Amboy?

Yes. The code exempts transfers between immediate family members and transfers made through probate proceedings from the certificate requirement.

How much can rent rise in a Perth Amboy rental I am selling?

Up to 3 percent a year where water is included and 2.5 percent where it is not, under the rent control cap in force since November 1, 2022.

Where is a Perth Amboy deed recorded?

At the Middlesex County Clerk's registry in New Brunswick. Title agents and attorneys can also submit electronically.

Owners here choose between a broker listing, a private sale and an as-is cash purchase. Each route still ends with the same paperwork: the compliance certificate, a recorded deed in Elizabeth, and the state transfer filings.

Plainfield had 57,141 residents in the mid-2025 estimate, and owners live in 44.8 percent of homes, so rentals make up the larger part of the housing stock. The median owned home is valued at $410,800 and median gross rent is $1,767. With 3.41 people per household, many homes serve larger families or hold more than one unit. Buyers and appraisers look closely at legal unit counts, which is one reason the city checks occupancy during a sale inspection.

What the Plainfield Certificate of Compliance covers

You file the Certificate of Compliance for Sale application with the city's Property Maintenance Unit and book an inspection before closing. The form asks about the property's legal occupancy, the buyer, the closing date, permits and smoke and carbon monoxide detectors. An LLC seller must add its Certificate of Formation.

An adult must be present to let the inspector in. Inspectors look at both the structure and the way the property is used:

  • Exterior walls, roofs, porches, stairs, railings and accessory buildings.
  • Yards, driveways, trash, tall vegetation and abandoned vehicles.
  • Kitchens, bathrooms, basements, crawlspaces and bedrooms.
  • Plumbing, hot water, heating equipment, outlets and fixtures.
  • Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, windows, doors and floors.
  • Signs of leaks, moisture or vermin, and the legal number of units.
  • Open permits or work that appears to have been done without one.

Other paperwork may be due as well. Sellers can be asked for a heating system certification on a professional's letterhead, a Fire Division certificate for smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms and a portable extinguisher, and permit approvals for completed work. A building with three or more units needs a current certificate from the state Bureau of Housing Inspection. Ask the Fire Division for its current fee.

What happens if a Plainfield house fails the inspection?

The owner receives a notice of violation, fixes the items, pulls any missing permits and requests a reinspection. A clear certificate is issued only after that. Most notices allow up to 30 days. Exterior items such as trash and overgrown vegetation can carry a deadline as short as five business days, and an immediate safety threat can require action within three days.

The city may approve a temporary certificate when the property is in substantial compliance. That route requires a $500 per unit escrow, and the buyer signs a notarized affidavit accepting responsibility for the remaining violations. Approval is discretionary, so do not count on it before you sign a contract.

Some transactions qualify for an exemption, and the city makes the final call after reviewing documents:

  • The construction official issued a certificate of occupancy or continued occupancy within 90 days before the sale.
  • The house is owned by the City of Plainfield.
  • A refinance with no change in ownership.
  • A building officially found unfit for habitation and headed for rehabilitation or demolition.
  • Certain documented foreclosure or short sale closings where the property cannot be reached for inspection.

If a notice of violation arrives, read each deadline. Trash and vegetation items can be short, while most others allow up to 30 days. Pull any missing permits, finish the repairs and request the reinspection before your attorney sets the final closing appointment. Historic districts

Plainfield has six residential historic districts, and a few carry real weight with buyers who want large older houses: Van Wyck Brooks, Netherwood Heights, Crescent Area, Hillside Avenue and Sleepy Hollow. Transfer fee and deed recording in Plainfield

The seller pays New Jersey's realty transfer fee. On a sale above $350,000 the schedule runs $2.90 per $500 up to $150,000, $4.25 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $4.80 per $500 from $200,000 to $550,000. The median value of $410,800 sits in that last band.

Your deed goes to the Union County Clerk's recording office at 2 Broad Street in Elizabeth. Weekday hours are 8:30 am to 4:30 pm, counter recording ends at 3:30 pm, and nobody needs an appointment. Deeds over $1,000,000 recorded after July 10, 2025 may carry a revised fee.

Your closing agent normally prepares the deed, the transfer fee affidavit and the Gross Income Tax residency form, and you sign them at the closing table.

Steps to take with tenants in place

If tenants live in the house, a rental unit needs its own Certificate of Compliance whenever the tenant named on the old one leaves. Give the buyer copies of the leases and ask the Property Maintenance Unit whether your rental certificate is current.

For a building with three or more units, confirm the state Bureau of Housing Inspection certificate is up to date before you list. Buyers' attorneys ask for it, and a lapsed certificate can cost you days at the end of the deal.

Which way of selling suits a Plainfield owner best?

It depends on repairs, timing and who is living in the house. A listing may reach more buyers, but it brings repair requests, showings and a lender's appraisal, all of which interact with the compliance inspection.

An as-is cash purchase lets you skip the repair list, though the inspection, fire certificate and recording steps still apply. Compare written terms before signing: who orders the compliance application, who carries the $500 escrow if a temporary certificate is used, and who pays the transfer fee.

Is a Certificate of Compliance required when I sell in Plainfield?

Yes. The Property Maintenance Unit asks sellers to file the Certificate of Compliance for Sale application and schedule an inspection before closing. A recent certificate of occupancy issued by the construction official within 90 days can support an exemption request.

The first residential unit costs $50 and each added unit costs $25 on the June 2026 application. A missed appointment adds $25 and an exemption application costs $75. A separate fire certificate fee may apply, so ask the Fire Division for its current charge.

Sometimes. The city can issue a temporary Certificate of Compliance when a property is in substantial compliance, but it requires a $500 per unit escrow and a notarized buyer affidavit. The decision is discretionary and does not apply to every violation.

Where is a Plainfield deed recorded?

At the Union County Clerk's recording office, 2 Broad Street, Elizabeth. Over the counter recording runs until 3:30 pm on weekdays and needs no appointment. The clerk requires a cover sheet with each land document.

Princeton housing at a glance

Princeton had an estimated 31,469 residents in mid-2025 and 9,300 households. Owners live in 55.4 percent of homes. The median owned home is valued at $1,050,600, median gross rent is $2,636 and median household income is $192,079.

Ask for recent sold prices on your own street instead of leaning on the citywide figure. Listing photos and descriptions that name a school should match the district's current attendance zones. Check with the district office before you repeat an assignment in marketing copy.

Princeton addresses and neighborhoods

Princeton's ZIP codes run from 08540 to 08544, with 08542 mostly covering the old borough. Cedar Grove, Port Mercer, Princeton Basin and Jugtown are unincorporated communities that keep their own identities within the larger municipality, so make sure your listing, deed and tax records all use the correct address and block and lot.

Buyers often weigh the rail link to Princeton Junction, where trains join Amtrak's Northeast Corridor and NJ Transit service toward Manhattan, and the public school system. The sewer affidavit with the Princeton Sewer Operating Committee covers sump pumps, roof drains and similar drains. An inspection is available for $50 if the owner asks for one, and the certification takes 7 to 10 business days.

Fire safety certificate timing

The fire certificate fee depends on timing. It is $45 per unit when the application is completed more than 10 days before closing, $90 per unit between 4 and 10 days before, and $161 per unit with less than 4 days left. Filing early saves $116 per unit.

State fees on a high-value Princeton sale

The seller pays the realty transfer fee. On sales above $350,000 the Division of Taxation schedule reaches $5.80 per $500 between $850,000 and $1,000,000 and $6.05 per $500 above $1,000,000.

A second charge, the Graduated Percent Fee, applies to residential deeds with consideration above $1,000,000. It is 1% of total consideration up to $2,000,000, 2% above that to $2,500,000, 2.5% to $3,000,000, 3% to $3,500,000 and 3.5% beyond. Form RTF-1EE is attached to every deed over $1,000,000.

Deeds go to the Mercer County Clerk's Office at 209 South Broad Street in Trenton. Deeds recorded after July 10, 2025 with consideration over $1,000,000 fall under the revised state fee.

How to line up the Princeton paperwork

The three city items run on separate clocks, so sequence them. Request the construction records clearance first, because the $35 rate needs 11 to 20 business days and the sewer certification takes 7 to 10 business days. Complete the fire safety application more than 10 days before closing to pay $45 per unit instead of $90 or $161.

Gather the sewer questions early: where the sump pumps and roof drains discharge, and whether you want the optional $50 inspection. If a house will be rebuilt, ask the Building Department what the records clearance covers before you agree to a closing date.

Your closing agent normally submits the deed and state affidavits to the Mercer County Clerk. Confirm with them whether the higher state fees apply at your price, and ask for the closing statement draft early so nothing about the transfer fee or the Graduated Percent Fee surprises you at the table. Keep receipts for the fire, records and sewer fees in one folder, since the buyer's side may ask to see each certificate before funds are released.

Which sale route fits a Princeton homeowner?

A broker listing gives you exposure to buyers who value the schools and the rail link, but it adds staging, showings and a lender's appraisal. A private sale saves a commission and leaves you to arrange the three city items yourself.

A cash buyer purchasing as-is can shorten the calendar, although the fire certificate, records clearance and sewer affidavit still need to be in hand. Compare offers by your net after fees, repairs and carrying costs.

On a high-priced house the state fees are a large line item, so ask each buyer who pays what and request a written estimate from your closing agent. A cash sale does skip the lender's appraisal and a long list of buyer repair requests, which can matter when a closing date is fixed. For a teardown or major rebuild, a buyer will usually want the construction records clearance in hand early, so settle who orders it when you sign the contract.

What does Princeton require before I sell my house?

Most sellers need a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate from the Bureau of Fire Safety, a construction records clearance from the Building Department and a sewer affidavit. Each is filed separately with its own fee, so contact all three offices once a closing date exists.

How much does the Princeton fire safety certificate cost?

The initial inspection is $50 per unit with one reinspection included. The certificate itself costs $45 per unit if you apply more than 10 days before closing, $90 between 4 and 10 days and $161 with less than 4 days left.

How long does the Princeton construction records clearance take?

Request it 11 to 20 business days before closing for $35. The fee rises to $70 at 6 to 10 business days and $125 at 1 to 5 business days, so earlier requests cost less.

Are there extra state fees on a Princeton sale above one million dollars?

Yes. The seller owes the Graduated Percent Fee, which starts at 1% of total consideration for deeds above $1,000,000, in addition to the realty transfer fee. Form RTF-1EE is attached to the deed.

Where is a Princeton deed recorded?

With the Mercer County Clerk, 209 South Broad Street, Trenton. Your closing agent normally submits the deed and the state affidavits there.

What does a Rahway seller need to arrange before closing?

Rahway issues a Certificate of Approval for Continued Occupancy, called a CACO, whenever ownership changes, and the Fire Prevention Bureau separately inspects the house for smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms and an extinguisher. Both items belong on your calendar the day a contract is signed.

Rahway is a compact Union County city of about 3.9 square miles of land, so the city's inspection checklist reaches nearly every sale. About half of its households own: owners live in 51.5 percent of homes. The 2025 estimate is 31,010 residents in 12,257 households. The median owned home is valued at $386,400, owners with a loan pay about $2,702 a month, and median gross rent is $1,845.

Rahway CACO inspection and fees

The Property Maintenance Division in the Department of Code Enforcement accepts the Application for Certificates of Approval for Continued Occupancy. You check the change of ownership box, list the closing date and give seller and buyer contact details.

Properties with two or more units, and commercial or mixed-use buildings, must first obtain a zoning permit and a Fire Department approval. A temporary CACO is possible once all fire prevention measures are met and the buyer signs an affidavit agreeing to handle the rest.

The city's list of common concerns tells you what to fix in advance:

  • Foundations, roofs, porches and stairs must be sound, with no open cracks or leaks.
  • Stairs with more than four risers need a handrail 30 to 42 inches high.
  • Windows need working glazing and screens on openings used for ventilation.
  • Habitable rooms need two outlets, kitchens need three, and any outlet within six feet of water needs ground fault protection.
  • Cellars and crawl spaces must be free of dampness, and drains must run clear.
  • Peeling paint, loose plaster and decayed wood on interior surfaces must be corrected.

What the Rahway fire inspection looks for

The Fire Prevention Bureau inspects single-family houses when a smoke detector compliance certificate is requested for a sale. A fire safety inspection also accompanies a change in ownership. The city's guidance sets these standards:

  • One smoke alarm on every level, basements included, and none farther than 10 feet from a bedroom door.
  • Battery units must carry sealed 10-year batteries, hard-wired alarms cannot be swapped for battery types, and no alarm may be more than 10 years old.
  • A carbon monoxide alarm within 10 feet of sleeping areas.
  • One extinguisher rated at least 2A:10BC, no heavier than 10 pounds, mounted within 10 feet of the kitchen and no more than 12 years old.

Replace expired alarms before you book the inspection so a failed visit does not push back closing.

What draws buyers to Rahway

Commuters are the natural audience. Rahway station sits on NJ Transit's North Jersey Coast Line and Northeast Corridor Line, and a typical ride to New York Penn Station takes 38 minutes. A 524-space parking deck stands across from the station, and Newark Liberty International Airport is about a 20-minute drive. Mean commute for local workers is 31.9 minutes.

The downtown has seen new housing, a hotel and shops since the late 1990s, and Merck's headquarters on its Rahway campus anchors local employment. Lead with the train in your listing, and be ready to show buyers that the certificates are in hand.

Flood status near the Rahway River

The Rahway River enters from Clark, takes in Robinsons Branch near Elizabeth Avenue and the South Branch near East Hazlewood Avenue, then leaves toward Linden and Woodbridge. If your street is near the water, ask the Building Department for the flood status of your lot, since buyers and insurers will ask for it.

State forms and recording after a Rahway sale

The deed is recorded with the Union County Clerk, whose record room holds land transactions from 1857 forward and whose Elizabeth recording office takes documents over the counter on weekdays. The county's online land records search lets you look up records by name, book and page, instrument number or date range.

Gross Income Tax forms depend on who is selling. A New Jersey resident individual, estate or trust signs the GIT/REP-3. A nonresident seller files the GIT/REP-1 at closing, with an estimated payment calculated as the gain times 10.75%, and never less than 2% of the consideration in the deed. The county clerk forwards that payment to the state. An out-of-state heir selling an inherited Rahway house should plan for this withholding. The seller also pays the state realty transfer fee at recording.

A working order of steps for a Rahway sale

Treat the two inspections as a pair. Put the CACO application in with the closing date, the seller's details and the buyer's details. Book the fire inspection in the same week, after replacing any alarms that are past 10 years or running on changeable batteries.

Walk through the house with the city's list: stairs and handrails, outlets, cellar dampness, peeling paint. Fix what you can before the visit. If something cannot be finished, ask whether a temporary CACO fits, which needs fire prevention measures complete and a buyer affidavit.

For a two-family or mixed-use building, begin with the zoning permit and Fire Department approval, because the CACO cannot go forward without them. A pre-1978 rental also gets dust wipes, so allow for that visit. Have your attorney confirm the deed and GIT forms before the closing appointment, and keep the certificates handy for the buyer's lender.

Is a cash sale a good fit in Rahway?

It can be when repairs would take longer than your closing window allows. An as-is buyer takes on the repair list, and a temporary CACO can let the sale proceed once fire prevention items are met and the buyer signs the affidavit.

Ask each buyer who files the CACO application, who pays the $100 fee, and who handles reinspection. Judge offers by what you net after payoff, repairs and fees. If the house has tenants, ask how the buyer will handle them, and remember that a rental built before 1978 carries a higher fee and dust wipes.

Frequently asked questions

Does Rahway require an inspection before a house sale?

Yes. A CACO is needed when ownership changes, and the Fire Prevention Bureau inspects single-family houses when a smoke detector compliance certificate is requested for a sale. Apply early so both inspections fit before closing.

How much is a Rahway CACO for a residential sale?

The 2025 application lists $100 per residential unit for a CACO and $100 per unit for a temporary CACO. A rental built before 1978 costs $125 per unit and receives dust wipes during inspection.

Can I close in Rahway with repairs still unfinished?

Possibly. A temporary CACO is available when all fire prevention measures are completed and the buyer endorses an affidavit agreeing to address the remaining inspection items. Properties with two or more units need zoning and Fire Department approval first.

What must a nonresident Rahway seller pay at closing?

A nonresident files the GIT/REP-1 and makes an estimated Gross Income Tax payment equal to the gain times 10.75%, subject to a 2% of consideration minimum. The payment goes through the county clerk with the deed.

Where can I look up Rahway property records?

The Union County Clerk's online land records search lets you search by name, book and page, instrument number or date range, and the record room in Elizabeth holds land transactions from 1857 to the present.

The Ridgewood certificate you need before closing

Before closing, a Ridgewood seller must hold a smoke detector and carbon monoxide certificate from the Fire Prevention Bureau. The village Building Department issues no certificate of occupancy when a one or two family house is resold, so this one inspection is the main local hurdle.

Ridgewood is a Bergen County village about 20 miles northwest of Midtown Manhattan, with an estimated 26,527 residents in July 2025 and 8,903 households. Of occupied homes, 82.5 percent are owner-occupied, the middle home value is $891,200 and median household income is $208,211. Most sales are family houses changing hands, and the price puts a typical sale in the top band of the state transfer fee schedule, covered below.

Inspection fees and timing

The fee depends on how far ahead of closing you book. The bureau charges per dwelling unit and takes appointments on weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. through the Inspection Office at 201-444-7898, extension 5480.

State law requires the certificate before transfer, which is why a late visit carries the penalty. Settle the fee at the bureau, 201 East Glen Avenue, with cash or a check made out to the Village of Ridgewood. Cards are taken in person only and add a 3 percent technology charge.

If the house has a monitored central station alarm, register it with the Ridgewood Fire Department at 201-444-8822, extension 4112.

Permits that can slow a Ridgewood closing

The village building FAQ lists work that needs a permit: replacing a furnace, boiler or water heater, creating habitable space in a basement or attic, adding a bathroom or laundry room, and building a deck, generator pad or accessory structure. Pools, patios, driveways, sheds and fences need a zoning certificate first.

Painting, flooring, trim, and replacing a window or door in the same opening need no permit. A permit lapses if work has not begun within 12 months, or if work stops for 6 months.

  • Cutting a tree with a trunk eight inches or wider at breast height on private land takes a permit. Trees in the public right-of-way belong to the village.
  • Sidewalk repair is the owner's job, and the village arborist assesses any shade tree whose roots lift the slab.
  • New Jersey allows an oil tank to be abandoned in place with a permit, though lenders and insurers increasingly want a buried tank removed, and that can come up at sale.

Older houses and historic review

Several Dutch-era homes in Ridgewood are on the National Register of Historic Places, among them the Ackerman houses on Doremus Avenue and Lincoln Avenue, the Archibald-Vroom House at 160 East Ridgewood Avenue and the Westervelt-Cameron House on East Glen Avenue.

The Historic Preservation Commission may review exterior changes. If you own an older house, ask the Building Department whether any approval applies before you advertise a renovation or addition as a selling point.

What to do if the inspection fails

Most failed visits come down to a missing or dead detector. Replace the device, then call the Inspection Office to book the follow-up. The fee climbs as the closing date nears, so the cheapest path is to call the week you list or sign, not the week you close.

  • Have every detector in place and working before the inspector arrives.
  • Put carbon monoxide protection where the code calls for it, and test each unit.
  • If the house has a monitored alarm, confirm the registration with the fire department.
  • Keep the certificate with your closing papers and hand a copy to your attorney.

A buyer paying cash can close quickly, but the same certificate is still needed, so a cash sale does not remove this step.

From contract to closing in the village

The local sequence is short, and following it in order keeps the fee at the low end.

  1. Call the Inspection Office as soon as the contract is signed and ask for the earliest weekday slot.
  2. Walk the house first. Check each detector, and look at any alarm panel for trouble signals.
  3. Bring payment to 201 East Glen Avenue, by check or cash if you want to avoid the card charge.
  4. Pass the inspection and keep the certificate with the file your attorney holds for closing.
  5. Close with the seller's transfer fee and any tax adjustments on the settlement statement.

Because Ridgewood houses are often older, a buyer's inspector may find more than the village does. Fixing small items before the village visit saves a second trip and keeps the buyer's repair requests short.

Many Ridgewood houses carry an old heating system, and some still sit over a buried oil tank. The state permits a tank to be closed in place under a permit, yet buyers' lenders and insurers have been leaning toward full removal. If you know a tank is underground, gather whatever paperwork exists about its closure and bring it up with your attorney before the first showing.

Replacing a furnace, boiler or water heater needs a village permit, so a seller who swapped one without a permit should talk to the Building Department before the buyer's inspector spots it. Closing the permit properly is quicker than explaining a gap after an offer is in.

Appealing a Ridgewood assessment

Bergen County takes assessment appeals through its Board of Taxation at Two Bergen County Plaza in Hackensack, 201-336-6300. The annual filing date is April 1, and hearings follow later in the year. When an assessment tops $750,000, a Ridgewood owner may skip the county board and file directly with the Tax Court by April 1.

Gather recent sales of similar houses nearby before you file. If an appeal is pending when you sell, tell your attorney so the buyer hears about it before closing.

Transfer fee and closing costs

The seller pays New Jersey's Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded. Each band of the state schedule applies only to the slice of price inside that band. At Ridgewood prices, a sale lands in the upper band of that schedule.

Above $1,000,000, a graduated percent fee also falls on the seller: 1 percent of the total price up to $2,000,000. Ask your closing attorney or title agent for the total before you set a bottom line on an offer, so the net you expect matches what the settlement statement shows.

No. The village Building Department does not issue one for the resale of a one or two family house. A smoke detector and carbon monoxide certification from the Fire Prevention Bureau is required before closing.

What happens if the Ridgewood inspection is done after closing?

The owner pays a $500 penalty on top of the $200 certification fee. The schedule is $120 more than 10 days out, $150 inside 10 days and $200 inside 3 days.

Do I need a permit to remove a tree before selling in Ridgewood?

Yes for a qualifying tree, meaning one eight inches or wider at breast height on private land. Trees in the public right-of-way need consent from the village arborist.

Is a Ridgewood buyer likely to ask about water quality?

Some will. Ridgewood Water entered a consent order with the state in May 2023 to treat PFAS in its groundwater supply, with a stated goal of finishing treatment by the end of 2026. The utility publishes current test data.

How is the transfer fee handled on a Ridgewood sale?

The seller pays it when the deed is recorded, and sales over $1,000,000 add a percentage fee. Your closing attorney can give you the exact amount for your price.

Two certificates before closing

A Sayreville seller needs a Certificate of Residential Resale Compliance from the borough and, separately, a smoke, carbon monoxide and secondary power source certificate from the Bureau of Fire Prevention. The fire marshal's 2026 sheet makes the second one a requirement for closing whatever the condition of the house and whatever the contract says about as-is terms.

Sayreville sits on the south bank of the Raritan River in Middlesex County, with an estimated 46,787 residents in July 2025 across 17,187 households. Median home value is $444,100, 63.0 percent of households own, and 33.3 percent of residents were born outside the United States, so listing material in more than one language reaches more buyers.

How to book the resale inspection

The borough takes resale applications online. Create an account, fill in the application and submit it. The office emails the fee, usually within one business day. After you pay online, request an appointment. Resale inspections run on Mondays and Wednesdays, and rental inspections on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

Call as soon as the house is listed so the office can check the file for open permits. The inspector looks hard at recently installed water heaters, furnaces and finished basements, and a permit that was never closed out can hold up the certificate.

Offices to call during a Sayreville sale
OfficePhoneWhat it handles
Code Enforcement732-390-7077Resale compliance application
Bureau of Fire Prevention, 167 Main Street732-390-7009Alarm inspection
Water Department732-390-7060Curb stop and final reading
Middlesex County Board of Taxation732-745-3350Assessment appeals

The 20-item resale checklist

Violations bring a correction notice and a reinspection before the certificate is released. Inspectors may also cite other violations of the International Property Maintenance Code and borough ordinances.

  • Exit doors must open from inside without a key, and double-keyed deadbolts are prohibited.
  • Stairs with three or more steps need a handrail, and house numbers must be at least 4 inches tall and visible from the street.
  • Kitchen stoves need anti-tip devices, and a single-family house may have only one working kitchen.
  • A basement, attic or garage used as a bedroom must meet habitable-space rules, including an approved egress window that needs a construction permit, or the house fails.
  • Pools deeper than 18 inches need a fence at least 48 inches high with a self-closing, self-latching gate.
  • The water curb stop must work, so call the Water Department before closing.

A house sold as-is is still subject to permit requirements. Any missing permit has to be applied for and finalized by a contractor, which is worth settling before an offer comes in.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Sayreville house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Alarm and labeling rules

Alarms are required on every finished level, within 10 feet of each sleeping area, at the bottom of basement stairs, and in finished attics with 7 feet or more of ceiling height. Smoke alarms must be under 10 years old, and stand-alone battery units must be 10-year sealed. Carbon monoxide alarms must be under 7 years old. Devices that belong to a home security system do not count, so stand-alone units go beside them.

Since February 3, 2025, a house with solar panels, battery storage or a generator must display a printed label reading "CAUTION: MULTIPLE SOURCES OF POWER," fixed within 18 inches of the main panel and the meter. Handwritten labels are rejected. Portable fire extinguishers are no longer part of resale inspections, and the fire marshal asks owners to drop old ones at a Middlesex County household hazardous waste day.

If the house fails the first visit

A failed visit is common and it is not the end of the sale. The borough sends a correction notice listing each violation. Fix the items, then ask the office for a reinspection before the certificate is released. Nothing is released until the list is cleared.

Finished basements, converted garages and attic bedrooms cause the most trouble. If a room was made into a bedroom without a permit, it must meet habitable-space rules, and that includes an approved egress window, which itself needs a construction permit. If the cost of bringing a room up to standard is more than you want to spend, say so to your attorney early, because the buyer will want to know before the contract is final.

Smaller failures tend to be cheap: a detector past its age limit, a missing handrail on stairs with three or more steps, an anti-tip device missing from the stove, or a house number too small to read from the street. Fix those before the first visit and the inspection becomes a formality.

Selling near the water

Low-lying ground near the river floods in storm surges. After Hurricane Sandy in 2012, residents accepted a federally funded offer in 2013 to buy out 250 floodplain houses. If your house is near the water, gather any flood insurance and elevation records before listing, since buyers and their lenders will ask for them.

The borough uses four ZIP codes, 08871, 08872, 08879 and 08859. Use the one on your deed and tax record when you list and when you fill in the resale application, so the file matches. A mismatch between the application, the deed and the listing is a small thing that can cost a day or two at the counter.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Sayreville houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Costs and tax steps at closing

The Middlesex County Board of Taxation is at 75 Bayard Street, fourth floor, New Brunswick, and takes petitions through an online portal. Its added or omitted assessment deadline is December 1. Ask the board for the regular filing date for Sayreville.

The seller owes the state transfer fee, with each band of the schedule applying to the slice of price inside it. A corporation, partnership or multi-member LLC signs a GIT/REP-3 and checks box 5. An individual seller who lives out of state pays at least 2 percent of the deed price in estimated tax unless an assurance applies.

A timeline for a quick Sayreville sale

Work backward from the closing date and give each office room to answer.

  1. As soon as the house is listed, call Code Enforcement so the permit file gets checked.
  2. Create the online account, submit the application and pay the emailed fee.
  3. Choose a Monday or Wednesday for the resale visit and run through the checklist the evening before.
  4. Arrange the alarm inspection with the Bureau of Fire Prevention.
  5. Fix anything on the correction notice and ask for the reinspection.
  6. Give both certificates to the closing attorney.

A cash buyer who accepts the house as it stands avoids repair haggling, but both certificates are still required for closing, so budget time for them whichever route you choose.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Sayreville Certificate of Residential Resale Compliance?

It is the borough's clearance after an inspection against a 20-item checklist covering life safety, interior conditions, building systems, exterior conditions and permits. It is separate from the fire marshal's alarm certificate.

Can I sell a Sayreville house as-is without these inspections?

No. The alarm certificate is required for closing despite any as-is terms, and as-is houses are not exempt from permit requirements.

On which days are Sayreville resale inspections held?

Mondays and Wednesdays. Rental inspections are on Tuesdays and Thursdays. You request a date after paying the emailed fee online.

No. Since February 3, 2025, state law no longer requires one for resale inspections. Solar, battery or generator systems need a printed power-source warning label instead.

Parts are. Low ground along the Raritan River floods in storm surges, and after Hurricane Sandy 250 houses in the floodplain were bought out under a federally funded offer in 2013.

Selling fast in Trenton

Cash to a buyer who takes the house as it stands is the quickest way out in Trenton, since that buyer deals with the city's transfer paperwork. An agent listing can suit a house in good shape, and you may sell without an agent, yet all three routes go through the same city inspection before the deed moves.

Trenton is the state capital and the Mercer County seat, with an estimated 91,506 residents in mid-2025 on 7.58 square miles of land. Houses sit tightly packed, and many are older rowhouses.

What Trenton homes cost and who owns them

The middle value of an owner-occupied home is $160,700 and median gross rent is $1,294. Only 37.9 percent of the city's 32,052 households own the home they live in, and median household income is $52,537. Many sellers are therefore landlords, heirs or owners of older houses that need work.

Owner costs median $1,717 a month with a mortgage and $752 without, so holding a paid-off house is cheap. That helps explain why inherited houses can sit a long while before anyone decides to sell.

Certificate of Housing Code Compliance

Trenton requires a Certificate of Housing Code Compliance before the change of ownership of any residential property. The Division of Housing Inspections issues it after confirming zoning and fire-safety compliance, working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, and substantial conformity with the city's habitability standards.

The seller or the seller's agent files the application, because the buyer has no legal right to enter the property before the sale. A buyer who has agreed to obtain the certificate may file instead. After the inspection the city hands over a list of violations, and the certificate is issued once they are corrected. A Certificate of Approval or a Certificate of Continued Occupancy can stand in for it. Commercial transfers need no inspection unless the structure contains a residential unit.

If the house cannot pass, the owner can file an affidavit with the Department of Inspections stating the property will stay unoccupied until a certificate is obtained. That is the usual path for a cash buyer who plans a full renovation.

Landlord and vacant-property rules

Trenton runs an Absentee Owner Program that requires every owner of rented residential or commercial property to hold a license, renewed each January. A single-family rental carries a $115 minimum fee. If you sell a tenant-occupied building, confirm the license is current, because a lapse can complicate the transfer.

Rental units also need their own inspection before a tenant moves in. The city no longer issues stickers, so a tenant or buyer calls to confirm a current rental certificate. Vacant structures face the steepest charge: a flat $500 registration fee, then $1,300 on the first renewal, $2,000 on the second and $3,000 after that.

  • A house that sits empty for a year or more costs its owner real money in registration fees.
  • Owners of vacant land and vacant buildings answer to the same Division of Housing Inspections.
  • Sidewalk damage from tree roots goes to the division's sidewalk inspection section, so check it before a buyer's walkthrough.

How does the inspection step work in order?

  1. The seller or the seller's agent files the application with the Division of Housing Inspections and pays the fee.
  2. The owner authorizes access, since the buyer cannot enter the house before the sale.
  3. The inspector checks zoning, fire safety, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors and general habitability.
  4. The city returns a list of violations, if any.
  5. The owner corrects them and requests a re-inspection, which carries its own fee after the first.
  6. The certificate is issued and stays good for six months, so closing needs to fall inside that window.

If the sale slips past six months, plan for a new inspection. A buyer who has agreed to handle the certificate takes this over, so spell out who is responsible in the contract.

Property taxes and appeals

Trenton bills quarterly, with payments due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1 and a 10-day grace period. Interest runs at 8% a year on delinquencies up to $1,500 and 18% above that, and a 6% penalty can apply to a delinquency over $10,000 left unpaid at year end. Bills go out twice a year, in late June or early July for the August and November quarters and in late December or early January for February and May.

Appeals of a regular assessment are due by April 1 each year, and appeals of added or omitted assessments by December 1. Forms come from the Tax Assessor or the County Tax Administrator.

Any municipal charge unpaid on May 11 of the fiscal year can go to tax sale before June 30. Trenton Water Works has also announced that eligible unpaid water and sewer balances can be certified to the tax sale. When a house sells, the tax bill goes to the new owner, and the seller's closing statement should show the quarter that was paid.

Selling with taxes or a failed inspection

Two problems turn up often with older Trenton houses: back taxes and a failed housing inspection. Both can be handled in a sale.

  • Ask the Tax Assessor or collector for the amount owed, including any water and sewer balance.
  • Ask the Division of Housing Inspections for the list of violations and whether a re-inspection fee applies.
  • Decide with your attorney whether to repair, price the work into a cash offer, or use the unoccupied-until-certified affidavit.

Interest on a delinquency builds at 8% a year up to $1,500 and 18% above that, so a long delay adds up. An owner who inherited a house and cannot afford the repair has a real reason to look at a cash sale.

Getting around Trenton

Trenton is the only New Jersey city served by Amtrak, NJ Transit and SEPTA. The Trenton Transit Center is the end of the Northeast Corridor line to New York Penn Station and of SEPTA's line to Philadelphia, and the River Line light rail runs to Camden. State employment keeps weekday demand steady, with roughly 20,000 state workers commuting in each day.

Frequently asked questions

Does a Trenton house have to pass inspection to sell?

Yes, a residential transfer needs a Certificate of Housing Code Compliance, or an affidavit that nobody will occupy the house until one is obtained. The base fee is $200, and the certificate lasts six months.

Can a buyer apply for the Trenton certificate instead of the seller?

A buyer can apply only when the buyer is the one responsible for obtaining it, because the buyer has no legal right to the property before the sale. Otherwise the seller or the seller's agent files, authorizes access and pays the fee.

What happens if my Trenton house fails the inspection?

The city gives the seller a list of violations, and the certificate is issued after they are fixed. Re-inspections cost $50 each after the first for one or two units, and $25 per unit for larger buildings.

What are the Trenton tax due dates?

Taxes are due on the first of February, May, August and November, with a 10-day grace period before interest starts. Interest is 8% on the first $1,500 of delinquency and 18% above it.

Do I need a landlord license to sell a rental in Trenton?

Owners who rent out property need a yearly license under the Absentee Owner Program, renewed in January. Call the Division of Housing Inspections to confirm the license is current before listing or accepting an offer.

Old place names in Vineland deeds

Landis Avenue and the Boulevard anchor the old downtown. North Vineland and South Vineland are the two traditional halves of the city. Unincorporated place names such as Clayville, Leamings Mill, Menantico, Parvins Branch and Willow Grove still appear in addresses and deeds, so confirm which name your property uses before you write the listing.

On a larger parcel, ask the closing attorney whether a current survey is needed before you list.

Certificate of Inspection before settlement

The city requires the owner to obtain a Certificate of Inspection before settlement on a house, duplex or multi-family building. A duplex or multi-family property with 15 units or fewer should be checked with the Zoning Department before listing, to confirm that its use conforms. The application is filed in person at the Fire Administration building at 400 W. Plum Street, in triplicate, and the process needs at least four business days.

If the house is uninhabitable or needs repair, the buyer can complete a Certificate of Transfer of Title (CTT) affidavit to take over the issues the inspector notes. The CTT application must be filed together with the Continued Certificate of Occupancy application, which secures two inspections, one before closing and one before occupancy. Skipping the inspection can delay settlement and bring fines.

Resale checklist

The city publishes a checklist, last revised in February 2025, and a house that meets it usually passes on the first visit. Utilities must be on at the time of inspection, which matters for vacant or inherited houses.

  • All construction permits closed before applying, including finished basements, garages and attic conversions done without permits.
  • No bedrooms in a basement without code-approved egress directly from the bedroom.
  • Open Code Enforcement violations closed out, and any duplex or triplex use approved through the Zoning Office.
  • House numbers at least four inches high and readable from the street, yards free of trash, and sound stairs, decks and porches.
  • Guard rails on landings 30 inches or higher, and handrails where there are three or more risers.
  • A smoke detector on each level and a carbon monoxide detector on every level with bedrooms.
  • Working heater and water heater, a bathroom fan or window, and a water heater pressure relief valve that extends 2 to 6 inches off the floor.
  • Fenced yards with self-closing, self-latching gates for any in-ground pool, working or not.

For houses built before 1978, the checklist flags excessive peeling paint on more than 25% of the home. An electrical certification may be required where wiring looks unsafe.

Step by step: from contract to certificate

Start with the date you expect to close, then count backward. Filing more than 10 days ahead costs less than filing 4 to 10 days ahead, and four business days is the floor for processing, so an early filing saves money and avoids a squeeze.

First, walk the house with the checklist and fix the cheap items: house numbers, alarms, a loose handrail, trash in the yard. Second, close any open permits, since an unpermitted finished basement or attic bedroom is the most common reason a house stalls. Third, turn on the utilities if the house is vacant. Fourth, bring the application to the Fire Administration building in triplicate. If the house needs more work than you want to take on, a buyer who signs the CTT affidavit can take over the repairs, which is why many cash buyers are comfortable with a house that would not pass today.

A failed item means a $50 re-inspection with a new application, so it pays to get the first visit right.

Appeals for regular billing must be filed by April 1, and added or omitted assessment appeals by December 1. Forms come from the Cumberland County Board of Taxation at 2745 S. Delsea Drive in Vineland, or by calling the County Tax Administrator. The City Hall tax office accepts walk-ins, drive-thru payments and drop boxes, and postmarks do not count. Online credit card payments carry a 2.95% fee and e-check payments $1.95.

Before closing, ask the tax office for a current balance so the title company can clear anything owed from your proceeds.

Zoning permits and local roads

The Zoning Division requires a zoning permit for changes of use, home additions, decks, pools and signs, in addition to the Certificate of Continued Occupancy. A garage turned into living space or an attic turned into a bedroom needs both zoning and construction permits, and those permits should be closed before the resale inspection. Call the Department of Licenses and Inspections to confirm what a particular project needs.

Vineland has roughly 335 miles of road. Route 47 (Delsea Drive) runs north and south in the western part of the city, Route 55 follows the western border, and Route 56 (Landis Avenue) crosses the city from Pittsgrove Township to Route 47. NJ Transit buses on the 313, 408 and 553 routes connect the city to Cape May, Philadelphia and Atlantic City.

A Certificate of Transfer of Title affidavit lets the buyer take over the repairs an inspector notes on a house that is uninhabitable or needs work. It costs $25 when filed more than 10 days before closing and $50 within 10 days.

Taxes are due on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, with a 10-day grace period. Postmarks are not accepted, and the collector cannot waive interest.

Roughly three of every four households rent, so the people who bid on a two- or three-family building are often landlords weighing rent rolls.

The sections below cover the town's housing figures, transit, the ownership certificate rules, tax payment habits and the county office that records deeds.

Housing figures

The town has 53,192 residents on 0.99 square miles of land, between Guttenberg, North Bergen, Union City, Weehawken and the river.

Transit and getting around

Bergenline Avenue, home to over 300 shops and restaurants, is the commercial spine, while 60th Street is the main crosstown road and the site of Town Hall. County Route 501 follows Kennedy Boulevard along the west edge and County Route 505 follows Boulevard East, so no state highway enters the town. The Turnpike, Route 1/9 and Route 495 sit in adjacent municipalities.

  • NJ Transit buses 128, 154, 156, 158, 159, 165, 166 and 168 reach Midtown's Port Authority Bus Terminal, and routes 181 and 188 go to the George Washington Bridge Bus Terminal.
  • The Hudson-Bergen Light Rail stops at Bergenline Avenue on the Union City line, and the Port Imperial ferry terminal is in Weehawken.
  • Jitneys along Bergenline Avenue can arrive as often as once a minute.

North Hudson Regional Fire and Rescue protects the town in place of a local fire department. Newark Liberty International Airport is 13.6 miles away, and LaGuardia is 13.5 miles away through the Lincoln Tunnel.

Ownership certificate before transfer

Chapter 148 of the town code bars anyone from selling a residential building, or taking title to one, until the town issues an ownership certificate following an inspection. The rule reaches one-, two- and three-family homes, buildings of four or more units, commercial and mixed-use buildings, and vacant land through a separate certificate. A missed certificate brings a $1,000 fine.

  • Seller or buyer may file the application, and both carry liability if none is obtained.
  • When the contract calls for an as-is sale, a copy goes in with the application, signed by both parties.
  • Inspectors look at housing, building, fire, electrical and property maintenance codes.
  • If repairs will not be finished by closing, the town can grant a temporary certificate lasting up to six months with no renewal, and the buyer takes on the duty to correct the violations.

State fire rules separately ask for an alarm certificate covering smoke and carbon monoxide detectors when a house of one or two units is sold, so ask the town which office issues it and book both visits once you have a signed contract.

Selling a building with open violations

An as-is sale is common here, and the temporary certificate is what makes it workable. The buyer agrees in writing to correct the violations within the six months, and the town decides which items qualify. Put the as-is language in the contract, have both parties sign the copy that goes with the application, and keep a record of every item the inspector lists.

If you are a landlord with tenants in the building, ask your attorney how the inspection fits around the leases. Access dates, notice to tenants and who pays for corrections are the points that usually cause friction, and settling them before the application goes in keeps the schedule intact.

Property tax payments and tax sales

The Tax Collector bills and collects municipal property taxes from the office at 428 60th Street, and the phone line is 201-295-5110. A ten-day grace period applies. Interest is counted from the original due date starting on day eleven, and a postmark does not count as payment.

The town holds its tax sale in December and announces the date by the end of November. Owners with a balance should request a payoff figure before listing so a lien can be cleared out of the proceeds.

Deed recording and the state fee

The Hudson County Register records the deed, not Town Hall. Paper filings need the county cover sheet, checks go to Hudson County Register, and a personal or LLC check cannot exceed $200. Questions can go to 201-395-4760.

The seller pays New Jersey's realty transfer fee on the price. A slice of a sale between $200,000 and $550,000 costs $4.80 per $500, which is where a typical West New York price falls, and anything above $1 million adds the Graduated Percent Fee. The closing statement shows the total.

How to sell a West New York property

Owners here usually weigh a listing, a private deal and a direct purchase for cash, and the town certificate applies to every one of them.

  • A listing fits a house or unit in good order that a lender can appraise, with the inspection and loan timeline that follows.
  • A private deal works when a tenant, relative or neighbor is already the buyer and a lawyer drafts the contract.
  • A cash purchase can fit a building with open violations, a tenancy you no longer want to run, or an estate that needs to close.

Write down who pays for certificate inspection and corrections before you sign anything.

Order of steps for a seller

Begin with the Tax Collector, since a payoff figure tells you what a lien or balance will take from the proceeds. Next, decide who will file the ownership certificate application, you or the buyer, and agree that in the contract. Once the contract is signed, book the town inspection and the alarm certificate visit together so the building is only opened to inspectors once.

Then give your attorney the deed, the county cover sheet requirements and the transfer fee estimate so the filing with the Hudson County Register is ready on closing day. A cash buyer can shorten the wait for financing, but the certificate and the recording still set the earliest closing date. Ask the buyer for proof of funds and a written closing date, and compare offers by what you keep after taxes, the state fee and any repairs the buyer wants you to cover.

Frequently asked questions

Is an inspection required before a West New York sale?

Yes. Under Chapter 148 an ownership certificate must be issued after inspection before a residential building transfers. Skipping it costs $1,000, and the seller and the buyer are both responsible.

Can I sell a West New York building with open violations?

Often, yes. The town may grant a temporary certificate for up to six months when violations remain at closing, and the buyer agrees to fix them. The Department of Public Affairs decides which items qualify.

How long is the West New York property tax grace period?

Ten days. Interest is charged back to the due date beginning on the eleventh day, and postmarks do not count. The Tax Collector at 201-295-5110 can give you a current balance.

Which office records a West New York deed?

The Hudson County Register. File with the county's cover sheet and a check made out to Hudson County Register, which your closing attorney or title agent normally arranges.

Do most West New York residents own their homes?

No. Only 23.0 percent of occupied homes are owned by the people living in them, and median gross rent is $1,716, so many buyers are investors who weigh rental income.

What a Westfield seller faces between signing and closing

Westfield sellers deal with a fire department alarm check, a deed filed in Elizabeth and tax bills that arrive every quarter. The town asks for no resale certificate of occupancy. The unusual feature is price. The typical home sells just below the million-dollar line where a state surcharge starts, which makes the final price unusually important.

Below: the alarm inspection, deed filing, the state's transfer fee, tax billing, and how an agent, a solo sale and a cash buyer compare.

Westfield housing and prices

Westfield counted 32,595 residents in mid-2025, compared with 31,032 in 2020, and about four of every five homes are lived in by their owners. Households average 2.84 people, and there are 10,900 of them. Buyers here often compare the town with Cranford, Scotch Plains and Mountainside, so the best pricing evidence is a handful of recent closings close to your own address.

Commuting access and your listing

Westfield station sits on NJ Transit's Raritan Valley Line. Off-peak trains run straight to New York Penn Station, and a few non-stop rush-hour trains head for Newark Penn. Bus 113 reaches the Port Authority terminal. By road, Route 28 follows the tracks, and Garden State Parkway Exits 135 and 137 and the Route 22 ramps are a short drive away.

Route 28 runs alongside the tracks for about two miles, and the town maintains 96.69 of its 108.63 miles of roadway. Give buyers the walk time to the platform and the drive to the nearest ramp in your description. Commuters weigh those two numbers heavily, and they are easy to state.
