Certificate of smoke detector and carbon monoxide alarm compliance

Westfield's building department confirms that a home sale needs neither a certificate of occupancy nor a continued one. The one paper it does want is a Certificate of Smoke Detector and Carbon Monoxide Alarm Compliance. Under state fire safety law, an owner of a one- or two-family house must obtain it from the Bureau of Fire Prevention before the buyer takes possession. Skipping it costs a $200 fine.

  • Crews inspect on Tuesday and Thursday mornings, and they do not phone ahead with an arrival time.
  • The fee depends on lead time: $100 for a slot more than ten business days out, $125 for four to ten, $150 for under four.
  • Someone aged 18 or over has to let the crew in, because they will not enter an empty house alone.
  • Sealed ten-year battery alarms pass, and so do hardwired detectors.
  • Close out any open construction permit before the visit.
  • Since March 14, 2025 the fire extinguisher is no longer part of the check.

The certificate arrives by email at the single address on the application, so use the one belonging to your closing attorney or agent. A house headed for demolition still needs one. With just two mornings a week on offer, request a date the moment you have a tentative closing day.

Recording the deed and the state transfer fee

Deeds for Westfield homes are filed with the Union County Clerk at the courthouse, 2 Broad Street, Elizabeth. The counter takes filings until 3:30 p.m. and wants no appointment. A second clerk's office in Westfield, on North Avenue East, handles passports, notary commissions and trade names, so deeds still go to Elizabeth. Most sellers never visit the counter, since the attorney or title company does it.

The state's realty transfer fee is the seller's cost. On sales above $350,000 the first $150,000 is charged $2.90 per $500, the next slice up to $200,000 is $4.25, then $4.80 runs to $550,000, and $5.30 and $5.80 brackets follow. Westfield's typical $953,400 value falls in the $5.30 bracket.

Residential sales above $1,000,000 also owe the Graduated Percent Fee, which is 1 percent of the full price up to $2,000,000. An offer near that line is worth a quick calculation by your attorney first.

Property tax bills around a sale

Westfield's Tax Collector, at 425 E Broad Street, issues four bills a year due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. Each gets a grace period of ten calendar days, moving to the next business day when day ten is a weekend or holiday.

Late payments accrue 8 percent interest on the first $1,500 and 18 percent on the remainder, counted from the original due date. A returned check costs $20 more. Sewer fees run on a different cycle, due April 1.

A bill that never arrived is no excuse, so new owners should ask for one. Get a written payoff for tax and sewer before closing, and have the closing agent divide the current quarter. Senior and veteran relief applications also pass through this office, so confirm any deduction on the account is settled.

Agent, solo sale or cash buyer?

Which route fits depends on the house and your calendar. An agent brings the widest buyer pool, a cash offer is the quickest to close, and selling on your own keeps the commission but hands you every chore.

  • An agent fits a Westfield house that shows well, if you can host weekend open houses and wait out a buyer's mortgage approval.
  • Going alone works if you already follow what nearby streets sold for and will pay an attorney to draft the contract.
  • An as-is cash buyer suits an inherited house, a tenant who stays, or a roof and kitchen you would rather not redo before moving.

A cash sale avoids open houses and the lender's underwriting wait, though the alarm certificate and the filed deed still apply. Judge written offers by what remains after the transfer fee, any surcharge over $1,000,000, taxes and your loan payoff.

Steps from contract to closing

  1. Hand the signed contract to your attorney.
  2. Book the Bureau of Fire Prevention for a Tuesday or Thursday morning.
  3. Close open permits and line up an adult to be home.
  4. Ask the Tax Collector for the tax and sewer payoff in writing.
  5. If you owe a mortgage, order a payoff letter from the lender.
  6. On closing day the deed goes to the clerk in Elizabeth.

Of all these steps, the alarm certificate most often delays a Westfield closing, since slots are scarce. Also remember that the certificate goes by email to one address, so use your attorney's.

Frequently asked questions

What costs come with selling a Westfield house?

The seller pays the state realty transfer fee, which follows the price, plus a fire department inspection of $100 to $150. Sales above $1,000,000 add a 1 percent surcharge. A listing agent's commission, if you use one, is separate.

Is an inspection needed before closing in Westfield?

Yes, an alarm and carbon monoxide inspection by the Bureau of Fire Prevention. No certificate of occupancy is needed. Crews come on Tuesday and Thursday mornings.

What are the Westfield tax installments?

Four bills fall due on the first of February, May, August and November, each with a ten-day cushion. Sewer is separate and due April 1. Late interest is 8 percent up to $1,500 and 18 percent beyond.

Can a Westfield house with problems still sell?

Yes. The alarm check covers only alarms and detectors, though open permits must be closed. A buyer can take on cosmetic or structural work, which is how as-is purchases function.

Which office files a Westfield deed?

The Union County Clerk in Elizabeth, at 2 Broad Street. Walk-in filing needs no appointment, and your closing attorney or title company normally files it for you.

Selling a house in Egg Harbor Township, NJ

Egg Harbor Township is a large Atlantic County municipality, 75.47 square miles of which 67.05 is land, and it is separate from Egg Harbor City. About 48,435 people live here. Owner-occupancy is high at 84.4 percent, the median owner-occupied home value is $312,700, and median household income is $97,190.

Because most houses here are owned rather than rented, the sale is usually a household moving on, and the one task to line up before closing is the state fire-safety certificate.

Smoke and carbon monoxide certificate

New Jersey's Division of Fire Safety runs an online smoke certification application with "Change of Ownership" as a stated reason, and it asks for the closing date, block, lot and whether you are the seller or the buyer's representative. Sheriff's sales, foreclosures, forfeitures and purchases from a federal agency work differently: the new owner must obtain the certificate before moving in. A building that is uninhabitable and will be rehabilitated or demolished can be exempt from the certificate, but it cannot be occupied until a new certificate of occupancy comes from the local construction official.

For the township's own form, fee and timing, call the Bureau of Fire Inspections before you set a closing date.

A settled housing market

The population rose 1.2 percent from the April 2020 base of 47,849 to 48,435. There are 17,261 households averaging 2.78 people, and 93.6 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so turnover is low and a well-priced house tends to draw local move-up households. Owners with a paid-off house pay far less each month than renters, which is why some heirs think twice before selling at all.

Median owner costs run $2,371 a month with a mortgage and $954 without one, and median gross rent is $1,456. That gap between owning and renting matters if you are deciding whether to keep an inherited house as a rental.

Building near the Pinelands

The township is one of 56 South Jersey municipalities in the Pinelands National Reserve, and part of it lies in the state-designated Pinelands Area. The Pinelands Commission classed Egg Harbor Township, Hamilton and Galloway as Regional Growth Areas, which steered residential construction into these towns so the preserved Pine Barrens could keep its trees.

  • If your lot sits near wetlands or protected land, ask the township's construction office about limits before planning a deck, shed or addition.
  • If a past owner added anything without a permit, a buyer's attorney may ask about it, so locate the paperwork first. Heirs selling an older home should look for old permits in the estate files.
  • Name the section of the township in your listing. The seat of government is in Bargaintown, and the township includes Cardiff, English Creek, Farmington, Scullville, Steelmanville and West Atlantic City.

Roads, buses and what draws buyers

The Atlantic City Expressway crosses the township for 5.3 miles and meets the Garden State Parkway at Interchange 7, which is Parkway Interchange 38. Routes 40, 322 and 9 plus county routes 559, 563, 575 and 585 carry local traffic. NJ Transit buses 502, 507, 508 and 509 link the township with Atlantic City, and Atlantic City International Airport lies mostly in the northern part. Mean travel to work is 23.3 minutes. Harbor Square, once the Shore Mall, is the regional shopping center, and the Atlantic County Bikeway runs 7.5 miles from it toward Hamilton Township.

  • Malibu Beach Wildlife Management Area covers 95.7 acres of marsh, dunes and back-bay shoreline and is known locally as Dog Beach, one of the few New Jersey beaches that permits dogs.
  • Storybook Land, a 20 acre children's park, opened in 1955 on the township's mainland side.
  • The township borders Ocean City and has Great Egg Harbor Bay shoreline in its eastern segment.

Name the nearest of these in your listing, since they are what a buyer from outside Atlantic County will recognize. Egg Harbor Township Schools run seven schools for pre-kindergarten through grade 12, with Egg Harbor Township High School at the top. Families moving in from elsewhere in the county often ask which school their street feeds, so call the district and put the answer in your listing before the first showing.

How to appeal an assessment in Atlantic County

Atlantic County's Board of Taxation sits in Mays Landing at 5909 Main Street and can be reached at (609) 645-5820. Petitions are due by April 1. Hearings usually take place from April through September at the Historic Courthouse. The board mails a hearing notice at least ten days ahead, and any comparable sales you rely on must reach the board, the municipal assessor and the municipal clerk at least seven days before the hearing. Comparables should be genuine sales in the same town during the year before the prior October 1. Most foreclosures, sheriff's sales, estate sales and short sales are treated as not usable. A reduction comes back as a credit through a revised bill from the tax collector, and you have 45 days from the judgment to go to the State Tax Court.

Recording the deed

On the deed, a seller who lives in New Jersey signs GIT/REP-3, while one who lives elsewhere signs GIT/REP-1 or GIT/REP-2 unless a listed assurance fits. Your attorney or title agent normally handles the recording, so the practical job for you is to supply the smoke certificate, payoff letters and any permit paperwork early.

Here is a quick order of operations: submit the state smoke certification application once the closing date is known, call the township fire bureau about its form and fee, collect payoff figures, then let your attorney schedule the closing. A cash buyer skips the appraisal and lender review, but the certificate and the deed work stay.

If the property was bought at a sheriff's sale or foreclosure, remember the rule runs the other way: the new owner obtains the certificate before moving in. If the building is uninhabitable, ask the local construction official before you list, because it cannot be occupied again until a new certificate of occupancy is issued. In every case, keep copies of the smoke certificate, the closing date you gave the state and the block and lot numbers, since the buyer's side may ask for them.

Is Egg Harbor Township the same as Egg Harbor City?

No. They are separate municipalities. This page covers the township, which has about 48,435 residents.

Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell in Egg Harbor Township?

Yes, a change of ownership calls for a state smoke and carbon monoxide certificate. Ask the township's Bureau of Fire Inspections for its form, fee and timing before you pick a closing date.

What is the median home value in Egg Harbor Township?

$312,700 for owner-occupied homes, and 84.4 percent of homes are owner occupied.

When is the Atlantic County tax appeal deadline?

April 1 of the tax year, filed with the Atlantic County Board of Taxation. Where a revaluation was done, the deadline is May 1.

How far ahead are Atlantic County hearing notices sent?

At least ten days before the hearing. Comparable sales evidence is due to the board, the assessor and the clerk at least seven days before.

What inspection does Galloway require on a resale?

Every residential resale needs a fire certificate covering smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and fire extinguishers only. Township code Chapter 153 requires the inspection before the new owners occupy the dwelling.

The application, inspection and certificate go through the Fire Department at 300 E. Jimmie Leeds Road. The fee depends on how much notice you give, so ask for the inspection as soon as you have a closing date.

Violating the ordinance can bring a fine of up to $2,000, up to 90 days in jail or community service, and each day counts as a separate offense. The resale inspection stays limited to the three fire safety items and does not cover the rest of the house.

Renting out the house

Rentals follow a separate and fuller inspection than resales. Under the rental ordinance, a certificate of occupancy is required on any rental, renewed every year or at each new occupant, whichever comes first, at $50 per inspection.

  • The lease must accompany the application and list every occupant's name and age.

  • A rental with a fireplace needs a chimney certification and proof that the dryer vent has been cleaned, or a notarized letter from the owner.
  • More than two follow-up inspections trigger another $50 fee.

The Housing Department handles applications at (609) 652-3700, extensions 241 or 249. Inspection requests must be emailed to the Construction office at inspect@gtnj.org with the permit number, address, type of inspection and your phone number.

The homeowner, not the contractor, is responsible for obtaining a permit. Residential contractors need a state Consumer Affairs 13VH number, so keep contractor names and permit numbers for any work you had done before selling.

What nonresident owners owe on a sale

A nonresident seller prepays estimated gross income tax at the closing table. The formula multiplies the gain by 10.75%, but the payment can never be below 2% of the consideration written in the deed, even if there is no gain.

The payment goes with the deed and the GIT/REP-1 form to the Atlantic County Clerk, who forwards it to the state. A seller who wants to avoid delays can prepay at a Division of Taxation regional office and receive a stamped GIT/REP-2 before closing.

  • A New Jersey resident signs the GIT/REP-3 instead and pays nothing up front.
  • A nonresident can still use the GIT/REP-3 if one of its listed assurances fits, such as a deed for $1,000 or less or a settlement with no net proceeds to the seller.
  • Selling a principal residence that qualifies under Internal Revenue Code section 121 is another listed assurance, when the entire gain can be excluded.

The GIT/REP Unit answers questions at 609-322-9275. Call at least two weeks before a complicated closing.

Parkway and commute

Buyers care about the Garden State Parkway. It runs 5.7 miles through the township, with Interchange 40 for U.S. Route 30, Interchange 41 for Jimmie Leeds Road and Interchange 44 for Pomona. Route 50 and County Routes 561, 563 and 575 also cross the township, and NJ Transit buses 508, 554 and 559 reach Atlantic City. The mean commute is 23.6 minutes.

Stockton University sits in the Pomona section, which keeps a steady pool of renters nearby. A house bought as a rental brings the inspection rules above into play.

A sensible order for a quick sale

Book the fire inspection the moment you have a closing date, because the fee rises as the date gets closer. Test your smoke and carbon monoxide detectors and check the extinguisher yourself. If the house is a rental, gather the lease and the latest certificate of occupancy for the buyer. Then have your closing attorney prepare the deed and the GIT/REP form that fits you, resident or nonresident, and file both with the Atlantic County Clerk.

Because Galloway is so spread out, tell a buyer exactly which part of the township the house is in. A buyer comparing a Pomona address with one in Leeds Point is looking at very different surroundings, and the fire certificate, permit history and any Pinelands limits follow the parcel, not the town name. A cash buyer will usually ask for the same documents a financed buyer does: the deed, permit records, any rental certificate and proof that the fire inspection passed.

If anything fails the fire inspection, the usual fixes are inexpensive, such as a new detector battery or a replacement extinguisher. Fix the item and ask for a re-check rather than waiting for the buyer to raise it.

Frequently asked questions

Does Galloway Township require an inspection to sell a house?

Yes, a fire certificate. Galloway inspects smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and fire extinguishers on every residential resale, and it must be done before the new owners occupy the home.

What does the Galloway Township resale fire certificate cost?

It costs $45 when the request arrives more than 10 business days before the change of ownership, $90 for four to 10 business days, and $161 for fewer than four business days.

Where do I apply for the Galloway Township fire certificate?

The Fire Department at 300 E. Jimmie Leeds Road handles the application, inspection and certificate. The Housing Department can be reached at (609) 652-3700, extensions 241 or 249.

How much tax does a nonresident owe when selling in Galloway Township?

At least 2% of the deed consideration is prepaid at closing as estimated New Jersey gross income tax. The actual figure can be higher, since the formula uses the gain times 10.75%, and the seller can claim a refund after filing a nonresident return.

Is Galloway Township in the Pinelands?

In part. Galloway is within the Pinelands National Reserve, and parts of it are in the state-designated Pinelands Area. Ask the Community Development office about your specific parcel.

Next, get a payoff figure from the tax collector so the title company knows what to clear out of your proceeds. Last, sign the deed and the residency or prepayment forms with the closing attorney, who files the deed with the clerk in Mays Landing.

Without an appraisal or underwriting, timing depends mostly on how soon the inspection is booked and whether the title is clean. Bring your deed, a recent tax bill, any mortgage payoff statement and the keys. Selling as is does not remove the inspection requirement, so plan for it even if you intend to make no repairs.

Back taxes get paid out of your proceeds at the table, so you need not pay them first. A failed alarm usually means a cheap battery or unit swap, followed by a reinspection. Tell any buyer when the certificate was issued, since the six months run from that date.

Before the closing date, confirm with the closing attorney that the payoff letter, the deed and the GIT forms are all ready. Missing paperwork, not the house, is what most often pushes a closing back a week or two.

A 14-mile stretch of the Atlantic City Expressway crosses the township with three interchanges, and U.S. Routes 40 and 322 and Route 50 cover other directions. NJ Transit buses 502 and 553 reach Atlantic City. Commuters care about those links, so mention them when you talk to buyers.

At the Atlantic County Clerk's Office, 5901 Main Street in Mays Landing, inside the township. A satellite office is at 1333 Atlantic Avenue in Atlantic City.

April 1 at 4 p.m., with December 1 as the date for added or omitted assessments. Filing works online, and a postmark does not satisfy the deadline.

No. They are separate municipalities in different counties, each with its own tax board, clerk and inspection office. This page covers the one around Mays Landing.

State rules move the usual April 1 appeal deadline to May 1 where a revaluation has been undertaken. Ask the Mahwah assessor or the Bergen board which date covers your parcel, and keep any notice of the new value because a buyer's attorney will want a copy.

Payment must reach the collector's office by the 10th to avoid interest, which state law sets at up to 8 percent a year on balances to $1,500 and 18 percent above that. Selling a house in Evesham Township

Evesham Township is a large Burlington County suburb in South Jersey. Speed here depends on the fire department's resale certificate, a clean permit history and the state forms that travel with the deed.

Evesham spreads over roughly 29 square miles. Residents numbered 46,826 in 2020 and an estimated 49,525 in 2025, the largest head count of any Burlington County municipality. Many people say Marlton when they mean Evesham. Marlton is the best known community inside the township and shares ZIP code 08053 with much of it, so mention both in your listing.

A slice of Evesham lies in the Pinelands Area, a state zone with separate land use rules. Owners near the wooded edge should look at the zoning map first, because those rules can limit additions or new structures for the next owner.

Home values and who owns them

Most Evesham homes are lived in by their owners, and values sit above the national median (2020 to 2024 estimates).

About 89 percent of residents stayed put over the past year. Few homes come up for sale, so one that lingers gets noticed. A price near the township median lands in the higher state fee band described under closing costs.

Roads and transit buyers ask about

Route 70 and Route 73 define the township, and buyers judge a house by how it connects to them. Route 70 cuts east to west across the north of the township, Route 73 runs along the western border, and County Route 544 (Marlton Parkway and Taunton Lake Road) links the two. A grade-separated interchange replaced the old Marlton Circle in 2011, and commutes toward Philadelphia and Cherry Hill became more predictable.

  • NJ Transit bus route 406 runs through the township between Berlin and Philadelphia.
  • The Atco station, just across the border in Waterford Township, carries Atlantic City Line trains to Philadelphia 30th Street and the Atlantic City Rail Terminal.

Resale certificate and permits

Resale certificate requests go to the Evesham Township Fire Department. Its site, eveshamfire.org, posts inspection scheduling and fees. Start that request early so the paper is in hand by closing day.

Permits go through Community Development, Room 204 of the Township Building at 984 Tuckerton Road in Marlton. Hours are 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays. The construction office is at 856-983-2914, then option 4. A construction permit confirms that work meets fire and building codes, and an insurer can refuse a claim tied to work done without one.

  • A shed or fence needs a zoning permit. A fence around a pool also needs a building permit that meets the pool barrier code.
  • A homeowners association may need to approve a shed or fence first.
  • Interior sump pump or French drain work needs a construction permit, while exterior-only drainage work does not.
  • For flood zone questions, use the FEMA Flood Map Service Center or the township mapping portal.

Did an earlier owner finish a basement, build a deck or add a pool with no paperwork? Fix that before listing. Ask the construction office whether an inspection or a closed-out permit is needed, then keep the paperwork with your closing file. Buyer attorneys request permit history, and a gap can hold up a sale for weeks.

Selling a rental or short-term rental

A rental house can be sold, though its registration and fire inspection records need to be pulled together first. Short stays booked through Airbnb or Vrbo are treated like long-term leases. The house needs a fire department inspection and a registration with the Township Clerk's Office.

Every change of tenant triggers a compliance certificate covering smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms and a portable fire extinguisher (N.J.A.C. 5:70-2.3). Skipping it costs a $500 penalty. The fire department sets inspection fees.

With tenants in place, expect the buyer to ask for the lease, the deposit figure and the latest inspection certificate. A cash buyer who needs vacant possession should put that in writing before signing, which leaves time to plan notice periods. For landlord and tenant disputes, the township points people to the Burlington County courts and Legal Services of New Jersey.

Costs and filings at closing

Two items fall on the seller at closing: the state Realty Transfer Fee and a Gross Income Tax residency form. Both go to the Burlington County Clerk along with the deed. The Division of Taxation prices the fee per $500 of the deed price, and on sales over $350,000 the $200,000 to $550,000 band costs $4.80 per $500. That band covers a house priced near Evesham's median.

Sales above $1 million carry an extra graduated percent fee, also the seller's, that begins at 1 percent of the whole price. Few Evesham sales reach that level.

New Jersey residents generally sign the GIT/REP-3. A form dated October 1, 2025 or later has to be the current edition or recording is refused. The state GIT/REP Unit, 609-322-9275, answers form questions. Sellers who live out of state owe at least 2 percent of the price as an estimated payment unless an exemption applies.

The county clerk offers a free Property Fraud Alert service that alerts owners when a document is recorded under their name. Sign up before you sell and keep it after.

How a fast as-is sale moves

The order below assumes clear title and no open permits.

  • Collect your deed, latest tax bill, rental registration if any, and a mortgage payoff statement.
  • Ask the fire department for the resale certificate. Fix what it flags, or write into the contract who will.
  • Your closing attorney orders the title search and prepares the deed plus the fee and GIT/REP filings.
  • Close, hand over the keys, and the attorney records the deed at the county clerk.

A cash buyer may take the house as it stands. That ends repair haggling but not the certificate or the state filings. On older parcels the title search can surface easements or old liens, and the attorney must clear them before the deed records. Before committing, get the price, closing date and the party paying for each inspection in a single written offer.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a certificate from the township to sell my house in Evesham?

Yes. The Evesham Township Fire Department issues it for residential resales, and eveshamfire.org lists scheduling and fees. Book the inspection once you decide to sell.

What happens if work on my Evesham house was done without a permit?

The buyer's attorney will probably want it settled before closing, and an insurer may deny a claim tied to unpermitted work. The construction office, 856-983-2914 option 4, can explain what a retroactive permit takes.

Who pays the realty transfer fee in an Evesham sale?

You do, as the seller. It is collected at recording and tied to the deed price, with a further graduated fee above $1 million. The closing attorney or title company gives you the exact number.

Can I sell a house in Evesham if I live out of state?

Yes. You file a GIT/REP form and, unless an exemption on it applies, prepay at least 2 percent of the price as estimated Gross Income Tax. That payment counts against what you finally owe when you file.

Is part of Evesham in the Pinelands?

Yes, a portion. The township zoning map and Pinelands Commission maps show which lots are covered, so check your parcel before you market it.

Allow extra time in your plans, because a township this large can mean a long drive between the house, the Fire Department and the county offices.

Pinelands rules that can affect a sale

Medford sits inside the Pinelands National Reserve, and part of the township falls in the state-designated Pinelands Area. The independent borough of Medford Lakes sits entirely inside the township. If your home is in the Pinelands Area, ask the township zoning office what that designation means for additions, tree removal or new outbuildings before a buyer's attorney raises it.

Buyers also recognize local landmarks such as Historic Medford Village, Kirby's Mill, Freedom Park and the Woodford Cedar Run Wildlife Refuge, a 170-acre preserve on the southern border. Nearly 30 glassworkers' homes survive on Trimble Street and Mill Street, and houses near the village carry some historic character that shows up in how they are marketed.

Resale certificate of occupancy

In Medford the Fire Department handles the resale certificate of occupancy, since the construction office inspects existing housing only when someone complains. A house on public water or sewer also needs a visit from the utility billing office for a final meter reading and a sewer inspection, and wells and septic systems fall under the Burlington County Health Department, reached at 609-265-5515 in Westampton.

The fire inspection checks these items:

  • Working smoke detectors on every level, basements included, and within 10 feet of sleeping areas. A system installed with the house and interconnected cannot be swapped for stand-alone battery units.
  • At least one carbon monoxide detector near the bedrooms, with more where bedrooms sit on more than one level.
  • A residential fire extinguisher rated 2A-10BC, no heavier than 10 pounds, mounted no higher than 5 feet and not hidden behind a door or inside a cabinet.

The township asks sellers to leave the detector manuals for the next owner. Contact the Fire Department and the utility office early, since each needs its own visit.

The seller owes the state realty transfer fee, which rises with the sale price. Above $1,000,000, a graduated percent fee starting at 1 percent applies to the seller for deeds submitted on or after July 10, 2025.

The old NJ Transit bus to Philadelphia that ended in Evesham has been discontinued, and Greyhound runs from nearby Mount Laurel. What are the choices for selling a Medford house quickly?

Medford owners can pick a listing agent, a private sale or a cash buyer for a house that needs work, and every route needs the Fire Department certificate and, where applicable, the utility and county health sign-offs.

  • A private sale avoids the commission, but the owner then manages disclosures, the contract and the certificate steps without help.
  • A cash sale works for estates, rentals with tenants, houses with septic or well problems, or owners who cannot take on a month of repairs.

Compare offers on the amount left after the mortgage payoff, the transfer fee, and the cost of any repair the inspector requires.

Start the sale by calling the Fire Department to book the resale inspection, and check the detectors and extinguisher yourself first so you do not pay for a second visit. If the house is on public water or sewer, contact the utility billing office for the final meter reading and sewer inspection at the same time. A house with a well or septic system needs the county health department involved before the buyer's attorney asks.

Gather the paperwork the attorney will want: detector manuals, any inspection results, and for a rental the registration and lead certificate. At closing the deed goes to the county clerk with the residency form and the summary sheet. Keep copies of everything in one folder so a delay on one item does not stall the rest. A cash buyer can often close without waiting on a lender's appraisal, but the township and county sign-offs still apply to the house.

Who inspects a Medford house before it sells?

The Medford Fire Department handles the residential resale certificate of occupancy. Homes on public water or sewer also need the utility billing office for a final meter reading and sewer inspection.

What if my Medford house has a well or septic system?

The Burlington County Health Department administers permits and inspections for wells and septic systems. Contact it at 609-265-5515 before listing so any needed work is known early.

Which smoke and carbon monoxide rules does Medford apply?

Smoke detectors are needed on every level, including basements, and within 10 feet of sleeping areas. At least one carbon monoxide detector must be near the bedrooms, and the home needs a 2A-10BC extinguisher of 10 pounds or less.

How is the transfer fee handled on a Medford sale?

The seller pays it at recording, and it grows with the price. Sales above $1,000,000 also pay a graduated percent fee starting at 1 percent.

Mount Laurel Schools teach pre-kindergarten through grade 8. Six neighborhood schools serve K-4: Countryside, Fleetwood, Hillside, Larchmont, Parkway and Springville. Certificate of Continued Occupancy

The township posts a Certificate of Continued Occupancy application and checklist under its Community Development / Construction pages, and emailed applications are not taken. Bring a paper application to the municipal building at 750 Centerton Road.

The Tax Collector bills in February, May, August and November, due on the first, with ten days of grace under N.J.S.A. 54:4-66. A postmark does not count, and arrears accrue 8% on the first $1,500 and 18% beyond it under N.J.S.A. 54:4-67.

Listing or direct cash sale?

A tidy house in a K-4 school zone with a passed CCO does well on the open market. A direct cash sale is better when the checklist looks expensive, an estate is involved, or you want a certain closing day.

Collect the CCO status, tax figure and payoff letter, then set each offer side by side on net proceeds.

Begin at the municipal building. Pick up the paper application, ask about fees and the inspection calendar, and learn whether any permit on your house is still open. Then go through the checklist room by room and make the fixes you can handle yourself.

While the inspection is pending, order the payoff letter from your lender and ask the Tax Collector for the current installment amount. At closing, the attorney or title agent sends the deed to Mount Holly with the residency declaration and the recording fees.

Keep copies of the application, the checklist and any inspection notes in one folder for the buyer's attorney. Pemberton borough is a separate municipality surrounded by the township, one of New Jersey's doughnut towns, so check which jurisdiction holds your parcel before you request forms.

  • Agent listing: reaches the most buyers, and puts showings, a buyer's home inspection and the township's resale inspection on your calendar.
  • Owner-run sale: keeps the commission, but you handle pricing, advertising and every municipal form yourself.
  • Investor purchase: a shorter path with fewer contingencies, and an offer priced for whatever repairs the buyer inherits.

Pemberton homes and owners

Pemberton skews toward owners who stay put. The July 1, 2025 estimate is 27,611 people, up from 26,903 in April 2020, in 9,785 households of about 2.73 people each. Owners live in 73.3 percent of homes.

A typical owner-occupied home is valued at $234,500, well under the national typical value of $332,700, and household income runs $80,843 at the midpoint. Price your house against nearby sales, since a house needing work will draw offers shaped by what the buyer must fix.

Resale inspection before a Pemberton closing

A Certificate of Occupancy Transfer is required every time a residential unit gets a new occupant, and a sale counts. The seller submits a resale application to Code Enforcement along with the inspection fee.

Under the township's packet, the first inspection costs $150 and each repeat visit costs $50. Staff will not book a visit until the paperwork is complete and the fee is paid, and inspectors in the field cannot accept either. Applications lapse after 60 days, so file when a closing is realistic.

A buyer who wants to take over the certificate must tell the office in writing before it is issued. That option helps when the buyer plans repairs after closing. Code Enforcement answers at 609-894-3376. Items the inspector looks for include:

  • House numbers in reflective material, at least 3.5 inches tall, visible from the road.
  • Battery smoke detectors on every level, in each bedroom and outside sleeping areas, with carbon monoxide detectors near bedrooms where a fuel-burning appliance or attached garage exists.
  • An anti-tilt bracket on the stove, rails on stairs with four or more risers, and a mounted ABC extinguisher of 5 to 10 pounds.
  • Window screens, egress windows that open easily, and GFCI outlets in kitchens, baths, garages and outdoors.
  • Every utility switched on for the visit.

What else gets reviewed on the Pemberton resale application?

The form follows the account history of the property as well as the structure. Each department initials its own box, so clearing balances early keeps the file from stalling.

  • The tax office confirms liens, taxes paid, and the solid waste, water and sewer accounts.
  • Public Works notes the water and sewer units billed.
  • The housing office checks open permits, open code violations, vacant property fees and any board-up or clean-up charges.
  • Houses on private water or septic attach a well report or a septic report.

The attached checklist also tells you what Pemberton skips. Inspectors pass over air conditioning, pools, hot tubs and termites, turn away basements with standing water, and will not remove leftover furniture or appliances. For the roof, wiring, structure or heating, a bonded contractor's certification may be requested.

Pemberton costs and due dates

These are the figures a Pemberton seller meets most often.

Pemberton resale and tax figures
Cost or dateAmount or deadline
First resale inspection$150
Each reinspection$50

Pemberton tax bills and your closing

Each installment is due on the first of its month, and a ten-day grace period runs to the 10th. After that, interest reaches back to the first. Balances left open on December 31 pick up a 6 percent year-end penalty on top.

One bill covers the township, Burlington County, the county farmland and open space fund, the local school board and the county library. Because the township collects for all five, a tax search before closing shows what is outstanding across the whole bill. Payments are credited on arrival, never by postmark, and a bill that never arrived is no excuse for a late installment. The tax office is at 609-894-3370.

A lien can be redeemed only by someone with a legal interest in the parcel. Requests go in writing to TaxOffice@pemberton-twp.com, and the payoff must arrive in full as certified funds. Title companies typically handle this step.

Do Pinelands rules touch a Pemberton sale?

They can. Pemberton is one of 56 southern New Jersey municipalities inside the Pinelands National Reserve, and part of the township lies in the narrower state-designated Pinelands Area. Congress created the reserve in 1978.

A plain change of ownership rarely hits those rules. They matter when a buyer wants an addition, a new outbuilding or a lot division. Ask the township's Community Development office whether your parcel is in the Pinelands Area before you make promises about future building.

State fee and Burlington County recording

The seller owes the state a realty transfer fee when the deed is recorded, set by bracket on the sale price. Nonresident sellers, including heirs who live elsewhere, also prepay Gross Income Tax at closing. That payment is the greater of a figure based on the gain and 2 percent of the price in the deed.

Burlington County's Clerk records the deed. Seller tax forms signed on or after October 1, 2025 must be the newest version, or the office returns them. The same office runs a free alert service that emails, texts or calls an owner when anything is recorded under their name. Call 609-265-5122 to ask about it. The county names seniors and owners of vacant properties as common targets of deed fraud.

When is a cash offer a good fit for a Pemberton house?

It suits a house that needs more work than the township checklist tolerates, a vacant property, or a seller with a firm move date. Ask any buyer who orders the transfer inspection, who pays the $150, and who signs for the repair list.

Judge an offer by what lands in your account after repairs, carrying costs and the state fee. Open permits and unpaid sewer or solid waste balances do not block a sale, though they have to be settled or credited at the table.

Do I need a certificate of occupancy to sell my house in Pemberton Township?

Yes. Pemberton requires a Certificate of Occupancy Transfer when a residential unit changes occupant. The resale application lists a $150 first inspection, a $50 reinspection and a 60 day life.

Can a buyer take over the Pemberton certificate?

Yes, once the code office has that request in writing before it issues the certificate. The buyer then owns the repair list, which suits as-is and investor purchases.

When are property taxes due in Pemberton?

They are due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, with a grace period to the 10th. After that, interest is 8 percent on the first $1,500 owed and 18 percent beyond it.

Who pays the state transfer fee on a Pemberton sale?

The seller pays it at recording, in brackets that rise with the sale price. Your closing attorney can give you the exact amount.

Does Pemberton borough follow the township's sale rules?

Check before assuming so. The borough is its own municipality inside the township, so ask the office serving your address which set of forms and dates applies.

How a Willingboro sale differs from most New Jersey sales

Before ownership of a Willingboro house can change, the township wants to issue a certificate of occupancy, and the inspection has to be booked a full 15 days before settlement. That lead time drives the whole schedule: heating certification, any repairs, a possible recheck, then the deed filing in Mount Holly.

Willingboro is a Burlington County suburb of Philadelphia with 32,824 residents. Below you will find local housing numbers, the resale inspection rules, deed and tax steps, and how an agent, a sale on your own and a cash buyer compare.

Willingboro homes and households

Willingboro grew out of one builder's plan, and the numbers still show it. Owners live in 84.3 percent of homes, households average 3.02 people, and the township packs about 4,128 people into each of its 7.73 square miles of land. The 2020 count was 31,889.

A typical value of $270,300 puts many sales under the $350,000 break in the state transfer fee schedule, so the lower rates described below apply to them.

Levittown neighborhoods and how buyers search

Levitt and Sons built its third and largest Levittown here in the 1950s and 1960s. The first homes sold in June 1958, and the population jumped from 852 in 1950 to 43,386 in 1970. Voters briefly renamed the place Levittown Township in 1959 and went back to Willingboro in a November 1963 referendum. The planning left a pattern buyers still use:

  • Neighborhoods are called parks, such as Pennypacker Park, Millbrook Park, Windsor Park and Hawthorne Park.
  • Streets in each park begin with the park's initial, so a Pennypacker address starts with P.
  • Country Club Ridge was laid out around a golf course in the 1960s.
  • Pennypacker Park and Country Club Park hold the community pools.

Many houses came from a small set of Levitt floor plans, so a buyer can often compare yours with the same model a few streets over. Mention additions and the age of the roof and furnace when you present the house.

Roads, buses and schools

U.S. Route 130 forms the northwest edge of the township, and Rancocas Creek drains the southwest side. Of 122.11 miles of road, 109.02 are township-maintained. Transit is by bus: NJ Transit routes 409, 417 and 418 run between Trenton and Philadelphia, BurLink operates two local routes, and Academy Bus connects to Midtown and Lower Manhattan.

Willingboro Township Public Schools covers Hawthorne, W.R. James Sr. and Twin Hills for grades 1 to 4, Levitt Intermediate for grades 5 and 6, Memorial Middle School for 7 and 8, and Willingboro High School. Families will ask which school serves your park, so find out before the first showing.

Certificate of occupancy and inspection

Chapter 199 of the township code, the housing standards chapter, bars a change of ownership or occupancy until the Department of Inspections issues a certificate of occupancy. The ordinance sets these steps:

  • The owner or agent applies and pays the fee in the township fee schedule.
  • The visit must be scheduled at least 15 calendar days before settlement, and a request made within four days of it adds an $80 expedite charge.
  • Cancel or move the appointment with a day's notice, or the first fee is charged regardless.
  • The inspector makes a visual check of accessible parts of the structure, which does not guarantee the electrical, plumbing or heating systems.
  • A qualified technician authorized by the township must separately certify the heating equipment, and that certification can be no more than 30 days old when the certificate issues.
  • If the house fails, the department sends a written list of defects, and the owner has 30 days from the visit to repair them and ask for a recheck.

Call the Department of Inspections for the current fee and application steps. If the buyer will take on repairs, write that into the contract so both sides know who pays.

Filing the deed and state fees

The Burlington County Clerk's main office, 50 Rancocas Road in Mount Holly, accepts deeds on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. The clerk also offers a free Property Fraud Alert service that flags any document filed under your name.

One paperwork rule is new. County staff reject any GIT/REP seller declaration signed on or after October 1, 2025 that is not on the latest state form.

For prices up to $350,000 the state's realty transfer fee is $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, then $3.35 per $500 through $200,000, then $3.90 per $500 through $350,000. Your closing agent will confirm the exact figure for your price.

Tax due dates and the October tax sale

Bills follow the calendar year, with installments due on the first of February, May, August and November and a ten-day grace period after each. From the eleventh day, interest is figured back to the first, and a postmark earns no credit.

Pay at the window in the municipal building, the Police Department drop box, by mail or on the township's online portal. The tax office is in Suite 205 at One Rev. Dr. M. L. King Jr. Drive, with window hours from 9 in the morning to 4:30. The portal rejects prior-year balances, so get an exact payoff figure from the collector before closing.

Earlier unpaid taxes and municipal charges still open after December 31 go into the township's electronic tax sale, held each October. Senior, veteran and disabled-person deductions are handled by the assessor's office at 609-877-2200.

Agent, own sale or cash buyer?

A listing can bring the strongest price for a clean house, a cash buyer removes the repair cycle, and selling alone falls between them. Timing is the real difference, because of the 15-day inspection lead.

  • An agent suits a house in good repair that can pass inspection without a long defect list.
  • A solo sale suits an owner who follows recent prices in the neighborhood and will hire an attorney for the contract.
  • A cash purchase suits a house with deferred repairs, a tenant or an estate, since the buyer can take over the defect list.

Book the township inspection the moment a closing date exists, and measure each offer by the cash that reaches you after transfer fee, taxes and payoff.

Order of events before closing

Work backward from the closing date. First, set the township inspection at least 15 calendar days ahead, since a late request costs $80 more. Next, hire the technician who will certify the heating equipment, remembering that the certification can be no more than 30 days old. If the inspector lists defects, you have 30 days to fix them and ask for a recheck, so a sale with many repairs needs more room on the calendar.

In parallel, ask the tax collector for a payoff figure, request a lender payoff if a mortgage remains, and make sure the seller declaration is on the current state form. Then your closing agent files the deed in Mount Holly. A cash buyer who agrees to take the house as is can absorb the defect list, which skips the recheck step.

Is an inspection mandatory before a Willingboro sale?

Yes. A certificate of occupancy is needed before ownership changes, and the visit must be booked 15 calendar days ahead. A qualified technician must also certify the heating equipment.

What if the inspector finds defects?

The department issues a written notice of defects. You have 30 days from the inspection to finish repairs and request a reinspection, and the certificate follows once the house passes.

What are the Willingboro installment dates?

The first of February, May, August and November, each followed by ten grace days. Postmarks are ignored, and balances still open after December 31 enter the October tax sale.

Which office records a Willingboro deed?

The Burlington County Clerk's main office, 50 Rancocas Road in Mount Holly, which serves the public on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Can a Willingboro house with tenants or repair needs be sold?

Yes. The certificate rules still apply, but an as-is buyer can agree to take over the defect list and the occupancy. Spell out who handles the inspection and repairs in the contract.

What sets a Cherry Hill sale apart

Cherry Hill sellers face two separate township inspections before closing, one covering the property's exterior and one covering smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, and each is booked through a different office. Booking both early keeps the closing date from slipping.

The township is large, mostly owner-occupied and built largely in the decades after World War II, so the typical seller owns a single-family house on a suburban lot with trees, fences, driveways and sidewalks that the township cares about.

Cherry Hill housing in brief

Cherry Hill is the most populous municipality in Camden County, with 79,965 residents. Its neighborhoods include Ashland, Barclay, Erlton, Greentree, Kingston Estates, Springdale, Woodcrest and the area around Cherry Hill Mall.

Roads, transit and schools

Cherry Hill is built around highway access to Philadelphia. Interstate 295 has three exits in the township, including exit 31, which leads directly to the Woodcrest PATCO station, and Routes 38, 41, 70 and 154 cross it. NJ Transit buses reach Philadelphia on the 317, 404 and 406 routes, and the Atlantic City Line stops at the Cherry Hill station.

Schools are the other big talking point. Cherry Hill Public Schools has two traditional high schools, Cherry Hill High School East and Cherry Hill High School West, plus three middle schools and 12 elementary schools. The two inspections before closing

A seller here needs a Certificate of Continued Occupancy from the township and a smoke alarm and carbon monoxide compliance certificate from the fire department. A single-family sale cannot reach closing without them, and they are separate appointments with separate costs.

The occupancy certificate comes from Community Development, which handles property maintenance, at 820 Mercer Street, Room 202. The property maintenance officer looks at exterior areas only. The township lists these items:

  • Sidewalks, driveways and fences.
  • Trees and natural growth.
  • Sanitation and exhaust vents.
  • Grading and drainage, including where sump pumps discharge.
  • Accessory structures and ground surface hazards.

The inspection costs $100, payable ahead of the visit, and you can apply online, in person or by mail. Online applications need office approval before a payment request is emailed, cancellations after payment are not refunded, and the property maintenance line is 856-834-3364. Some condominiums and townhomes are excluded, and the township posts a list of properties that skip the inspection.

The fire department certificate is a different step. It is required for one- and two-family homes before settlement, and sellers are asked to request the appointment three to four weeks early. If the home passes and payment is made, the certificate is handed over at the visit; temporary certificates are not issued, and fire extinguishers are no longer required. The fire department's inspection line is (856) 429-7441. Because the two appointments run on separate calendars, book both the week the contract is signed.

Move-out trash after a sale

Cherry Hill offers a one-time courtesy collection for house clean-outs after a sale, covering furniture, carpets, bedding and similar household items. Proof that you applied for a Continued Certificate of Occupancy is required before Public Works will schedule it, pickups happen on Fridays, and the number to call is 856-424-4422.

No trash or recycling service goes to dwellings under construction, vacant lots or properties lacking a valid certificate of occupancy, so a vacant house waiting on its paperwork may go without pickup. Plan the clean-out around the certificate date, and keep contractor debris out of the cart, because construction waste generated by a contractor has to be hauled away by that contractor.

Property tax due dates and collection

The four installments land on the first of August, November, February and May, and a ten-day grace period rolls forward to the next business day if it ends on a weekend or holiday. The township mails two bills a year: July covers the third and fourth installments, and January covers the first and second. Money has to be in the tax office by the last grace day, because postmarks do not count.

Late payments accrue 8 percent a year up to $1,500 of arrears and 18 percent on any amount beyond that, running from the original due date. The tax collector also bills sewer rent: residential sewer is a flat annual fee due April 1, with a 10 percent discount for owners 60 or older who live in the property. Ask the tax office at 856-488-7880 for a closing figure that includes any sewer balance. The bill you pay includes shares for the school district, the fire district and Camden County along with the township.

Appeals follow state deadlines, April 1 or May 1 after a revaluation, and go to the Camden County Board of Taxation.

Transfer fee and deed filing

The Camden County Clerk files the deed, and the seller owes the state realty transfer fee when it is filed. Above $350,000 the state schedule runs $2.90 per $500 for the first $150,000, $4.25 per $500 for the slice from $150,000 to $200,000 and $4.80 per $500 for the slice from $200,000 to $550,000. Confirm the exact figure with your closing attorney, since senior, disabled and low-income rates run lower.

The county's recording schedule lists $30 for page one of a deed, $10 for every added page, a $10 abstracting fee and a $5 homeless trust fund charge, with a $55 floor. The clerk's office answers at 856-225-5300. A New Jersey resident signs a residency certification at closing, while a seller who is leaving the state prepays estimated income tax, so tell your attorney early if you are relocating.

A sensible order for a quick sale: book the township and fire inspections the week you sign, request the trash collection once the occupancy application is filed, ask the tax office for a closing figure including sewer, and give your attorney the deed details so the county filing is ready. Keep both certificates and every receipt in one folder to hand to the buyer's side.

Frequently asked questions

Are inspections required to sell in Cherry Hill?

Yes, two of them. The township requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy for single-family resale, and the fire department requires a smoke alarm and carbon monoxide compliance certificate before settlement.

What does the Cherry Hill resale inspection cost?

The occupancy inspection is $100, paid before the inspector arrives. The fire department sets its own charges, which are posted on its checklist.

How early should the Cherry Hill fire inspection be scheduled?

Three to four weeks before settlement. The certificate is given at the appointment if the home complies and payment is made, and temporary certificates are not available.

What are the Cherry Hill tax installment dates?

August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. A ten-day grace period applies, and the money must reach the tax office by then because postmarks do not count.

Who files a Cherry Hill deed?

The Camden County Clerk. The posted schedule lists $30 for page one of a deed, $10 for each added page, a $10 abstracting fee and a $5 homeless trust fund charge.

What helps a Gloucester Township house sell quickly

The township covers 22.95 square miles of land. Communities inside it include Blackwood, Glendora, Grenloch, Chews Landing, Erial, Glen Oaks, Lambs Terrace and Turkey Foot, and a listing should name the one that matches your street.

One useful first step is to pull your tax bill and any loan statements and line them up beside the closing date you want. If the house will go to a cash buyer, ask the buyer to confirm in writing who orders the fire-district certificate and who pays its fee. Those two decisions are where as-is sales most often slip.

Also decide early how you will hand over the keys. If tenants live in the house, a buyer will want to know the lease terms and whether the unit will be empty at closing, and that should be written into the contract.

Numbers that should guide your price

Gloucester Township housing and tax figures
Local figureAmount

The 2025 general tax rate is 4.179 per $100 and the effective rate is 2.703. Sales averaged about $149,000 over the average assessment, which is why recent closings, not the tax card, should set your price.

Smoke and carbon monoxide certificate

The fire district serving your street handles it, because the township is split into several fire districts. Fire District No. 4's Bureau of Fire Prevention posts the application form for this certification and accepts inspection requests by phone or email.

To find your district, search your street address in the township's property tax lookup and read the Special Taxing Districts line on the record. FIRE DISTRICT=F04 means District No. 4. The state wants the certificate in place before a one-family or two-family house is sold. Once issued it lasts six months, so time the inspection near your closing.

Alarm requirements can vary with a property's age and layout, and a failed inspection brings a list of fixes and a re-inspection. Fix the listed items quickly, since a re-check is what gets the certificate issued. Before listing, ask the township construction office if any further resale paperwork applies.

How does the tax office handle a sale?

Taxes are billed in four installments, due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, each with the longest 10-day grace period state law permits. Overdue balances earn 8 percent yearly interest up to $1,500 and 18 percent past that, and a balance above $10,000 still open at year end adds a 6 percent penalty. Current-year taxes unpaid after November 11 can go to tax sale before December 30, and anyone paying in that window must use cash or certified funds.

Two $250 deductions exist, one for qualifying seniors and disabled residents and one for veteran owners. Bill dates can move if the tax levy certification is late, so get a written payoff figure before closing.

An assessment appeal goes to the Camden County Board of Taxation, due by 4:00 p.m. on April 1 (May 1 after a town revaluation). The $25 filing fee for assessments from $150,000 to $500,000 covers the township's average residential assessment. Keep paying taxes during an appeal, or it can be dismissed.

What a seller pays at closing

Your loan payoff and the state Realty Transfer Fee are normally the biggest costs. For prices at or below $350,000 the fee starts at $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, and it is the seller's to pay when the deed is recorded. Ask your closing attorney for the exact figure before you sign.

  • Transfer fee, from the state's rate table.
  • Payoff of the mortgage, credit line or tax lien.
  • Certificate fee charged by the fire district.
  • The GIT/REP-3 residency certification attached to the deed.

Deeds are recorded by the Camden County Clerk, 520 Market Street in Camden, which accepts electronic recording. Sellers living out of state prepay at least 2 percent of the price as Gross Income Tax unless an assurance on the GIT/REP-3 applies.

Schools, roads and buses

Local public schools run from prekindergarten through eighth grade. High schoolers attend Highland Regional in Blackwood, Timber Creek Regional in Erial or Triton Regional in Runnemede, assigned by address within the Black Horse Pike Regional School District.

The Atlantic City Expressway clips the southwest corner, Routes 42 and 168 run through the west, and County Routes 534 and 544 cover the center and the northern edge. NJ Transit's 400 bus reaches Philadelphia, and the 403 and 459 serve local trips.

Selling a rental or a house with liens

Landlords register through a Landlord Identity Registration form on the township's downloads page, so confirm yours is current before listing. Renters live in about 27 percent of homes at a typical rent of $1,592, so a tenant-occupied sale is nothing unusual. The fire certificate also applies to a lease or change of occupancy.

Liens do not block a sale as long as the price covers every payoff. That includes a mortgage, credit line, tax lien or pending foreclosure. Ask each lender and the tax collector for written figures, because tax sale charges add fees beyond the posted tax total. Have those numbers before you accept an offer, so the closing statement holds no surprises. On the day of closing the attorney or title company pays off each lender, records the deed with the transfer fee and GIT/REP form, and sends you the remaining proceeds.

Does Gloucester Township require a resale certificate of occupancy?

The certificate you need covers smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and comes from the fire district for your address. The construction office can say whether anything else applies.

How can I tell which fire district my house is in?

Search your street address in the township's property tax lookup and read the Special Taxing Districts line. F04 means Fire District No. 4.

What are the Gloucester Township tax due dates?

February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, each with a 10-day grace period. Late balances accrue interest, and unpaid current-year taxes can go to tax sale after November 11.

By when must I appeal a Gloucester Township assessment?

Before 4:00 p.m. on April 1, or on May 1 if the town did a revaluation or reassessment. The county Board of Taxation sits at 509 Lakeland Road in Blackwood and offers a summary hearing with no appearance needed.

May I sell a Gloucester Township house with liens or a foreclosure pending?

Yes, if the sale price covers every payoff. Request written figures from each lender and the tax collector, because tax sale charges add fees on top of the posted tax total.

What makes selling a house in Pennsauken different?

Pennsauken requires a housing resale inspection and a fire certificate on every one- and two-family house before settlement. The inspections happen on the township's schedule, so owners who plan around them close with fewer surprises.

The township sits in Camden County directly across the Delaware River from Philadelphia, joined to the city by the Betsy Ross Bridge. It had an estimated 37,742 residents in mid-2025. The typical owner-occupied home is valued at $232,900, owners occupy 73.9 percent of homes, and median gross rent is $1,209. Median household income is $87,680, and households average 2.87 people across 12,900 homes.

Housing resale inspection

Township ordinance calls for an interior and exterior inspection plus a Certificate of Occupancy before settlement. The Building Department's packet lists a combined $175 fee, made up of $100 for the housing resale certificate and $75 for the fire certificate.

Sellers send both forms and payment to the Building Department, then wait about two to three days after the visit for a written report. The housing office takes scheduling calls at 856-665-1000, extension 145, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Certificates cover one change of ownership or six months, whichever ends first. The application also asks whether the buyer plans to flip the house, rent it or live in it, and whether the property is vacant, rented or owner-occupied.

If the report lists repairs, the buyer may sign a notarized affidavit for a temporary certificate, accepting the report and responsibility for the final certificate. When the report forbids occupancy before a final certificate, the temporary version covers work only. Open construction permits must be inspected and closed first, and missed permits can push back a settlement date.

Which fire safety items does Pennsauken check?

The fire certificate looks at alarms and extinguishers, with smoke alarm rules that depend on the year the house was built.

  • Before 1975: sealed 10-year battery alarms only.
  • 1975 to 1977: a hardwired detector on the top level and sealed battery alarms elsewhere.
  • 1977 to 1983: interconnected hardwired alarms on the top level and in the basement, battery alarms on other levels.
  • 1983 to 1991: interconnected hardwired alarms on every level.
  • 1991 on: interconnected hardwired alarms with battery backup on every level and in each bedroom.

A carbon monoxide alarm must sit within ten feet of every sleeping area, and combination units are accepted. At least one extinguisher rated 2A:10-BC, no heavier than ten pounds, must hang within ten feet of the kitchen with its top three to five feet above the floor, and carry a service tag from the last 365 days or a dated receipt if new.

  • Systems: roof, plumbing, mechanical and electrical certifications, hazard checks, at least two outlets per room except bathrooms, and GFCI protection near sinks and outdoors.
  • Records: open permits and occupancy limits, such as minimum room widths and bedroom access.

Rental registration and a lead paint visual assessment application sit on the same housing forms page, so a house that has been a rental may need extra paperwork. With 13.59 percent of the township's area water, buyers often ask about drainage and basement history, so have those answers ready. A short written history of any water problems and repairs makes a buyer's inspector easier to deal with.

Taxes and recording in Pennsauken

The township mails one bill each summer. It combines a final bill for the current year and a preliminary bill for the next, with four stubs due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. Late payments after the grace period, usually the 10th, accrue interest from the due date at 8 percent on the first $1,500 and 18 percent above it, and a December 31 delinquency over $10,000 adds a 6 percent penalty.

Office hours at 2400 Merchantville Avenue run 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. weekdays, with a drop box outside. Online payments carry a processing fee set by the provider, not the township. Owners who change mailing address should tell the assessor.

Deeds are recorded at the Camden County Clerk's office, Room 102, 520 Market Street in Camden, phone 856-225-5300. Electronic recording and online record searching are both available. Sellers who live in New Jersey use the residency certification form with the deed, and a co-signer who gets no proceeds can use the no-net-proceeds box, entering zero consideration. The seller also owes the state transfer fee at recording.

Timeline for a Pennsauken closing

Work backward from the closing date. Send the resale and fire forms with payment to the Building Department as soon as you have a signed contract. Allow about two to three days after the visit for the written report, and schedule the inspection close enough to settlement that the six-month certificate does not expire first.

Before the visit, confirm that open construction permits are closed, because the packet warns they can delay settlement. Check alarms against the year the house was built, and hang a fire extinguisher with a current service tag within ten feet of the kitchen. Ask the tax office for your open balance across all four stubs, then line up the deed with the Camden County Clerk through your attorney or title agent.

If the report lists repairs you would rather not make, talk to the buyer about the notarized affidavit for a temporary certificate.

When is a cash sale practical in Pennsauken?

Cash tends to suit a house that cannot pass the resale report without major work, a vacant property that has sat, or an inheritance the heirs want settled. The buyer can sign the affidavit for a temporary certificate and take over repairs, which lets the closing proceed.

Ask every buyer who pays the $175, who books the inspection, and how long the offer stands if the report is long. Judge offers by your net after repairs and carrying costs.

Does Pennsauken require an inspection before I sell?

Yes. All one- and two-family dwellings need a housing resale inspection and a Certificate of Occupancy before settlement, and the Building Department lists a $175 combined fee with the fire certificate.

Can the buyer take responsibility for repairs in Pennsauken?

Yes. A buyer who accepts the report can sign a notarized affidavit for a temporary Certificate of Occupancy and take on the listed items. If the report bars occupancy, the temporary certificate covers work only.

How long is a Pennsauken resale certificate good for?

It covers one change of ownership or six months, whichever comes first. Schedule the inspection close enough to settlement that the certificate does not expire first.

When are Pennsauken property taxes due?

The stubs are due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. A grace period, usually to the 10th, applies before interest runs back to the due date.

Where do I record a deed for a Pennsauken sale?

At the Camden County Clerk, Room 102 at 520 Market Street in Camden. Electronic recording is also accepted, and the office can be reached at 856-225-5300.

Selling fast in Voorhees

The Voorhees housing market

Voorhees covers 11.47 square miles of land in western Camden County and has 31,571 residents. Most of the housing stock went up in the decades when the population climbed from 12,919 in 1980 to 24,559 in 1990, so many houses are now old enough to need roofs, boilers and updated systems. Unpermitted work is the usual snag. A finished basement, deck or converted garage built without a permit can hold up the certificate until the permit is closed or the work removed, so pull your permit history before you sign a contract.

Your closing attorney sends the transfer fee affidavit in with the deed, because the county clerk may turn away a deed that arrives incomplete.

Assessments and appeals

Disputes over a Voorhees assessment go to the Camden County Board of Taxation, 509 Lakeland Road in Blackwood, phone 856-225-5238. Camden County keeps the regular calendar: April 1, or May 1 after a municipal revaluation. A property valued above $1,000,000 can go straight to Tax Court.

Evidence from comparable sales carries the day at the board, not your own view of fair value. A seller who is about to close gains little from filing, but a buyer or heir who keeps the house could. Which elementary school a street feeds is a question buyers raise early, so have the answer ready from the school district before you list.

A cash buyer does not need a mortgage approval or a lender's appraisal, so the sale avoids the repair demands that often come with a loan. You still owe the township sign-off, the state's closing forms and the transfer fee, and the deed still goes through your closing attorney.

The practical order is simple. Pull your permit history and close open permits. Call the construction office about the certificate and book the inspection. Ask the buyer for proof of funds and a closing date in writing. Then have your attorney review the contract, including who pays for any item the township flags. April 1 in Camden County, or May 1 after a revaluation. Use Form A-1 and call the Camden County Board of Taxation in Blackwood at 856-225-5238.

What a Winslow sale requires

A Winslow closing depends on two separate approvals: a township resale certificate from the Construction Official and an alarm certificate from the Winslow Township Fire District. The township is the largest in Camden County by area, and much of its land lies in the Pinelands, which affects some lots and buyers.

This page covers market figures, both inspections with their fees, the Camden County filing and the township's tax rules, and ends with a plain comparison of an agent listing, a sale by yourself and an as-is cash buyer.

Winslow housing and prices

The 2020 census put Winslow at 39,907 people, and the mid-2025 estimate is 40,562. Those residents are spread across 57.42 square miles of land, only 695 per square mile, which fits the pine woods and farm parcels between its villages. Communities include Sicklerville, Cedar Brook, Blue Anchor, Tansboro, Braddock, Albion and Williamstown.

The Pinelands and large lots

Much of Winslow is protected land, and the New Jersey Pinelands span 1.1 million acres. For a large lot, or a buyer who plans a new structure, call the Pinelands Commission at (609) 894-7300 and ask which approvals apply before you promise anything in a contract.

The Winslow resale certificate

Under Chapter 205 of the township code, retitled Resale Certificates by a February 2025 ordinance, every existing dwelling needs a certificate of continued occupancy before occupancy changes. Applicants go to the Township Construction Official, who inspects for habitability and compliance with the code.

  • Residential applications cost $100.
  • Payment by check triggers a 10 working-day wait before the inspection.
  • The Construction Official has 10 working days from a complete application and fee to inspect and then issue the certificate or list the violations.
  • The first reinspection is free, and each later one costs $50.
  • No one may occupy the dwelling until life-hazard violations are corrected.
  • Violating the chapter carries a penalty from $250 up to $1,000.

The ordinance has an unusual option. A buyer can assume the seller's duty through a written waiver acknowledging responsibility for the certificate, and the waiver is filed with the Construction Official.

What happens at the fire inspection

State law calls for an alarm inspection before a home is sold, and the Winslow Fire Prevention Division performs it. A firefighter sprays test smoke into each smoke alarm, presses the carbon monoxide test button and checks for a secondary power source label. A passing house earns a certificate to carry to settlement.

  • The fee is $65 with eight or more days of notice, $100 with four to seven days and $150 with three days or fewer.
  • A senior aged 62 or older with proof of age pays $30.
  • Reinspections and missed appointments cost $35 each.
  • Alarms past ten years of age must go, and the manufacture date is printed on the underside of each device.
  • Solar panels, a generator or battery storage call for a permanent printed label at the panel and meter warning of multiple sources of power.
  • The fire district will not go in on a lockbox, and its office says it answers online applications within 24 hours.

An all-electric house with no fireplace or attached garage needs only smoke alarms. Questions about your layout go to the Fire Marshal at 609-561-4225.

Recording the deed and paying taxes

Camden County's Clerk records Winslow deeds from Room 102 at 520 Market Street in Camden, phone (856) 225-5300. The clerk offers electronic recording and appointment booking, so a title company can usually file on your behalf.

Tax installments come due on the first of February, May, August and November. A ten-day courtesy period follows, but the collector must physically hold the payment by the end of the tenth day, since postmarks do not count. Delinquent amounts up to $1,500 carry 8 percent interest and larger ones carry 18 percent, and a balance above $10,000 at year end adds a 6 percent penalty. Anything left in the township drop box counts as received the next business day.

Added and omitted assessment bills go out in October and fall due November 1. The township holds a tax sale each October, and taxes and utility charges attach to the property itself. Request a payoff figure from the tax office before closing.
