Hills, flood zones and what buyers inspect

The township is shaped like an inverted L, with the Hudson River on its eastern edge facing Manhattan and the Hackensack River on the west toward Carlstadt. The Palisades rise from the waterfront, and a steep slope on the west side drops toward the Meadowlands.

Steep driveways, retaining walls and stairs up to the front door are features a buyer will want to inspect, so photograph and describe them honestly. Low-lying ground on the west side is part of the New Jersey Meadowlands, so ask your insurance agent whether your parcel sits in a flood zone before you quote a closing date.

Of 64.74 miles of road, the township maintains 50.00, Hudson County 7.85, the state 5.49 and the Turnpike Authority 1.40, so a complaint about a street goes to a different office depending on who owns it.

Neighborhoods to name in a listing

Name the section, since housing type and transit access vary across the township.

  • Bergenline Avenue, a commercial strip with more than 300 stores and restaurants.
  • The Racetrack section, on the plateau between Bergenline Avenue and Kennedy Boulevard.
  • Bergenwood, clinging to the west-facing slope of the Palisades.
  • New Durham, near the Bergen Turnpike and Tonnelle Avenue.
  • Meadowview behind the Municipal Building, and Babbitt out in the Meadowlands.
  • Bulls Ferry and Woodcliff, toward the Hudson and North Hudson Park.

About 71.4% of residents are Hispanic or Latino and 74.5% of residents age 5 and up speak another language at home, so Spanish-language listings can reach a large share of local buyers.

Transit and commuting

Commuters buy here for buses and light rail. Route 495 links the Lincoln Tunnel with the Turnpike, and NJ Transit lines such as the 121, 125, 127 and 128 terminate at Midtown Manhattan's Port Authority terminal. Jitneys on Bergenline Avenue can run as often as one a minute. The Hudson-Bergen Light Rail stops at Tonnelle Avenue and reaches Weehawken, Hoboken, Jersey City and Bayonne.

Residents take 33.1 minutes on average to reach work, so a block near a bus line or a light rail stop is worth highlighting in your description.

Rent control and short-term rentals

The township runs its own rent control program, and its office explains which apartments are covered, the legal base rent, capital improvement surcharges and annual registration. Files on residential properties are open for public inspection. The yearly increase is 2.5 percent of base rent, allowed once in any twelve months, with at least 30 days' notice to tenants after approval.

Renovations go through the Rent Control office, with inspections before and after. Ask the office whether your building is covered before you hand a buyer a rent roll.

Short-term rentals are tightly restricted. Ordinance 610-23, adopted September 20, 2023, bars them for anyone who had not registered a dwelling by September 6, 2023. Do not market a house on the strength of Airbnb income unless it already holds a registration certificate.

Code Enforcement and certificates of occupancy

The township's Code Enforcement office inspects and issues residential and commercial certificates of occupancy, and it investigates illegal occupancy. The number is 201-392-2051. The township website also lists a Residential Owner Certificate form and an illegal apartment hotline, so ask whether any unit count in your deed differs from what is actually in the building.

If a mortgage goes into default, Ordinance 325-17 has the lender inspect the house and register it with the Building Department within 10 days, stating whether it is vacant or occupied. Owners facing default can ask that department how the registration works.

Fees, forms and the Hudson County recording office

The state's realty transfer fee falls on the seller. A deed from an executor or administrator to an heir or devisee under a will or intestacy law is exempt, which helps with inherited houses, and so is a deed recorded within 90 days after a divorce decree. Prices above $1,000,000 add a graduated percent fee, 1% up to $2,000,000 and more above that.

A seller or heir who lives out of state prepays at least 2% of the deed price toward state income tax. The estimate is 10.75% of the gain when that comes out higher.

Hudson County deeds go to the Hudson County Register of Deeds and Mortgages at 257 Cornelison Avenue, second floor, in Jersey City. Cashier and search hours run weekdays from 9:00 am to 2:00 pm, and phones are answered from 8:00 am to 3:45 pm at 201-395-4760. The Register also runs a free Recording Notification Service that warns owners when a document is filed against their property.

A sensible order of steps

Start with paper. Pull the deed, the tax bill, the certificate of occupancy and, for rentals, the rent control registration and leases. Call Code Enforcement if the unit count in the deed may not match the building, because an unapproved apartment is easier to deal with before an offer than after one. Keep the lease copies and rent ledgers where you can find them, since a buyer's attorney will ask for them in the first week.

Next, decide how the house will be sold. A buyer paying cash can take it with its flaws, including hillside stairs or an old addition, and can often close on your schedule. A buyer relying on a mortgage brings an appraisal and a lender's checklist. Whichever you choose, your attorney or title company files the deed and the seller's residency form at the Hudson County office in Jersey City.

Frequently asked questions

Is a North Bergen house with an unapproved apartment sellable?

A sale can go ahead, but tell buyers up front. The township's Code Enforcement office investigates illegal occupancy and keeps an illegal apartment hotline, so call 201-392-2051 and ask what a buyer or lender will need before closing.

Does the township control rents?

Yes. The Rent Control office administers the ordinance, which allows an annual increase of 2.5 percent of base rent, once in twelve months, with at least 30 days' notice to tenants. Covered rentals must register.

May a buyer turn my house into an Airbnb?

Generally no. Ordinance 610-23 ended new short-term rental registrations after September 6, 2023, and only dwellings holding a registration certificate by then are grandfathered. Confirm with the township before advertising it that way.

Is the transfer fee owed on an inherited house?

Start with the fire prevention certificate

Raritan will not let a house close without a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate from the borough fire prevention office. Book it the week you sign a contract, because everything else on your closing calendar waits on it. The same office also inspects rentals, so a house with a tenant adds a second set of paperwork.

Raritan is a small Somerset County borough on the Raritan River. It had 7,835 residents in 2020 and an estimated 8,516 in July 2025, an increase of 8.7 percent. The borough covers only 1.99 square miles of land, so lots are small and buyers judge a house that needs work against the neighbors within a block or two. About half of households own their home (49.9 percent), which means plenty of landlords and tenant-occupied sales.

Raritan housing numbers

Rents are well above the national figure and the typical owner-occupied home is worth more than the national midpoint, so a repaired house has a real market here.

The borough has 3,326 households averaging 2.50 people. About 42.7 percent of residents age five and older speak a language other than English at home, so listing material and disclosure forms often need to reach buyers in more than one language.

What the fire prevention office checks

The borough fire prevention office handles smoke detector certification for the sale of dwellings. Older homes with battery detectors need one on every occupied level. Homes with hard-wired interconnected detectors must have every unit sound together when one is tested.

  • A carbon monoxide detector must be mounted within 10 feet of every sleeping area, and a house with bedrooms on more than one level needs more than one.
  • Fire detection systems must be inspected every year under state rules, so a house with a monitored alarm needs its alarm company or an electrician to put the system on test during the visit.
  • New Jersey dropped the portable fire extinguisher from resale inspections effective February 3, 2025. Ask the office which items it checks before you buy one.

Fire code violations in Raritan have no statute of limitations, so one that turns up late must still be corrected. Talk to the office before you pick a closing date. If a device fails, replace it and rebook promptly.

Selling a rental or two-family house

The Property Maintenance office keeps the register of rental properties and inspects each rental unit before it is reoccupied. Own a duplex or a house with a renter? The buyer's attorney will want proof that the unit sits on the register and passed its inspection.

The same office responds to complaints about upkeep on residential and commercial buildings and enforces the rules for putting out trash, recycling and bulk items. A complaint still open against your address can hold up the closing. Phone the office and find out if one exists.

Before you call, collect the rental registration, the date of the last inspection, the names on the lease and any notice the borough sent about the building. One folder with all of it lets your attorney answer a buyer in a single reply.

How do I appeal my Raritan assessment?

Somerset County sets April 1, 4:30 p.m., as the deadline for an assessment appeal from Raritan to reach the county tax board. File a paper petition with the fee, by mail or at the office, and send copies to the municipal assessor and the municipal clerk.

The thing you contest is the assessed value. The board starts from the assumption that the assessment is right. Your job is to show otherwise with comparable sales from the year before the October 1 assessment date. Taxes and charges also have to be current through February 1 of the hearing year, or the board can throw the appeal out.

The Somerset County Tax Board is at 27 Warren Street, fourth floor, Somerville, and its number is 908-541-5701. An added assessment appeal, for new construction picked up mid-year, has a December 1 deadline.

Closing costs and tax forms

New Jersey charges the seller a Realty Transfer Fee, collected as the deed goes on record. Each band of the state schedule applies only to the part of the price inside that band, so the bill climbs with the sale price. Ask your attorney or title agent for the exact number before closing day.

A landlord who lives outside New Jersey fills out a GIT/REP-1 at the closing table unless a seller assurance covers the sale. The prepayment is the gain times 10.75 percent, with a floor of 2 percent of the deed price. Residents of the state sign the GIT/REP-3. If a county clerk refuses a deed, go back to that clerk, then to the state GIT/REP unit at 609-322-9275.

What to have ready for the closing attorney

A complete file on day one shortens a Raritan closing. Gather these before you sign.

  • The fire prevention certificate, or the appointment date if the visit has not happened yet.
  • For a rental, the borough registration and proof of the last unit inspection.
  • Any permits for work done on the house, with the final sign-off.
  • Your current tax bill, and a note of whether taxes are paid through the quarter due.
  • Your residency status for the GIT/REP form, since an owner who lives out of state follows a different path from a New Jersey resident.

Cash buyers move as fast as the paperwork does. Mortgage buyers add an appraisal and underwriting, and an unclosed permit or missing detector tends to stall there.

How a cash sale changes the Raritan steps

An as-is cash offer removes the lender's appraisal and repair list. It does not remove the borough's certificate, and the seller normally still arranges it.

The order is short: contract, call to the fire prevention office that day, repairs to any missing detector, passed visit, certificate to the attorney. With a tenant in place, raise the rental registration with Property Maintenance in the same week. Selling for cash also tends to mean fewer showings, which matters when tenants live in the house and every visit disrupts them. Agree on a closing window up front so the certificate, the payoff of any balance and the handoff of keys all land on the same week.

Frequently asked questions

Does Raritan require a certificate of occupancy to sell a house?

The borough fire prevention office certifies smoke detectors for the sale of dwellings, and that is the document you need. Ask the borough whether any other resale paperwork applies to your address.

What smoke alarm rules apply to a Raritan sale?

Every occupied level needs a working smoke detector, and hard-wired interconnected units must all sound together. Carbon monoxide detectors go within 10 feet of each sleeping area. The state removed the fire extinguisher item from resale inspections on February 3, 2025.

When is the Raritan appeal deadline?

April 1 at 4:30 p.m. Hearings come later in the year. Added assessment appeals are due December 1.

Who inspects rentals in Raritan?

The borough's Property Maintenance office. It keeps the rental register and inspects each unit before it is reoccupied, so a seller with a tenant should confirm the unit is on the register.

Who pays the transfer fee on a Raritan sale?

The seller pays it when the deed is recorded with the county clerk. The amount rises with the price, and your closing attorney can quote it.

Match the method to your deadline. East Windsor owners can work with an agent, go it alone, or take a cash offer, and the best fit depends on condition, tenants and timing. The township adds a step of its own: a fire prevention check of smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and an extinguisher before a single-family home or condominium is sold.

  • Working with an agent: reaches financed buyers, and takes the longest.
  • Going it alone: you handle price, contract and the township check yourself.

The township fire inspection

The Bureau of Fire Prevention checks smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and the fire extinguisher before a sale. Start by completing the Fire Inspection Form, then deliver or mail it with a $50 check or money order payable to East Windsor Township. Cards are refused, and the township asks for a week to process. A call follows to set the inspection, held mornings on varying days.

The resulting certificate lasts 60 days, so fix a closing date before booking. The inspector reviews how well the detectors work and how old they are, the extinguisher, the record of work and site conditions. Smoke detectors may be no older than 10 years and carbon monoxide detectors no older than 7, going by the manufacturer's label. A 2A10BC extinguisher with this year's tag must be in the kitchen, though it need not be mounted. Do not count on the inspector coming back quickly after a failure. Failing means repeating the process and paying a $25 re-inspection fee.

The township answers at 609-443-4000, extension 406, from the Municipal Building at 16 Lanning Boulevard.

Does East Windsor require a Certificate of Occupancy at resale?

The township's Certificate of Occupancy page names three residential triggers: new construction, additions, and reconstruction after fire, storm or vehicle damage. A plain resale is not one of them. The Construction Department also issues continued certificates and certificates of approval, so ask whether anything applies to your property, particularly if a reconstruction job never received a final sign-off.

For a rented house, owners are sent to the East Windsor Health Department at extension 416 for lead-based paint inspections in rental dwellings.

Highways and transit

Turnpike Exit 8 is inside the township and feeds Route 33 and Route 133, the Hightstown Bypass. U.S. Route 130 crosses the western part, with county routes 535 and 539 adding local links. Suburban Transit's 300 line goes to Port Authority in Midtown and its 600 line to Wall Street. The nearest NJ Transit rail stop is Princeton Junction, with a rush-hour shuttle, and Mercer County runs a shuttle along Route 130. The average commute is 26.8 minutes. Penn Medicine Princeton Medical Center is about 7 miles away in Plainsboro, which buyers sometimes ask about.

One district, East Windsor Regional School District, serves East Windsor and Hightstown. Name the school for your street in the listing, since buyers with children ask early.

What an East Windsor seller pays and where the deed goes

The state realty transfer fee is the seller's. The Mercer County Clerk's page adds that the graduated charge on sales of $1 million and up, starting at 1 percent, moved to the seller as of July 10, 2025.

A sensible order of steps

For a fast East Windsor sale, work backward from the date you want to close. Fix the closing date first, because the township certificate lasts only 60 days. Mail or drop off the Fire Inspection Form with the $50 payment about a week and a half ahead so the township has its week to process and the inspection can be scheduled. Replace any smoke detector older than 10 years, any carbon monoxide detector older than 7, and put a 2A10BC extinguisher with a current tag in the kitchen, so you pass the first time and skip the $25 re-inspection.

In parallel, ask your attorney or title agent to prepare the deed and the GIT/REP certification, and ask the Construction Department whether a past rebuild or addition needs a final certificate. Cash buyers can close as soon as these items are finished, while a mortgage buyer adds an appraisal and lender timeline on top.

If tenants live in the house, tell them about the inspection date in advance, since the inspector needs access to the kitchen and to each level with detectors. A vacant house is simpler to schedule, which is one reason owners of empty inherited properties often prefer a cash sale. Keep the receipt for the $50 payment and the certificate itself in the same folder as your closing documents, because the buyer's attorney will usually ask to see both. If the closing slips past 60 days from the inspection, plan on repeating the process, so it is better to book the inspection late than early.

Yes for a single-family home or condominium. The Bureau of Fire Prevention certifies detectors and an extinguisher before the sale, at $50, with a certificate good for 60 days.

What detector ages does East Windsor accept?

Smoke detectors up to 10 years old and carbon monoxide detectors up to 7, going by the manufacturer's label. The kitchen also needs a 2A10BC extinguisher with a current-year tag.

What if the East Windsor inspector fails my house?

Fix the items and run the process again with a $25 re-inspection fee. The certificate expires after 60 days, so book early enough to leave room for a second visit.

Will a resale in East Windsor require a Certificate of Occupancy?

The township's residential list covers new construction, additions and reconstruction. If your house was rebuilt after a fire or storm, ask Code Enforcement whether a final certificate was issued.

Who files an East Windsor deed?

The Mercer County Clerk. A regular deed runs $43 for page one and $10 for each page after, and the transfer fee has to arrive by an accepted method such as cash, cashier's check, money order or attorney trust account.

Drainage and the inspection

Rain is frequent in Ewing, so inspectors look hard at grading, drainage, roofs, gutters and foundation walls. Pointing a downspout away from the foundation costs little and takes an easy objection off the table.

What does Ewing's resale inspection check?

Every dwelling or commercial building offered for resale must be inspected and approved by the Ewing Division of Housing. The residential fee on the township's 2025 form is $125. State residents sign the GIT/REP-3 at the closing table. An owner living out of state prepays at least 2 percent of the price unless an exemption applies.

Steps for a quick sale in Ewing

The inspection sets your timeline, so book it first, through the portal or the Construction Office. Ask what the inspector will check at your address. Handle the cheap fixes yourself: alarms, extinguisher, outlets and handrails. Close open permits, and get the well water certificate if you have a well.

After the Division of Housing signs off, your closing attorney drafts the deed and the transfer fee and GIT/REP paperwork. Take the deed, your newest tax bill and a mortgage payoff figure to the first meeting. Recording costs $43 for the first page of a regular deed and $10 per added page. The transfer fee is a separate payment tied to the sale price, due when the deed is recorded.

Do I have to register a rental before selling it in Ewing?

Registration is yearly under ordinance 10-07, with forms due January 31, so it should already be on file. Landlords also need a property maintenance inspection on each tenant change. Have the paperwork ready so the buyer sees a clean record.

Can I sell a Ewing house with open permits?

Not as they stand. The house cannot pass the resale inspection until open permits are closed. The Construction Office can tell you which final inspections are still outstanding, and new repairs may need their own permits first.

Certificate of Approval before closing

Before any change in occupancy of a house or apartment, the Office of Housing Inspection and Landlord Compliance has to issue a Certificate of Approval. It confirms the building and premises meet township ordinances, and life safety comes first in the inspection.

Postcards with the new assessment go out at the end of January, so read yours before deciding to file. The county's Property Information Portal shows property record cards, sales, deeds and tax information, which helps you find comparable sales near your street. About 28 percent of occupied homes in Hamilton are rented, and typical rent is $1,634. The same housing inspection office that approves owner sales handles any change of occupancy in a house, dwelling unit or apartment. A rental passing to a new tenant or a new owner goes through it too.

Gather leases, move-out dates and repair records before you apply. A buyer who plans to keep renting the house will need approval for the next tenancy, so a clean inspection record helps the sale.

Then meet the closing attorney or title company to sign the deed and the residency or prepayment forms. The deed goes to the clerk's office on South Broad Street.

Bring your deed, a recent tax bill, any mortgage payoff statement, leases if tenants live there, and the keys. If taxes are owed, the amount is taken from your proceeds at closing, so you do not have to pay it beforehand. Water comes from Aqua New Jersey or Trenton Water Works, so confirm which utility serves the house and have a final reading arranged.

Highways and trains

Hamilton is the only New Jersey municipality hosting Interstate 95 along with both of its auxiliary routes, I-195 and I-295, plus U.S. Routes 130 and 206 and Routes 29, 33 and 156. With the Mercer County Board of Taxation at 640 South Broad Street in Trenton by April 1. Appeals over added or omitted assessments are due December 1.

No, it does not test houses for lead on request. A seller who wants a test has to hire a private inspector.

Selling in Lawrence Township

Lawrence Township sits in Mercer County between Trenton and Princeton. Begin there, because it often takes longer than the rest of the paperwork combined.

The July 2025 population estimate is 34,165 on 21.73 square miles of land, up from 33,077 in the 2020 count. Most addresses carry a Lawrenceville mailing label, while some use Princeton or Trenton. Put the legal municipality, Lawrence Township, on any contract so the township's rules clearly apply regardless of the postal name.

Housing numbers and neighborhoods

Owners live in about two thirds of Lawrence homes. Median household income is $130,142, well above the $80,734 national figure, and a typical owner-held house is valued at $439,700. Rent and ownership costs sit close together: gross rent is about $2,020 a month and owners with a mortgage pay $2,933. Buyers look at the commute first, and the average one-way trip is 28.7 minutes. Interstate 295 loops through the township and U.S. 1 splits it, while U.S. 206 (Lawrence Road) is the main local artery from Trenton to Princeton. County routes 533, 546 and 569 handle cross-town trips.

Certificate of Inspection for a sale

The housing office issues a Certificate of Inspection for sales, and the seller normally pays for and obtains it. It is a different document from a Certificate of Occupancy, which the Construction Official issues after new construction or a major renovation. The inspection certificate is needed before title passes, for condos and foreclosed properties too.

  • Cost and filing: $80 with the application, handed in at the office or mailed. Emailed forms and online payments are refused.
  • Scheduling: the office books a visit only after it holds the form and fee, and a slot usually opens within two weeks, though busy periods run longer.
  • Visit length: roughly 60 to 90 minutes for a house, about 30 for a condo or townhouse.
  • Validity: the certificate expires one year after the inspection. Return visits cost nothing.
  • Safety checks: alarms, detectors and extinguishers are examined in the same visit, so no separate certificate is issued.

If the inspection finds problems

A buyer can take on most violations by writing to the township, listing them and giving a repair date. Life safety items are different: they must be corrected and checked again before anyone lives there. A failed septic system or open permits fall to the seller to resolve before closing.

In an as-is or bank-owned sale the buyer may be the one to get the certificate, so settle that point in the contract. The township's Pre-Inspection Checklist lists the usual items, and walking through it a week before your visit gives you time to replace a dead smoke detector or fix a loose railing. Recording the deed in Mercer County

The Mercer County Clerk, at 209 South Broad Street in Trenton, records Lawrence deeds. A regular deed costs $43 for page one and $10 for every page after that, and the public records room keeps weekday hours from 8:30 to 4:30.

The seller pays the state's transfer fee. With a median near $439,700, many Lawrence sales fall under the schedule for prices over $350,000, and the rate rises in steps with the price. Deeds over $1 million recorded from July 10, 2025 onward carry a revised fee under a new state law, again paid by the seller.

Paperwork to gather

Lawrence buyers and their attorneys will want a short list of papers early, and most of it you already have.

  • Septic records if the house is not on sewer, since a failed system is the seller's problem to solve.
  • Permit history for decks, finished basements and additions, because open permits also fall to the seller.
  • Leases and deposit details for any tenant, along with a note on whether the buyer wants the house empty.
  • The latest tax bill and your mortgage payoff, so the closing attorney can total what comes out of your proceeds.

Handing this folder over with the contract keeps the closing on schedule.

Listing or cash sale?

A house in good shape with time for showings does well on the open market, given the Trenton and Princeton pull. A house needing repairs, occupied by tenants or facing a tight inspection date may suit an as-is cash purchase better. Whichever buyer you pick, get in writing who orders and pays for the Certificate of Inspection and how a failed item is handled.

A workable order of steps: book the inspection first, gather the survey, tax bill and any permit papers, compare written offers on price, closing date and fees, then let the closing attorney or title agent file the deed with the county clerk. A cash buyer removes the appraisal and bank approval, but the inspection certificate and recording still have to be finished before title passes, so start the township paperwork the day you decide to sell.

Is an inspection mandatory for a Lawrence Township sale?

Yes. A Certificate of Inspection must exist before title passes. It is normally the seller's job, costs $80 with the application, and lapses one year after the visit.

How soon can Lawrence Township inspect my house?

Usually within two weeks, though holidays and busy periods can stretch it. Appointments cannot be expedited, and the office books nothing until it holds the application and fee.

May a buyer assume inspection violations?

For most items, yes: the buyer writes to the township naming them and a fix date. Life safety violations still have to be corrected and re-inspected before move-in, and the seller must clear a failed septic system or open permits.

Which office takes a Lawrence deed for recording?

The Mercer County Clerk, 209 South Broad Street, Trenton. A deed costs $43 for the first page and $10 for each extra page.

Does Lawrence Township have rent control?

No, apart from a short list of affordable-housing complexes named by the housing office. Most single-family rentals and owner-occupied houses are not covered.

If the owner is an estate, the executor or administrator signs the residency paperwork, so line up the letters of authority before you list. Frequently asked questions

Is an inspection required to sell in North Brunswick?

Ask the township's Community Development department. It handles building and occupancy certificates, and staff can say whether a Certificate of Continued Occupancy or another inspection applies to your sale and how long it takes.

What is a typical home worth in North Brunswick?

The median owner-occupied value is $431,500 for 2020 to 2024. Actual prices depend on the section, condition and lot, so treat the median as a rough guide.

Where does the deed get filed?

With the Middlesex County Clerk's registry in the County Administration Building at 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick. Title companies often file electronically through the county's e-recording portal.

Is the transfer fee due if I deed the house to my child?

No, a deed between parent and child is exempt from the realty transfer fee. You still file the seller residency form, because the GIT/REP-3 has no special assurance for family transfers.

What changes if I live in another state?

You complete a GIT/REP form and, unless an assurance on the GIT/REP-3 applies, prepay at least 2% of the deed price toward New Jersey income tax. A refund is possible later if your actual tax is lower.

Where an Old Bridge seller begins

Old Bridge Township has 70,228 people in the 2025 federal estimate, and a sale there should begin with a call to the township's Housing Inspection Division. Whatever route you pick, agent, private buyer or cash, the same municipal and state paperwork stands between you and a recorded deed.

Old Bridge spreads over 38.18 square miles of land in Middlesex County, roughly 25 miles from New York City and across Raritan Bay from Staten Island. Laurence Harbor, Madison Park, Brownville and the Route 9 corridor are all different settings within one municipality, so describe your house by its section of the township, because buyers search that way.

Much of the housing stock dates from the postwar boom, when subdivisions replaced fields and the population rose from 7,366 in 1950 to 48,715 in 1970. Roofs, windows and heating systems are common repair topics at sale.

Housing numbers and commuting

Owned homes in Old Bridge are valued at $461,000 in the 2020 to 2024 figures. Roughly 70 percent of households own, and 94.4 percent of residents did not move in the past year, so many houses change hands rarely.

At 36.1 minutes, the average commute is long, so buyers weigh access to the Parkway, Route 9 and the commuter buses heavily.

What to ask the Housing Inspection Division

The township maintains a Housing Inspection Division with a requirements page of its own. Before listing, ask it whether a resale inspection applies to your address, and get the present checklist, fee and booking steps directly, since the township sets and can change them.

State fire rules add a second layer. A house with one or two units needs a smoke alarm compliance certificate, issued through the municipality and good for six months. Ask the township which office issues it for your address.

  • Close open building permits first, since an unfinished permit can hold up a municipal sign-off.
  • For a deck, a finished basement or a new furnace, find the permit and final inspection paperwork.
  • Swap out dead smoke and carbon monoxide alarms ahead of the visit.

An owner who cannot afford needed repairs may qualify for the township's Home Improvement Program, which funds health, safety and code fixes for low- and moderate-income households. Ask whether you qualify before choosing between repairing and selling as-is.

Sections, parks and flood questions

Four areas sit inside the township: Old Bridge, Madison Park, Laurence Harbor and Brownville. Laurence Harbor has a 70-acre bayfront with a boardwalk, playgrounds and fishing, and Cheesequake State Park spans about 1,600 acres.

Nearness to the bay or a park helps a listing, though homes beside the water also raise flood questions. Streams in the township include the South River, Matchaponix Brook, Deep Run and Cheesequake Creek. Collect your flood insurance history and elevation details before a buyer asks.

Old Bridge Township Raceway Park, off Englishtown Road near the Manalapan and Monroe borders, has kept kart and motocross racing, car shows and concerts. Houses near it are a different sale from houses near the bay, and buyers will ask about event noise.

Humid summers make basement moisture and attic ventilation points that buyers and inspectors check, so a dry, clean basement helps a listing.

Roads, buses and schools

About 1.9 miles of the Garden State Parkway pass through, with Interchange 120 signed for Laurence Harbor and Matawan. U.S. 9 and Routes 18, 34 and 35 also cross the township, along with county roads 516, 520, 527 and 615. Drivers reach the New Jersey Turnpike at Exit 9 in East Brunswick or Exit 8A in Monroe. Of the township's 222 miles of roadway, about 179 are municipal.

NJ Transit buses on Route 9 serve the Port Authority terminal, Newark and Jersey City, and a park and ride sits on Route 9 northbound near Ernston Road. For trains, riders drive to Aberdeen-Matawan or South Amboy on the North Jersey Coast Line.

The public school district has 14 schools, including Old Bridge High School and two middle schools, Jonas Salk and Carl Sandburg. County magnet schools also admit eighth graders from across Middlesex County.

State charges and the appeal deadline

A Realty Transfer Fee falls on the seller at recording, and the amount comes from the state's rate schedule applied to the deed price. Buyers face an added 1 percent only above $1,000,000. A seller's GIT/REP form is filed with the deed as well.

Assessment appeals go to the Middlesex County Board of Taxation in New Brunswick, where petitions can be filed online and evidence uploaded as late as seven calendar days before the hearing. April 1 is the default deadline, and the appeal covers value only, never the tax amount.

Cash can suit a house with deferred maintenance, an estate property or a short timeline. Weigh the offer against a listing's net after commissions, repairs, carrying costs and the charges above. With any buyer, put in writing who obtains the township approval and the smoke alarm certificate and who pays for repairs the inspection demands.

  • Ask what the buyer will do if the township or fire inspector finds a defect that cannot be fixed before the closing date.
  • Ask who is responsible for permits left open by earlier owners.
  • Ask for the closing date and the proof of funds in the same written offer.

Steps from first call to recorded deed

Begin with the township. Call the Housing Inspection Division, get the checklist and fee, and ask which office issues the smoke alarm certificate. Close any open permits and replace dead alarms before the visit. Once a buyer is lined up, your attorney or title company prepares the deed, the transfer fee is figured from the price, and your GIT/REP form goes in with the filing.

If a price looks wrong to you for tax purposes, the appeal runs on a separate track at the county board and covers value only. It does not hold up the sale itself.

A cash buyer who accepts the house as it stands can skip the lender's appraisal, but the township and fire paperwork still has to be sorted out. Ask the buyer to name in writing who handles it. Keep the permit closeouts, the alarm certificate and any repair receipts together so your attorney can hand them over in one packet.

Is there an Old Bridge inspection before a resale?

Ask the Housing Inspection Division what applies to your address and get its checklist and fee in writing. The state separately requires a smoke alarm compliance certificate for homes with one or two units.

How long is an Old Bridge smoke alarm certificate valid?

Six months. It is issued through the municipality, and the Division of Fire Safety requires it before such a dwelling is sold, leased or changes occupancy.

What is the Old Bridge assessment appeal date?

April 1 for the Middlesex County Board of Taxation, or May 1 after a town-wide revaluation. The challenge can address assessed value only.

What is a typical Old Bridge home worth?

The typical owned-home value is $461,000 for 2020 to 2024, against $332,700 nationally. Your own house will differ by section, age and condition.

Is the 1 percent state fee the seller's cost?

No. Buyers pay it, and only on prices above $1,000,000. Sellers owe the standard transfer fee, which has partial exemptions for qualifying senior, blind or disabled owners.

What should a seller know about Piscataway before listing?

Piscataway will not let a home change occupants without a Municipal Certificate of Continued Compliance. The requirement has applied to sales and rentals since January 1, 2019, and it is the step that most often sets the calendar for a closing.

The township covers 18.79 square miles of Middlesex County and had an estimated 62,253 residents on July 1, 2025, up 2.4 percent from the 2020 base. Values run well above the national figure of $332,700: the median owner-occupied home is $449,900, median gross rent is $2,024 and median household income is $127,832. Owners live in 63.8 percent of homes, across 17,664 households. Rutgers University's Busch and Livingston campuses lie inside the township, which keeps demand steady. Neighborhoods such as Arbor, Johnson Park, Lake Nelson, New Market, North Stelton, Riverview Manor and Society Hill appear in listings, so use the one buyers recognize.

How the Piscataway MCCC inspection works

The Community Development Department inspects each dwelling for fitness for habitation and issues the certificate if it passes. Inspections take place weekdays from 8 a.m. to noon and 1:30 to 3:30 p.m., excluding holidays, and inspectors show a township vehicle and photo identification at the door.

The township asks sellers to apply at least four weeks before closing. Applications and fees go to the MCCC office at the Public Works Center, reachable at (732) 562-2393 or mccc@piscatawaynj.org. Section 14-4 of the municipal code governs the program.

Certificate typeFee

One rule catches many sellers: if work was done without a required permit, the permit must be obtained and any open permits closed before the certificate is issued. Dig out old deck, basement and kitchen permits early.

Getting a Piscataway house ready for the MCCC

Preparation starts with paperwork, because unpermitted work holds up the certificate. The partial checklist on the township site is a guide to what homes most commonly fail, and it is not a full list of every possible reason.

  • Submit the application and fee at least four weeks before the closing date.
  • Walk the house with a permit list in hand and note anything built or replaced since you bought it. Collect permits for decks, finished basements, additions, water heaters and electrical work, and close any that are still open.
  • Plan the visit for a weekday window, and expect inspectors to show photo identification.
  • Budget for the third inspection onward, which costs $100 per unit.
  • Ask whether a temporary certificate fits your timeline if repairs will run past closing.

Older housing stock is part of the picture. The Road Up Raritan Historic District holds nine historic homes along River Road, and a house dating to 1741 operates as a county museum. Owners in or near historic areas should ask the Planning Division what local review applies before promising a buyer exterior changes.

Property taxes when you sell in Piscataway

Ask the township Tax Collector for a current statement before you set a closing date, because balances and installments change through the year. The tax office also publishes the township's rates.

In April 2026 the township announced a budget that lowered the municipal tax rate by another 4.72 percent to offset gains in property value. A lower rate does not guarantee a lower bill, since assessed values and county and school levies move too, so compare your own bill line by line.

Taxes and sewer charges can be paid online through the township website, which helps when a title company needs proof that accounts are current.

Who records the deed for a Piscataway sale?

The Middlesex County Clerk's registry in New Brunswick records deeds for Piscataway properties. The office opens weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 4:10 p.m. and asks walk-in filers to arrive by 4 p.m.; appointments are optional but get priority.

A deed must say "Prepared by" and name the drafter, show the tax block, lot and consideration, and give a record-and-return address. Signatures must be original with the names printed beneath. A re-recorded deed needs a new affidavit, a new seller's residency form and a new cover sheet. Title companies commonly file electronically through the New Jersey County Recording system instead.

State forms go with the deed. Married sellers who file a joint state return may sign one Gross Income Tax form, while unmarried co-owners each sign their own, matched to their ownership share. A nonresident seller prepays at least 2 percent of the sale price. Heirs selling an inherited house sign the form that fits their own residency. The seller also pays the state realty transfer fee at recording.

A step-by-step plan for a Piscataway closing

Work from the closing date backward. At least four weeks out, file the MCCC application with the Public Works Center office and pay the fee. Before that, collect every permit for past work and close the open ones, since that rule applies to any house.

Plan for the inspection window on a weekday, remembering that inspectors work mornings and early afternoons only, with an adult available to let the inspector in. If the house fails, fix the items and book the reinspection. Reinspection fees start with the third inspection, at $100 per unit. Should repairs run past your closing date, ask about the $125 temporary certificate once the application is filed.

In the final weeks, request the tax statement, confirm the deed details with your attorney or title company, and decide who signs which Gross Income Tax form. Keep copies of the certificate and any closed permits, since a buyer's lender or attorney may ask for them.

Is a cash sale worth considering in Piscataway?

It can be, when a house is likely to fail the MCCC inspection, has open permits or has sat vacant. A cash buyer may accept the property without the repairs a seller would otherwise fund, but the certificate still comes before any change of occupancy, and the township also offers a temporary version at $125 per unit once an application is filed.

Call the MCCC office before you sign to confirm the process for your address. Ask any buyer who files the MCCC application, who pays the fees, and what happens if reinspections run past the second visit. Because the certificate must be in hand before anyone moves in, a buyer who plans to rent the house needs one too. Weigh the offer against what you would net after repairs, the seller's transfer fee and the months a listing may take.

Yes. A Municipal Certificate of Continued Compliance is required when selling or renting a home, and the township asks for the application four weeks before closing.

How much does a Piscataway MCCC cost?

It costs $150 per unit for a single-family home, condo or townhome, $300 for a two-family, and $125 per unit for a temporary certificate. Reinspections cost $100 per unit starting with the third.

What happens if I did work in Piscataway without a permit?

The permit must be obtained and any open permits closed before the certificate is issued. Start that step early because it can hold up a closing.

Where is the Piscataway MCCC office?

It operates from the Public Works Center. Call (732) 562-2393 or email mccc@piscatawaynj.org for an appointment.

Where are Piscataway deeds recorded?

At the Middlesex County Clerk's registry at 75 Bayard Street in New Brunswick, or electronically through the county's e-recording service for title companies.

Start with the resale certificate of occupancy

Every sale in South Brunswick, whether you list with an agent, sell privately or accept an as-is cash offer, meets the same township step: a Residential Resale Certificate of Occupancy, issued before the deed changes hands. The township will not release it while any permit or inspection is still open, so sort out your permit history before anything else.

A direct sale gives up some price for speed and usually skips repair negotiations. A listing reaches the most buyers, but it adds commissions, showings and a township inspection to schedule around the sale.

What the certificate covers

Under section 22-425 of the township code, the certificate rests on a general inspection of the visible parts of the dwelling. The application confirms three things: no work was done that needed a construction or zoning permit, no permits or inspections remain outstanding, and no visible violations or unsafe conditions exist. If an inspector finds a problem, you must obtain the missing permits and satisfy the inspections before the certificate is released.

Past projects to check before you book

The application asks whether the home has had any of the following, and for the permit number if so. Anything done without a permit has to be permitted and inspected before the certificate can issue, even if a previous owner did the work.

  • Replacement central air conditioning, furnace or water heater
  • Generator or radon system
  • Addition or finished basement
  • Fireplace or wood stove
  • Shed larger than 200 square feet
  • Swimming pool, hot tub, deck or gazebo

The Building Department administers the state Uniform Construction Code and handles permits, but resale certificates go through the Zoning office. Permits and certificates of approval that come out of the process are passed to the Tax Assessor, so new work will show on the property record.

Why many homes here have replaced systems

South Brunswick grew fast after World War II and again after 1980, so many houses are old enough that a furnace, water heater or central air unit has been replaced at least once. The resale form asks about each replacement, so keep invoices and permit numbers together before you apply.

The township is a set of unincorporated villages, each with its own mail address, and buyers often search by village name. Dayton uses 08810, Kendall Park 08824, Monmouth Junction 08852 and Kingston 08528. Name the village clearly in your listing and on the application. Buyers who search by village will otherwise miss it.

When the inspector finds a problem

The inspection is visual, so it looks at what can be seen without opening walls. When something shows up, the process is simple but it takes time. You obtain the missing permits, satisfy the inspections that go with them, and then the certificate is released. Work that a previous owner did counts as yours once you hold the deed.

Ask these questions before you list. Was the finished basement permitted? Does the shed fit within the 200 square feet allowed without a permit? Did a contractor pull a permit for the water heater, or did a handyman swap it? A yes to any of these needs a permit number in hand when you apply.

If the cost of legalizing old work is high, talk to your attorney about whether the contract should shift that cost to the buyer. Some cash buyers will price the work into their offer and take the repair list off your hands, though the township still wants the permits satisfied before the certificate goes out. Ask each buyer how they plan to handle that step and who will pay the permit fees, so no one is surprised in the last week.

Who owns and buys here

The township has an estimated 47,454 residents in July 2025 and 16,770 households. Of those, 76.9 percent own their home, and the average household has 2.81 people. The middle value of an owner-occupied home is $582,700, median household income is $150,933 and median gross rent is $1,935.

About 52.7 percent of people age five and over speak a language other than English at home. Sellers who advertise in more than one language, or who hand buyers a floor plan and an inspection summary ahead of a tour, tend to avoid repeat questions.

Kingston historic district

The Kingston Mill Historic District covers 49 acres around the village of Kingston, where South Brunswick meets Princeton and Franklin Township. It includes the 1888 Kingston Mill and the 1798 Kingston Bridge. If you own an older Kingston house, ask the township Planning office whether your address lies inside the district before you plan exterior changes ahead of a sale.

State paperwork at closing

New Jersey puts the Realty Transfer Fee on the seller, collected at recording and scaled to the price stated in the deed. A deed that claims an exemption, such as a transfer between spouses or between parent and child, needs Form RTF-1. For Class 2 residential sales above $1,000,000, a supplemental graduated fee starts at 1% of the total price.

The seller also signs a Gross Income Tax residency form, GIT/REP-3 for New Jersey residents. A nonresident seller prepays at least 2% of the total consideration unless a stated exception applies. Your closing attorney or title agent will prepare the forms.

Timeline for a quick sale

Work backward from the closing date.

  1. Pull permit numbers and invoices for any replaced systems, additions, sheds or decks.
  2. Call the Zoning office and schedule the inspection.
  3. Fix any violation the inspector lists and ask for a recheck.
  4. Call the Planning office the day after the inspection passes to pick up the certificate.
  5. Check the validity window. If the sale drags past 120 days and an extension, a new application is needed.

A buyer paying cash can close inside that window without trouble. The window matters more for a listing that sits on the market. Keep a copy of the certificate in your closing folder.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Is a township inspection required before closing in South Brunswick?

Yes. South Brunswick requires a Residential Resale Certificate of Occupancy under section 22-425 of the township code. The inspection looks at visible components and checks for unpermitted work, open permits and unsafe conditions.

How long does the South Brunswick resale certificate last?

It is effective for 120 days, and the inspecting officer may grant one extension of up to 30 days. If the house has not sold by then and is still on the market, the owner must apply again.

Which township office handles resale certificates?

The Zoning office does, at 732-329-4000 ext. 7240. The Building Department handles construction permits and new construction certificates, and sends resale questions to Zoning.

Can I sell with work that was done without a permit?

The township wants the permits and inspections satisfied before it issues the resale certificate, so unpermitted work has to be brought into compliance first. Ask your attorney how the sale contract should address any cost of doing so.

Who pays the New Jersey realty transfer fee in South Brunswick?

The seller does. The state collects it at recording, and the rate rises with the price in the deed. Sales above $1,000,000 also carry the graduated percent fee, starting at 1%.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Woodbridge?
We buy Woodbridge houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

What a Woodbridge seller must clear before closing

Woodbridge Township skips the certificate of continued occupancy, yet a house still needs an alarm certificate and a sanitary sewer discharge inspection to close. The sewer check is where sellers stumble, because floor drains, sump pumps and downspouts tied into the sewer must be fixed first.

Roughly 105,000 residents live across ten communities, from waterfront flood zones to older streets in the Rahway Valley and neighborhoods beside the highways, so one inspection list lands very differently from section to section.

Woodbridge housing and prices

The 2020 census recorded 103,639 residents, and the mid-2025 estimate is 104,802. Owners occupy about 66 percent of homes, which leaves roughly a third of households renting.

Woodbridge Township housing costs and income, 2020-2024 estimates
MeasureWoodbridge
Median value of an owner-occupied home$433,000
Monthly owner cost, with a mortgage$2,758

A typical value of $433,000 lands above the $350,000 break, which moves a Woodbridge seller into the higher rate set of the state transfer fee: $2.90, $4.25 and $4.80 per $500 across the first three bands. Your closing attorney will confirm the exact amount.

Which community is your house in?

Woodbridge Township is an umbrella over ten unincorporated communities, and their 2020 populations show the scale:

  • Iselin, 20,088 residents;
  • Woodbridge Proper, 19,839;
  • Colonia, 18,609;
  • Avenel, 16,290;
  • Fords, 12,941;
  • Port Reading, 3,921, with Keasbey, Sewaren, Hopelawn and Menlo Park Terrace making up the rest.

A mailing address may say Iselin or Colonia, but the municipality that bills the tax and requires the inspections is Woodbridge Township in every case.

Transit, highways and your listing

The New Jersey Turnpike and the Garden State Parkway meet here. The Parkway covers 7.5 miles of town between Exits 127 and 132, while the Turnpike crosses for about 5.25 miles and has Exit 11. With U.S. 1 and 9 and several state routes, the road network totals 303.32 miles, 244.16 of them municipal.

Three train stations serve the township. Metropark, on the Northeast Corridor, recorded 3,702 average weekday boardings in 2025, seventh highest on NJ Transit, with Amtrak service as well. Avenel and Woodbridge stations sit on the North Jersey Coast Line, and buses 115 and 116 head to Port Authority.

Houses near Metropark or a Parkway ramp suit commuters, while houses beside the highways face road noise, so describe both plainly in a listing.

Flood risk and a Woodbridge sale

About 19 percent of the township sits inside FEMA flood hazard areas. Water wraps three sides: the Arthur Kill to the east, the Raritan River to the south and the Rahway River to the north, and some built-up land lies only five feet above sea level.

Hurricane Sandy in October 2012 struck the Watson-Crampton area beside the Woodbridge River hard, and the township afterward used the state's buyout program to purchase and remove many homes in flood hazard areas. For a house near the Woodbridge River, Heards Brook, the Raritan in Keasbey, or the Arthur Kill in Sewaren and Port Reading, expect questions about flood zone status and insurance history.

Pull together your flood insurance policy, any elevation certificate and past claim records before listing. A cash buyer cares about the same facts but can price the risk straight into an offer.

Required inspections for a resale

The township's certificate of compliance sheet says no Certificate of Continued Occupancy is required, but a smoke detector inspection applies under an ordinance from April 15, 1980, and a sanitary sewer discharge inspection under one from March 3, 1998. There is no online form, so you book by phone and need the buyer's name, address, email and phone number plus a closing date.

  • Smoke detectors must be on every level, mounted with screws, and battery models must be the ten-year sealed type since January 1, 2019.
  • Carbon monoxide detectors go within 10 feet of sleeping areas.
  • Open permits and violations must be closed before the inspector releases the certificate.
  • The owner or a representative has to be at the house for the visit.
  • The finished certificate stays valid for 60 days.

The sewer rules are where houses fail. Banned connections include roof drains and downspouts, basement floor drains, sump pumps, yard and driveway drains, and missing or cracked trap caps. Floor drains get plugged and covered with concrete, and sump pumps and downspouts must send water to the street rather than the sewer. Fix these before you request the inspection.

Recording the deed and tax due dates

Middlesex County records the deed at the County Clerk's Registry, 4th Floor of the County Administration Building, 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick. The office stays open until 4:10 p.m. on weekdays, but you must be in line by 4. Appointments are optional, though booked customers go first. A deed must include the words "Prepared by," the tax block and lot and the consideration, and a paper filing with no cover sheet draws a $20 indexing charge.

Bills are mailed every January and July, with payment dates on the first day of every February, May, August and November. The Tax Collection Office, on the first floor of Town Hall at 1 Main Street, opens at 8:30 in the morning and closes at 4:30 on weekdays, staying open until 6:30 on Tuesdays. A drop box stands in front of Town Hall. Sewer has its own bill, with the second half due October 1, and the township counts the date it receives the money, not the postmark.

Agent, solo sale or cash buyer?

An agent listing suits a well-kept house in a strong section, a cash buyer suits one with flood, sewer or repair problems, and a solo sale fits an owner who can run showings and the contract. Sewer and flood questions often tip the balance here.

  • Use an agent if your sewer connections are clean and the house shows well.
  • Go solo if you will handle the inspections and the Middlesex County recording yourself or through an attorney.
  • Pick an as-is cash buyer if the house has an illegal sewer connection, flood damage in its past, open permits or tenants, since that buyer can absorb the cost.

Whatever you choose, book the township inspection once a closing date is set, and judge written offers by the amount you keep after the transfer fee, taxes and payoff.

Steps before a Woodbridge closing

Start with the sewer. Walk the house for floor drains, sump pumps, downspouts and yard drains that feed the sanitary sewer, and fix them before calling for the inspection. Then phone the township with the buyer's name, address, email and phone number plus the closing date. Check alarm placement on every level and near bedrooms, and close any open permits.

Because the certificate stays valid for 60 days, time the visit so it has not lapsed at closing. The owner or a representative must be present. Finally, ask the Tax Collection Office for tax and sewer figures, and have your attorney or title company file the deed in New Brunswick before 4 p.m.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Must a Woodbridge house have a certificate of occupancy to sell?

No. The township says a Certificate of Continued Occupancy is not required. A smoke and carbon monoxide inspection and a sanitary sewer discharge inspection are.

What does the sewer discharge inspection look for?

It checks that no roof drains, floor drains, sump pumps or yard drains feed the sanitary sewer and that trap caps are intact. An ordinance adopted March 3, 1998 requires it before a resale.

How long does a Woodbridge compliance certificate last?

Sixty days from the inspection. Time the visit so the certificate has not lapsed by closing.

When do Woodbridge tax installments fall due?

The first day of February, May, August and November. Bills are mailed in January and July, and payments are taken in Town Hall at 1 Main Street.

Which office records a Woodbridge deed?

The Middlesex County Clerk's Registry, 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick, on the fourth floor. Weekday service ends at 4:10 p.m., and you must arrive by 4.

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Freehold, NJ sale

Sell Your Freehold House for Cash

Tell us about your Freehold house.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Freehold?
We buy Freehold houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Freehold Township or Freehold Borough?

They are different places. Freehold Township and Freehold Borough are separate municipalities with separate offices, and the township wraps completely around the borough. Check which one your deed and tax bill name before you call anyone.

The township covers 38.65 square miles of land in western Monmouth County. It has an estimated 36,052 residents in 2025, up 1.9% from the April 2020 base but still below the 36,184 counted in 2010.

Homes here skew toward owners: 83.7% of housing is owner-occupied, and 94.2% of residents lived in the same house a year earlier. For 2020 to 2024 the median value of owner-occupied homes is $553,600 and median gross rent is $2,194. Mean commute to work is 30.9 minutes.

What the township requires before a sale

Freehold Township requires both a Certificate of Continued Occupancy (CCO) inspection and a fire inspection whenever a residential property is sold or rented. File the two applications together with the Housing Department, each with its own check or money order. No cash or cards are taken.

The inspection appointment can be scheduled only after both applications and payments are in. A CCO issued for a resale is valid for up to 120 calendar days, or until occupancy changes, so do not apply so early that it lapses before closing. To schedule, call the Department of Zoning and Housing Enforcement at 732-294-2066.

CCO and fire inspection rules for resales
RequirementTownship rule
ApplicationsCCO and fire application filed together, one payment each
PaymentCheck or money order only
Validity of a resale CCOUp to 120 calendar days
Validity of a rental CCOUp to 60 calendar days
Open permitsAll permits must be closed before the CCO is issued
Well or septicHealth Department approval, 732-294-2060

What the inspector looks for

The township's checklist is mainly about safety and open permits, and buyers should still hire a private inspector. Any violation the inspector considers a safety issue must be fixed even if it is not on the list.

  • Permits: work done without permits, such as water heaters, furnaces, AC, decks, sheds, fences and finished basements, must be permitted and closed first.
  • Utilities must be on, and the house number must be six inches high and visible from the street.
  • Doors: entry doors with deadbolts need an inside thumb latch, and double-key deadbolts and slide bolts are not allowed.
  • Electrical: GFCI outlets within six feet of every sink, and covers on all outlets, switches and junction boxes.
  • Garage: entry doors need a solid core wood or steel door with a 20-minute fire rating.
  • Dryer vents must be flexible metal, and a sump pump needs its own outlet and must discharge outdoors.
  • Pools need self-closing, self-latching gates and must be running or closed.

Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are handled on the separate fire checklist. Alarms are required on every level including the basement and within ten feet of bedrooms, and detectors must be replaced every ten years.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Freehold house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What if the house cannot pass the CCO before closing?

The township offers a document called Transfer of Title, No Occupancy, which lets a closing go forward while the buyer fixes the remaining items. The state still requires every property to pass the fire inspection before the sale, so the smoke and carbon monoxide work cannot be skipped.

It runs in steps. Both applications and payments go in first, and the inspector lists deficiencies, sometimes marking the house as having too many items to list. The buyer's attorney then writes a letter on the township's sample, agreeing there will be no occupancy until a new inspection and CCO, and agreeing to hold the township harmless. After the fire inspection passes and the letter is filed, the Housing Department emails the document for closing.

After closing the buyer owns the repair list and schedules the final CCO inspection. This path suits a cash buyer who plans to renovate. Rental properties follow stricter rules: they must be registered, vacant at inspection, freshly painted and, if built before 1978, supported by a lead-safe certificate that lasts two years.

Estates, trusts and co-owners at closing

Each seller on the deed completes a GIT/REP residency form, and the Monmouth County Clerk will not record the deed without one. Married couples who file a joint New Jersey return can sign one form, but unmarried co-owners each sign their own.

  • Estates: the estate completes the form under its own residency status, signed by the executors or the administrator if there was no will. One form can carry several executors' signatures.
  • Trusts: the trustee signs for the trust, and a trustee who is also a beneficiary signs a second form in a personal capacity.
  • Percent of ownership: if one owner holds 50% and two others hold 25% each, each form shows that share.
  • LLCs and corporations complete the GIT/REP-3 and check the box for sellers that are not individuals.

For a nonresident seller, the formula multiplies gain by 10.75% but never lets the estimated payment fall below 2% of the deed consideration. Sheriff's sales and bankruptcy trust sales are the only exceptions to the form requirement.

Roads and commuting

Buyers weigh the commute first. Route 9, Route 33, Route 18 and Route 79 cross the township, along with county routes 522, 524, 527 and 537. Interstate 195 is reachable through Howell on Route 9 or Jackson on County Route 537, and Garden State Parkway Exit 100 is about ten miles east.

NJ Transit buses 131, 135 and 139 run along Route 9 to the Port Authority Bus Terminal. The nearest rail stops are Aberdeen-Matawan, Asbury Park and Long Branch, and the SeaStreak ferry from Highlands is a 25 to 30 minute drive from the east side of the township.

High school students attend Freehold Township High School or Freehold High School, both in the Freehold Regional High School District, and assignment depends on the home address.

Putting the sale in order

Send both CCO and fire applications first, because nothing gets scheduled until they and the payments are in. Close out open permits while you wait. If the house will not pass in time, ask the Housing Department about the Transfer of Title, No Occupancy document and have the buyer's attorney prepare the hold-harmless letter. Meanwhile, have each seller on the deed ready to sign the GIT/REP form, and send the deed to the Monmouth County Clerk for recording at closing.

Frequently asked questions

Does Freehold Township require an inspection when I sell?

Yes. Freehold Township requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy inspection and a fire inspection for every residential sale or rental. Both applications go to the Housing Department together, each with a check or money order.

How long is a Freehold Township resale CCO good for?

Up to 120 calendar days from the date of issue, or until the occupancy changes, whichever comes first. A rental CCO lasts only up to 60 days.

Can a Freehold Township house close without passing the CCO?

Yes, with a Transfer of Title, No Occupancy document. The buyer's attorney signs a letter agreeing there is no occupancy until the final CCO is issued, and the property must still pass the fire inspection first.

Which phone number do I call to schedule a Freehold Township CCO?

Call the Department of Zoning and Housing Enforcement at 732-294-2066. Other lines are 732-294-5109 and, for the zoning office, 732-294-2068.

Do estates in Freehold Township need special state tax forms?

They need the same GIT/REP form as any seller, filled out in the estate's name. If there was a will, the executors or beneficiaries who sign the deed sign the form; with no will, the administrator signs it.

Selling in Howell?

Ways to sell a house fast in Howell

A Howell owner can list with an agent, sell alone, or take a cash offer. Each route still passes through the township fire inspection, the one local step no seller avoids. Howell is a large, mostly single-family township in Monmouth County, so many sellers own a detached house on a sizeable lot, sometimes with older systems.

  • Agent listing: widest reach, best for a house that shows well, but appraisals, mortgage approval and repair requests stretch the calendar.
  • Private sale: you save the commission and take on pricing, contract and alarm inspection yourself.
  • Cash buyer: no lender and no repair haggling, which fits an inherited home, a vacant house or a short move deadline.

Book the Fire Bureau visit early on any route. Failing for a missing detector is the easiest delay to prevent.

The Howell housing market

Howell covers roughly 61.21 square miles, making it Monmouth County's biggest municipality by area. It borders Colts Neck, Freehold Township and Wall in Monmouth County and Brick, Jackson and Lakewood in Ocean County. Communities inside the township include Ramtown, Adelphia, Ardena, Land of Pines, Southard and Squankum. The township completely surrounds the borough of Farmingdale.

Owner occupancy is 88.8 percent, and the median owned home is valued at $507,200. Typical monthly costs are $2,846 for owners with a mortgage and $1,133 for those without. There are 19,134 households with a median income of $134,854. The 2020 count was 53,537 people, and the estimate for July 2025 is 55,156.

Horse farms and nurseries are still part of the township, so rural lots and acreage show up in local listings. A house needing work still sells, and a buyer who accepts its condition shortens the path.

Commuting and schools

Most working residents leave the township, and more than 70 percent of employed residents work outside the Monmouth-Ocean labor area.

  • Roads: Interstate 195, U.S. 9, Route 33 and Route 34 all cross the township, plus County Routes 524, 547 and 549. The Garden State Parkway is reached from I-195 and Route 33 at exits 98 and 100.
  • Buses: NJ Transit routes 131, 135 and 139 head to the Port Authority Bus Terminal. Resident-only park-and-ride lots sit at Aldrich, in Land of Pines, and in Adelphia. Belmar is the nearest train station.
  • Schools: the Howell Township district serves pre-kindergarten through grade 8 in 12 schools. High schoolers attend Howell, Freehold Township or Colts Neck High School in the Freehold Regional district depending on address.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Howell house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Fire Bureau inspection before closing

Resales in Howell need a Certificate of Smoke Alarm, Carbon Monoxide Alarm and Secondary Power Source Compliance from the Fire Bureau, 4567 Highway 9 North, second floor. Dust and test each alarm before the inspector shows up. What counts as compliant depends on the year the house was built or renovated.

Smoke alarm minimums by construction date
Built or renovatedMinimum alarms
Before 197710 year sealed battery alarms on all levels
January 1977 to September 1978Electric alarm on each sleeping level, sealed battery elsewhere
October 1978 to January 1983Electric on sleeping level and basement, sealed battery elsewhere
February 1983 to July 1984Electric alarms on all levels
August 1984 to February 1991Electric on all levels, interconnected
March 1991 onwardElectric on every level and in each bedroom, interconnected, with battery backup

Sellers often miss these details.

  • Every alarm must be under 10 years old by its manufacture date, and an electric alarm cannot be replaced with a battery model.
  • One and two family homes with a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage need carbon monoxide alarms on each sleeping level and near every bedroom door.
  • A solar array, generator or battery system calls for a printed label reading CAUTION: MULTIPLE SOURCES OF POWER within 18 inches of the main panel and the meter.
  • Street-visible house numbers at least 4 inches tall that contrast with the background.
  • Fire extinguishers are no longer part of the check for one and two family homes that change hands.

The Fire Bureau's number is 732-938-4500, extension 2900.

Property tax appeals and payoffs

Howell appeals are due January 15, not the April 1 date used in most of the state, because Monmouth County keeps its own calendar. Form A-1 goes to the Monmouth County Board of Taxation, phone 732-431-7404.

Unhappy with the board's judgment? The Tax Court of New Jersey must receive your appeal within 45 days of it. Property assessed over $1,000,000 can bypass the board and go straight to the Tax Court.

Lien redemption figures, bank code removal and prepaid taxes are all requests to the township Tax Collector. If a tax lien exists, ask for the redemption figure early, because the closing statement must show the payoff.

Deed recording and state rules

Howell deeds are recorded by the Monmouth County Clerk, which takes real property filings, offers e-recording and publishes a fee schedule. The title company ordinarily sends the deed and tax forms in together.

The state Realty Transfer Fee is the seller's cost. A house at Howell's $507,200 median falls in the over-$350,000 schedule, where the rate is $4.80 per $500 between $200,000 and $550,000. Sellers staying in New Jersey sign GIT/REP-3. Someone relocating out of New Jersey becomes a nonresident for tax purposes on this sale, and an estimated payment of 2 percent of the price or 8.97 percent of the gain may come due at the table unless an exemption covers it.

Selling a Howell house with tenants

The township keeps rental forms, including a combined rental certificate, a landlord registration for multi-unit property and a single unit rental application. Pull those filings and the current lease before you list, since buyers on either side will want to see the terms.

What a cash closing looks like

A cash buyer removes the lender's tasks but not the township's. Once a contract is signed, schedule the Fire Bureau visit, swap out any alarm past its age limit, and add the power-source label if the house has solar or a generator. If a lien exists, request the redemption figure from the Tax Collector, and let the title company draw up the deed.

Take identification, the deed, a recent tax bill, any mortgage payoff letter and the keys with you. Leaving the state? Ask the closing attorney about the nonresident estimate ahead of time so the table holds no surprises.

Frequently asked questions

What inspection does Howell require before I sell?

A smoke alarm, carbon monoxide alarm and secondary power source compliance inspection by the Howell Fire Bureau. The alarm type required depends on the year the house was built or renovated. Test and clean the alarms first, then confirm the appointment at 732-938-4500, extension 2900.

Do I need fire extinguishers to sell a Howell home?

No, for a one or two family dwelling. Extinguishers no longer come into play when ownership or occupancy changes in those homes and in attached single-family units. Alarms, carbon monoxide detectors and any power-source label do still need to pass.

Which county office records the deed on a Howell sale?

The Monmouth County Clerk. The office handles real property recordings and e-recording, and its website carries the recording fee schedule. The title agent usually bundles the deed, the transfer fee affidavit and the GIT/REP form.

Speeding up a Manalapan sale

Speed here comes from clearing the township's Housing Certification early and choosing a buyer with no long loan process. Cash offers shorten the timeline most, though a well-prepared listing can also move in a township where owners occupy nearly nine in ten homes.

The steps that most often decide the calendar are these.

  • Apply for the Housing Certification, which is the seller's responsibility.
  • Close out every open building permit before the inspection.
  • Get Health Department approval first if the house has a well or septic system.
  • Confirm the quarterly tax payment and get a payoff figure for closing.

Manalapan at a glance

Manalapan is a large township of 30.65 square miles in western Monmouth County, and it completely surrounds the borough of Englishtown. Older hamlets include Clarks Mills, Gordons Corner, Millhurst, Smithburg and Taylors Mills, and Yorketown is the largest populated area inside the township.

Manalapan is car-oriented. U.S. Route 9 runs through the northeast, Route 33 passes near the south, and County Routes 522 and 527 cross the township. NJ Transit bus 139 goes to the Port Authority Bus Terminal, and routes 64 and 67 reach Newark and Jersey City. The nearest rail stations are Metropark, Metuchen, New Brunswick and Princeton Junction on the Northeast Corridor. The average trip to work takes 43.2 minutes, so buyers study highway access closely.

Manalapan housing figures

This is an affluent township of long-time owners. Because most sellers are owner-occupants rather than landlords, the typical Manalapan sale is a family house, and the permit file matters to the buyer's attorney.

  • The 2025 estimate is 40,987 residents, and the 2020 count of 40,905 was the highest on record.
  • Owners live in 89.7 percent of homes.
  • The midpoint home value is $655,500.
  • Owners with a mortgage pay about $3,251 a month at the midpoint.
  • Households earn $152,832 at the midpoint and average 2.72 people.

Manalapan Housing Certification

The township now calls its Certificate of Continued Occupancy a Housing Certification, required when a home is sold or rented. The cost is $225, paid either in exact cash or with two separate checks or money orders: $150 for the certification and $75 for the smoke certificate. Both are payable to Manalapan Township.
