Mount the extinguisher within 10 feet of the kitchen or in the cabinet under the sink. Ask the Construction Office for the inspector's checklist and fix items beforehand, because a failed item means a re-inspection.

Open permits before the inspection

All existing open permits must be closed out before the Housing Certification inspection, and closed permits are what become part of the block and lot file. Walk through the house and list every deck, finished basement, addition, water heater, furnace or fence that was permitted or should have been.

If a permit is open, the contractor who pulled it or you as owner must schedule the final inspection. That step can take longer than the certification itself, so start with permits and only then pay for the Housing Certification inspection.

What older Manalapan houses face

Most of the housing dates from the 1970s onward, since the township grew from 14,049 people in 1970 to 40,905 in 2020. Buyers will therefore check the age of roofs, windows and mechanical systems. Schools and the Recreation Center, which covers 162 acres with tennis, basketball and sports fields, often come up before the house itself, so mention them in your marketing even if you sell for cash.

Choosing between a listing and a cash sale

A listing reaches the widest group of buyers and can bring the highest price when the house is updated, but it adds showings, a buyer's loan approval and an appraisal. A cash sale trades some price for certainty and speed, and it suits inherited houses, houses with deferred repairs and owners with a fixed moving date. In both cases the township certification and the deed filing apply.

Ask each buyer for written terms. Compare the price, the closing date, who applies for the Housing Certification, who pays for any items the inspector cites, and who covers the filing costs at the county clerk. The best-looking number is not always the largest check at closing.

What a Manalapan seller pays at closing

The seller pays New Jersey's transfer fee as the deed is filed. Above $1,000,000 a graduated percent fee joins it, starting at 1 percent of the total price, and with a midpoint value of $655,500 a good number of larger Manalapan homes can reach that range.

At the Monmouth County Clerk, a deed costs $40 for its first page and $10 for each added page, with transfer tax due at filing. A seller living outside New Jersey submits the nonresident GIT/REP form and prepays income tax estimated at no less than two percent of the price.

Property tax bills arrive in four installments, the first on February 1 and the last on November 1, and state law lets a town allow up to 10 days of grace, so ask the collector how Manalapan applies it. Because Monmouth County runs an alternate calendar, assessment appeals are due January 15; the county board of taxation answers at 732-431-7404.

What to gather before you list or accept cash

Manalapan buyers and their attorneys tend to ask for the same documents, and most are in your files already.

  • Permit records for every deck, finished basement, addition and mechanical replacement, with final sign-offs.
  • Health Department approval paperwork for a private well or septic system, if the house has one.
  • The latest quarterly tax bill, plus a payoff figure from the collector.
  • Receipts for roof, window and furnace work, since many houses here date from the 1970s onward.
  • Your mortgage payoff statement, so the closing agent can total what leaves your proceeds.

Having this folder before the first showing or cash offer cuts the back and forth that stretches a closing.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Timeline from contract to closing

Book the Housing Certification inspection as close to the closing date as the schedule allows, because the certification is good for 90 days and the smoke certificate for six months. Before the visit, close open permits, confirm Health Department approval if the house has a well or septic system, and mount the extinguisher. After the pass, collect the tax payoff, and let your attorney file the deed with the county clerk. A cash buyer removes the appraisal and loan approval, so the township inspection and permit file are what remain.

Frequently asked questions

Does Manalapan make sellers get a Housing Certification?

Yes. The township requires it on a sale or a rental, and the seller is responsible. The cost is $225 in all.

How long does the Manalapan certification last?

The Housing Certification is good for 90 days from issuance, and the smoke detector certificate lasts six months. If your closing slips past those dates, you will need to reapply and pay again, so time the inspection close to the closing day.

Do I need Health Department approval for a well or septic system?

Yes. Homes with well and septic systems must have Health Department approval before the Housing Certification is issued.

What is the Manalapan assessment appeal date?

January 15, since Monmouth County follows an alternate assessment calendar. The county board of taxation can confirm the date for your filing year.

Can a cash buyer take my Manalapan house as-is?

Yes. A cash buyer can purchase it in its present condition, though the Housing Certification inspection still has to be passed or its items handled in the contract.

Retirement communities are part of the mix. Greenbriar North has more than 750 homes, and Marlboro Greens has 341 homes built from 1986 to 1988. The township is spread out as scattered villages rather than one downtown, with Morganville and Robertsville the two largest named areas, so buyers compare streets and neighborhoods more than a town center. Many owners are long-term residents, which means older houses with original systems are common and the inspection items below deserve attention early.

Continued Certificate of Occupancy

Marlboro Township requires a Continued Certificate of Occupancy for every home sale or rental. The Zoning/Code Enforcement Division issues it, and the paperwork is available on the township website or at the zoning office. Old oil tanks and environmental records

Buyers and their lenders sometimes ask about contaminated sites, and Marlboro has some history here. The practical step for an owner is to know what is buried or stored on the lot.   • A cash purchase can fit an inherited house, a vacant property, or a house with an old oil tank or unpermitted work that would complicate a mortgage-financed buyer.

Put in writing who orders the HVAC form, the chimney inspection and the well or septic certification, and who pays for any fix the inspector requires.

Start with the zoning office. Call the number above, ask for the current application, and find out which permits on your house are still open. Open permits are the item most likely to hold up a closing, so clear them before you list.

Next, line up the contractors. Book the HVAC company and the chimney sweep if you have a fireplace, and arrange Board of Health certification if the house has a well or septic system. Then pay the fees and schedule the inspection. Because the certificate is good for 90 days, time the visit so it will still be valid on the closing date. If the inspector finds something, each re-inspection costs $75.

Keep a folder with the certificate, the HVAC form, the chimney report, any septic or well certification and the permit closeouts. Hand a copy to the buyer's attorney early, because a missing page is a common reason a closing date slips by a week or more. If the house is vacant or inherited, say so when you call the zoning office, since the person who signs the application must be able to give access for the inspection.

At closing, the title company or attorney handles the transfer fee, the residency form and the deed for recording with the county clerk. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and mortgage underwriting, which removes the most common source of delay, though the township certificate is still required.

An HVAC company fills out the heating and cooling form, a certified chimney sweep inspects any fireplace, and a house on a well or septic system needs certification from the Monmouth County Board of Health.

The seller pays it at recording, and it rises with price. Sales above $1,000,000 also pay a graduated percent fee that starts at 1 percent.

Where is a Marlboro deed recorded?

The Monmouth County Clerk records it, at the Market Yard, 33 Mechanic Street, Freehold. The fee is $40 for the first page of a deed and $10 per added page.

Should I worry about an old oil tank on my Marlboro property?

Yes, check it before listing. The state lists 39 underground storage tank contamination locations in Marlboro, so a buyer's attorney is likely to ask whether a tank was removed and whether closure records exist.

Selling in Middletown: the basics

Middletown Township sells like a large shore suburb with one gate every seller passes through: a Residential Certificate of Occupancy that must be issued before title transfers. Start that inspection early, then fit the rest of the sale around it.

The township has about 67,135 residents and 25,211 households. Roughly 85.7 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, the median owner value is $608,300, and median household income is $141,810. Workers spend an average of 34.9 minutes getting to their jobs, which fits a township built around commuter rail, ferries and the Garden State Parkway.

Addresses read "Middletown," but local descriptions use section names such as Belford, Lincroft, Fairview, Leonardo, Navesink, New Monmouth and Port Monmouth. Houses from different eras carry different electrical, plumbing and addition histories, so pull the permit record before the inspector arrives.

Certificate of Occupancy application and fees

Middletown requires a Certificate of Occupancy before transfer of title, and violators may face fines or a summons. The same form covers a sale or a rental, goes to the Housing Department at 1 Kings Highway, and asks for the block, lot, number of bedrooms and the prospective transfer date. If the house is occupied, an adult must be home for the inspection, and the visit time depends on the inspector's daily workload.

The township also lists a 60-Day Conditional Residential Certificate of Occupancy form. Ask Building & Inspection at (732) 615-2104 whether it fits a sale where the buyer plans to make repairs after closing.

What the Middletown inspector checks

The township's checklist follows the International Property Maintenance Code and is not all inclusive, so other items can be noted on the day. Open permits need a final inspection, and recent construction needs approvals before a certificate can issue.

  • Address numbers at least 4 inches high, readable from the street.
  • A water heater relief valve discharge pipe ending no more than 6 inches above the floor, in copper, galvanized, black or CPVC pipe. PVC is not permitted.
  • Ground fault outlets in the garage, outdoors, on kitchen counters, in unfinished basements and in bathrooms, plus no extension cords in place of wiring.
  • Handrails where stairs have more than four risers, and guards on any open side more than 30 inches above grade.
  • A metal flex hose on the dryer, working burners on the range and no leaks or missing shingles on the roof.
  • A debris-free yard, no peeling exterior paint, a septic system that is not visibly failing, and a self-latching 48 inch barrier around any pool deeper than 24 inches.

The Fire Prevention Office at 732-615-2270 inspects smoke detector and carbon monoxide compliance, and the Building & Inspection Department issues the certificate once every requirement is met.

Commuting and flood zones

Buyers rank Middletown by how it gets them to New York, and the township offers more than one route.

  • Ferry: NY Waterway runs from a slip in Belford, a trip of roughly 50 minutes to West Midtown, and SeaStreak sails from neighboring Highlands.
  • Roads: Garden State Parkway exits 109 and 114, Routes 35 and 36, and County Routes 516 and 520.
  • Bus: NJ Transit local routes 817, 833 and 834.

A buyer's inspector will look hard at roofs, gutters and grading in a shore town. Elevation certificates are needed for new construction in mapped flood zones, so ask the township floodplain manager whether your lot sits in one.

Property tax appeals

If you think the assessment is too high, act early because the window is short. Monmouth County follows an alternative assessment calendar, so an assessment appeal must be received, not just postmarked, by the County Tax Board on or before January 15. A separate petition goes in for each parcel, the owner needs three to five comparable sales, and hearings run from January through April. Taxes themselves cannot be appealed, only the assessment, and a change-of-assessment postcard gives 45 days to file.

Transfer fee at closing

The state charges the seller a Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded, and the amount rises with the price. Deeds above $1,000,000 add a graduated percent fee of 1 percent to 3.5 percent of the full price. Deeds between spouses, parent and child, or from an estate to an heir are among the listed exemptions.

Where a Middletown deed is recorded

Deeds for Middletown are recorded with the Monmouth County Clerk in Freehold. The fee is $40 for the first page of a deed, $10 for each additional page and $10 for a marginal notation, and transfer tax must be paid when the deed is recorded. Mortgage discharges are $30 for the first page and $10 for each added page, so ask your closing agent which pieces are being filed.

Deeds over $1,000,000 received after July 10, 2025 may be subject to a revised transfer fee under P.L. 2025, c. 69. Anyone selling a higher priced home should confirm the amount with the Division of Taxation before closing.

Sequence for a quick Middletown sale

Call Building & Inspection first and request the permit history for the house. Close any open permits, because a final inspection is required before the certificate can issue. Next, submit the application with the $150 fee and the separate $15 filing check, and ask Fire Prevention to schedule the smoke and carbon monoxide inspection.

Walk the house with the checklist above before the inspector does. Fixing a missing dryer hose, an unprotected outlet near a sink or a peeling porch rail ahead of time can save you the $75 reinspection charge. Keep an adult available on the inspection day.

On closing day the title company or attorney collects the transfer fee and sends the deed to the county clerk. Bring the certificate of occupancy, the smoke and carbon monoxide approval and any permit closeouts so the buyer's side has a complete file, including anything the township asks to see again, and nothing waits on a missing signature.

A cash buyer who takes the house as is can still need the certificate, and the 60-Day Conditional form may let repairs continue after closing. Ask the township before you sign a contract that promises a closing date.

The township application lists $150 for each house sold, plus a $15 filing fee on a separate check. A reinspection at the third inspection costs $75.

Who issues the smoke and carbon monoxide certificate in Middletown?

The Fire Prevention Office handles it as part of the Residential Certificate of Occupancy. Building & Inspection issues the final certificate once everything is met.

What is the Middletown deadline to appeal an assessment?

January 15. Monmouth County uses an alternative calendar, and the petition must be received by the County Tax Board, not just mailed, with separate paper copies to the assessor and municipal clerk.

Can a Middletown house with open permits still sell?

It can go under contract, but open permits need a final inspection before a certificate of occupancy can issue. Ask Building & Inspection for the permit history before you list.

Which office records a Middletown deed?

The Monmouth County Clerk records it. The fee is $40 for the first page and $10 for each additional page, and the seller's Realty Transfer Fee is paid at recording.

Five state routes (18, 33, 35, 66 and 71) pass through, and Garden State Parkway access comes at Exits 100 and 102. Bradley Beach station on the North Jersey Coast Line takes riders to Newark Penn, Secaucus Junction, New York Penn and Hoboken. NJ Transit buses 317, 830, 832 and 836 serve the township.

Neptune Township Schools run Gables, Green Grove, Midtown Community, Shark River Hills and Summerfield for PreK-5, then Neptune Middle School and Neptune High School.

Certificate of Inspection checklist

Selling, buying or renting without the certificate risks a fine up to $2,000 and as many as 90 days in jail. The Transfer of Title application costs $65, is non-refundable, and has the buyer swear not to occupy the home until the certificate is clear, with a fine up to $1,250 otherwise.

Before an inspection is booked, every construction permit and violation must be closed and municipal charges, meaning property taxes and sewer, must be current. An estate needs the surrogate's certificate naming the executor. The application expires after 30 days, and the home must be empty on inspection day.

  • Outside: house numbers at least 3 inches tall, no flaking paint, gutters and downspouts attached, safe railings and walks, and a trash and recycling cart left behind.
  • Inside: smoke detectors on every level, carbon monoxide alarms near bedrooms where required, GFCI outlets in kitchens and baths, and a marked furnace shut-off.
  • Unused oil tanks come out or get filled, which requires a demolition permit.
  • Wood stoves and fireplaces need a certified chimney sweep's letter.

Code Enforcement works from 25 Neptune Boulevard, phone 732-988-5200, extension 260, and the township's forms page takes online applications.

Rentals and short-term rentals

Neptune separates rentals into categories. A standard rental application is for leases of a year (365 days) or longer, and a pre-1978 building needs a lead certificate or lead inspection.

Tenants complicate a sale because the unit must be vacant when the inspector visits. Match move-out dates to your closing date, and ask Code Enforcement whether the buyer needs an owner-occupancy certificate or a rental certificate once the deed is recorded.

Taxes and assessment errors

Installments are the first of February, May, August and November, each with ten days of grace. Arrears up to $1,500 carry 8% a year and larger balances carry 18%, and a penalty of up to 6% may be added to unpaid balances above $10,000 at year end. Sewer bills come separately, on March 1 and September 1. A municipal charge still open on November 11 can be sold at tax sale.

The Tax Collector cannot adjust an assessment, so errors go to the assessor. Seniors and Social Security disability recipients can apply for property tax relief on the PAS-1 form, and forms for a military service deduction are on the Tax Office page. Call 732-988-5200, extension 251, for the exact payoff.

Deed recording in Freehold

Recording happens at the Monmouth County Clerk's main office, Market Yard, 33 Mechanic Street, Freehold, where recording runs 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays. The clerk's phone is 732-431-7324.

The fee is $40 for a deed's first page and $10 for extra pages, and transfer tax is due when the deed is recorded. A revised fee for sales over $1 million took effect on July 10, 2025 under P.L. 2025, c. 69. Confirm current numbers with your closing attorney.

Listing or direct cash purchase?

The inspection step makes a conventional sale slower when a house needs work. As-is buyers suit estate properties, houses with tenants and homes with unfinished permits.

  • Listing: broadest exposure, especially for Ocean Grove and Shark River Hills.
  • Owner sale: you keep the commission and do the paperwork.
  • Cash purchase: no repairs asked, a closing date that fits you, and the inspection still due before anyone moves in.

Subtract inspection costs, the tax payoff and closing costs from each offer, then pick the timeline you prefer.

Timeline for a Neptune sale

Work backward from the closing date. The application expires after 30 days, so do not file it too early, but file it soon enough that the inspector has an opening. Before filing, close all permits and pay any open tax or sewer balance, because Code Enforcement will not book the visit without them.

Empty the house before inspection day and leave the trash and recycling cart behind. Test each detector, check the GFCI outlets in the kitchen and baths, and have a chimney sweep's letter ready if there is a fireplace or wood stove. For an estate, bring the surrogate's certificate naming the executor.

Keep every receipt and approval in one folder for the buyer's attorney, including the permit closeouts, the tax and sewer payoff and the chimney letter. If you live far away, ask whether a relative or agent can let the inspector in, since a vacant house is required and a missed appointment only delays the closing and may require a new application.

On closing day the attorney sends the deed to Freehold, and the buyer must wait for a clear certificate before moving in. A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal, but the township still requires the certificate.

Frequently asked questions

Must a Neptune house have a Certificate of Inspection to be sold?

Yes. The township checklist lists fines up to $2,000 and up to 90 days in jail for buying, selling or renting without one, and the Transfer of Title application costs $65.

Can buyers move into a Neptune house before the inspection clears?

No. The Transfer of Title affidavit commits the buyer not to occupy the home until a clear certificate exists, and the form lists a fine up to $1,250 for doing so.

What dates does Neptune use for property tax installments?

The first of February, May, August and November, each followed by ten days of grace. Sewer charges fall due on March 1 and September 1.

Which items does Neptune Code Enforcement look at?

Permits and violations, current taxes and sewer, house numbers, detectors, GFCI outlets, the furnace, stairs, gutters and trash carts, among others. The Certificate of Inspection checklist has the full list.

Which county office records a Neptune deed?

The Monmouth County Clerk at 33 Mechanic Street in Freehold, open for recording on weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Selling in Ocean Township

Ocean Township occupies east central Monmouth County, and no buyer may move into a house there until the Housing Division has issued a Code Compliance Inspection Certificate. The requirement follows the property, so it applies to an agent listing, a private sale and a cash purchase alike.

The population is 28,088 across 10.87 square miles of land, up from 27,672 in the 2020 count. This page covers the Monmouth County township, which is a different place from Ocean Township in Ocean County. There is no central downtown. Homes cluster in three communities, Oakhurst, Wanamassa and Wayside, so people usually describe a house by its neighborhood.

A five-member council sets policy and an appointed manager runs daily administration, so permit and inspection questions go to staff offices rather than to elected officials.

Oakhurst, Wanamassa and Wayside

The township touches Eatontown and West Long Branch on the north, Long Branch, Deal, Allenhurst and Interlaken on the east, Neptune and Asbury Park on the south and Tinton Falls on the west.

ZIP code 07755 covers Oakhurst, and 07712 covers Wanamassa and Wayside. Deal Lake, 158 acres shared among seven municipalities along roughly 27 miles of shoreline, touches the township. A house near the water should be ready for questions about basement moisture, which is also something the inspector checks.

Home values and who owns

A typical owned home carries a $678,300 value in the 2020 to 2024 figures, and 62.7 percent of households own their place. More than one in five residents is 65 or older, and many houses change hands rarely, so they may be due for updates.

What the Housing Division inspects

The Housing Division covers every sale and every rental that changes hands. Sale permits must be closed before you call for the visit, post-dated checks are sent back and the office keeps weekday hours from 8:30 to 4:30. The checklist is a visual look at:

  • The outside: flaking paint, gutters and leaders, doors, windows, screens, siding, sheds, fences, trash and weeds.
  • A street number at least 3 inches tall that can be read from the road.
  • A handrail once stairs pass four risers, and a guardrail on any open porch or landing above 30 inches.
  • The inside: kitchen and bath plumbing, walls and ceilings, leaks or cellar water, outlets with covers, locks and ventilation.
  • A water heater fitted with a pressure and temperature valve and extension pipe.
  • An anti-tip bracket for stoves manufactured after 1991.

Before the visit, line up three things:

  • Close every open permit.
  • Keep gas, electric and water running on inspection day.
  • Gather a lab report if the house has its own well.

A private well needs a certified lab report that meets state environmental standards. The township also offers a lead paint information sheet.

Fire district forms

Smoke and carbon monoxide forms are separate from the Housing Division visit. Ocean Township has Fire District No. 1 and No. 2, and the township's online forms cover a smoke detector, carbon monoxide and extinguisher application for both. Ask the district covering your street which one applies.

State rules also demand a smoke alarm compliance certificate, issued through the municipality, for a house with one or two units. It stays valid for six months, so schedule the fire visit so it still covers your closing date.

State fees and the appeal deadline

Recording the deed triggers the seller's Realty Transfer Fee, and the state's schedule shows lower rates for qualifying senior, blind or disabled sellers. The buyer's extra 1 percent starts above $1,000,000, a level that most local sales will not reach with a median near $678,300.

The seller also signs a GIT/REP form that goes to the county with the deed.

Monmouth County has an assessment appeal calendar of its own. The Monmouth County Tax Board must receive a petition by January 15, or 45 days after notices are mailed if that is later, and a petition that arrives after the close of business that day is dismissed.

Roads, trains and schools

Route 18 runs through the western side and Route 35 through the east. Route 66 marks the southern edge with Neptune, and Route 71 follows the eastern boundary beside Deal, West Long Branch and Long Branch. The Garden State Parkway lies just west, in Tinton Falls. Of its roughly 132 miles of road, about 120 belong to the township. Retail gathers along the main routes, with Ocean Commons on Route 35 and Seaview Shopping Center off Route 66.

A brief piece of the North Jersey Coast Line crosses the east side, though the nearest stops are Allenhurst and Elberon. NJ Transit buses 832 and 837 serve the township, and the SeaStreak ferry terminal in Highlands is a 25 to 30 minute drive.

Expect buyers to ask which elementary school serves a given address, since the district has elementary schools in Oakhurst, Wanamassa and Wayside. Joe Palaia Park, the township's largest, hosts the July 4 event, and the township also runs a membership pool and tennis club open from Memorial Day to Labor Day.

When a cash offer fits

A cash price deserves a look when the house would struggle with the checklist and repairs are unwelcome, when it came to you through an estate, or when a firm closing date matters. Have the buyer put in writing who orders the Housing Division visit and who covers corrections.

Landlords should note that the township requires rental registration and payment before March 1. If a tenant-occupied house is being sold, agree with the tenant and buyer how the change of occupancy will be handled.

A simple order of work: close open permits, request the Housing Division visit, ask the district for the fire forms, and book the smoke alarm certificate close enough to closing that its six months still cover the date. Then your attorney or title company handles the deed and the GIT/REP form. Keep copies of the certificate, the permit closeouts and any lab report for the buyer's attorney, who will ask for them early. If the house has tenants, tell the buyer when the lease ends and whether rental registration is current, with the lease and rent history in hand.

Frequently asked questions

Must an Ocean Township house be inspected before it changes hands?

Yes. The Housing Division performs the code compliance inspection on sales and on rentals with a new occupant. Open sale permits have to be closed first, and nobody may move in before the certificate exists.

What is on the Ocean Township checklist?

A visual review inside and out: paint, gutters, a 3-inch street number, handrails beyond four risers, plumbing, leaks, outlet covers, the water heater valve and extension pipe, and an anti-tip bracket on newer stoves.

What is the Monmouth County assessment appeal date?

January 15, unless notices were mailed late enough to extend it. Monmouth, Burlington and Gloucester have this earlier date, while other New Jersey counties keep April 1.

How long does an Ocean Township smoke alarm certificate last?

Six months. The certificate comes through the municipality, and in Ocean Township the fire districts supply the application forms.

Does the seller pay the extra 1 percent state fee?

No, the buyer does, and only above $1,000,000. A seller pays the regular Realty Transfer Fee, which follows the price in the deed and any exemption claimed.

Selling quickly in Wall Township

With a median home value above $700,000, the percentage-based charges at closing deserve a close look.

Owners choose between hiring an agent, handling the sale alone, and signing with a buyer who pays cash. Each route runs through the same township offices and the same state forms, so the sections below walk through those steps.

The Wall housing market

Wall covers 30.66 square miles of land in eastern Monmouth County and has about 26,753 residents. It is a large, mostly suburban township with the named areas of Allenwood, West Belmar, Glendola, Old Mill, Allaire and Remsen Mills. The population has barely moved since 2020, which points to a settled housing stock and fewer listings.

About 83.4% of homes are lived in by their owners. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $720,400, and owners report median monthly costs of $3,162 with a mortgage and $1,378 without. Median household income is $142,768. Long ownership often ends in a downsize, an inheritance or a relocation, which is where a fast sale usually comes in.

Wreck Pond, a tidal pond on the Atlantic coast, lies on the township's edge with Spring Lake, Spring Lake Heights and Sea Girt. If your lot is near a pond or tidal stream, ask your surveyor or insurer whether it falls in a mapped flood zone, since buyers will ask.

Roads, rail and who maintains your street

The Wall Building Department enforces the state Uniform Construction Code and issues a certificate of occupancy or approval once final inspections pass. The office is at 2700 Allaire Road, phone 732-449-8444, extension 2225. The Land Use Office reviews residential zoning permit applications.

Ask both offices whether your sale needs a resale or transfer approval, what it costs, and what permits the property has on file. Fire inspections for the whole township come from the Fire Prevention Bureau, which also has an office at 2700 Allaire Road.

Staff can check that list against the permits on file and tell you quickly whether anything is open. Closing out a permit can take longer than the sale itself, so this is the first task to start, ideally before you accept an offer.

If the house sits on a private well or septic system, tell the buyer early, because a lender will usually want those systems checked. A buyer paying cash may waive that, but it is better to know the answer than to learn it a few days before closing.

Fire districts

Wall has three fire districts: West Belmar (District 1), Glendola (District 2) and South Wall (District 3). Ask the Fire Prevention Bureau which district your address falls in, and book the inspection for the sale through the Bureau at 2700 Allaire Road.

Realty transfer fee and closing forms

At a median value over $700,000, many Wall sales land in the upper rows of the state's Realty Transfer Fee chart, which shows $5.30 per $500 for the slice from $550,000 to $850,000. A residential deed over $1,000,000 also carries the seller's Graduated Percent Fee: 1% of the price up to $2,000,000, then 2%, then more, reaching 3.5% beyond $3,500,000. Form RTF-1EE goes with that deed.

Every co-owner has to fill out a GIT/REP form for the deed. Sellers who stay in the state use GIT/REP-3. If you are moving away, the state may collect a prepayment of 2% of the price or 8.97% of the gain, whichever applies. Federal law may also shield some or all of the gain on a home you owned and lived in during two of the last five years. Your attorney confirms the amounts before signing.

Because Monmouth County runs on the alternative calendar, assessment appeals are due January 15. The county board sits at the Hall of Records in Freehold (1 East Main Street, 732-431-7404). Assessments above $1,000,000 can skip the county board. Wall's township site offers an online page for tax account lookup and payment.

Bring comparable sales as evidence. Winning rarely helps a seller on the way out, though a buyer or heir who keeps the house could benefit.

Look up your account online before closing and pay any open balance, which keeps the title search clean.

A cash buyer removes the lender from the timeline, so no appraisal or loan approval holds up the closing. The township steps remain. Call the Building Department early to learn its timing, ask about open permits, and confirm the smoke alarm requirement. If an item fails, you can fix it yourself or agree in writing with the buyer on who handles it and when.

A listed sale usually takes a couple of months once showings, the buyer's loan and township inspections are counted. A cash sale can close in a few weeks. By January 15, since Monmouth County uses the alternative assessment calendar. File with the Monmouth County Board of Taxation in Freehold, or call 732-431-7404.

Budd Lake and Flanders

There is no single downtown. Budd Lake (ZIP 07828) and Flanders (ZIP 07836) are the two census-designated places, with Bartley, Saxton Falls and Waterloo as smaller localities. Route 46, the train and schools

U.S. Route 46 cuts through the center, Route 206 bypasses Netcong on the east, and Interstate 80 runs along the northern edge. The Mount Olive station on NJ Transit's Morris and Essex and Montclair-Boonton Lines connects to Hoboken, Newark Broad Street, Secaucus Junction and New York Penn Station, and the Morris on the Move bus follows Route 46 between Netcong and Dover.

One school district runs from pre-kindergarten to grade 12: Mountain View, Sandshore, Chester M. Stephens and Tinc Road elementary schools, Mount Olive Middle School and Mount Olive High School.

Fire Marshal's Private Home Inspection

The township's Private Home Inspection, handled by the Fire Marshal's Office, has to be done before a house is sold, because state rules require it. The inspector looks for a smoke detector on every level and a carbon monoxide detector within 10 feet of the bedrooms on each level.

Township ordinance section 89-1 also calls for house numbers on the front of the home and on the mailbox. The fee schedule prices the inspection by how far ahead of the change of occupant you apply, so late requests cost more. The application can be picked up at the municipal building or downloaded from the Fire Marshal's page.

  • Test or replace detectors on each floor first.
  • Mount visible house numbers.

Tax bills, rates and deductions

Installments come due on 2/1, 5/1, 8/1 and 11/1. A ten-day grace window applies, and when the tenth day lands on a weekend or holiday, payment is accepted the following business day. The 2026 residential rate is 3.657, built from a 3.547 base and a 0.11 sanitation district rate, with an assessment ratio of 66.12%. With 208.45 miles of road the township has the most of any municipality in the county. Interstates 80, 280 (which ends here) and 287 cross it along with U.S. Routes 46 and 202 and State Routes 10 and 53. Housing numbers

Payment by check or money order is due before the inspector arrives, and an adult has to be at the house.

New owners who move in before the inspection face a $500 penalty. Requests made inside ten days are not always accommodated, so file when the contract is signed. Rental properties also need a separate certification from the Housing Department.

The standard follows the year the house was built or last altered. Homes built before 1977 need at least one ten-year sealed battery smoke alarm on each level, while houses built from 1984 on need hard-wired, interconnected alarms, with battery backup added to the rule from 1993. Flood answers are mandatory as well. The disclosure statement must say whether the house sits in a FEMA flood hazard area and what the seller knows about past flooding, before the buyer is bound.   • An assessment over a million dollars may bypass the board and go to the State Tax Court.
  • An unhappy owner has 45 days from a board judgment to go on to Tax Court.

To win, show that the figure misses market value or falls outside the common level range, set at 15 percent either side of the district's average ratio. Ask the township tax collector for your balance ahead of closing.

Sign the contract, then request the fire prevention inspection that same day to get the lowest fee. Test every alarm, check their dates and replace any that are too old. If the house has solar panels or a generator, add the required label. Pull the deed, payoff letter and any estate papers for your attorney, who will prepare the deed and the GIT/REP form.

The $60 fee becomes $90 at four to nine business days out and $150 inside three business days. A failed or missed appointment adds $60 for reinspection.

The township charges new homeowners or renters a $500 penalty for occupying a home before the inspection.

Does the seller cover the transfer fee in Morris County?

Yes. The state charges the seller at recording, in brackets that climb with price, with lower rates for qualifying seniors and disabled sellers.

What is the cutoff for an assessment appeal here?

April 1 in most years, or May 1 after a township revaluation. The Morris County Board of Taxation has to receive the petition by then.

The borough's sheet on selling a home names three items due before closing: a Certificate of Compliance for Fire Prevention, a final water reading, and property taxes paid in full. Each comes from a different office with its own fee, so start all three the day you have a contract.

This page covers Rockaway Borough, a Morris County municipality of 2.07 square miles. It had 6,598 residents in 2020 and an estimated 6,631 in July 2025. Rockaway Township borders the borough and runs its own separate offices, so check your tax bill to see which one holds your address before you phone anyone.

Zoning questions go to the borough zoning officer at Zoning@rockawayborough.org. The zoning office books appointments through 973-627-2000, extension 229.

The Bureau of Fire Prevention issues the certificate. Schedule by calling 973-625-3473 (973-625-FIRE) and leaving your name, address and phone number. Staff answer on weekdays and close at 4:30 p.m. The borough sheet, dated October 1, 2022, sets the fee by how early you ask.

Call the Water Clerk at 973-627-2000, extension 223, for the final reading. The fee is $60 with 72 hours or more of notice and $95 with less, so ask early. Do not wait for the week of closing, since a short notice costs more and the clerk may not be able to fit the reading in.

Morris County appeals and estate sales

The Morris County Board of Taxation, at P.O. Box 900, Morristown, holds appeal hearings in person only. Ask the board for the Rockaway filing date for the tax year you care about.

If you inherited the house, an executor signs the deed and the New Jersey GIT/REP form. A New Jersey estate uses the GIT/REP-3, and an executor who is also a beneficiary signs two forms. The seller owes the state transfer fee at recording, and each band of the rate schedule applies only to the slice of price inside it.

A sensible order of steps

With three offices involved, the order matters more than the speed of any one of them.

  2. Ask the Construction Office whether any permit is still open and finish it.
  3. Request the final water reading with at least 72 hours of notice.
  4. Pay property taxes in full through the closing date.

The borough's property maintenance article requires one for nonresidential and mixed buildings, and it exempts residential structures. Ask the Construction Office at 973-627-8035 whether anything else applies to your address.

Contact the Water Clerk at 973-627-2000, extension 223. The fee is $60 with at least 72 hours of notice and $95 on shorter notice.

Is Rockaway Borough the same as Rockaway Township?

No. They are separate Morris County municipalities with separate offices, and the borough was split off from the township in 1894. Check your tax bill to see which one you are in.

What is it like to sell a house in Barnegat Township?

Barnegat Township in Ocean County is a fast-growing, mostly owner-occupied community where sellers deal with a township resale letter, a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate and, in many cases, environmental approvals tied to the location of the lot. It covers about 34 square miles of land between the Garden State Parkway corridor and Barnegat Bay.

Owners live in nearly nine in ten homes, which makes most sales household to household rather than investor deals. What follows covers the local numbers, the township paperwork and the county steps after a contract is signed.

Barnegat housing numbers

The township reached 24,296 residents in the 2020 census, up from 20,936 in 2010, and the estimate for mid-2025 is 26,151, a 7.6% rise over April 2020. That 2020 count was the highest in the township's history.

With nearly nine in ten homes owner-occupied and almost a third of residents 65 or older, many sales here involve downsizing, estates or a move to be near family. Single-level homes and low-maintenance lots stay in demand.

Roads matter to buyers. North to south through the township's middle runs the Garden State Parkway, with U.S. Route 9 along the east side. Route 72 and County Route 539 serve the western part, County Route 554 crosses west to east, and NJ Transit bus route 559 connects the area with Atlantic City. The average commute is 27.8 minutes. Buyers with children ask first, so name the Barnegat Township School District in the listing.

What paperwork does Barnegat Township require for a home sale?

Barnegat Township requires a Letter of No Interest on resales, and the township lists a Resale Complete Letter of No Interest and a state smoke detector and carbon monoxide certification. Call the township's Rentals and Resales line at 609-698-0080, extension 159, before you list.

The township's construction office also handles permit history, which counts if you finished a basement, built a deck or added a shed. Work done without permits can hold up a sale, so ask the office if yours are closed. Calls are routed by extension on the same main line: construction permits at 135, 150 and 153, the planning and zoning board at 155, and the fire, electrical and plumbing subcodes at 157, 158 and 115. Having the right extension saves a round of transfers when a buyer's inspector asks for sign-offs.

  • Zoning permits cover sheds, fences, decks, pools, driveways, patios and additions.
  • A fence needs a zoning permit and a survey or plot plan prepared by a New Jersey surveyor.
  • Tree clearing permits are required before cutting trees.
  • Vacant properties must be registered with the township, and registration and de-registration forms are available.

Do Pinelands, DEP or septic rules affect a sale in Barnegat?

They can, depending on where the lot sits. Some approvals come before any local permit: Pinelands approval for land west of the Parkway only, state environmental approval for waterfront and freshwater wetland areas, and Department of Transportation approval for Route 9 and Route 72 properties.

County health department approval covers septic systems, wells and food handling, and the county soil conservation district reviews soil disturbance of 5,000 square feet or more. If your house is on septic, ask a buyer's inspector which records they will want. If part of your lot lies west of the Parkway, tell your agent early so buyers understand what Pinelands rules may mean for later projects. Route 9 and Route 72 frontage can trigger state highway approvals for work on the lot.

Rentals and senior buyers

Rental properties in Barnegat need a certificate of occupancy before every new tenant and must be registered with the municipal clerk. Units rented for fewer than 30 days need a yearly certificate, and failure to file can bring a summons to the owner.

On the state side, New Jersey publishes a reduced realty transfer fee schedule for senior citizens, blind or disabled persons, and for low and moderate income housing. For a standard sale above $350,000 the first $150,000 costs $2.90 per $500, against $1.40 on the reduced schedule. Ask your closing agent whether the transaction qualifies. The township's forms also include affordable housing applications for purchase and rental, which matter if your house sits in a program.

Deed recording and transfer fees

Deeds for Barnegat sales are recorded with the Ocean County Clerk, whose office handles land records and property search for the county. The state realty transfer fee is paid by the seller as the deed is recorded, and a seller who lives out of state also files a GIT/REP form and prepays at least 2% of the deed consideration.

Closing day brings a handful of deductions from your proceeds: payoff of any mortgage, the transfer fee, township certificate costs, and unpaid taxes or water and sewer charges. Ask the cash buyer or title company to walk through each line before you sign.

Order of work before you sell

Start with the township. Call the Rentals and Resales line, ask which resale letter applies and whether the smoke and carbon monoxide inspection must come first. Then check permits with the construction office and close out anything still open.

Next, look at the lot itself. Know whether any part lies west of the Parkway, whether it touches wetlands or the waterfront, and whether the house is on septic. Those answers tell you which outside approvals a buyer might ask about.

Last, line up the closing items. Selling to a cash buyer as-is spares you repair requests and a lender's appraisal, but the township certificate, the deed recording and the transfer fee still apply. Getting each one scheduled early is what keeps a fast closing fast.

Sellers who are downsizing or settling an estate often want to move quickly, so roles are worth knowing. The township office issues the resale letter and tracks permits. The county clerk records the deed. Your closing agent or title company collects the payoff, the transfer fee and any unpaid tax or water and sewer balance from the proceeds. If a family member is helping you sell, give them this list of offices and extensions so they can make the calls on your behalf.

One more point for lots that border the bay or the wetlands: environmental approvals can show up in a buyer's due diligence even when the house itself has never been altered. Pulling those records together at the start, instead of waiting for a buyer's inspector to ask, avoids a renegotiation near the end. Barnegat buyers who come from outside the township often ask about flood zones and septic, so be ready with a plain answer on both.

Frequently asked questions

Does Barnegat Township require anything special to sell a house?

Yes. The township asks for a Letter of No Interest on resales, and sellers also need the state smoke and carbon monoxide certification. Call the Rentals and Resales line at 609-698-0080, extension 159, to confirm current steps.

Is Barnegat mostly owner-occupied?

Yes. The owner-occupied rate is 88.0% for 2020 to 2024, with a median home value of $399,000, so most sales are between homeowners.

Do Pinelands rules apply to every Barnegat property?

No. Pinelands approval applies to land west of the Garden State Parkway only. Lots east of the Parkway may still need state environmental approval if they are on the water or near wetlands.

Which roads serve Barnegat Township?

Expect the Garden State Parkway through the middle and U.S. Route 9 on the east side. Route 72 and County Route 539 serve the west, and County Route 554 crosses west to east.

Who pays the realty transfer fee on a Barnegat sale?

The seller does. The state sets the fee by sale price in steps per $500, the county clerk collects it with the deed, and seniors may qualify for a reduced schedule.

Ways to close a Berkeley Township sale

Owners here usually choose among a broker listing, a do-it-yourself sale and an as-is cash purchase. Whichever you pick, the township requires a Certificate of Occupancy for the resale, and a house inside an age-restricted community also needs an approval letter from its homeowners association.

The township skews older: people 65 and over are 42.6 percent of residents. That makes many sales a downsizing move, a transfer to assisted living or heirs clearing out a parent's place. A listing rewards a tidy house and a seller who can sit through showings and wait on a buyer's loan approval. A cash buyer is the more practical match for an estate, a house that needs work or an owner who has already relocated.

  • Broker listing: most buyers see it, you pay a commission and you negotiate repairs.
  • Do-it-yourself sale: you arrange the inspection, the certificate and the attorney.
  • Cash purchase: condition becomes the buyer's problem, and the price reflects the repair bill.

Prices and ownership in Berkeley Township

Berkeley has 45,550 residents, up 4.1 percent from 2020. Nearly nine in ten homes (88.9 percent) are owner-occupied, and the median value of those homes is $310,000. The typical household has only 2.01 people, which fits a retirement community. Owners with a mortgage spend $1,925 a month at the median, and those without one spend $661. Bay and river frontage, flood maps and Pinelands rules can shape what a buyer's lender, insurer or surveyor asks for, so gather survey and flood paperwork before you list if your lot touches the water or the preserved woodland.

Township approvals for a resale

A Certificate of Occupancy is needed every time a Berkeley home is sold or rented. For a transfer, rental or resale in an age-restricted community, an original approval letter from the homeowners association must go with the application, bearing a live signature and not a duplicate.

Inspectors apply the township's written rules for battery-powered smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. Separately, state rules call for a compliance certificate before a one- or two-unit house is sold, available only from the municipality. Town Hall sits at 627 Pinewald-Keswick Road in Bayville; call 732-244-7400 for the current forms.

  • File the resale application the week a contract is signed.
  • Ask the association how long its letter takes to issue.
  • Confirm that decks, additions and finished basements each have a final inspection on file.
  • Test every alarm against the township's written requirements before the inspector arrives.

If the inspector finds a problem, you fix it and book a second visit, which can push the closing date. A seller who checks alarms and permits first usually avoids that delay.

Due dates, interest and penalties on property tax

Bills go out once a year, normally in July. Two quarters are billed as estimates, and the other two are adjusted so the year adds up to the real tax. The Ocean County Board of Taxation sets the rate once the township, the school districts and the county file certified budgets.

Berkeley Township installments and late charges

In a mid-year sale the closing statement divides that quarter's tax by days of ownership. Before closing, have the Tax Collector's office confirm what is owed so no installment remains open under your name.

South Seaside Park owners

Residents of this barrier island neighborhood petitioned in 2014 to leave Berkeley Township for the borough of Seaside Park, and the New Jersey Supreme Court sided with them in 2025.

Taxes on South Seaside Park properties remain payable to Berkeley Township through the end of 2026, and any change in collection starts January 1, 2027. If you own there, call both municipalities to learn which office issues the resale approval and the tax bill for the year of your closing.

Do roads and schools affect resale?

Garden State Parkway exits 77 and 80 serve the township, and Route 9 and Route 35 run through it. NJ Transit bus 559 links to Atlantic City, and Ocean Ride operates routes OC1, OC2, OC7 and OC8.

Four township schools teach pre-kindergarten through sixth grade. Seventh through twelfth graders go to Central Regional Middle School and Central Regional High School. Only 11.6 percent of residents are under 18, so age-restriction rules and single-level layouts tend to drive buyer questions more than school ratings.

Is a cash buyer worth considering?

A cash buyer is worth a call when certainty matters more than the top price: deferred maintenance, an association whose approval drags, or an estate with several heirs. The buyer may still have to secure the township certificate and the association letter, so decide in writing who files and who pays.

Judge any offer against a realistic listing net. Subtract commission, repair credits and the months of tax, association dues and utilities you would carry while waiting. A New Jersey attorney should read the contract and the deed language before you sign.

A cash sale skips the buyer's loan approval and the appraisal, and it usually skips repair requests after an inspection. The steps that stay are the township certificate, the association letter if one applies, the tax payoff and the deed recording. Start the certificate application and the association request as soon as you have a signed contract.

What to bring to the township office

Have your deed, your latest tax bill and the contract of sale in hand when you apply for the resale certificate. If the home is in an age-restricted community, bring the original association letter. Ask the clerk which forms the inspector wants on the day, and keep the alarm test results with you so the visit goes once and not twice.

After the certificate is issued, your attorney schedules the closing. On that day the mortgage and any lien are paid off, the tax is prorated to the closing date, the deed is signed and you hand over keys and garage openers. Keep copies of every township approval in your sale folder.

Frequently asked questions

Is a resale inspection mandatory in Berkeley Township?

Yes. Every sale needs a township Certificate of Occupancy, and landlords need one each time a tenant changes. Have working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms in place before the inspector visits.

What does an age-restricted community add to a Berkeley sale?

An original letter of approval from the homeowners association. The township does not take copies, and the letter must carry an original signature, so request it once a buyer is lined up.

What are the Berkeley Township tax installment dates?

Quarterly: February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, each followed by 10 grace days. Late interest is 8 percent on the first $1,500 and 18 percent beyond it, with a 6 percent penalty once a delinquency tops $10,000.

Where do South Seaside Park owners send their property tax?

To Berkeley Township through the end of 2026. Any change in collection takes effect January 1, 2027, so confirm the arrangement with the Tax Collector before a closing.

Can a senior seller pay less in New Jersey realty transfer fee?

Possibly. Senior citizens, blind persons and disabled persons can claim a partial exemption, which is personal and not available to a trust or an estate. Your attorney files the seller affidavit.

Quickest ways to sell in Brick Township

A seller in Brick has three realistic paths: hire an agent, handle the sale alone, or sign with a cash buyer who purchases the property untouched. Cash moves fastest and generally pays least. Listing adds commission and fix-up costs and takes longer. The right choice turns on the roof, the flood history, your deadline, and what the house would net after each route.

Brick has about 77,402 residents, up 5.1% from 2020. Buyers are active, but the housing stock is mostly decades old. Sellers meet the same questions again and again: flood zones, inspection paperwork and quarterly tax bills.

Brick housing and neighborhoods

Brick is a mature shore suburb where owners dominate. Of 30,289 households, 82.2% own, the median home value is $410,600 and median income is $106,130. Rent runs $1,756 a month at the median, so a rental is a realistic fallback for some owners, though not a cheap one to maintain under the township's inspection rules.

The mainland sits along the Metedeconk River and Barnegat Bay, and a separate set of ocean beaches (Brick Ocean Beaches I, II and III) lies on the barrier peninsula. Because the two parts do not touch, a street address can mean very different insurance and elevation questions.

  • Many homes date from the 1950s through the 1980s, so roofs, septic or sewer connections, and electrical panels are common negotiation points.
  • Waterfront and bayfront lots near Cherry Quay, Havens Cove and Shore Acres carry their own flood and elevation questions.
  • Herbertsville and Parkway Pines sit near Parkway exit 91, away from the rest of the township, and attract commuters.

How flood risk changes a Brick sale

Flood history is the biggest local variable. Hurricane Sandy in October 2012 devastated parts of Brick, and barrier island and waterfront properties took the worst of it. Roofs and heating systems matter even away from the water, since winter storms can bring heavy snow and power outages.

The township's floodplain office provides flood zone data to realtors, lenders, insurers and owners, including base flood elevation, whether a lot is in a coastal barrier area, and whether flood insurance is mandatory. Elevation certificates on file can be searched through the township's mapping tool, or requested from the engineering office by address or block and lot. Pull the certificate before you list, because a buyer's lender will ask for it.

Brick takes part in the federal Community Rating System, which can lower flood premiums. A seller who can show an elevation certificate, a recent flood policy, and any raised-utility work usually faces fewer price cuts.

Roads and commuting

The Garden State Parkway crosses the western side with exits 89, 90 and 91. Routes 70, 88 and 35 and county routes 528 and 549 handle local traffic. NJ Transit runs the 137 bus to the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Manhattan and the 67 to Newark, and a Park and Ride at exit 91 serves express commuters. Average commute time for workers is 28.2 minutes.

Buyers also check which elementary school zone a street falls in, so mention it in your listing.

Township paperwork when a Brick house is sold or rented

The Division of Inspections, which is the Building Department, issues construction permits and handles requests for certificates under the New Jersey Uniform Construction Code. Open or unclosed permits are the usual cause of delay at closing, so have the division confirm the status of past work before you sign.

Brick also treats rental homes strictly. Owners must register the landlord with the clerk, apply for a Rental Certificate of Occupancy, and file a mercantile license with proof of at least $500,000 in liability coverage. Code Enforcement then inspects every rental each year, at $100 per inspection and $50 per failed re-inspection. The annual checklist covers smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, ground-fault outlets near water, a mounted fire extinguisher, and lead-safe status for structures built before 1978. Creditors must also register foreclosed or vacant residential and commercial properties with the township within 10 days of filing a foreclosure action.

Property tax billing and closing

Installments fall on the first of February, May, August and November, with a ten-day grace window after each. Each bill covers a calendar quarter (the February bill pays for January through March), which matters at closing because the seller owes tax only through the closing date. A missing bill is no defense against interest, so make sure the closing agent has the current quarter's figure.

Work done on the house can add a second layer. After construction is finished, the township places an assessment on the improvement and mails an Added Assessment Bill in October, due November 1 and again on February 1 and May 1 of the following year. If you finished a deck or addition, ask the assessor whether that bill is still coming.

  • Assessment notices go out each year, usually by February 1, and an owner who thinks the value is wrong may appeal on or before April 1 to the Ocean County Board of Taxation.
  • Properties assessed above $1,000,000 can file directly with the State Tax Court of New Jersey.
  • The assessor processes veteran and senior or disabled deductions, each currently $250.

What New Jersey charges a seller

The state Realty Transfer Fee is the seller's cost, collected as the deed goes on record. It is charged per $500 of the price in tiers, starting at $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000 and rising on higher slices of the price. Because Brick's median value is $410,600, many sales land in a higher tier, so ask your attorney for the exact figure on your price before you accept an offer.

Closing costs also include deed recording, any payoff of liens, and whatever the buyer negotiates for repairs. A cash buyer typically absorbs repairs, so the realistic comparison is your net after repairs, carrying costs through the winter and agent fees against a single offer with a closing date you choose.

When a cash sale makes sense

A cash sale fits best when the home has defects an inspector would flag, when flood or storm damage is unrepaired, when the owner has inherited a house in another town, or when quarterly tax bills and a mortgage are piling up. It also helps landlords who do not want to carry the annual rental inspection cycle. It makes less sense for a move-in-ready home on a good street where a listing will draw several offers.

Whatever the buyer, get the offer on paper, set it beside the proceeds of a listing after commission, and confirm who pays for the certificate and recording steps. If you are close to a foreclosure filing, speak to a housing counselor or attorney in addition to any buyer, because the township's vacant property registration and the lender's timeline both affect your options.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell my Brick house if it was damaged in a storm?

Yes. Houses with storm damage change hands regularly, mostly to investors and cash buyers who subtract the repair bill. Collect your elevation certificate, flood claim paperwork and permit history first. The engineering office can look up certificates by address or by block and lot.

Which Brick office handles permits and certificates?

Start with the Division of Inspections voicemail line, 732-262-4604, or the permit status email on the township's building page. Rental certificate matters belong to Code Enforcement, 732-262-1033, weekdays.

What is the cutoff for contesting a Brick assessment?

April 1 each year, filed with the Ocean County Board of Taxation. Owners of property assessed above $1,000,000 may file directly with the State Tax Court of New Jersey instead.

Does a landlord need a certificate before selling a rented house in Brick?

A landlord needs the Rental Certificate of Occupancy to keep tenants in place, and the township inspects each rental every year. Ask the Division of Inspections what is required for your property when the sale closes and whether tenants move out first.

Who pays the realty transfer fee on a Brick sale?

The seller pays it. Recording the deed triggers the charge, which follows the price written in the deed and the state's published rates. Sales above $1,000,000 add a graduated percent fee.

Jackson owners generally weigh three paths: hire an agent, sell without one, or accept a direct cash offer from a buyer who takes the house in its current shape. The cash path skips staging, open houses and lender appraisals, the steps where slow closings usually stall. A listing may fetch more, though the mortgage, tax and utility bills keep running while it sits.

Delays in a Jackson sale tend to be local: a fire-code certificate, permits still open on the file, and tax balances. Deal with those three before anything else, and the rest of the timeline gets much shorter for you.

Jackson housing and buyers

Jackson is a big residential township in Ocean County, with an estimated 61,281 residents, 4.6% above 2020. At 99.17 square miles of land it is the largest municipality in the county, so streets run long between pockets of homes and wooded tracts. Interstate 195 carries most traffic through town.

The big housing wave came late. Builders averaged about 100 new homes a year in the late 1950s, roughly 750 a year in the 1960s, and over 1,000 a year through the 1970s and 1980s. A house built in that stretch will draw a buyer's inspector to the roof, heating system, septic or sewer link and electrical panel.

Owners live in 87.0% of housing units, so most buyers are moving from another owned house. Children under 18 are 26.6% of the population, which brings family buyers who ask about school zoning first.

Schools and commutes

Families will look at the Jackson School District, which runs 10 schools. The district has announced changes to how its middle and high schools are used, so check its current attendance map before you promise a buyer a particular school.

Commuters care about access. Jackson is the one Ocean County municipality with an interstate, and I-195 links directly to the Parkway, the Turnpike and I-295. NJ Transit runs the 317 bus between Philadelphia and the shore.

Ordinances that reach a seller

Signs, inspections and rentals are where Jackson's own code touches a sale. A lawn sign needs a $25 zoning permit: one per lot, at most six square feet and four feet high, 15 feet back from the curb, and removed within three days of closing or when the listing agreement ends. Up to five open house directional signs are allowed without their own permit. A sign violation costs $500 to $1,000.

  • Inspections: requests go through the township's SDL online portal, and inspections run from 7 AM to 3 PM.
  • Rentals: owners register each rental ($125) and apply for a rental continued certificate of occupancy ($100); code officers inspect before the tenant arrives.
  • Vacant property: registration is yearly, $500 the first time and $1,000 on each renewal.
  • Alarms: state fire code asks for a smoke alarm compliance certificate, issued by the municipality, before a one- or two-family house is sold. It lasts six months.

Clear any open building permits before listing. The township makes sign permits wait until open ones are closed, and the buyer's title search will flag them regardless.

Pinelands rules and what a buyer can build

Part of Jackson lies inside the Pinelands National Reserve, where state Pinelands rules layer on top of township zoning. The Pinelands Comprehensive Management Plan sorts land into nine management areas. In the Rural Development Area, clustered one-acre lots are allowed at an average of one home per five acres. The Forest Area averages one home per 28 acres, and Regional Growth Areas allow two to six homes per acre where sewers exist.

The category a lot falls into decides whether a buyer can add a second dwelling or split the parcel. Ask the Pinelands Commission for the lot's classification and mention it when you market the house or talk to a cash buyer. Late land-use surprises often reopen price talks.

Tax bills and deed recording

Jackson bills by calendar year, in installments due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. Interest backdates to the due date after the 10th day. The annual bill is mailed in late June or early July, and the township will not accept a postmark in place of receipt. Keep your latest bill on hand, since the closing agent must know the next installment due.

State law puts the realty transfer fee on the seller, collected as the deed is filed. The state's band schedule sets the amount, and a sale over $1 million adds a graduated percent fee. File the deed at the Ocean County Clerk, 118 Washington Street in Toms River (Monday to Friday, in-person service until 4 PM). A balance from an earlier year can be sold at a tax lien sale, which is one more reason to pay it off first.

A cash sale in Jackson from start to finish

Start by asking the construction office which certificate your house needs, then book the smoke alarm inspection through the SDL portal. Check the file for open permits and close them. Request a current tax balance from the collector and, if the house sits vacant, confirm the yearly registration is paid.

With a cash buyer there is no appraisal and no loan approval, so closing can follow soon after the certificate and title are in order. Take your deed, a recent tax bill, your photo ID, any payoff letter and the keys to the closing. Back taxes come out of your proceeds at the table.

If the house needs repairs, you do not have to make them before a cash sale, but safety items tied to the alarm certificate still have to pass. Tell the buyer about any open permit or past water problem up front, because the title search and inspection will find them anyway, and an early disclosure keeps the price steady. Ask the closing agent for a short written list of what each side signs so nothing is left for the final day.

Frequently asked questions

How fast can Jackson owners close?

Listings run longer because buyers need tours, a loan and an appraisal. Order the alarm certificate and look for open permits first, since those stall more closings than price does.

Does a Jackson house need a certificate before it sells?

A one- or two-family house needs the state smoke alarm compliance certificate, which the township issues and which lasts six months. A rental has its own rental continued certificate of occupancy, required before a tenant takes the unit. The construction office can tell you which forms fit your house.

Do I need a permit for a For Sale sign in Jackson?

Yes, a $25 permit from the zoning office. The sign can be six square feet and four feet tall at most, and must sit 15 feet from the curb. Open house signs follow a separate rule and need no permit.

Who covers the state transfer fee on a Jackson sale?

The seller does. The fee climbs with price in bands, and a sale over $1 million adds a graduated percent fee. The closing agent works out the exact amount from the deed.

What if my Jackson house sits vacant or has back taxes?

A vacant house has to be registered with the township each year, $500 at first and $1,000 on renewals. Back taxes can be sold off as a lien, and the payoff comes from your proceeds. Ask the township tax collector for a current balance before setting a date.

Selling a Lacey Township house without a long wait

The quickest sale in Lacey is a direct cash purchase, since it removes the buyer's loan, the appraisal and most repair negotiations. Listing with an agent usually earns a higher price and takes more weeks. Selling on your own sits between the two, and you handle the paperwork, the showings and the negotiation yourself.

Lacey is a shore-side township in Ocean County with an estimated 30,297 residents, up 5.7% from 2020. Owners occupy 88.1% of housing units. Population jumped from 1,940 in 1960 to 22,141 in 1990, so much of the housing dates from that rush.

The Parkway split and the Pinelands

Lacey is split by the Garden State Parkway, and the split decides what a house is worth and what can be built next to it. East of the Parkway sit more than 95% of the township's homes, mostly in Lanoka Harbor and the Forked River area. West of it, roughly two-thirds of the township's area is mostly pine and cedar forest governed by the Pinelands Commission under the 1979 Pinelands Act.

The township covers 83.25 square miles of land and another 16.55 of water, so the shoreline and the creeks matter. If your property is west of the Parkway, tell buyers early, since the Pinelands Commission limits building and land use there.

  • Forked River, Lanoka Harbor and Cedar Creek are among the named communities east of the Parkway.
  • Bamber Lakes and a handful of farms sit west of it, in the Pinelands.

Oyster Creek's closing and your tax bill

The Oyster Creek Nuclear Generating Station, which came online on December 1, 1969, closed in September 2018. It had contributed roughly a third of the township's budget through taxes.

For a seller, the effect shows up indirectly, through the municipal tax rate rather than anything in your house. Keep your most recent tax bill available when you price, because buyers will want to see what a year of ownership costs.

Schools, roads and transit

There is no rail service, and the nearest train station is in Bay Head.

What a Lacey seller needs from the township

Start with the building department at 124 South Main Street in Forked River, which handles inspections and certificates. Property taxes and the deed

Lacey bills property tax once a year and collects it in four installments on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, each with a 10-day grace period. The township collects for Ocean County and the Lacey Township Board of Education as well as itself, so the bill covers all three. A new bill is mailed when ownership changes, and a buyer should confirm the amount due with the tax collector at 818 West Lacey Road in Forked River.

New Jersey's realty transfer fee falls on the seller and is collected at filing. The county's Manahawkin office, 179 South Main Street, Room 106, phone (609) 597-1500, accepts deeds and stays open until 8 PM Tuesday through Thursday.

  • Credit cards are taken online or at the office for current-year taxes until November 10, with a 2.95% fee charged by the card company; an e-check costs a flat $1.95.
  • After November 28, payment must be cash, certified check or money order.
  • Any open tax, water or sewer balance on November 11 is subject to the tax sale list.

A cash closing in Lacey

With no lender, the steps are short. Send the building department a written inspection request at least a day ahead, close any open permits, and ask the tax collector for the amount due. Then meet the closing agent to sign the deed, which goes to the county clerk.

Bring your deed, a recent tax bill, any mortgage payoff letter and the keys. Back taxes and water or sewer balances come out of your proceeds, so clear them early if you want a smooth day.

Timing depends mostly on the township. The building department wants inspection requests in writing at least 24 hours ahead, so file the request the day you have a contract instead of the week of closing. The smoke alarm certificate stays valid for six months, which gives you room to close without a second inspection. If the house is a rental, the same smoke alarm rule applies, and a buyer will expect to see current leases.

Check the tax side early too. Because the bill covers the township, Ocean County and the school board, ask the tax collector at 818 West Lacey Road for one total and the next installment date. An open tax, water or sewer balance on November 11 can reach the tax sale list, so settle anything old before then. Finally, confirm with the closing agent whether the deed goes to the Toms River or the Manahawkin office, so nobody drives to the wrong counter.

Does the Pinelands hurt a Lacey sale?

Mostly no, because more than 95% of Lacey's homes sit east of the Garden State Parkway. West of the Parkway the Pinelands Commission limits building, so buyers of those parcels need to ask what uses are permitted.

How soon can a Lacey sale close?

With a clear title, a cash sale can finish in one to two weeks. A listing drags longer through tours, buyer financing and inspection scheduling, and Lacey's building department wants each inspection request in writing a day ahead.

Whose taxes appear on a Lacey bill?

Three: the township, Ocean County and the Lacey Township Board of Education, since New Jersey law makes the municipality the billing and collection agent for all of them. Installments come due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1.

Is a smoke alarm certificate required for a Lacey sale?

Yes, for a one- or two-family home. The municipality issues the state fire code certificate, which stays good for six months, so schedule the inspection early.

Where does a Lacey deed get recorded?

At the Ocean County Clerk's office. The main location is 118 Washington Street in Toms River, and a Manahawkin branch at 179 South Main Street sits closer to Lacey.

A posted notice reminds owners of the smoke and carbon monoxide alarm requirement. Ask the staff what resale paperwork and inspection your closing date needs, and request the form list in writing.

The township's FAQ raises the question of a certificate of occupancy when selling a home, so get the current answer by phone. Ask about open permits too. Work done without a permit can cost up to $2,000 in penalties, plus $2,000 more for each additional week.

  • Permit review under the state construction code can take up to 20 business days.
  • The engineering section covers flood zone lookups, elevation certificates, property surveys and wetlands questions.

Who records a Lakewood deed, and what does the seller owe?

The Ocean County Clerk records Lakewood deeds. Its main office sits at 118 Washington Street in Toms River and answers at (732) 929-2018. Selling with back taxes owed
