Sequence matters here. Phone Code Enforcement first and learn what your closing date demands, so an alarm check or certificate never lands in the final week. Next collect the tax and water or sewer payoff figures, then the survey, permit records and leases. Only after that sign a contract that spells out who pays which fee. The closing attorney or title agent finishes by sending the deed to the Ocean County Clerk.

Cash buyers skip appraisal and bank underwriting, the two steps that most often slip a closing date. Township paperwork and recording still apply, so the calendar depends on how quickly those offices answer. Tenants in place are workable: give the buyer the lease and ask Code Enforcement about the rental certificate before a date is chosen.

Two offers with the same headline price can pay you different amounts, so line up closing date, transfer fee and certificate responsibility side by side.

  • The property survey, plus any flood zone or wetlands paperwork the engineering section gave you.
  • For Leisure Village homes, the community's written resale rules.

A seller who hands over this folder at the first showing or cash offer usually gets cleaner terms and fewer late renegotiations once the contract is signed.

Choosing a sale route

Think about speed against condition. An agent listing exposes the house to the most buyers but adds showings, an appraisal and a township inspection. Going without an agent keeps the commission and puts every deadline on you. A cash buyer taking the house as-is removes repair requests and loan approval. Put the survey, permits, leases and latest tax bill in one folder before offers arrive, and ask your title company for a copy of your recorded deed.

Yes. The state bases it on the price in the deed and collects it when the Ocean County Clerk records the deed. Sales above $1 million also trigger a graduated percentage fee, again on the seller.

Which office records a Lakewood deed?

The Ocean County Clerk. The main office is in Toms River at (732) 929-2018, and a Lakewood location at 225 4th Street, Room 211 answers at (732) 370-8850.

You can still sell, but deal with them first. Code Enforcement can tell you which permits are open, and unpermitted work can draw fines that grow weekly. A buyer or lender may require the permit closed before the sale.

Often, because a cash sale skips mortgage approval and an appraisal. A listing may reach more buyers. Deed recording, the transfer fee and any township certificate apply either way, so compare the written terms.

Who sells in Manchester Township

Manchester Township sellers skew older: nearly half the population, 48.1 percent, is past 65, and the average household has only 1.92 people. That mix points to retirees moving closer to family, heirs settling an estate, and owners who no longer want to maintain a house.

The township in Ocean County had an estimated 46,556 people in mid-2025. Owners occupy 86.7 percent of the housing, the middle home value is $219,100, and tenants pay $1,477 at the median (2020 to 2024 survey). Median household income was $56,885. A quick, as-is sale is a practical option for some owners, especially when a house needs work that a retiree or an estate does not want to fund.

Where the house sits matters

Manchester Township is a wide, mostly wooded township of 81.42 square miles of land, so a sale here depends heavily on which neighborhood the house is in. Lakehurst Naval Air Station lies within its borders, and the borough of Lakehurst is completely surrounded by the township.

Several age-restricted and planned communities sit inside the township, including Pine Lake Park, Crestwood Village, Leisure Village West, Pine Ridge at Crestwood, Leisure Knoll, Cedar Glen Lakes and Cedar Glen West. Whiting is the largest section by area and population, with 33,180 of the township's 45,115 residents in 2020. When the house belongs to a planned community, ask the association for its resale package and any rules on who may buy before listing, since those can add weeks.

Certificate of Re-occupancy

Manchester Township requires a Certificate of Re-occupancy for a resale, applied for through the Building Department's online citizen portal. The owner creates a login, chooses the non-rental application, notes whether the house is vacant or occupied (a lockbox or combination can be left for the inspector), submits, and pays the fee online by check or card. The township then emails or calls to schedule the inspection.

The inspection list covers a good deal of the house:

  • Water, electric and gas on, with heating and plumbing in working order.
  • Smoke detectors on every level and within 10 feet of sleeping areas, less than 10 years old, at least 3 feet from vents.
  • Carbon monoxide detectors within 10 feet of bedrooms but not inside them.
  • GFCI outlets that trip on the test button, and covers on every electrical box.
  • House numbers at least 4 inches high, visible from the street.
  • A warning label within 18 inches of the electric panel and meter if solar, a generator or battery storage supplies a second source of power.
  • Open permits closed out, and any unpermitted work cited as a violation.

Houses on well water need a water analysis certification from the Ocean County Health Department. Since April 15, 2025, the state fire code also calls for 18 inches between mulch and combustible parts of a building such as decks and porches.

From contract to recorded deed

Steps from contract to recorded deed in Manchester Township
StepWho handles itWhat to expect
Re-occupancy inspectionTownship Building DepartmentOnline application, fee paid online, inspector schedules a visit

Recording the deedOcean County Clerk, Toms RiverMain office at 118 Washington Street

Because the inspection runs through the township's portal, starting it early keeps the closing date from slipping. If the inspector cites a problem, the repair and a second visit have to happen before the certificate issues.

The state transfer fee

New Jersey puts the realty transfer fee on the seller, collected at recording and based on the price in the deed. The fee schedule gives partial relief to sellers who are qualifying senior citizens aged 62 or older, blind persons, or disabled persons, which matters in a township where so many owners are over 65. A seller claiming the reduction files an Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller, which must be notarized and recorded with the deed. Sales above $350,000 use a higher rate table, and a graduated percent fee applies only above $1,000,000.

Roads and transit

Buyers weigh the drive more than anything else, since no limited-access highway crosses the township. Route 70 runs through the heart of the township and Route 37 through the east, with County Routes 530, 539, 547 and 571 also in use. The nearest Garden State Parkway entrances are in Toms River, Berkeley and Lacey, and Interstate 195 is reached through Jackson Township. Ocean Ride local bus service runs the OC1 Whiting, OC1A Whiting Express and OC2 Manchester routes. The average commute is 33.3 minutes.

Getting the house ready for the inspector

Walk through the house a few weeks before you apply, with the inspection list in hand. Test each GFCI outlet, replace any smoke detector past its age limit, check that detectors sit clear of vents, and make sure no electrical box is missing its cover. Pull back mulch from decks and porches, put up house numbers that can be read from the street, and confirm that gas, water and electric are on for the visit.

If the house is vacant, leave a lockbox or combination in the application notes so the inspector can get in. Owners who live out of town often forget this step, and a missed visit pushes the closing date. Close any open permits before you apply, because unpermitted work gets cited as a violation and holds up the certificate.

Your options for selling

An owner can hire an agent, go it alone, or take an offer from a cash buyer that takes the house without repairs. Each route needs the same township certificate and the same state forms, so the difference comes down to timing and cost.

  • Hiring an agent usually reaches the widest pool of buyers, at the cost of a commission, and the house often needs repairs to pass inspection and satisfy a buyer's lender.
  • Going without an agent saves the commission, though the owner handles pricing, showings, the contract and the paperwork alone.
  • Selling for cash without repairs removes the lender from the picture, which suits inherited, vacant or tenant-occupied houses. Settle in the contract who obtains the re-occupancy certificate and who pays for any repairs it requires.

Whichever route fits, get offers from more than one buyer or agent and compare the net proceeds after the transfer fee, any mortgage payoff and unpaid township charges.

Frequently asked questions

Does Manchester Township require an inspection before I sell?

Yes. The township issues a Certificate of Re-occupancy for resales after an inspection, and the application goes through its online citizen portal. Open permits must be closed first, and wells need an Ocean County Health Department water analysis.

Who pays the realty transfer fee on a Manchester Township sale?

The seller does, at the recording counter. Qualifying seniors aged 62 and older can claim a reduced rate by filing an Affidavit of Consideration.

Where is the deed recorded for a Manchester Township house?

The Ocean County Clerk records deeds, and its main office is at 118 Washington Street in Toms River. The seller's residency form (GIT/REP) goes in with the deed, and the clerk can reject paperwork that is incomplete.

Can I sell a Manchester Township house that needs major repairs?

Yes, though the re-occupancy inspection still applies. A cash buyer will often accept the condition, but the contract should say who fixes anything the inspector cites and who pays for it before the certificate is issued.

Do mulch and secondary power labels really matter at inspection?

They can. The checklist calls for a label near the electric panel for solar, generators or battery storage, and the state fire code has required 18 inches between mulch and combustible building parts since April 15, 2025. Fixing both ahead of time avoids a failed visit.

Under Chapter 81 of the Stafford code, a house that changes occupancy needs an inspection by the Code Official, after which a continuing certificate of occupancy is issued.

You submit the Application for Existing Structure Certificate of Occupancy and can reach the office at 609-597-1000, extension 8532. The township describes the review as visual only, not a structural investigation, so a buyer will still want a private home inspection.

Stafford housing at a glance

Stafford sits on the Jersey Shore in southern Ocean County, and many owners have been in their homes a long time. The estimated population is 30,958 as of July 2025, up 8.2 percent from April 2020. Of 12,007 households, 90.3 percent own, the middle home value is $426,200 and median household income is $117,612. Residents 65 and older make up 22.0 percent. Median gross rent is $1,800.

Many houses date from the 1950s to the 1980s, and some are converted summer homes. Heating systems and electrical panels are where the township inspector tends to look closely.

What the inspector looks for

The township's list of common violations works as a pre-listing checklist. Walk the house with it before you apply.

  • Missing outlet plates and uncovered junction boxes
  • Open spaces in an electrical panel and unsecured fixtures
  • Leaking pipes, and relief valves not piped to within 6 inches of the floor
  • Metal dryer vents, chimney caps, and house numbers at least 3 inches high
  • Handrails on stairs with more than 3 risers, and guardrails where a deck or stair is 30 inches or more above grade
  • Smoke detectors within 10 feet of sleeping areas and on every floor including the basement
  • Carbon monoxide detectors in one- and two-family homes with fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage

The township posts more on its rentals and resales page. Small fixes made before the visit save a second trip and keep the certificate on schedule.

Heating systems and solid-fuel burners

The Heat Certification is the item sellers most often leave to the last minute. A professional has to inspect the heating system, and any fireplace, wood stove or other solid-fuel burner, before the seller or agent signs the statement. Book that visit as soon as you decide to sell, since a tradesperson's calendar can run longer than the township's.

Once the professional has finished, bring the statement to the counter. Staff can notarize it there, which saves a separate trip to a notary. Keep a copy, because your attorney and the buyer's lender may each ask for one.

Older houses in Stafford, especially converted seasonal cottages, may have had heating added piece by piece over the years. If you know of an old burner that no longer works, say so to the professional and fix or remove it rather than leaving it for the inspector to question.

Where Stafford sits

Stafford is the mainland gateway to Long Beach Island. Route 72 is the only road onto the island and crosses Barnegat Bay on the Manahawkin Bay Bridge into Ship Bottom. The Garden State Parkway meets Route 72 at Exit 63. The main areas are Manahawkin around Route 9 and Route 72, Beach Haven West, Ocean Acres, Warren Grove, and smaller places such as Mayetta. Flood rules and raised houses

Stafford's house raising page refers to the Base Flood Elevation regulations and to the storm of October 27, 2012, and it describes two permit routes. In the first, the owner raises the home under a construction permit and does not reoccupy it until a Certificate of Occupancy is issued. In the second, the owner repairs the home to safe living conditions first, receives a Temporary Certificate of Occupancy, and raises it later.

Either route needs a zoning permit with a survey showing setbacks and structure height, engineered plans for the new foundation, and releases from every utility serving the building. Insurance Increased Cost of Compliance payments are tied to the permit and the final certificate.

A seller with a raised house should keep the permit, the engineering sign-off and the final certificate in one folder for the buyer's lender. A seller near the bay should ask the Zoning office which flood zone and base flood elevation apply to the address.

Seasonal and long-term rentals

Shore properties often have a rental history. The township's seasonal rental page lists a $100 fee plus $50 for a reinspection. The applicant also supplies proof of paid property taxes, proof of water and sewer payment, and a floor-by-floor drawing. Long-term rentals built before 1978 need lead-based paint inspections.

If you are selling a house that has been rented, give the buyer the tax and utility proofs, the drawing and any lead inspection record.

Transfer fee and out-of-state sellers

The seller owes New Jersey's Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded, calculated from the price in the deed. Many shore owners live elsewhere, and a seller who is not a New Jersey resident must prepay estimated Gross Income Tax at closing, never less than 2% of the sale price, unless a listed exception applies. Your closing attorney will complete the forms.

  2. Order the heating system inspection and get the Heat Certification notarized.
  3. Request the utility authority letter, or arrange the well water test.
  4. Walk the house against the violations list and fix what you find.
  5. Pass the visual inspection and collect the certificate for your attorney.

A cash buyer who takes the house as it is can still ask you to complete these steps. Ask early whether the buyer will take them over.

Frequently asked questions

Does Stafford require an inspection when a house is sold?

Yes. Chapter 81 of the Stafford code calls for an inspection by the Code Official on every change of occupancy, followed by a continuing certificate of occupancy. Apply with the Existing Structure Certificate of Occupancy form.

What is the Heat Certification?

It is a notarized statement from the seller or the seller's agent that a professional inspected the heating system and any fireplace, wood stove or other solid-fuel burner. Clerical staff can notarize it at the counter.

How is a private well handled in a Stafford sale?

The well water must be tested by a well driller or tester and approved by the Ocean County Health Department. That approval takes the place of the utility letter that houses on public water and sewer provide.

Is the Stafford inspection a full home inspection?

No. The township calls its review visual only and says a complete overview of the property comes from a registered home inspection agency. Buyers usually order their own inspection as well.

What does a Stafford seasonal rental license cost?

The fee is $100, plus $50 for a reinspection. The applicant also supplies proof of paid property taxes, proof of water and sewer payment, and a floor-by-floor drawing.

Options for selling in Toms River

Three routes are open to a Toms River owner: an agent listing, a private sale, or an as-is offer from a cash buyer. Which one fits turns on the house, your deadline and how much repair money you want to put in before closing.

The township spans mainland neighborhoods, bayfront streets and barrier-island blocks, so a house in Silverton does not sell the same way as one in West Dover or Ortley Beach. Listing puts the house in front of the most buyers and lets nearby sales set the price. Selling direct is faster and usually hands the repairs and the township paperwork to the buyer.

The Toms River market

The estimated population is 100,899 as of July 1, 2025, up 5.7 percent from April 2020. Of 38,047 households, 82.1 percent own their home, and the middle home value is $416,700. Median gross rent is $1,726 and median household income is $99,547. About 21.0 percent of residents are 65 or older.

Mainland addresses use ZIP codes 08753, 08754, 08755, 08756, 08757 and 08739. Ortley Beach, on the barrier strip, shares the 08751 ZIP code with Seaside Heights, so use the right one on your listing.

Dover Township on old records

Dover Township became Toms River by a voter-approved name change that took effect on November 14, 2006. Older deeds, title records and tax documents may still say Dover Township, so ask your title company to confirm that the legal description matches the property.

Flood history and paperwork

The October 2012 storm caused the township's worst flooding on record in low-lying areas, including Silverton and the downtown area. The barrier-island neighborhoods suffered even more severe damage. A mainland or barrier house that was flooded, raised or rebuilt after that storm carries paperwork that buyers and their lenders will want to see.

  • Elevation certificate and flood insurance history, if the address is in a mapped flood zone
  • Construction permits and the final Certificate of Occupancy for any raising or rebuilding
  • Records of repairs to utilities and heating equipment

Roof age, gutters and basement or crawlspace moisture are the items a buyer's inspector checks first. If you have a private well, keep a current water test on hand.

Rental registration and inspection fees

Many Toms River sellers have run a rental, either a year-round tenant or a seasonal unit near the beach. The Division of Property Maintenance's rental packet, revised October 2024, sets the rules.

Applications go through the township's online portal and must be complete.

Documents for a rental inspection

Hand the same papers to a buyer who plans to keep the tenants.

  • A lead-safe certificate for any one-, two- or multi-family rental built before 1978, except seasonal rentals under six months

Smoke alarm rules depend on the age of the house. Homes built before 1984 need 10-year sealed battery alarms on each level, homes from 1984 to 1990 need interconnected hard-wired alarms with battery backup, and homes from 1991 on need them in every bedroom, outside the sleeping rooms and on every level including the basement. Carbon monoxide alarms go within 10 feet of sleeping areas where a home has fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage. Mainland versus barrier-island houses

Buyers sort Toms River into two kinds of property. Mainland houses sit in neighborhoods such as Silverton, West Dover and downtown. Barrier-island houses sit on the Barnegat Peninsula, in the areas called Dover Beaches North and Dover Beaches South, which includes Ortley Beach.

Each kind brings its own questions. A mainland buyer asks about roof age, drainage and the basement. A barrier-island buyer asks about flood zone, elevation, insurance cost and whether the house can be rented seasonally. Put the answers in a folder before the first showing, and a buyer's attorney can move straight to the contract.

Selling an owner-occupied house

Before you sign a contract, phone the construction and property maintenance offices and ask whether a resale certificate or inspection covers your address. The township's building page covers permits and final certificates of occupancy for new homes and raised homes, and any open permit should be closed out before listing.

The clerk's forms page also lists an Application for No Knock and an Affirmative Statement to Receive Real Estate Solicitations. Ask the Municipal Clerk how those forms work if buyers you did not invite keep contacting you.

State forms and fees at closing

The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee as the deed goes on record. It follows the price written in the deed, and the Division of Taxation lists the exemptions. A price over $1,000,000 adds a graduated percent fee. A seller who has moved out of state prepays estimated Gross Income Tax at closing, never less than 2% of the sale price, under the GIT/REP rules. Ask your closing attorney to run the numbers early.

A practical order of steps

  1. Check with the construction office for open permits, then close each one.
  2. Gather flood, elevation and repair records if the house was affected in 2012.
  3. If the house was a rental, collect the certificate, insurance and lead-safe papers.
  4. Confirm the legal description with your title company in case it says Dover Township.
  5. Give everything to your attorney before the contract is signed.

A cash buyer who takes the house as it stands can skip repairs, but the paperwork still has to be in order for the deed to record. Ask that buyer for a closing date early, and give your attorney time to review the title, the legal description and any rental records. If the house was a seasonal unit near the beach, include the registration paperwork, because the buyer may want to keep renting it. Every document you hand over in advance is one fewer question later.

Is Toms River the same place as Dover Township?

Yes. Dover Township became Toms River Township by a voter-approved name change that took effect November 14, 2006. Old deeds and tax records may still use the Dover name.

How much does a Toms River rental inspection cost?

The township packet lists $150 for each unit, $50 for a failed re-inspection and $50 to amend a registration. The fees are non-refundable.

Are seasonal rentals allowed all year in Toms River?

No. Barrier-island seasonal and short-term rental certificates run from April 1 through November 30, and such rentals are not permitted outside that period.

Do I need a lead-safe certificate to sell?

The packet requires it for rentals built before 1978, with an exception for seasonal rentals under six months. Ask the township and your attorney whether anything applies to an owner-occupied sale.

What is the median home value in Toms River?

The middle value of an owner-occupied home is $416,700 for 2020 to 2024. Your own house may sit well above or below that depending on its location, condition and flood exposure.

Selling a house fast in Wayne, NJ

Selling a house in Wayne, New Jersey is shaped by one township rule that many sellers do not expect: a Continued Certificate of Occupancy, or CCO, that must be issued before most sales close. Add the state's closing fees and Passaic County's assessment calendar, and you have the three items that decide how fast a Wayne sale can move.

Whether you hire an agent, go it alone or sign with a cash buyer, the CCO applies, so start there.

Wayne housing snapshot

Wayne spreads over 23.72 square miles of land in Passaic County and is a bedroom suburb of New York City, less than 20 miles from Midtown Manhattan. Water defines many neighborhoods. Lake communities surround Packanack Lake, Pines Lake, Lions Head Lake and Tom's Lake, and the Passaic River crosses the township and often floods near Willowbrook Mall and the riverside neighborhoods. Ask your insurer and surveyor about flood-zone status before you list a house in those areas.

Highways and trains

Interstate 80, U.S. Routes 46 and 202, Route 23 and county routes 502 and 504 cross the township, and the 229.48 miles of public road include 180.59 miles kept up by the municipality, 41.05 miles by Passaic County and 7.84 miles by the state. NJ Transit's Mountain View and Wayne Route 23 stations on the Montclair-Boonton Line run to Hoboken, with Midtown Direct connections to New York Penn Station. Buses reach the Port Authority Terminal on several routes.

If your street is close to a station, say so in the listing. Wayne Hills High School serves students who live on or north of Ratzer Road and Wayne Valley High School serves those south of it, so buyers with children will ask which side of that line your house is on.

Continued Certificate of Occupancy

Wayne requires a CCO for the sale or rental of one- and two-family homes, duplexes, townhouses and condominiums. No residential premises may change ownership, tenancy or use without a CCO from the Enforcement Officer under Township Code Section 100. A transfer between spouses, from parent to child, or between siblings does not need one.

  • Apply and pay the base fee online. The Building Department then checks for open permits, and open permits must be closed before an inspection is scheduled.
  • After that, the enforcement officer has 15 business days to inspect and either issue the certificate or list the failed items.
  • Inspections sooner than 10 days after the application and permit closure carry an expediting fee.
  • A CCO is valid for 90 days. If closing slips past that, you must reapply.

The inspection checks the house against the zoning and property maintenance ordinances, including any addition, finished basement, shed, second kitchen, deck or pool, and each must have a permit or a variance.

If the house fails inspection

If the house fails or permits are still open, the township may allow the sale to close on a signed purchaser's agreement that names who will fix the items. That agreement cannot run longer than 60 days, and the buyer schedules the follow-up inspection. This is the route many cash buyers use for a house that needs work.

A separate CCO fire inspection is also needed. Call the CCO Office at 973-694-1800, extension 3263, and the Fire Bureau at extension 3300. The township's CCO page links a search for open permits, so check it before you apply.

Step by step: timing the CCO

The CCO clock controls most Wayne closing dates, so work backward from the day you want to close. Search for open permits first, since nothing can be scheduled until they are closed. Then apply online and pay the base fee. Allow up to 15 business days for the inspection decision, and remember the certificate lasts only 90 days.

Do not wait until you have a signed contract if you suspect a permit problem. A deck, a finished basement or a second kitchen without paperwork can take longer to sort out than the inspection itself. If you are short on time, ask whether an expedited inspection is available and what it costs, or ask the buyer whether a purchaser's agreement would work.

Taxes and fees at closing

On the state chart for prices above $350,000, the slice from $550,000 to $850,000 costs $5.30 per $500 and the slice to $1,000,000 costs $5.80. Anything higher adds a Graduated Percent Fee that begins at 1%. Every owner files a GIT/REP form with the deed.

A New Jersey resident files GIT/REP-3. Sellers who have moved out of state file GIT/REP-1 or 2 and may prepay 2% of the price or 8.97% of the gain. The township has also warned residents about a phone scam claiming a property is in a tax sale. To confirm what you owe, call the township at 973-694-1800, extension 3330, and do not send money to a caller.

Appealing your assessment

Passaic County keeps the usual calendar. Appeals are due April 1, moving to May 1 after a revaluation or reassessment. Form A-1 goes to the Passaic County Board of Taxation in Totowa (930 Riverview Drive, Suite 250; 973-720-7399). Assessments above $1,000,000 may go to the Tax Court.

The burden of proof is yours, so bring recent sales of comparable homes. Sellers rarely benefit from an appeal, but an heir or buyer keeping the house might.

Quick-sale choices

  • Agent listing: broad exposure to commuters and university-area buyers, with weeks of showings and lender timelines.
  • Private sale: saves a commission, and you handle the CCO, disclosures and contracts.
  • Cash offer: no mortgage contingency, and a buyer willing to close on a purchaser's agreement if an item fails.

Whatever you choose, start the CCO early and find open permits first.

On closing day, the buyer's attorney and the title company will ask for the CCO, proof that open permits were closed or the signed purchaser's agreement, and the township's confirmation of your tax balance. Having those papers in one folder is the simplest way to keep a Wayne closing on schedule, and a cash buyer will usually accept the house with whatever the inspector found, so long as the agreement says who fixes what.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a Wayne CCO take?

The enforcement officer has 15 business days to inspect and decide once the permit check is clear. Expedited inspections inside 10 days carry an extra fee, so apply as early as you can.

Is a CCO required when I give my house to a family member?

No for transfers between spouses, from parent to child, or between siblings. Other transfers of one- or two-family homes need the Continued Certificate of Occupancy.

How long does a Wayne CCO last?

Ninety days from issue. If closing has not happened by then, the certificate expires and a new application is needed.

When is the deadline to appeal a property tax assessment in Wayne?

April 1, unless the township did a revaluation or reassessment, in which case it is May 1. File with the Passaic County Board of Taxation in Totowa at 973-720-7399.

Can I sell my Wayne house if it fails the CCO inspection?

Possibly. The township may allow closing on a purchaser's agreement that says who corrects the items, for no more than 60 days, and the buyer schedules the follow-up inspection.

What to sort out first in West Milford

West Milford is a sprawling, lake-dotted township in northern Passaic County, and a sale here turns on three things: a fire-safety certificate from the township, the assessment calendar kept by the Passaic County Board of Taxation, and a deed filed with the county clerk in Paterson. Nearly nine in ten houses have the owner living in them, so most buyers will be families moving in, with investors a smaller group.

The sections below cover the local market, what its lakes and watershed mean for a listing, the alarm certificate, the tax calendar and the filing that ends the process.

West Milford housing figures

At 75.93 square miles of land, West Milford is the biggest municipality in Passaic County. It has 25,216 residents, and workers face a long drive, with a commute near 40 minutes.

About 95 percent of residents lived at the same address a year earlier, so few houses change hands in a given year. A lakefront cottage and a hilltop colonial can sit far apart in value, so ask an agent for sold prices on your own road rather than rely on the township middle figure.

Lakes, watershed and the Highlands

The township describes itself as many small towns, with the township center, Hewitt, Newfoundland and Oak Ridge as the four main communities. After the war, the cottages around the lakes gradually became year-round houses. Greenwood Lake runs about nine miles and crosses into New York, and smaller waters such as Upper Greenwood Lake, Wonder Lake and Lake Lockover have their own clusters of homes.

  • Large tracts around the Pequannock watershed belong to the City of Newark, so a view of that land will not be built over.
  • The 2004 Highlands Water Protection and Planning Act puts West Milford in the Highlands preservation area, which brings extra state rules. Check with the township before telling a buyer that an addition or a new lot is possible.
  • Jungle Habitat, a safari park open from 1972 to 1976, passed to the state in 1988 and is now a mountain biking destination that outdoor-minded buyers like.

Roads and buses

Route 23 carries most through traffic, with County Routes 511 and 513 close behind. The township counted 198.30 miles of roadway, of which 163.20 miles belonged to the township and the rest to the county or the state, so find out which agency maintains the road in front of your house. NJ Transit buses 194 and 196 run to the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Midtown, and the township operates two limited local bus routes.

Families will want the elementary school for your street named in the listing, so get that from the school district office.

Smoke and CO alarm certificate

A house for one or two households cannot change owners until the Fire Marshal's office certifies that its smoke and CO alarms pass inspection. The state rule is N.J.A.C. 5:70-2.3, and skipping it can mean a fine of up to $2,500. Inspections are booked for Wednesdays, so start early.

  • Fees on the township's February 2025 sheet run $55 for a request made more than 10 business days ahead, $100 for four to ten days, and $165 inside four business days. A second visit costs $50.
  • Alarms must carry a UL listing and be under 10 years old, and plain battery units must use sealed 10-year batteries.
  • Any home with a fuel-burning appliance, fireplace, wood stove or attached garage needs a CO alarm.
  • No certificate is issued unless house numbers at least four inches tall can be seen from the street.
  • A solar array, generator or battery backup calls for a label by the electric panel and meter that reads "CAUTION: MULTIPLE SOURCES OF POWER."
  • A fire extinguisher is no longer part of the requirement for one- and two-family homes.

The certificate lasts six months and does not transfer to a later owner. The Fire Prevention Bureau is at 13 Edgar Drive, and its phone is 973-728-2840.

Walk the house with the list before you book. Check the age printed on each alarm, confirm the house number is visible from the road, and look at any solar or generator equipment for the required label. Fixing these items costs little, and a failed visit means a second fee and a later closing date.

Tax assessments and appeals

The assessor mails a postcard to every owner on February 1 listing the assessment for the current tax year. If you think it is too high, a petition goes to the Passaic County Board of Taxation by April 1, and forms are available from the township assessor at 973-728-2793. Added or omitted assessments, which appear when new construction is added to the roll partway through a year, have a separate December 1 deadline.

The county board sits at 930 Riverview Drive, Suite 250, in Totowa. When you sell, ask the township tax collector for your current balance and any sewer charge so the title company can build an exact payoff.

Deed filing and the state transfer fee

The Passaic County Clerk's Registry Division, at 401 Grand Street, Room 113, in Paterson, records West Milford deeds. A deed must show a "Prepared by" line, the tax block and lot, the price and a return address. The office asks for an official cover sheet, and without one it adds $20 per document.

The seller also pays the state realty transfer fee, a tiered charge that rises with the price and is paid by trust account check. Your closing attorney will compute it from the state schedule, and the county adds a $5 homelessness trust fund charge per document.

Which sale route fits

The lakes, long drives and low turnover here affect which route makes sense, and each one still needs the alarm certificate and a clean title.

  • An agent listing helps most when the house is far from Route 23 or on a lake road, because the wide buyer pool includes commuters who will trade drive time for space.
  • A sale on your own can work with a neighbor or relative as buyer, though you take on pricing, disclosures and the contract.
  • A cash purchase suits an inherited house, a camp-style cottage needing work or an owner who has already moved away.

Compare offers by the amount left after the certificate, taxes, state fee and repairs, not by the headline price.

Frequently asked questions

Is an alarm certificate required to sell in West Milford?

Yes, for houses of one or two units. The Fire Marshal's office issues it, the township sheet lists fees of $55, $100 or $165 depending on how near closing you apply, and it expires after six months.

Can I sell a West Milford house that needs major repairs?

Yes. The alarm certificate looks at alarms, house numbers and a few related items, not the overall condition of the house. A mortgage lender may still demand repairs, while a cash buyer can take it in its current condition.

By what date must a West Milford assessment appeal be filed?

Every April 1, with the Passaic County Board of Taxation, once the February postcard has arrived. Appeals about added or omitted assessments are due December 1.

Which office records a West Milford deed?

The Passaic County Clerk's Registry Division in Paterson. The closing attorney or title agent files it and sends the seller's transfer fee at the same time.

Does the Highlands Act affect a West Milford sale?

It can shape what a buyer may build. West Milford lies in the Highlands preservation area, so additions and new lots face added state rules, while an existing house sells like any other.

Routes to a closing in Bernards Township

You can list the house, sell it to a buyer you find privately, or accept a cash bid for the property as it stands. The township adds its own pre-sale steps to the state rules, so your pace depends on how quickly permits and inspections get cleared.

With median home values around $814,800, many buyers finance, and a listing draws them. A cash bid answers different problems: an inherited house in Basking Ridge, a property whose permits were never closed, a rental after the tenant leaves, or a seller who needs a closing date that will hold.

  • Private sale: no agent fee, with pricing, marketing and township paperwork on your desk.
  • Cash buyer: condition does not stall the sale, and the bid is reduced for the work required.

Home values and ownership

Bernards Township has 28,594 residents, and owners live in 83.1 percent of the housing units. Median household income is $194,107 and median rent is $2,476. Home values sit far above the national median of $332,700. At these price levels buyers expect a clean permit file, and the township checks for one before any residential sale anyway.

Because buyers here often borrow large amounts, lenders look hard at the file. Gather your deed, your recent tax and sewer bills, permit records for any addition or finished basement, and the fire safety certification in one folder before the first showing. A seller who hands over complete records early tends to keep a contract on schedule.

What a seller must obtain before closing

Two things, both issued from 277 South Maple Avenue in Basking Ridge. The first is an inspection and certification of smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and a fire extinguisher from the Bureau of Fire Prevention. The second is a Construction Records Clearance from the Code Enforcement Division. Create a free account on the township's online portal to apply.

The township code requires a Construction Records Clearance before the sale of any residential structure, and both owner and purchaser can be held responsible if one is not issued. The inspector checks records for open construction or zoning permits, and any open permit must have its final inspection before the clearance issues. File at least 10 business days before the change of ownership. A violation carries a fine up to $1,000, up to 90 days in jail or up to 90 days of community service.

The code exempts several transfers when no one changes occupancy, including title corrections, a transfer between spouses and a transfer by or to an executor or administrator distributing an estate. Mortgage refinancing and home equity loans are exempt as well.

If the inspector lists open permits, contact the permit holder or the contractor first. The Tax Collector posts a 2026 total rate of $1.661. Of that, $0.275 funds the county, $0.030 county open space, $1.077 the school district, $0.246 the municipality and $0.033 the library. Four installments fall on the first of February, May, August and November, and the 10th of each of those months is the last day of grace. Postmarks do not count; the payment must be physically in the office.

Sewer bills follow their own cycle, due January 1 and July 1 with a 30-day grace period. A closing in the middle of a quarter is prorated, so get a current balance on both the tax and sewer accounts from the Tax Collector.

Senior and veteran deductions exist. Seniors qualify at 65 or older on October 1 of the prior year, if they live in the home and stay under the income limit. Tell your attorney if a deduction is in place.

Do floods affect a Bernards sale?

They can. The Passaic River runs along the township's edge, and the township keeps a flood information page with flood zone maps for buildings, floodways, open space and township property. It also links to FEMA maps and elevation guides.

Ask a buyer's lender whether the property needs flood insurance, and look up the parcel on the township and FEMA maps before you list. A seller who can show an elevation certificate or a clear zone designation answers a common buyer question in the first week.

Transit and schools buyers mention

Interstate 78, Interstate 287 and U.S. Route 202 serve the township. NJ Transit's Gladstone Branch stops at Basking Ridge and Lyons stations on the way to Hoboken Terminal, and Lakeland Bus Lines runs a Route 78 rush-hour service from Bedminster to the Port Authority Bus Terminal.

The Bernards Township School District runs six schools, ending with William Annin Middle School and Ridge High School. Private options include Pingry School's upper campus in Basking Ridge and Saint James School. Name the commuter stations and schools in your listing so buyers see them early.

What changes when the buyer pays cash?

Paying cash takes out the lender's appraisal and most repair haggling. The Construction Records Clearance, the Bureau of Fire Prevention certification and the state transfer fee all stay in place. Agree up front who files each application, because the clearance fee climbs as closing nears.

Weigh offers by what you keep. A listing may fetch more, but commission, staging, inspection credits and holding costs come out of it. Above $1,000,000 the buyer owes an extra 1 percent fee beyond the seller's own transfer fee.

A workable order of steps: sign the contract, open the portal account the same day, book the fire safety inspection, file the clearance request, and ask the Tax Collector for balances. Your attorney then schedules the closing, the deed is recorded and you hand over the keys.

Frequently asked questions

Is a smoke detector certificate the only thing Bernards Township asks for?

No. The Code Enforcement Division also issues a Construction Records Clearance before a residential sale. Its review looks for open construction or zoning permits, which need final inspections before the clearance is released.

How much does a Construction Records Clearance cost in Bernards Township?

It costs $40 if the request reaches the township more than 10 calendar days ahead of closing, $75 inside 10 days and $125 inside 4 days. File the application at least 10 business days before ownership changes.

When are Bernards Township property taxes due?

The first of February, May, August and November, with grace through the 10th. The money must be in the Tax Collector's hands by then, since a postmark proves nothing. Sewer bills are due January 1 and July 1.

Which transfers skip the Bernards clearance?

A transfer is exempt when occupancy stays the same. That covers a deed correction, a transfer between spouses, an estate distribution by an executor or administrator, and refinancing or home equity loans.

Does the buyer ever pay a transfer fee in New Jersey?

Only when the price is above $1,000,000. The seller pays the standard realty transfer fee in every sale, and the buyer owes an added 1 percent above that line.

The township mixes older neighborhoods with large newer developments. Buyers talk about it in sections that have no formal borders:

  • Green Knoll, the central area with Bridgewater Commons, the municipal building and the high school.
  • Finderne, in the southeast, with older streets and newer developments.

Commuting and shopping

Average travel time to work is 31.4 minutes. Interstate 287 is the main limited-access road, Interstate 78 passes through the north without exits, and U.S. 22, Route 28 and Routes 202-206 cross the township. The Raritan Valley Line stops at Bridgewater station, and NJ Transit buses run to the Port Authority Bus Terminal (route 114) and Newark (route 65). Newark Liberty Airport is about 25 miles away.

Buyers moving from New York or north Jersey often ask which streets are closest to the station and the highways, so put that in the listing.

Schools buyers ask about

The Bridgewater-Raritan Regional School District covers nearly the whole township and the borough of Raritan too. Families often search by elementary zone, so ask the district which primary school your street feeds before you advertise.

Permits before you renovate or sell

Code Enforcement administers construction permits and issues certificates of approval and occupancy after final inspection. A permit is generally needed for decks, pools, additions, garages, finishing a basement, new electrical outlets, and new or replacement furnaces, water heaters or air conditioning. A shed needs one if it is over 200 square feet or has utilities, a fence only if it is over 6 feet or serves as a pool barrier, and roofing only where sheathing is replaced. State law lets the construction official fine unpermitted work up to $2,000 per violation, which is why open or missing permits surface during a buyer's review. Plan review can take up to 20 working days.

Home fire safety requirements and applications are handled by the Fire Safety office. Call the main line at 908-725-6300, extension 5560 for construction questions and extension 5550 for fire safety, to confirm what a buyer's inspection will check. The municipal offices are at 100 Commons Way.

Property tax billing and appeals

Bridgewater bills in four installments, with a ten-day grace period. If the lender escrows your taxes, the lender must supply the correct bank code to the tax office, and when a mortgage is paid off at closing the office should be told to remove it. The assessor runs an annual reassessment program, and each property is inspected on a four-year cycle, so a visit from the township's appraisal contractor before a sale is not unusual.

When the price tops $1,000,000 for a residential property, a supplemental Graduated Percent Fee applies, and the seller owes it. The band starts at 1% for sales up to $2,000,000 and climbs in steps to 3.5% on the very top prices. Exemption forms, including RTF-1EE, are posted by the Division of Taxation. Compare a cash buyer's lower price against these fees plus commission, not just the headline number.

Flood and site issues

The Raritan River forms much of the southern edge, and the North Branch of the Raritan marks the western border. If your home is low-lying near the river, ask the township engineering office about flood information before you list, and keep any flood insurance and repair records for the buyer. The northeastern part, by contrast, is hilly because the First Watchung Mountain runs through it.

Steps from contract to closing

Once a contract is signed, phone Code Enforcement to verify each permit was finaled, and phone Fire Safety to find out what a buyer's inspector will look at. The Tax Collector can give you the current quarter's balance, and should hear when a payoff of your mortgage is planned for closing. Title work is ordered by your attorney, the county records the deed, and the seller's transfer fee is due at recording. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, but these township and state steps still apply, so start them in the first week.

Put your deed, permit records for any deck, basement or addition, the last two tax bills and flood or repair paperwork into one folder. Buyers at these prices request documents early, so a full folder cuts the back and forth. Planning to move out first? Say so to your attorney, who can fit the final walk-through, key handover and utility transfers around your date. May 1 of the tax year. Confirm the date against the notice you receive from the Tax Assessor at 908-725-6300, extension 5121.

Only in some cases. A shed needs a permit if it is over 200 square feet or has electric or plumbing, and a fence needs one if it is over 6 feet tall or serves as a pool barrier.

Which school district covers Bridgewater?

The Bridgewater-Raritan Regional School District, which covers pre-kindergarten through grade 12 for Bridgewater and the borough of Raritan.

Selling a house in Franklin Township

Franklin Township is a large Somerset County township with no resale certificate of occupancy for home sales. That keeps the timeline short, since the fire inspection and the deed recording are the two fixed steps.

The township has an estimated 69,105 residents spread over 46.17 square miles of land. That is about 1,481 people per square mile at the 2020 count. For 2020 to 2024, 69.3% of homes are owner-occupied, the median home value is $457,900 and median gross rent is $2,115. Median household income is $124,648, and the mean commute to work is 33.5 minutes.

Franklin is a collection of villages that grew together, and buyers search by village name, so use the right one in your listing or when you talk to a cash buyer: Somerset, Franklin Park, East Franklin, Middlebush, Griggstown, Kingston, Six Mile Run, Pleasant Plains, East Millstone, Blackwells Mills or Weston.

Is a certificate of continued occupancy required?

No. The township's construction office confirms that a Certificate of Continued Occupancy inspection is not required when a residential home is sold. What is required is an inspection from the Fire Prevention Department, reachable at 732-873-2500, extension 6303.

That fire inspection is the state's smoke alarm, carbon monoxide alarm and portable extinguisher compliance check, and the township posts a smoke alarm application among its forms. Commercial sales are different: a commercial building or a new tenant needs a Certificate of Continued Building Compliance.

In practice, schedule the fire inspection as soon as you have a buyer, test every alarm yourself beforehand, and replace any that fail. Keep the passing result with your closing file so the buyer's attorney can see it. Skipping the resale certificate saves time, but it does not remove the need for open permits to be sorted out before closing.

Offices that touch a home sale in Franklin Township

Permits and historic districts

Check two things: whether past work on the house was permitted, and whether the property sits in a historic district. Under the Uniform Construction Code, replacing roofs and siding on one- and two-family detached homes no longer requires a construction permit, with polypropylene siding as the exception.

That relief does not apply in a historic district. All siding and roof replacements there still need Historic Commission review and approval before work starts, and the township publishes a map of the districts.

  • Look at your last roof, siding, deck and basement jobs and confirm the paperwork exists.
  • Check the township's district map if you plan any exterior repair before selling.
  • Call the Construction Department at 732-873-7283, extension 6224, when you are unsure whether a job needed a permit.

Vacant or foreclosure properties

Chapter 183 of the township code, amended by Ordinance 4393-23 effective March 26, 2023, covers vacant and abandoned residential properties in foreclosure. A mortgagee must inspect after filing a foreclosure complaint and register the property with the Township Clerk within 10 days. The nonrefundable annual fee is capped at $500.

The ordinance spells out what happens at transfer. When a covered property is sold, the owner is responsible for all code violations and must meet the Code Enforcement office within 45 days for a final courtesy inspection report. Failing to maintain a covered property can lead to a summons with a fine of up to $1,500.

If your house is headed toward foreclosure, selling before a complaint is filed avoids this registration track altogether. Ask the Clerk's Office whether your address already appears on the vacant property register.

How does the reduced transfer fee for seniors work?

New Jersey charges a lower realty transfer fee when the seller is a senior citizen, blind or disabled. About 18.3% of Franklin residents are 65 or older, so this schedule applies to many local sales.

For a price of $350,000 or less, the reduced rates are $0.50 per $500 on the first $150,000 and $1.25 per $500 on the portion from $150,000 to $350,000. Above $350,000, the schedule starts at $1.40 per $500 and climbs to $2.65 per $500 for the slice between $550,000 and $850,000.

A seller claiming the reduced schedule files the RTF-1 affidavit with the deed at the Somerset County Clerk's office. Have your closing attorney confirm that you qualify before you count on the lower figure.

A separate GIT/REP residency form travels with the deed as well. The person who signs the deed completes it, and a New Jersey resident uses the GIT/REP-3.

Roads and open space buyers care about

Buyers look at the school district, Interstate 287 and open space. Franklin Township Public Schools serve pre-K through grade 12 across 10 schools. Interstate 287 crosses the northern part of the township with two interchanges, and county routes 514, 518 and 527 carry local traffic. The New Jersey Turnpike lies just outside the township, with its closest interchanges two towns away in Edison, East Brunswick and Monroe.

  • Colonial Park, a 685.5-acre Somerset County park, includes the Arboretum, a rose garden and a golf course.
  • Six Mile Run Reservoir Site, a 3,037-acre state parcel, offers multi-use trails.
  • The Ten Mile Run Greenway covers 684 acres and runs over four miles in length.

The old Delaware and Raritan Canal towpath is now a state park along the northern and western edges of the township.

Which sale route fits?

  • A traditional listing works well for a house in good condition when you can wait on a buyer's financing.
  • A private sale suits an owner who already has a buyer and an attorney.
  • A cash offer fits a house with deferred repairs, an estate or a foreclosure notice, as long as the fire inspection is scheduled early.

Call Fire Prevention first, then set the closing date with the buyer's attorney. Bring the deed, your latest tax bill and any permit paperwork to the attorney, and confirm which GIT/REP form the signers need before closing.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a resale certificate of occupancy in Franklin Township?

No. The construction office confirms a Certificate of Continued Occupancy is not required for a residential sale. You still need the Fire Prevention Department's smoke alarm, carbon monoxide alarm and extinguisher inspection.

Who inspects smoke and carbon monoxide alarms before a Franklin Township sale?

The Fire Prevention Department. Its number is 732-873-2500, extension 6303, and the township posts a smoke alarm application among its fire prevention forms.

Can I replace my roof before selling without a permit in Franklin Township?

Usually yes for a one- or two-family detached home, since the Uniform Construction Code no longer requires a permit for roof replacement. A house in a historic district is the exception and needs Historic Commission approval first.

What is the senior citizen realty transfer fee in New Jersey?

It is a lower schedule for senior citizen, blind or disabled sellers. For prices up to $350,000 it is $0.50 per $500 on the first $150,000 and $1.25 per $500 on the portion up to $350,000, claimed on the RTF-1 affidavit.

What happens to a foreclosure property when it sells in Franklin Township?

The owner becomes responsible for all code violations at transfer and must meet the Code Enforcement office within 45 days for a courtesy inspection report. Mortgagees register covered properties with the Township Clerk within 10 days of their inspection.

Ways to sell a house fast in Hillsborough

You can go three ways in Hillsborough: list with an agent, sell on your own, or find a cash buyer willing to take the house as is. The township lies in Somerset County, in the Raritan Valley.

What sets the pace is paperwork more than price. The smoke detector certificate, open building permits and your tax record determine how soon a closing can be scheduled.

  • Agent listing: most exposure, though showings, the buyer's mortgage and a repair list each add weeks.
  • Without an agent: the commission stays in your pocket, while pricing, the contract and the alarm inspection become your job.
  • Cash buyer: no lender and no repair talks, which leaves title work and the certificate inspection as the main clock.

Judge each route by what you keep after fees and repairs.

The Hillsborough housing market

Hillsborough Township is large, at 55.10 square miles, and includes communities such as Belle Mead, Neshanic, Flagtown, Amwell and Woods Tavern. Nearly 40 percent of the land is protected or preserved open space, including Duke Farms, a 2,700 acre estate in the northeast corner. A house near preserved land often keeps its farm or woodland views for good.

About 79.5 percent of housing units are owner-occupied, and an owned home has a median value of $547,600. Owners carrying a mortgage spend a median of $3,017 a month on housing, and owners without one spend $1,470. The township has 16,388 households with a median income of $154,031, and turnover is low, since 91.1 percent of residents lived at the same address a year earlier. Population is estimated at 45,061, up 4.1 percent from 2020.

Expect a commuter household with solid income as your buyer, and expect to compete with only a modest supply of similar homes. Buyers who need cash certainty or no financing contingency are a smaller group, but a real one.

Commute and schools buyers ask about

Ask any Hillsborough agent and you will hear that commute and school questions come before kitchen questions.

  • Roads: U.S. Route 206 is the main route. A 3.75 mile bypass finished in 2021, and the old road is meant to become a downtown main street. County Routes 514 and 533 also cross the township, while Interstate 287 sits just outside in Bridgewater and Franklin.
  • Transit: D.H.I.L.A.N. buses link to Manville, Bridgewater and Somerville, and Coach USA runs four weekday morning express trips to Midtown Manhattan.
  • Schools: the Hillsborough Township School District runs pre-kindergarten through grade 12 in nine schools, including five K to 4 elementaries, Auten Road Intermediate for grades 5 and 6, a middle school for 7 and 8 and the high school.

Closing paperwork checklist

Four offices have a hand in a Hillsborough closing: the Fire Safety Department, the Building Department, the Tax Collector and the Somerset County Clerk.

Hillsborough seller checklist
TaskOfficeWhat to know
Smoke detector certificationFire Safety DepartmentFor a resale, the Building Department does not issue a certificate of occupancy. Schedule this inspection instead.

The township's SDL portal shows permit status and inspection results, so pull the permit history for your address early. Fixing a stale permit takes less time than explaining it to a buyer's attorney.

Property taxes and selling

An estimated third-quarter bill goes out each July, figured from the current year's assessed value. Multiplying it by four gives a wrong annual number, because adjustments land in the third and fourth quarters.

The township runs a reassessment each year, so assessed values track the market. The rate fell from $2.419 per $100 of assessed value in 2018 to $2.143 in 2024, even as values climbed. A check mailed on the 9th but received on the 12th is late, because the office ignores postmarks.

If you pay by ACH direct debit, tell the Tax Collector as soon as you list, since debits continue until the office is notified. A seller with unpaid taxes should request a payoff figure ahead of closing. Delinquent charges can end up in the township's online tax lien auction, so clear them before a buyer's title search turns them up.

How to appeal your assessment

Appeals go to the Somerset County Board of Taxation. The statewide date is April 1, pushed to May 1 in a district that has been revalued or reassessed, so ask the board or the township assessor which one fits your parcel. If the board rules against you, the Tax Court takes a petition for 45 days after the ruling.

State costs of selling in Hillsborough

When the deed is recorded, the state charges a Realty Transfer Fee, and it lands on the seller. A house priced near the Hillsborough median of $547,600 falls under the schedule for sales above $350,000, where the $4.80 per $500 band covers most of the price. Every band is posted by the Division of Taxation.

Sellers who remain New Jersey residents sign GIT/REP-3 at closing, which means no income tax is held back from the proceeds. If the house was your main home for two of the last five years, the federal gain exclusion that New Jersey follows may apply: $250,000 for one filer, $500,000 for joint filers.

What a cash sale skips

A cash buyer skips the appraisal, the underwriting and the repair demands that tend to follow an inspection. Three things still apply: the township's smoke detector inspection, payoff of any taxes owed, and a recorded deed. Book the inspection once a contract is signed, look for open permits in the SDL portal, and get a payoff figure from the Tax Collector.

At the attorney's office, have your deed, a recent tax bill, any mortgage payoff letter and a list of open permits. A house in poor shape can still sell for cash, but any permit left open has to be closed by you, so settle that first and the closing date will hold.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a certificate of occupancy to sell my Hillsborough house?

Not from the Building Department, which issues none for a residential resale. The Fire Safety Department handles a smoke detector certification inspection, and that is the visit you book. Your closing attorney can say whether a buyer's lender wants anything more.

When are Hillsborough property taxes due?

Bills are dated the first of February, May, August and November. Payment is on time through the 10th, or the next business day if the 10th is a weekend or holiday. Later payments owe interest back to the first, and postmarks do not count.

What is the deadline to appeal a Hillsborough assessment?

Usually April 1, on Form A-1 with the Somerset County Board of Taxation. Where a revaluation or reassessment has been carried out the date shifts to May 1. The board or the township assessor can tell you which one governs your parcel.

Who records the deed when I sell in Hillsborough?

The Somerset County Clerk, whose office files deeds, mortgages and related papers. Every filing needs a county cover sheet, and recording costs $45 for page one and $10 for each page after. Your title company normally submits it.

Can I sell a Hillsborough house that has open permits or needs repairs?

Yes, though open permits stay attached to the house. Whoever owns the property must close an open permit, even one a prior owner pulled. Cash buyers will take a house needing repairs, but resolving the permit first avoids a snag at closing.

Selling a house fast in Union, NJ

The quickest sale in Union is a cash purchase by an investor or family buyer who takes the property in its present state and orders the township's resale inspection. A listing suits a well kept house in a sought-after pocket, and selling without an agent is permitted. Every route needs a resale certificate before closing, so the inspection decides your timeline more than the buyer does.

Union here means Union Township in Union County, not Union City in Hudson County. The township has 63,675 people on 9.05 square miles of land. About 71.5% of its 21,374 households own their home, and the median owner-occupied value is $451,300. Owners with a mortgage pay a median of $3,015 a month, and those without one pay $1,292. Homes range from older houses in Putnam Manor to newer pockets near Kean University and the train station.

Neighborhoods buyers ask about

People in Union describe where they live by neighborhood more than by township name, so use the name buyers know when you write a listing.

  • Five Points, around the junction of Galloping Hill Road, Chestnut Street and Salem Road.
  • Union Center, near Morris and Stuyvesant Avenues.
  • Vauxhall, north of Interstate 78, with its own ZIP code, 07088.
  • Putnam Manor and Putnam Ridge, an older residential section off Colonial Avenue and Morris Avenue.
  • Battle Hill, in the west near the Rahway River and Route 22, and Larchmont Estates by the Larchmont Reservation.
  • Green Lane, a newer community between Kean University and Union Station.

Residential resale certificate

Union requires a Residential Resale Certificate, also called a certificate of continued occupancy, before a sale. Requests must be made at least ten business days before the inspection date, and the certificate is not issued until the inspection fee is paid. The visit verifies smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and fire extinguishers. Every open permit must be closed with the proper inspections first.

Inspections run on weekdays from 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. The owner or a representative must be at the house during those hours, or a second visit is scheduled at an added charge. The certificate is issued two full business days after final approval and stays valid for three months unless occupancy or ownership changes. It cannot be transferred.

What the inspector checks

The checklist is short and concrete, so a seller can prepare in a weekend.

  • At least one smoke detector on each level, plus one within 10 feet of each separate sleeping area. Two-family houses also need one at the top of each common stairwell.
  • Carbon monoxide alarms outside each sleeping area, within 10 feet of the bedroom doors.
  • A fire extinguisher within 10 feet of the kitchen, no smaller than 2A:10B:C and no larger than 10 pounds, mounted no more than five feet off the floor and in plain view.
  • Smoke alarms mounted to the manufacturer's directions with no double-sided tape, and the extinguisher on a hanger or bracket.
  • Existing hardwired detection systems from a newer build or renovation kept working, since battery units are not accepted as replacements.

Test every alarm before the inspector arrives. A failed visit means another $80 and another wait. A cash buyer will often fix these small items before closing so the certificate can issue.

How long the resale process takes

Plan on at least two to three weeks from request to certificate. The township wants ten business days of notice before the inspection, and the certificate comes two full business days after final approval. If the first visit fails, the housing inspector books a second one, which adds the $80 fee and another wait.

Because the certificate lasts three months, you can apply as soon as a contract is signed without much risk of it lapsing before closing. When the buyer wants a quick closing, apply the day the contract is signed. Ask the township whether any permits on the house, such as a finished basement or a deck, are still open, since the inspection cannot pass until they are closed.

A short order of operations helps. Pull your permit history first. Close anything open. Replace old alarms and mount an extinguisher near the kitchen. Then submit the request and put the inspection date in the sales contract so the buyer knows what to expect.

On closing day, bring the certificate to the table. The title company and the buyer's attorney will want to see it, along with proof that open permits were closed and the Tax Office's latest payment status. A cash buyer usually skips the lender's extra conditions, so these papers are often all that remains between the signed contract and the deed.

Property tax due dates

Union property taxes are due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, with a 10-day grace period. Postmarks do not count as proof of payment, so a payment must be physically in the Tax Office by 4:30 p.m. to be credited that day. A drop box at the front door of the municipal building on Morris Avenue works around the clock, and cash should never go in it.

The Tax Office collects municipal, county and school taxes and sewer utility bills. Bills equal assessed value times the tax rate, and the Union County Board of Taxation certifies the rate. The collector cannot lower a tax or waive interest. Ask the Tax Office for the quarter-by-quarter status before closing so the title company can prorate correctly. The township's tax page links to a property tax relief page for owners who may qualify.

Getting around: roads, rail and Kean University

Union has about 145.85 miles of roads, crossed by the Garden State Parkway, Interstate 78, U.S. Route 22 and Route 82 on Morris Avenue. Parkway interchanges 139A, 139B, 140, 140A and 141 serve the township. The Union station on NJ Transit's Raritan Valley Line runs to Newark Penn Station, and its lot holds over 450 cars. Bus routes 113, 114 and 117 go to the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Midtown Manhattan, and Newark Liberty International Airport is about six miles east.

Kean University moved to the township in 1958 and serves almost 16,000 students, which keeps rental demand steady nearby. If your house is close to the station, a highway ramp or the campus, say so in the listing.

Frequently asked questions

Is a resale certificate mandatory in Union, NJ?

Yes, the township requires a Residential Resale Certificate of continued occupancy before a sale. The inspection costs $175 and must be requested at least ten business days ahead.

How long does the Union resale certificate last?

It stays valid for three months from issue unless occupancy or ownership changes in the meantime. It cannot be transferred to another property or owner.

What does the Union inspector check?

The visit checks smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and fire extinguishers, and confirms that every open permit has been closed. Test the alarms before the inspector arrives.

What if my Union house fails the resale inspection?

A re-inspection costs $80, and the seller calls the housing inspector for a new appointment instead of reapplying. Fix the listed items first, since each extra visit adds cost and delay.

What are the Union tax due dates?

Bills fall due each February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, followed by a 10-day grace period, and postmarks earn no credit. Payments must be in the Tax Office by 4:30 p.m. to count that day.
